recognition also refused zero-argument calls outright, and `do_call_intrinsic`
returned early for `argc == 0`, which is why `pop` could not be classified as an
intrinsic at all.

`Intrinsic::ArrayPop` is now in the table (`%Array.prototype.pop%`, recognized
by name and gated on the realm's function identity). `pop_fast` serves the
dense-Array truncate through `array_pop_dense` and returns the hole sentinel for
every other receiver (a non-Array, a spilled array, or a hole at the end), which
keeps the general call. Zero-argument calls are allowed for this kind in both
`try_compile_intrinsic` and `do_call_intrinsic`.

Measured: `arrays/push_pop` **6.48 → 4.70 ms (1.38x)**, `call_slow` 960k → 0
and `array_pop` 0 → 1.2M on the row; gap to node **55x → 40x**. Corpus values
unchanged on all 77 rows and the full-corpus median is flat (1.003).

## Array.prototype.reverse inlines for a dense array (2026-10-18)

`reverse` had no intrinsic splice, so every compiled `a.reverse()` ran the
spec's pairwise read/`HasProperty`/`Set` loop through the general call (the two
element swaps per call went through the generic property machinery).
`opcost/array_reverse` measured 23.9 ms for 100k four-element reversals against
node's 0.51 ms.

`Intrinsic::ArrayReverse` joins the table (`%Array.prototype.reverse%`) and
`reverse_fast` reverses a fully-populated dense Array in place:
`JsObject::array_reverse_dense` requires dense mode, an integral non-negative
length, and no hole in the populated range (a hole makes the swap consult the
prototype chain), reverses the buffer, stamps the GC's dirty bound at 0 (the
values moved, so a minor must trace the whole buffer) and bumps the generation.
Everything else, a non-Array receiver, a spill, a hole, or a frozen array
whose elements are non-writable, keeps the general call, which is what makes
the frozen case throw its TypeError.

Measured: `opcost/array_reverse` **23.92 → 4.56 ms (5.2x)**, gap to node
**47x → 9.0x**; `array_reverse` 2M calls on the row and no `call_slow`. Corpus
values are unchanged on all 77 rows and the full-corpus median is flat.

## Iterator results fork their shape once per realm (2026-10-18)

`CreateIterResultObject` built `{ value, done }` with two sequential
`create_data_property` calls on a fresh object. Each is a `CreateDataProperty`
through the descriptor machinery (~100-140 ns), so a generator `next()` spent
about 160 ns of its 375 ns in the result object alone (`control/generator_loop`
measured 82.3 ms for 200k resumptions).

The five implementations of the operation (generator, async generator, array
iterator, keyed iterator, iterator helpers) now share
`context::create_iter_result_object`, which forks the two-key shape once per
realm and adopts it with `JsObject::adopt_vector_free_fields` in one step,
falling back to the two defines if adoption declines. The shape is cached on
the agent (`iter_result_map`) and keyed on the realm handle
(`iter_result_realm`): a realm switch refork, but the hot path never has to
resolve `%Object.prototype%` through the intrinsic table, that lookup was the
remaining cost after the first version still resolved it per call. A cache hit
reads the prototype back from the map (`Map::prototype`), and the map's own
trace keeps that prototype alive.

Measured on the `scratch/ab/gen` probe (generator applying `next().value`):
**82.3 → 57.5 ms (1.43x)**, i.e. ~411 → ~288 ns per resumption, over five
interleaved runs. Corpus: `control/generator_loop` **89.6 → 67.4 ms (1.33x)**;
the other 76 rows' names and checksums are unchanged and their median ratio is
inside the documented ±10% run noise.

Trap: `adopt_vector_free_fields` requires the object to start on the empty
canonical map, so the result must be created with `ordinary_object_create`, not
`ordinary_object_create_with_map` (the latter starts on the non-empty final
map and fails the fresh-map guard). The cached map's all-true attributes are
what make the adoption equivalent to two CreateDataProperty calls; a shape
forked with any non-default flag would change the descriptors the caller
observes.

## Array.prototype.at reads a dense element inline (2026-10-18)

`at` had a JIT splice, but its fast path called `Helper::ArrayAt` on every
call: the helper re-decodes the receiver and the index in Rust
(`to_integer_or_infinity` + `at_dense`) and returns the hole sentinel to
decline. `opcost/array_at` issued 2.8M helper calls for its 100k-iteration
loop.

Both JIT tiers now inline the read. The gate is a Number index and an
Object-tagged receiver with a non-null `array_dense` cursor. The index is
ToIntegerOrInfinity'd in machine code (truncate toward zero, with NaN mapped
to +0 explicitly, the saturating conversion's NaN result is not the spec's),
a negative index is rebased by `ArraySlots.length`, and the load is bounded by
`elem_len`. Those two lengths must stay separate: `length` may exceed the
materialized prefix when the tail is holes, and those elements must reach the
general call (the prototype chain can serve a hole), while an index outside
`[0, length)` answers `undefined`, a result, not a decline. A hole inside the
materialized prefix also declines.

Measured: `opcost/array_at` **3.09 → 2.60 ms (1.19x)** and the `array_at`
helper leaves the census entirely (2.8M → 0). The other 76 rows keep their
names and checksums and the corpus median is flat (0.996).

Trap: rebasing with `elem_len` instead of `length` would turn
`new Array(5).at(-1)` into `undefined` instead of a prototype lookup at index
4; bounding the load by `length` alone would read uninitialized buffer slots.

The row is now dominated by the `small.at` member read, not the call: the
identical loop with `small[2]` measures 0.60 ms against 2.60 ms, and
`GetMemberName` still runs ~2.8M times. The next slice on this shape is the
named method read, not `at` itself.

## Vector-free field stores stay inline (2026-10-18)

`objects/warm_store` (`o.d = i; s += o.d` on a literal) measured 55.7 ms
for 4M iterations and issued a `SetMemberSlot` helper call on every store.
The literal is vector-free (Option-3): `object_fast_create` adopts the
`{a,b,c,d}` shape and writes the fields, leaving `props_deferred` set.
The compiled store's deferred arm was therefore available, but two things
kept the helper on the hot path.

First, the warm-store record path called `JsObject::property_slot`, which
materializes the property vector and clears `props_deferred`, one cold
store and the object was never deferred again. `warm_store_record` now
resolves the descriptor ordinal through a new read-only
`JsObject::deferred_field_value` and records that ordinal as the store
cell's slot; `write_data_property_slot` gained a deferred arm that routes
the cell hit to `deferred_field_write`. The first store no longer
destroys the representation it needs.

Second, the optimizing tier had no deferred store at all: the per-step
path served a value-cell hit through `emit_deferred_inline_store`, while
`opt_lower::emit_member_store` called `SetMemberSlot` on a cell hit.
`emit_deferred_update_store` is the opt-tier mirror of the per-step
update arm, the deferred bit, the map cell's ordinal in
`in_fields`, a written field, writability, a barrier-free store (young
receiver or non-heap value), and the non-global receiver gate, and the
store now reaches it through the shared map-keyed shape probe. Both warm
paths also warm `member_map_cells`, which the compiled probe reads; the
write-side `member_write_map_cells` table is interpreter-only. The shape
cell matters beyond the value cell because `clear_derived_caches` empties
`member_value_cells` at every collection while the map cells survive.

Measured: the standalone store probe (`o.d = i`) **47.6 → 18.8 ms
(2.5x)** with the `SetMemberSlot` census 28M → 0; store-then-read
**57.7 → 27.5 ms**. Corpus: `objects/warm_store` **55.72 → 27.88 ms
(2.0x)** and `objects/compound_assign` **60.33 → 37.39 ms (1.61x)**. The
other 75 rows keep their names and checksums, the corpus median is flat
(1.003), and p90 is 1.031.

Trap: never resolve a store cell's slot with `property_slot` on a
receiver whose `props_deferred` may be set, the materialization is
permanent for the object and silently returns every later compiled store
to the descriptor-resolving helper. The deferred branch of
`warm_store_fallback` had the same gap in the shape cell (it warmed only
the value cell), which a store loop with no preceding read exposed.

## Dense Array.prototype.push appends inline (2026-10-18)

`push` had a Stage-B intrinsic splice, but each call dropped into
`Helper::ArrayPush` (`push_fast`): re-derive the receiver, `array_length_dense`,
then `array_element_write` with its dense/spill/grow branching. The
machine-code append that already served `a[a.length] = v` was not reachable
from the intrinsic, and the optimizing tier had no append arm at all.

Both tiers now inline a single-element dense append. The gates are the
append's: an Object-tagged receiver with a non-null `array_dense`, extensible,
not a registered prototype, a current clean-chain verdict
(`store_chain_clean == PROTOTYPE_EPOCH`), the 2^53-1 length cap,
`elem_len == length`, cursor room (`elem_len < elem_cap`), and a barrier-free
store (young slots or a non-heap value). The success path writes
`elements[elem_len]`, bumps `elem_len`, the f64 length, and the generation,
and answers the new length as a Number. A grow, a hole, a spilled buffer, a
frozen array, or a stale verdict falls to the narrow `array_push` helper,
whose hole sentinel still routes to the general call.

Measured: the probe's `array_push` helper count falls **960k -> 100** (the
grows) with the checksum unchanged, and the isolated 60k push/pop cycle runs
**~5.0 -> ~4.4 ms**. The full-corpus pass in this session ran thermally
skewed (median 0.84 against the earlier baseline, with unrelated rows such as
`warm_store` moving 27.9 -> 31.3), so it is not quoted as evidence; the row's
checksum is unchanged and the push helper is gone from the census.

Trap: `push` answers the new length, not the stored value, so the inline path
must go through the same result-and-restore protocol as every other intrinsic
hit (`emit_intrinsic_value` / `emit_intrinsic_hit`). Jumping straight to the
merge block without writing the call region leaves the stack pointer and the
argument slots in the caller's frame corrupted, which the loop case in the new
jit test exercises.

## Registered builtins run on the JIT argument buffer (2026-10-18)

A compiled call to a registered builtin (`String.fromCharCode`,
`Array.prototype.join`, `RegExp.prototype.test`, the Map/Set members) left
`call_slow` through the interpreter funnel: push `this`/callee/args onto
`vm.stack`, run `do_call_fast` -> `fast_call_core`, let the registered-builtin
arm call the handler, then truncate the stack and read the result back. The
handler itself is a plain `(agent, this, args)` call; only the round trip
around it is overhead.

`call_slow` now offers the builtin verdict first: the same per-function-id
`builtin_call_lookup` cell `fast_call_core` uses, with the JIT's argument
buffer as the args slice and the result returned directly. The lane is gated
on a single-realm agent, no direct eval, no termination request, and a
non-reentrant verdict; a reentrant host callback still withdraws to its own
activation, and an engine-defined ECMAScript body keeps the funnel.

Measured on a one-element `join` loop, the stable probe: **19.0 -> 17.4 ms
(1.09x)**. The other builtin-heavy rows moved in the same direction but the
machine was thermally variable this session, so they are not quoted. Corpus
names and checksums are unchanged on all 77 rows.

Trap: the args slice points into the compiled body's working buffer, which a
re-entrant handler can move when it resizes `vm.stack`, that is exactly what
the `reentrant` gate excludes. The lane also returns before the pending-call
completion check the funnel performs, which is sound only because a
non-reentrant handler never withdraws.

## Prototype-chain method reads serve the opt tier (2026-10-18)

A method read (`arr.push`, `p.get`) resolved through the full `[[Get]]` on
every compiled iteration: the value cell is keyed by the receiver's id, but
the method lives on the prototype, so the guard could never hit it. A
map-keyed chain cell now caches the RESOLUTION (receiver map id, walked links'
(id, generation), the found data property's vector slot) and the compiled
guard reads it before the exact helper. A hit re-validates each link and
re-reads the found property through the link's member value cell under its
live generation, so a value write to the prototype method is observed. The
shape probe runs first, so object loops that read map-described fields keep
their inline path instead of paying a chain-probe gate that only bails.

Three latent opt-tier bugs kept the probe from executing; all were found by
dumping the runtime cells at the moment the helper ran:

- `emit_chain_probe` emitted its first `iconst` before `switch_to_block(entry)`.
  In release the whole probe was appended after the caller's terminator (dead
  code); in a debug build Cranelift panicked with "cannot add an instruction
  to a block already filled".
- `emit_chain_value_read` was called with `(hit, miss)` against `(slow, merge)`
  parameters, so a VALID value cell branched to the miss block. Every hit
  declined. The parameters are now named `miss`/`hit` to match the callers.
- `emit_array_push_inline` called `Helper::ArrayPush` with `sig_binary` (four
  parameters) while passing two arguments, so Cranelift's verifier rejected
  the whole body and `opt_lower::compile` returned `None` silently. Every body
  containing `.push` fell back to the per-step tier. `CreateFunction` and
  `CreateFunctionDecl` had the same class of mismatch with `sig_tdz`. Both
  silent fallbacks now print under `JIT_DUMP_CLIF`.

Measured (release, one file each): `opcost/array_push` 6.69 -> 1.50 ms,
`array_reverse` 9.57 -> 2.55, `array_includes` 7.90 -> 2.67, `array_indexof`
7.05 -> 2.40, `array_at` 3.87 -> 1.42, `arrays/push_pop` 4.38 -> 1.94. The
push/pop helper census drops `GetMemberName` from 1.4M calls to 2. The full
corpus pass was thermally noisy (unrelated rows moved both ways depending on
the pass); the array rows reproduced across three passes.

Trap: the canonical empty-array map is collectable, so two array literals in
SEPARATE evaluations can get different map ids. `resolve_chain_cell` records a
map-keyed cell; a collection between scripts drops that map from the cache and
the next literal gets a fresh id, which correctly misses. The unit test must
create both arrays in one evaluation.

Trap: `chain_cell_read` must re-warm the found link's value cell when it falls
back to the vector slot. A collection clears the derived cells
(`Agent::clear_derived_caches`), and without the re-warm the compiled probe
would miss on every iteration for the rest of the run while the helper served
the read from the slot.

## Fused plain-argument `new` (2026-10-18)

A plain-argument `new` compiled to three helpers per construct: `ArgsBase`
(push the argument boundary onto the VM's args vector), one `ArgsPush` per
argument, and `Construct` (pop the boundary and run the construct). The
optimizing tier now fuses `ArgsBase; <arg eval>; ArgsPush*; Construct` into
one `Op::ConstructArgs`, whose arguments are written to the working region
and handed to a `construct_args` helper. `Vm::step_construct_from_args` is
the construct core over an arbitrary slice; the interpreter's
`step_construct_impl` detaches its vector and calls the same core.

Exactness: a pending run flushes back to the interpreter's vector form
whenever a step can disturb it, a nested `ArgsBase` (a construct inside an
argument), `ArgsSpread`, and every boundary-consuming call (`Call`,
`TailCall`, `TailCallSelfVector`, `SuperCall`, tagged templates). A run never
crosses a block (the block-end flush covers `new A(x ? 1 : 2)`), and the
diagnostic deopt probe flushes first so an interpreter resume sees the
boundary and the pushes. The arguments are written to the working region only
at the fused op, after argument evaluation, so an argument's own calls cannot
clobber them.

Measured on a construct-only loop (`new Item(i)`, 2M iterations): 287.7 ->
272.6 ms mean (5.3%, `SLAG_NO_FUSE_CONSTRUCT` A/B in one binary).
`calls/construct_churn` is neutral within the thermal noise, the construct
machinery, not the argument vector, dominates it. The helper census drops
`ArgsBase`/`ArgsPush` (one per iteration each) and keeps `ConstructArgs` at
one per iteration; the full-corpus checksums are unchanged.

## Construct/leaf profile, and the fill-path gate (2026-10-18)

Isolated probes (2M iterations each unless noted; the corpus runner reports
one call, so the figures are per-call ms with ns/iter in parentheses): a `{}`
literal 70 ms (35 ns/iter, incl. the `ObjectBegin` helper), `new Object()`
93 ms (46 ns/iter), `new Empty()` 115 ms (57 ns), `new Item(x)` with one
field store 195 ms (98 ns), `new Item(x, y)` with two 240 ms (120 ns), and
`new Item(i).sum()` 85 ms per 500k (170 ns/iter). The leaf call and own reads
are cheap: `p.sum()` on a stable receiver 75 ms (37 ns), two own reads 1.5 ms
(~0.4 ns each). A field store on a stable receiver is ~4 ns; the constructor's
first field store costs 44 ns, the second 19 ns.

The first-store gap is the object's fill. `construct_this_object` starts the
receiver on a presized map and vector-free (`props_deferred`), so the first
`this.x =` is a HOLE fill. The per-step compiler has that inline
(`compiler.rs::emit_deferred_field_store`'s fill block: write the field, bump
the generation, refresh the value cell). `opt_lower`'s
`emit_deferred_update_store` only has the UPDATE path (`not_hole`), so under
the optimizing tier every constructor store falls to the `SetMemberSlot`
helper, the census shows 1-2 calls per iteration that the per-step tier does
not pay.

This was the gate that kept constructors on the per-step tier. It is now
ported: `opt_lower::emit_deferred_update_store` emits both paths, the
in-place UPDATE of a written field (no generation bump) and the FILL of a
presized hole (write the field, bump the generation, refresh the value cell at
the NEW generation). The fill gates mirror the per-step ones: the deferred
bit, an inline slot, every field above the slot still a hole (the layout must
stay prefix-dense), a clean chain record whose direct prototype is still the
live one, and a young receiver (a fill into an old object would need the write
barrier).

With the fill path in, the lift also answers `undefined` for a body that falls
off the end, so constructors, functions with no explicit `return`, and scripts
opt-compile. The `SetMemberSlot` helper leaves the constructor census (one
call per field before). Measured: `calls/construct_churn` 91.5 -> 83.6 ms
(9%), the one-field construct probe at per-step parity (195 -> 200 ms) and the
two-field one 241 -> 256 ms (inside this session's spread), `new Item(i).sum()`
85 -> 84 ms. The full corpus has no checksum changes and no regression beyond
the noise floor; the largest rows moved in both directions with the thermal
drift.

Trap: the fill path trusts the map cell's `clean`/`proto_id`/`proto_gen`
record. A read-recorded cell (`clean == 0`) must decline to the exact helper,
it never validated the chain, so filling through it could skip an inherited
setter or a non-writable descriptor.

## Intrinsic-named calls take the leaf lane (2026-10-18)

Bodies containing `NewClosure`/`FunctionDecl` are now opt-compiled. The
earlier explicit decline was a workaround for a 3x regression on
`opcost/proto_method_call`, but the cause was the intrinsic slow path, not
closures: a method whose NAME matches a lifted intrinsic (`get`, `set`,
`has`, ...) is lifted as `Intrinsic` because only the name is known at lift
time; the runtime identity gate then declines, and `emit_intrinsic`'s fallback
went straight to `call_slow` instead of the leaf-call lane `Op::Call` uses.
The per-step tier withdraws to `fast_call_core`, which has that lane, so the
opt tier was ~3x slower. With the fallback routed through `emit_leaf_call`,
`CallSlow` on that body falls from 1.2M calls to 4 and the row measures
8.3 -> 3.18 ms (per-step 3.17). A same-binary A/B after the fix put
`construct_churn` at 98-103 ms opt vs 94-98 per-step and `recursive_fib` /
`method_call` at parity, so the decline is removed.

## Map/Set key index drops SipHash (2026-10-18)

`KeyedIndex`, the Map/Set collection key word -> entry slot index, was a
plain `HashMap<u64, usize>`, so every `has`/`get`/`set`/`add` re-hashed an
already-hashed 64-bit word through std's SipHash. The index now uses
`BuildHasherDefault<MixHasher>` (a splitmix64 finalizer). Plain identity
hashing would be wrong here: a small integer's f64 bit pattern has all-zero
low bits, so every numeric key would land in one bucket; the mixer is a few
instructions and still spreads them.

Measured with a same-session baseline: `builtins/map_churn` 40.8 -> 36.4-39.2
ms and `builtins/set_churn` 58.9 -> 53.5 ms (the thermal noise this session is
comparable to the win, so treat it as ~9%).

The same probes show the allocation path is NOT the bottleneck for the churn
rows: `opcost/object_alloc` runs 100k `({ a: 1 }).a` iterations in 0.33 ms
(~3.3 ns per allocation). The remaining gap on `construct_churn` and
`spread_assign` is the call/builtin lane, not GC.

## Minor GC: root dedup and the young-cohort scan (2026-10-19)

The previous entry's `opcost/object_alloc` reading was wrong: `({ a: 1 }).a`
in a loop is folded, `JIT_HELPER_STATS=1` shows 174 `ObjectFast` calls for
the whole 36-row corpus, not 100k. The row does not allocate and cannot be
used as an allocation floor.

Measured properly on a `{}` probe (2M literals, one allocation per iteration):
the bare loop costs 3.3 ns/iter, `JsObject::ordinary_object_create` measured
hot in a crux-only bench is 14.5 ns (a 32 B box is 6.3 ns, so allocation +
init is ~8 ns of it), and the safe-point minors cost ~16 ns per allocated
box. `--gc-trace` on the probe reports 617 minors per call, avg 52-53 us for
a ~3k-box cohort: half the row is GC. A temporary stage breakdown inside
`collect_minor_inner` attributed one minor as: sort 1.6-21 us (bimodal),
stack scan 2.5 us, sweep 20-27 us, pinned/root seeding 7-8 us, mark ~0.

Two changes in `crates/crux/src/heap.rs`:

- The stack scan binary-searched a sorted copy of the young cohort. The free
  list is LIFO, so a cohort that reuses the previous sweep's slots arrives in
  scrambled order and the sort becomes the dominant term. It is now an
  open-addressed membership table (`Heap::young_table`: 2x next power of two,
  linear probing on `addr >> 4`, zeroed at build, reused across collections).
  This drops the cohort microbench (4096 hot boxes) from 43.4 us to 25.0 us
  per collection.
- Root dedup was an `AddrSet` insert per traced root. The root sources push
  the same boxes once per record (the documented ~6200 roots over 34
  addresses), so the set was pure overhead on every collection. Dedup is now
  `FLAG_MINOR_SEEN` on each old box, with a small clearing list; a young root
  is deduped by its mark bit in the work drain.

Same-binary A/B (`SLAG_GC_SORT_SCAN` selected the sorted scan for the old
arm), interleaved 3x:

| row | sorted | table |
| --- | --- | --- |
| isolated `{}`, 2M | 67.0-67.3 | 57.5-58.4 (-13%) |
| isolated `new Empty()`, 2M | 110.9 | 100.8 (-9%) |
| `calls/construct_churn` | 82.0 | 78.0-78.6 (-4%) |
| isolated `new Item(x,y)`, 2M | 236.5-238.6 | 228.5-230.8 (-3%) |

The sweep (20-27 us, ~8.8 ns per dead box: drop glue + free-list push) is now
the largest per-minor term; the allocator's TLS + `RefCell` path (~6 ns of
the 14.5 ns create) is the next.

## Skipping the drop for a plain object (2026-10-19)

Follow-up to the cohort-scan change, where the sweep became the largest per-minor term. Isolating it in the crux bench: a 432 B box with a trivial drop costs 4.0 ns per box in a minor, a same-sized `JsObject` 12.5 ns, and `drop_in_place::<JsObject>` on a plain, never-mutated object measures 6.96 ns standalone. The cost is the chain of ownership checks the synthesized drop runs: the `ObjectKind` match (the `Host` variant holds an `Rc`), `SmallProps::heap`, `property_index`, `private_elements`. A plain object owns none of them.

`Trace` gains `DROP_MAY_RELEASE` (default `true`) and `drop_releases_heap`; the vtable's `drop` slot still calls `request_finalize` first, then consults the predicate when the type opted out. `JsObject` opts out: kind is `Ordinary`, the spilled property vector has capacity 0 (up to `INLINE_FIELDS` keys live in `in_fields`, and `properties` stays empty), the key index is unbuilt, and the private-element vector has no capacity. Capacity rather than length, so a vector that spilled and was truncated still frees its buffer; a failed `try_borrow` answers "owns", so a mid-collection borrow can never turn into a skipped drop. A non-ordinary kind, a spilled vector, a built index or reserved private elements all still take the drop, a false negative would leak, which is what `drop_releases_heap_tracks_owned_storage` pins.

Measured: the 4096-box cohort minor drops 12.5 -> 5.3 ns per box (a cohort whose objects hold a spilled vector stays at 9.8). End to end, the isolated `{}` probe (2M) went 57.0-58.6 -> 50.0-50.8 ms (-12%) and `new Empty()` 100.8 -> 96.2 (-5%); `construct_churn` moved 78.0-78.6 -> 77.2 because its cost is the construct lane rather than the sweep.

## Allocation latency is hidden by the payload init (2026-10-19)

Two attempts at the allocation path, both measured and both reverted.

The GC-5 allocation counter and the GC-2 `--gc-stress` flag sat in two thread-locals, so every allocation paid two TLS accesses plus a branch. Folding them into one word (the stress flag in the top bit) is a strict work reduction, and isolated it is real: `Gc::new(Unit)` in a hot 4096-box ring went 6.32 -> 5.20 ns per allocation (-18%). End to end it moved nothing: `p_obj_lit` 49.1-49.4 -> 50.2-51.5 ms (thermal drift the wrong way), `fresh_join` 36.2-36.3 -> 37.0-37.4, `closure_nocap` 10.85-11.25 -> 10.94-11.03, `mapchurn` 34.8-35.0 -> 34.4-35.2.

`canonical_empty_map`'s lookup is a TLS `RefCell` borrow plus a vector scan, 2.7 ns standalone, and object creation measured 14.1 ns on the lookup path against 12.0 with a map supplied directly, which looks like a 2 ns win. A one-entry `Cell` inline cache took the lookup to 1.98 ns (-0.7) but `ordinary_object_create` stayed at 14.3 ns: only ~0.3 ns of the saving surfaces once the 408 B payload init is in the same path.

The lesson for this area: plain-object creation is store-bound on the payload init, not latency-bound on the calls around it. A latency win in a helper is invisible unless it removes stores. The layout lever that would pay is fewer bytes written per object (a smaller ordinary-object initial state or a bulk-initialized slot), not a smaller struct (see the object-layout skill) and not a cheaper lookup.

## Constructor fills scan only described fields (2026-10-19)

Decomposing the construct lane on isolated probes (2M iterations each, per-call ms and ns/iter): a plain method call `p.sum()` 72 (36), `new Empty()` 94 (47), a one-store constructor whose store never executes (`if (x < 0) this.x = x`) 134 (67), one fill 172 (86), a fill plus an update of the same field 184 (92), two fills 220-226 (110-113), the same two stores out of order 227 (113). So the lane itself is ~11 ns over a plain call, the presize receiver ~19 ns, an in-place UPDATE ~1.5 ns, and a FILL ~18-20 ns each.

The fill gate required every one of the seven inline slots above the target to still be a hole, a serial chain of seven loads. Only map-described ordinals can ever hold a written field (a map is immutable for its id), so the scan can stop at the map's descriptor count. `MemberMapCell` now carries `count`, recorded from the map at every cell site, and both emitters (opt and per-step) loop from `slot + 1` to `min(count, INLINE_FIELDS)`: a constructor store that targets the last described field loads nothing.

Same-binary A/B (stashed baseline, three runs each): out-of-order two-field construct 227 -> 201 ms, `construct_churn` 79-80 -> 74-77, one-field construct 172-175 -> 163-169, two-field 220-226 -> 206. The empty construct and the presize-only probe are unchanged, which attributes the win to the scan rather than to thermal drift.

Also tried and reverted: a constant-template memcpy for the object init. Copying the whole 408 B payload (including the 112 B uninitialized inline array and the full `Option<HashMap>`) costs more than the targeted ~30 stores; creation went 12.1 -> 19.6 ns.

Correction to the decomposition above: the ~19 ns attributed to the presize receiver is not the presize machinery. A constructor with no `this` store at all but a local binding (`function Item(x) { var y = x; }`) measures 138 ms, the same as the presize probe (134) and the explicit-return body (136), while `function Item(x) { x; }` measures 94 like the empty body. The trigger is `steps_are_leaf`: any identifier reference (a local read) disqualifies the body, so it takes the C2a certified lane instead of the shared leaf construct. That lane costs ~21 ns per construct: an `ecma_functions` lookup, `lookup_info`, `ir.clone`, and the scratch save/restore, none of which the leaf path pays. The next lever there is a construct-site record like `leaf_records` so the lane can take the `cached` arm; it is a JIT/ABI feature, not a local edit.

## Construct-site record: scoped and not worth it (2026-10-19)

A construct-site record in the `leaf_records` style would let the C2a lane skip the work it redoes per construct: the `ecma_functions` lookup (identity hasher, ~2-4 ns), `ir.clone` (an `Rc` bump), the eligibility flag scan, and `lookup_info`. `lookup_info` is already a load + compare in the hot case (`jit_info > 1` returns the cached pointer), and the eligibility verdict is a handful of field tests, so the whole skip is ~3-5 ns of the ~21 ns lane overhead.

The lane's cost is its per-construct construction, not its lookups: `vm.stack.resize` for `frame_len + stack_usage + slack` (then a per-slot rewrite of the frame), `install_nested_frame`, `vm.save_scratch` and five saved fields, and a fresh `JitCallContext` (around 550 B, including a 15-entry `intrinsic_bits` array). To also skip `ecma_functions` the record would have to own the `Rc<CompiledBody>`, the `EnvRef` and the `Handle<Realm>`, which makes it a traced GC root and needs code-gen invalidation, for 3-5 ns.

The next real lever in this lane is reusing the caller's `JitCallContext` in place (save, overwrite and restore the ~a dozen fields the nested run changes) instead of building the whole struct per construct. That is a redesign of the lane's frame protocol, not a record.

## Shared-leaf construct with environments: neutral, reverted (2026-10-19)

The follow-up to the scoping: `try_shared_construct_leaf` was extended to accept environment-using leaves (install the closure environment for the run, restore the caller's `body_context`/`lexical_env` afterwards, refuse only a body that needs a fresh per-call capture context), so a constructor whose body reads an identifier would run on the caller's context instead of the private-buffer `run_jit_leaf` path.

Measured neutral: `function Item(x) { var y = x; }` 138 -> 133 ms per 2M (-3.6%, within the noise floor), `this.x = x` 167 -> 165, `construct_churn` unchanged. Reverted. The run also showed that the 94 ms (empty body) vs 138 ms (one local) gap is not lane selection, both are leaf constructs, so the difference is inside the leaf run/frame setup and remains unattributed. The lesson from the three failed attributions in this area: instrument the specific path (`construct_inline`, `environment.is_none()`, the shared-leaf entry) before naming a cause; the compile-time verdicts (`ir.leaf`, `construct_inline`, `leaf_uses_env`) do not predict which run is taken.

## Inline headroom: the shared construct leaf was room-starved (2026-10-19)

A sampled diagnostic inside `try_shared_construct_leaf` (fired at construct 1,000,000, with `Instant` marks) settled the 94-vs-138 ms cliff: the shared leaf was returning `no-room`. The caller's buffer leaves `(caller_max_stack - current_depth) + JIT_STACK_SLACK` slots above `sp`, and the callee needs `frame + working + JIT_STACK_SLACK`. The slack appears on both sides and cancels, so the real condition is `callee_frame + callee_working <= caller_max_stack - current_depth`, which is **zero** at the caller's deepest call site. Only a callee with `frame + working <= 1` could ever fit; `var a;` (frame 2) and `this.x = x` (frame 2 + working 1) both fell back to `run_jit_leaf`'s private frame and per-call global resolution (~20 ns).

Fix: `JIT_INLINE_HEADROOM = 4` slots, reserved in the buffers of bodies that can call (`run_jit_body`, its resume region, `certified_lane_inline`, and the shared call lane). Leaves reserve nothing (they make no calls). The headroom slots are initialized like the rest of the segment, the shared leaf carves into slots the caller already filled.

Measured (three runs; `fib`, `mcall`, `p_call_only` and `p_obj_lit` also measured against a stashed baseline binary):

| row | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `calls/construct_churn` | 72.2-74.4 ms | 61.8-64.5 (-12-15%) |
| `new Item(x)` 2M | 165-172 | 123-133 (-25%) |
| `new Item(x,y)` 2M | 206-225 | 163-170 (-20%) |
| presize pattern, store skipped | 134-137 | 92.8-96.8 (-30%) |
| `fib` (recursive calls) | 49.5-50.1 | 49.5 (neutral) |
| `mcall` | 55.9 | 53.8 |
| `p_call_only` / `p_obj_lit` | 71.9-72.8 / 51.2 | 72.2-74.4 / 50.8-51.4 (noise) |

A 32-slot headroom measured the same on the construct rows and on `fib` (the added initialization is L1-cheap at this depth); 4 is the smallest value that serves the common shapes and is what ships. This is the first construct-side change that moved `construct_churn`; the earlier fill-scan win was in the compiled body, this one is in the call machinery around it.

## Loop counters: a shared delta constant blocked narrowing (2026-10-19)

The loop-counter pass narrowed `i + 1` only when the constant `1` had exactly
one use. `narrow` CSEs identical literals, so in `for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
n += 1; }` the increment and the accumulator share that constant, the counter
stayed a tagged-double `Add` (its range guard intact), and the loop ran at ~2.6
ns/iter instead of the ~1 ns an int counter gets.

`prove` no longer demands a private constant. `run` counts, per constant, how
many proven increments use it, re-types it in place when *every* use is one of
them (all of those become `IntAdd`/`IntSub`, so an `Int` constant is what they
need), and otherwise appends a private `Const` with `imm: Imm::Int(delta)` and
repoints that increment's arg 1. The clone is inserted immediately before its
increment, not at the end of the constant's block, a same-block use before the
definition fails dominance (`UseNotDominated`). Insertions are applied from the
highest index down so they cannot shift a position still to be inserted at.
Verified IR for `n += 1`: `v5:num = Add(v15, v4); v12:int = IntAdd(v19, v23)`.

Same-binary A/B (`--jit-bench`): `bare loop` 2.664 -> 2.283 ms (-14%);
`arithmetic` unchanged (2.476 -> 2.489), whose increment constant was already
private. Corpus A/B, three runs each side, 77 rows: mean JIT gap 13.26 -> 12.64,
with the loop-heavy rows `strings/search_slice` 21.0 -> 15.7,
`strings/concat_loop` 10.7 -> 9.3, `control/generator_loop` 70.6 -> 62.2,
`opcost/typed_array_for_each` 67.9 -> 61.1, `opcost/array_for_each` 31.1 ->
28.1. Rows under ~0.3 ms are one timer tick and are not evidence either way.

Correction to a near-miss: `opcost/baseline` reads 2.3 ms in the 2026-10-19
dump's *second* column, which is slag jitless; its JIT column is already 0.1 ms
before this change. The 23x "win" that number suggests is not this pass.

## Arithmetic chains stay in f64 registers (2026-10-19)

The optimizing tier canonicalizes every arithmetic result against the NaN-box
tag region (`canon_double`: mask, compare, select) and keeps the word in an
i64 SSA value, so `n += 1` round-trips through a general-purpose register every
iteration. The per-step lane does not: its deferred numeric register keeps the
value in an f64 register and boxes once, at the store. Measured on the two rows
the opt tier compiles, before and after the loop-counter slice above:

| row | opt tier | per-step lane (`SLAG_OPT=0`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bare loop` | 2.28 ms | 0.71 ms |
| `arithmetic` | 2.42 ms | 0.61 ms |

`pass/unbox.rs` adds `Type::Float` (a raw f64) and `Op::Canon` (raw -> Value).
A value is raw when it is an arithmetic result whose operands are proven
Numbers, or a block parameter that receives a raw value on any edge; the
fixpoint is what carries an accumulator across the back edge. Every use that
observes the value word, a helper, a store, a return, a tag test, a branch
condition, an edge into a non-raw parameter, gets a `Canon` inserted in front
of it, so the canonicalization lands where the chain ends rather than on every
iteration. `repr(Float)` is `F64`, so the register allocator keeps the chain in
an xmm register with no `vmovq`s. `emit_bare_numeric` works in f64 and skips the
canonicalization for a raw result.

Safety: a raw float is not a canonical `Value` word (a NaN whose bits are
`0x7FF8...` decodes as a tag), so the lowering refuses the opt body
(`Unsupported::Step("opt:raw-float-boundary")`) if one ever reaches a path that
is not the bare f64 op. A pass bug is therefore a fallback to the per-step body,
never a misread value.

Measured, same binary via the `SLAG_UNBOX=0` seam, three interleaved pairs over
the 77-workload corpus: mean speedup 1.024, 1.025, 1.003. The rows that move are
the ones with a proven-Number accumulator (`arrays/index_loop` ~1.08,
`opcost/array_length_write` ~1.12, `control/switch_dispatch` ~1.08); per-row
swings beyond that are thermal (a single row changed direction between pair
orders). Micro-suite: `bare loop` 2.28 -> 0.586 ms and `arithmetic` 2.42 ->
0.723 ms, i.e. `bare loop` is now faster than the per-step lane and `arithmetic`
is 18% behind it.

That last gap is the counter, not the accumulator: `arithmetic` is
`n += i * 2`, the loop-counter pass proves `i` an int32, and each use of it in
a float op converts (`vcvtsi2sdl`). It is still the right choice. Keeping the
counter a raw f64 when it feeds a float expression was implemented and
measured: `arithmetic` went 0.711-0.721 -> 0.762-0.777 ms (three runs each),
while `bare loop` was unchanged. The generated loop is shorter either way
(4 f64 ops), so the loss is the counter's loop-carried dependency: an int32
back edge is one `lea` (1 cycle) and its `fcvt`+`fcmp` ride off the critical
path, whereas an f64 back edge is a 4-cycle `vaddsd` feeding the compare. The
int counter stays; the different rule was reverted.

## Prototype reads: the chain cache ran after the own-field miss work (2026-10-19)

`get_member_name` tried `member_cell_get` first, and its miss path does the
proto-keyed cell lookup plus a properties-vector probe; only then did it try
`member_chain_get`. For a prototype read (a method like `arr.push`,
`o.method`, `s.charAt`) that miss work is pure overhead: a chain cell is
recorded only when the receiver owns no `name`, and a hit validates the
receiver generation and every recorded prototype link, so a hit already proves
the own-property lookup would miss.

Moving the chain probe ahead of the own-property resolution costs nothing for
an own read (the chain lookup misses) and removes the redundant work for a
prototype read. Isolated, 300k reads: a one-link prototype data read 5.39 ->
3.48 ms (1.55x), an own data read 1.15 -> 1.17 (unchanged), a String-primitive
method read unchanged (that path goes through `get_primitive_member`, not the
chain cache). Corpus rows driven by prototype reads: `objects/proto_read` 73.1
-> 50.2, `opcost/proto_method_call` 3.1 -> 2.2, `opcost/map_get` 4.3 -> 3.2,
`control/for_in` 14.0 -> 10.8, `calls/apply_call` 36.8 -> 30.3,
`builtins/map_churn` 34.1 -> 28.4, `opcost/regexp_test` 51.5 -> 40.5. The
corpus total is flat within thermal noise: the three largest rows are language
fixtures whose hot loops do not read members.

`GetMemberName` is still the corpus's most-called helper (91.7M calls in one
run of all 77 workloads, ahead of `CallSlow` 38.9M and `LoadContext` 38.8M).
This change removes work inside the helper; inlining the chain probe into
compiled code (the own-data cell already has `emit_member_cell_probe`) is the
next lever.

## Deferred function boilerplate: a measured regression (2026-10-19)

An isolated closure creation costs ~350 ns (`var f = function(){}` 300k times
= 97-105 ms; adding a call adds ~40 ns). A one-sample phase probe inside
`register_function` (100 ns Windows timer) suggested `alloc` 100 ns,
`ecma_functions insert` 100 ns and "rest" 200 ns, so the eager
`length`/`name`/`caller`/`arguments` defines looked like the target. They were
made lazy exactly like `prototype_pending`: a `props_pending` record flag, an
`ensure_function_properties` materializer, the existing own-property barrier
extended to the four atoms, and `set_function_name` recording the name on the
pending record instead of defining it (so the hot anonymous-definition path
does not force materialization).

Measured, same binary, three alternating pairs: worse.

| probe | eager (HEAD) | deferred |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 300k anonymous closures | 97-100 ms | 108-113 ms |
| ...with one call each | 138-141 ms | 177-178 ms |

An instrumented counter confirmed no materialization happened in either probe,
so the deferral really was lazy. The regression is the replacement work: the
batched adoption is four field writes plus a pre-forked map assignment, and
the eager `SetFunctionName` lands as an in-place update of the already-created
`name` field, both cheaper than the lazy path's `ecma_functions` lookup plus a
`name` clone per creation. Reverted.

The methodological point: a single-sample phase split on a 100 ns timer is
noise (`rest` read 200 ns here, but the defines are a small fraction of the
cost). Accumulate per-phase totals over at least a thousand calls before
attributing closure-creation cost.

## Closure creation, profiled properly (2026-10-19)

An accumulated phase profile (means over 19,000 `instantiate_function_with_
source` calls, `SLAG_FNPROF`, instrumented build; subtract ~16 ns of
`Instant::now()` overhead per phase). Uninstrumented total is ~333 ns
(300k anonymous closures in 100 ms):

| phase | ns |
| --- | --- |
| `capture_source` (the source slice) | 27 |
| `shared_function_body` | 56 |
| `shared_params` | 17 |
| setup (strict check, realm/contexts, parse_text) | 16 |
| `Function::new_with_prototype` + env edge | 59 |
| `shared_compiled_body` + `set_compiled` | 30 |
| **`ecma_functions.insert` + patterns** | **97** |
| `set_function_properties_batched` | 31 |

The registry insert dominates. `EcmaFunction` is **408 bytes** (six `Vec`
fields, 144 B, plus `Option<JsString>` `source`/`parse_text`, ~90 B, all empty
or tiny for an ordinary closure), and the identity-hashed map still pays a
full value copy per insert.

Measured alternatives (isolated `rustc -O` bench, 300k inserts with removals,
a 248-byte stand-in record):

| shape | ns/insert |
| --- | --- |
| `HashMap<u64, Big>` (today's shape) | 52 (with growth: 224) |
| `HashMap<u64, Box<Big>>` | 128 |
| `Vec`-slab by id (value) | ~77 MB at 300k ids, not viable |

So boxing the map value is a regression (the allocator costs more than the
copy it saves), and a value slab is too much memory. The lever is the record's
SIZE: moving the class-only fields (`fields`, `private_methods`,
`decorator_initializers`, `computed_keys`) behind one optional box and the two
inline source strings behind a handle would roughly halve it. That is a record
layout change across every field access, so it is a slice of its own.

Methodology: this supersedes the earlier single-sample phase split, which read
`rest=200 ns` from a 100 ns timer and led the boilerplate-deferral attempt
astray.

The staged follow-up (shrink the record: class-only state behind one box, the
two inline source strings behind a shared per-site `SourceInfo`; the GC-arena
record as the last option; and the stop rule) is
`.notes/closure-cost-plan.md`.

### LANDED (2026-10-19): share the per-site source info (closure Stage B)

`EcmaFunction`'s inline `source`/`parse_text` (`Option<JsString>`, 96 B) are
now one `Option<Rc<SourceInfo>>` (8 B) holding `{ slice, full, key }`, built
once per declaration site and shared by every closure the site creates. The
cache key mirrors `shared_function_body`'s `(node, realm, span start, span
end, slice hash)` and lives on the `SourceInfo`, so the body cache no longer
rehashes the same slice per closure. Record: **408 -> 320 bytes**.

A non-leaf enclosing text (`ConsString`/`Rope`/`Sliced`, e.g. an eval of a
concatenated string) is materialised to a leaf once before it enters the
thread-local cache, which is not traced; records still trace through the
`Rc` for the uncached paths.

Interleaved same-binary release A/B (base = `021f80a5`, 10-12 pairs):

| probe | base | Stage B | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `e7` 300k closures, no call | 104.78 ms | 99.88 ms | **-4.7%** |
| `e5` 300k closures + one call | 153.93 ms | 142.80 ms | **-7.2%** |
| for-in head-let row (6 pairs) | 765 ms | 708 ms | -7.4% (last 5 pairs 749 -> 673, -10%) |

The first build also passed the slice to `shared_function_body`, which
rehashed it: that measured only -1.5% on `e7`. Carrying the hash in the
`SourceInfo` is what makes the win visible.

The slice caching alone is *not* the lever, the 2026-09-08 negative probe
already showed a no-slice build within noise. The measured win is the record
shrink: 88 B off a value that is moved into the identity-hashed map on every
create (and cloned on the call path, hence the larger `e5` delta). Stage A
(the class-only fields behind one box, 320 -> ~208) is the next slice.

Gates: `cargo test --workspace`, clippy `-D warnings`, corpus parity 0,
`test262` sweeps 48,633 + 3,365 at 100%.

### LANDED (2026-10-19): box the class-only slots (closure Stage A)

The five class-only slots, `fields`, `private_methods`,
`decorator_initializers`, `super_constructor`, `computed_keys`, moved into
`ClassParts`, stored as `Option<Box<ClassParts>>`. `EcmaFunction` drops from
**320 to 216 bytes** (408 at the start of the session, so -47% total). An
ordinary closure never allocates the box; `class_parts_mut` creates it on the
first class write (a derived constructor's heritage, or the class definition's
field/private-method/computed-key write).

One planned deviation: `private_environment` stays **inline**. Every closure
created inside a class body inherits it, so boxing it would allocate a
`ClassParts` for those closures, the opposite of the goal. The record is 8 B
larger than the plan's 208-byte estimate and avoids that allocation.

Interleaved same-binary release A/B, Stage B vs Stage B+A (6-12 pairs):

| probe | Stage B | + Stage A | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `e7` 300k closures | 102.38 ms | 96.51 ms | **-5.7%** |
| `e5` 300k closures + call | 147.10 ms | 136.24 ms | **-7.4%** |
| for-in head-let row | 788 ms | 753 ms | -4.5% |
| `construct_churn` corpus row | 60.55 ms | 58.89 ms | -2.7% |

Base (Stage B's parent) vs Stage B+A in one interleaved run: `e7` 106.65 ->
97.39 ms (-8.7%), `e5` 143.76 -> 130.68 ms (-9.1%). Class/call rows did not
regress (`construct_churn`, `method_call`, `recursive_fib`, `apply_call`,
`closure_capture`, `direct_leaf` all flat or better).

The stop rule in `.notes/closure-cost-plan.md` (do not start Stage D unless
B+A take `e7` below ~85 ms from a 97-105 baseline) is **not met**: this machine
measured 106.65 ms for the pre-Stage-B binary on the same runs, and the final
binary is 96.5-97.4 ms. Stage D is therefore not started.

Gates: clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`, corpus parity 0,
`test262` 48,633 + 3,365 at 100%.

### LANDED (2026-10-19): computed-key loops register-lower (interpreter)

The `--jitless` corpus column still had three large register-lane holes: a
computed member store whose key is derived from the loop counter
(`a[k & M] = k & N`) and its read (`s += a[k & M]`). Bytecode dumps
(`SLAG_DUMP_FUNCS`, a temporary probe) showed both statements staying on the
step path at ~6 ns/step. Two lowering rules were responsible:

1. `Step::GetMemberComputed` rejected an `Acc` key unconditionally. With a
   frame-slot object the object read never touches the accumulator, so the
   fused `GetMemberComputedLocal` can consume the live `Acc` directly.
2. A computed key held in the accumulator was overwritten by the value
   expression (`LoadCounter`/`BinImm`), and the old `spill_live_acc` only
   looked at the top of the shadow and pushed the value onto the value stack,
   which no store op can consume.

The fix spills a live accumulator to a **hidden scratch frame slot**
(`alloc_scratch_slot`) and rewrites the shadow entry as a plain `Reg`, so the
key stays re-readable by the existing `StoreMemberComputedLocal` /
`GetMemberComputedLocal` ops. The spill scan now finds the `Acc` marker
anywhere below virtual operands and is applied before every op that loads into
the accumulator (`Binary`/`BinaryImm` loads, `LoadCounter`, member reads),
which also lets nested arithmetic register-lower. The scratch grows the frame
by one word per spill site, is unnamed, and turns `args_alias` off (the
inline-leaf alias gate compares `argc == frame_size`, which a later frame
growth would otherwise make admit an extra argument).

No new `LeafOp` variant: the first attempt added
`StoreMemberComputedSpilled` and measured a ~5-13% icache/layout hit on
unrelated rows even after outlining its executor, so the scratch-slot shape
reuses the existing ops instead.

Isolated `--jitless` A/B, alternating run order (8-10 pairs, min/mean):

| row | HEAD | landed | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `arrays/index_loop` | 124.1 ms | 94.6 ms | **-23.7%** |
| `arrays/typed_array` | 188.8 ms | 159.1 ms | **-15.7%** |
| `objects/many_objects_read` | 108.3 ms | 69.5 ms | **-35.8%** |

JIT (default) on the same isolated rows: `many_objects_read` 21.5 -> 20.3 ms
(-5.6%), `typed_array` 22.9 -> 23.6 (+2.7%), `index_loop` 16.7 -> 18.1
(+8.6%). The CLIF for `index_loop` is nearly identical (three prologue stores
differ), so the last two are code-placement/alignment effects of the register
body's smaller loop.

Measurement caveat: `globals/object_read` (17.4 -> 18.3) and
`control/nested_loops` (105 -> 112) move in the wrong direction while their
dumped IR is **byte-identical** across the two builds, and a HEAD rebuild
reproduces the HEAD timing exactly. Those deltas are LTO/code placement, not
the lowering; the corpus numbers carry the same caveat.

Gates: clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`, corpus parity 0,
`test262` 48,633 + 3,365 at 100%.

### LANDED (2026-10-19): typed-array prototype reads hit the chain cache

`opcost/typed_array_for_each` was 75 ms jitless / 63 ms JIT for 100k
`ta.forEach(cb)` calls on a four-element view. The decomposition:

| probe (100k iterations, jitless) | ms |
| --- | --- |
| `var f = ta.forEach` only | 33.3 |
| `var f = ta.nope` (missing) | 41.6 |
| `var f = a.forEach` (plain array) | 3.5 |
| `var n = ta.length` | 3.3 |
| four direct `cb(ta[j])` calls | 20-24 |
| `ta.forEach(cb)` | 75.7 |

A typed-array **method read** cost ~333 ns while the same read on a plain
array cost ~35 ns. The cause is `Vm::cell_object`, which excludes
`ObjectKind::IntegerIndexed` from the member caches, so `member_chain_get`
never ran for a typed-array receiver and every `ta.forEach`/`ta.map` read
paid the full `[[Get]]` prototype walk.

The chain cache now takes a wider `chain_object` (Ordinary, Array, and
Integer-Indexed; functions unchanged) while the own-DATA cells keep the old
narrow `cell_object` (typed-array elements are not in the property vector).
Soundness for the exotic kind: an Integer-Indexed receiver intercepts every
**canonical numeric index** key, valid (`"0"`) or not (`"1.5"`, `"NaN"`,
`"Infinity"`), so `resolve_chain_cell` refuses to record one
(`crux::object::is_canonical_numeric_index`, newly public). Own shadowing
bumps the receiver generation; prototype mutation/setPrototypeOf miss through
the recorded link ids/generations. Element writes do not bump the generation,
but they cannot shadow a non-index name. Proxies stay on the exact path.

Measured (isolated, alternating order, 10 pairs):

| row | HEAD | landed | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `opcost/typed_array_for_each` jitless | 76.9 ms | 34.5 ms | **-55%** |
| `opcost/typed_array_for_each` JIT | 62.7 ms | 29.6 ms | **-53%** |
| `ta.forEach` read probe | 33.3 ms | 3.3 ms | **10x** |
| `ta.map` read probe | 34.0 ms | 3.3 ms | **10x** |

Full corpus (min of 3, interleaved): default JIT mean -0.74%, jitless mean
-0.86%; the row is the only double-digit mover. A read of a *missing* name on
a typed array pays a little more now (the chain probe runs before the exact
fallback): `ta.nope` 41.6 -> 49.0 ms, a cold path.

Verified: a targeted probe covers canonical index atoms (valid/invalid),
own shadowing and deletion, prototype method reassignment, setPrototypeOf,
symbols, Float64/BigInt arrays and proxies; `cargo test --workspace`;
clippy `-D warnings`; corpus parity 0; test262 48,633 + 3,365 at 100%.

The same probe decomposition for `opcost/array_to_sorted` shows it is not a
read problem: `small.toSorted()` is 144 ms jitless, `small.slice()` is 26 ms,
and `slice().sort()` is 153 ms. The sort itself costs ~1.3 us for four
elements because `sort_indexed_properties` pays a string-keyed
`HasProperty`/`Get`/`Set` per element. A dense-array fast path for the
default comparator landed below.

### LANDED (2026-10-19): dense-array default sort

`sort_indexed_properties` now takes a direct-slot path when the comparator is
`undefined`, the receiver is a `dense` Array whose element count equals its
length, every element is present (no `Value::hole()`) and every element is a
primitive that runs no user code (Number, String, Boolean, Undefined, Null,
BigInt). The path copies the element buffer, precomputes each `ToString` once
(pure and deterministic for those kinds, so the per-comparison reduction is
unobservable), sorts on the text, writes back through
`write_barrier_element`, and bumps the receiver generation. Holes, objects,
Symbols (their `ToString` throws and the throw order is observable) and a
supplied `comparefn` keep the generic string-keyed
`HasProperty`/`Get`/`Set` path unchanged.

The cost the path removes is the generic machinery, not the comparison: the
old path materialised a `PropertyKey` string and did a prototype-aware
`HasProperty`, `Get` and `Set` for each of four elements, ~1.3 us per sort.

Same-source interleaved A/B (baseline built from the commit without the fast
path, alternating order, 16 pairs, min/mean ms):

| probe (100k sorts) | jit base | jit new | jitless base | jitless new |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `opcost/array_to_sorted` (`toSorted`) | 129.1/134.2 | 32.9/34.3 (-74%) | 142.7/146.6 | 44.8/46.0 (-69%) |
| `slice().sort()` | 139.9/144.4 | 39.0/40.0 (-72%) | 152.9/154.5 | 50.1/50.8 (-67%) |
| `[4,2,3,1].sort()` | 124.9/128.5 | 28.9/29.4 (-77%) | 136.5/138.2 | 38.2/39.1 (-72%) |
| `["d","b","c","a"].sort()` | 117.2/118.7 | 27.1/27.7 (-77%) | 130.1/131.1 | 36.6/36.8 (-72%) |
| control: `sort(cmp)` (generic path) | 148.5/150.2 | 148.8/150.9 (+0.5%) | 156.0/158.3 | 155.1/159.1 (+0.5%) |
| control: `slice()` only | 18.3/18.6 | 18.1/18.6 (+0.1%) | 25.2/25.8 | 24.9/26.0 (+0.6%) |

Whole corpus, 5 interleaved pairs, per-row min: default JIT total
2891.6 -> 2784.1 ms (-3.7%, `array_to_sorted` 142.0 -> 36.3), jitless total
5891.5 -> 5866.7 ms (-0.4%, `array_to_sorted` 144.9 -> 46.1), value parity 0.
Two jitless rows move the wrong way consistently: `arrays/index_loop`
89.1 -> 101.8 ms and `control/nested_loops` 102.5 -> 124.1 ms (focused
16-pair rerun: +12% and +20% by mean). Neither calls sort; the change touches
only `sort_indexed_properties`, so this is the usual LTO placement effect of
adding code, recorded rather than chased.

Verified: the semantic probes (numbers, string order, mixed primitives,
holes including prototype-provided hole reads, `toSorted` copy/immutability,
stable generic sort, Symbol TypeError, frozen array TypeError with the array
unchanged, sealed array, `new Array(n)` tail holes, `-0`/NaN, non-writable
element, preventExtensions) print identically on the baseline and new
binaries in both modes; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace`; corpus
parity 0; test262 48,633 + 3,365 at 100%.

The class-parts commit also dropped the GC edge for `EcmaFunction`'s inline
`private_environment`; that is fixed separately and is not part of this
measurement.

### MEASURED (2026-10-19): Goats client, a real workload

[Goats](https://github.com/sdgoij/goats) is an external game built on Slag.
Its optimized dev client run, one scripted run, 7 bots and 4 mods, after
warm-up, is the first real workload measured against this engine rather
than a corpus row. The clean steady-state window is `n=240` frames with
zero slow frames.

The two columns are the Slag revision the client was built against:
`f491e69` (2026-10-18) and `178f92f` (2026-10-19).

| phase | `f491e69` | `178f92f` | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| phase sum | 22.98 ms | **18.74 ms** | **-18.5%** |
| fps | 40 | **50** | **+25%** |
| `tufts` (largest) | 10.47 | 7.77 | -26% |
| `mods_upd` | 1.46 | 1.29 | -12% |
| `sky2d` | 1.65 | 1.16 | -30% |
| `shadow_grass` | 1.65 | 1.34 | -19% |

The engine loop probes in the same client (`perf loop`, ns/iteration):

| kind | `f491e69` | `178f92f` | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `mapget` | 104.84 | 74.78 | **-29%** |
| `maphas` | 163.68 | 102.75 | **-37%** |
| `arith` | 13.34 | 13.75 | noise |
| `new` | 386.19 | 406.52 | noise |

`perf probe`'s pure-JS `Math.sin` loop went 7457 -> 6540 ns (-12%), while
`callNs`, `propNs` and `pureNs` are unchanged. The native boundary is not
faster; the win is inside the runtime and JIT for the same operations.

Attribution: the Map rows line up with the key-index mixer
(`aa57dbf perf(runtime): hash Map/Set key index words with a mixer`),
`has` gains more than `get` because it skips the value read. The broad
phase movement lines up with the GC work (`edfed74 perf(gc): scan the
young cohort by hash table`, `6a1b771 perf(gc): skip the drop for a plain
object`): less scanning and less teardown per allocation shows up in every
allocating phase. The rest of the range `f491e69..178f92f` is the JIT
inline batch (dense `push`/`pop`/`reverse`/`at`, field stores,
prototype-chain reads, direct builtin calls), the closure-record work and
the dense default sort. Two builds many commits apart mean the attribution
is by mechanism, not by bisection.

The phase sum is the honest headline: -18.5%. The fps jump (40 -> 50) is
part frame-budget quantization but is the number a player sees. `arith`
and `new` staying flat are the controls: this is not a global speedup, it
is less work in the paths a frame actually uses. `new` at +5% is within
noise and is worth watching if allocation-heavy phases regress later.

Next real-workload target: `tufts` is still the largest phase at 7.77 ms
after -26%; a sampling profile of that phase is the useful next input. That
profile is below.

### MEASURED (2026-10-19): Goats `tufts`, one global write, not allocation

The phase-internal split (`perf on`) put almost all of `tufts` in the draw
loop, and the draw loop's floor was a single global read-modify-write:

| part | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `tuft_setup` (shader + uniforms) | 0.09 | 0.09 |
| `tuft_field` (hash, `EATEN`, height cache) | 0.62 | 0.65 |
| `tuft_draw` (water test + cubes) | **6.70** | **0.50** |
| tail (`endShaderMode`) | 0.03 | 0.03 |
| `shadow_grass` (same work) | 1.27 | **0.41** |

The field is cheap: ~625 cells of `Set.has` / `Map.get` / hashing / terrain
sampling cost 0.64 ms, matching the `mapget`/`maphas` micro-results.

Ablations inside the draw loop:

| ablation | `tuft_draw` ms |
| --- | ---: |
| none | 6.70 |
| water check removed | 4.65 |
| cube submissions removed | 4.96 |
| both removed | 2.84 |

The 2.84 ms floor was `perfCubes += t.d ? 2 : 1;` running once per tuft.
Replacing it with a local accumulator and writing `perfCubes` once after the
loop made `tuft_draw` 0.50 ms and `shadow_grass` 0.41 ms with identical
geometry and cube count.

The global **reads** are not the issue: the same loop with a local
accumulator and `TUFT_POOL` / `waterSubmergedAt` / `rl` still reads 0.50 ms.
The write was not just its own cost, with the global reads present it made
the rest of the loop pathological.

Frame-level, same session, clean `n=240` window:

| | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| CPU sum (all phases) | 16.53 ms | **9.61 ms** |
| `boundary` (swap wait) | 0.05 ms | **6.72 ms** |
| worst / slow frames |, | 17.9 ms / **0** |
| fps | CPU-bound | **59-60** |

About 42% less CPU per frame, and genuinely vsync-bound. The next-largest
phases are `mods_upd` (1.13 ms), `tuft_field` (0.65 ms) and `bots` (0.48 ms).

This was a client-side fix (accumulate locally, publish once), not an
allocation-latency result.

An engine-side probe isolates the write (5,000,000 iterations, min of 5):

| shape | JIT ms | jitless ms |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `var acc` local to the function | 3.6 | 114.9 |
| top-level `var acc` compound assign | **960.0** | 1084.8 |
| top-level `let acc` compound assign | **362.5** | 504.4 |
| top-level `var acc` simple assign | **698.9** | 755.1 |
| read-only `g` from the global | 3.9 | 43.0 |
| `globalThis.acc += ...` | 147.5 | 258.4 |

`JIT_HELPER_STATS=1` shows one `ResolveVarIdent`, one `GetVarReference` and
one `PutVarReferenceOp` per iteration, the generic reference machinery,
while a global read is a single `LoadIdent` cell hit. The compiler classifies
a function body's script-global write as `BindingLoc::Env`, and there is no
`StoreIdent` analogue of `LoadIdent`; the inlined global-value store cell
exists only for certified top-level script code (`StoreGlobal`).

The engine-side fix is a `StoreIdent` step gated exactly like `LoadIdent`
(env-constant body + unshadowed chain), with the JIT inlining the same
global-value cell `StoreGlobal` uses and falling back to the reference path
when the cell is stale or the property is not a writable data slot. Both
`var` shapes (global object) and `let` shapes (declarative record) want the
same step; the declarative record additionally needs a slot for its value.
That slice landed below.

### LANDED (2026-10-19): environment-resolved global stores

A certified body's `BindingLoc::Env` write no longer goes through the
generic reference machinery. `Step::StoreIdent` (with its
`ResolveIdentStore` companion) now stores through the same direct-mapped
global-value cell `LoadIdent` reads, and a declarative binding keeps the
environment resolve.

The write was three helpers per iteration (`ResolveVarIdent`,
`GetVarReference`, `PutVarReferenceOp`) while a read was a single `LoadIdent`
cell hit. The compiled sequence is now `ResolveIdentStore` + `LoadIdent` +
RHS + `Binary` + `StoreIdent`. `ResolveIdentStore` branches on the ctx's
`globals_unshadowed`: the clean path skips the walk entirely, and the
shadowed path resolves the reference before the RHS, preserving spec 13.15.3
steps 1 and 5 (a `with` binding the RHS deletes is still the PutValue
target). `StoreIdent`'s cell fast path writes an own writable data property by
slot, and a declarative binding by its binding-vector index (`declarative`
= 1 in the cell); the global env bumps the global object's generation on
every declarative mutation, which validates the index. The name-keyed
resolve remains the fallback for a moved index, an immutable binding, or an
undeclared name.

Measured (5,000,000 iterations, min of 5, same scripts):

| shape | before JIT | after JIT | before jl | after jl |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| top-level `var` `+=` | 960.0 | **39.1** | 1084.8 | **179.7** |
| top-level `var` `=` | 698.9 | **21.4** | 755.1 | **72.7** |
| top-level `let` `+=` | 362.5 | **113.1** | 504.4 | **239.4** |
| local `var` (control) | 3.6 | 3.7 | 114.9 | 108.5 |
| global read (control) | 3.9 | 4.0 | 43.0 | 39.9 |

The JIT inlines the object-slot cell probe (the `StoreGlobal` shape:
name/id/generation/slot validation, then `set_global_slot`), so the fast path
is a branch and one helper call for the vector write; every miss (a shadowed
chain, a declarative cell, a stale cell) goes to `store_ident`, never to
`set_global`. A declarative write is one helper call and a binding-vector
index write, which is why `let` lands at 113 ms rather than the `var` path's
39.

Whole corpus (5 interleaved pairs): default JIT -1.1%, jitless -1.7%, value
parity 0. The `let` shape is no longer a resolve per write: it records the
binding index and writes it in place. The `var` shape is the client's case
and is now close to a quarter of the `globalThis.acc +=` member path (39 vs
152 ms).

Two fixtures shaped the slice: the JIT declarative read/write test caught
`store_global_value` creating a shadow property for a `let`, and
`statements/with/set-mutable-binding-binding-deleted-with-typed-array-in-proto-chain-strict-mode.js`
caught the missing pre-resolve ordering. A `DeclarativeEnv::set_value_at`
test pins the cached index, the moved-index fallback, and the const
sloppy/strict split.

Verified: clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace`; corpus parity 0;
test262 48,633 + 3,365 at 100%.

### LANDED (2026-10-19): keep-jump branches in the optimizing tier

`JIT_DUMP_STEPS=1` on the `language/statements/try` workload showed the
optimizing tier refusing `completion-values` on exactly two shapes:

```text
opt-blockers: JumpIfFalseKeep,JumpIfTrueKeep
```

The baseline tier lowered them (`top()` + truthiness, no pop), but the SSA
lifter's `TermRec::Branch` only knew the popping pair, so any body with `&&`,
`||` or a ternary that keeps its value never reached the optimizer. The lift
now treats the keep variants as branches on the top value with the condition
left on both edges: the terminator record, the branch emission, `jump_target`
(which also makes them terminators and gives `block_successors` its
`[target, end]` shape), and the blocker diagnostic. The stack-depth fixpoint
needed no change, its conditional-pop edge only matches the popping pair,
so a keep conditional falls into the `out` arm as it should.

Whole-corpus effect (one pass each; the change is JIT-only, so the jitless
column is noise): JIT total 2878.4 -> 2815.7 ms (-2.2%). The rows that were
waiting on the shape:

| row | before JIT | after JIT |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `language/expressions/template-literal/evaluation-order.js` | 312.1 | **286.3** |
| `language/statements/for-in/head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration.js` | 669.0 | **633.8** |
| `language/statements/try/completion-values.js` | 407.3 | **394.0** |

`completion-values` now lifts, but barely moves: its cost is the completion
record and list-stack work (`ListBegin`/`ListEnd`/`NormalizeCompletion`),
not the blocked branch. The other two bodies in the template workload are
still blocked by `ConcatStr`/`ConcatStrConst`/`PushStr`/`UpdateLocal` and
`UpdateContextSlot`, and the for-in body by the per-iteration steps
(`EnterPerIteration`, `PerIteration`, `LoadPerIteration`,
`StorePerIteration`). The for-in row's helper stats put the real cost in the
call path (about 9 `CertifiedCall`, 2 `CallSlow` and 21 `LeafCallProbe` per
body iteration), not in the three per-iteration environment ops.

Verified: clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace`; corpus parity 0;
test262 48,633 + 3,365 at 100%. A new lift test covers a `&&` body.

### MEASURED (2026-10-19): the env-leaf call lane

Four minimal 1M-iteration loops isolate the call shapes (`JIT_HELPER_STATS`;
the counts include the corpus runner's warm/timed calls):

| probe | JIT ms | probe | fill | env | cert | slow |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| leaf, no env | 5.9 | 20 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 4 |
| leaf reading a captured var | 22.0 | 11 | 7.0M | 7.0M | 7 | 4 |
| non-leaf (calls a leaf) | 53.5 | 16 | 0 | 0 | 6.0M | 1.0M |
| two leafs, alternating | 11.2 | 22 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 8 |

The probes are **cold** for monomorphic sites (20 first visits over 7M
calls), so the probe is not a per-call cost. The for-in row's three
probes/iteration are its `fns.a/b/c()` sites: the closures are recreated by
every `__t262Body` call, so the callee identity changes and the per-site
record misses by construction. The env leaf is the clear inefficiency: it
paid two FFI calls per call (`leaf_call_fill` then `leaf_call_env`).

`leaf_call_env` now rebuilds the frame itself and performs the call in one
round trip, returning `u64::MAX` on a fit/eligibility failure so the site
falls to `cert`/`call_slow` as before. Both lowerings (the baseline
`compiler.rs` and the optimizing `opt_lower.rs`) pass the receiver with the
six-parameter signature; the now-unused five-parameter `Abi::sig_call` is
gone.

Env-leaf probe: 22.0 -> 19.7 ms (-10%). The corpus is flat within noise
(few rows call env-reading leaves), and parity is 0. The remaining call
floor is `CertifiedCall` at ~53 ns for a non-leaf callee; moving it needs
the C3 frame work, not another helper merge.

Verified: clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace`; corpus parity 0;
test262 48,633 + 3,365 at 100%.

### MEASURED (2026-10-20): the template-literal lift, and what the row is really made of

The optimizing tier now lifts `PushStr`, `ConcatStr`, `ConcatStrConst`,
`TaggedTemplate` and `UpdateLocal`, so a loop body that builds a template no
longer falls back to the per-step path. `PushStr`/`ConcatStrConst`/
`TaggedTemplate` keep the quasi payload in the running body and read it back by
step index; `ConcatStr` threads the accumulator as an SSA value; `UpdateLocal`
is `FrameLoad` + `UpdateValue` + `FrameStore`, pushing the new value for the
prefix form and the loaded one for the postfix form (the same shape the
baseline `emit_update` emits, including its TDZ check on lexical slots).

The corpus row under change moved from 288.5 to 280.3 ms (-2.8%), but the
honest reading is that the row is not compiler dispatch-bound at all. An
ablation of its body (100k iterations, the real fixture minus the harness
noise, one factor removed per run):

| probe | ms | per-iter |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| full body (closure + plain template + tagged template) | 199.9 | 2.0 us |
| without the tagged template | 107.1 | 1.07 us |
| without the plain template + its `assert.sameValue` | 104.9 | 1.05 us |
| without the per-iteration closure (hoisted tag) | 208.7 | 2.09 us |
| closure creation alone | 38.8 | 0.39 us |
| tagged template alone | 150.1 | 1.50 us |
| plain template + one `assert.sameValue` | 57.1 | 0.57 us |
| one `assert.sameValue(0, 0)` call | 17.9 | 0.18 us |
| `tag("x", 0, 1, 2)` (a plain 4-arg call) | 119.0 | 1.19 us |
| `tag`abcd`` (tagged template, no substitutions) | 18.2 | 0.18 us |

Two things follow. The tagged-template machinery itself is cheap: 0.18 us
including the call, so template-object caching is not the cost. The cost is the
ordinary JS call: `assert.sameValue(0, 0)` is 179 ns, and the tag invocation
plus its three nested calls is 1.19 us. That is the same floor the C3 work is
aimed at (`CertifiedCall` ~53 ns is only the non-leaf *callee* half; a
method-call site pays the read, the guard and the binding around it). The lift
is therefore a coverage win, not a row win, and the next real move on this row
is the call path.

A pure template loop (200k iterations of `s = `a${i}b${i + 1}c``) is unchanged
by the lift, as expected, it is allocation-bound: 49.5-52.1 ms opt-on versus
50.0-51.9 ms opt-off across five runs each. The first measurement suggested a
19% regression; it was one hot-machine outlier (42.6 ms), and it did not
reproduce.

`UpdateContextSlot` was lifted in the same slice and then taken back out. With
it supported, `built-ins/Iterator/zip/basic-longest.js` starts failing under
`sweep all` (wrong padding function observed inside a `map` callback: a
mis-typed `expected` array), and it passes with `SLAG_OPT=0`, with
`SLAG_NOLIFT_CTX` (a temporary seam), with `SLAG_GUARD=0` and with
`SLAG_TYPER=0`. Both of those switches remove or keep every `GuardType`, so the
fault is not the helper lowering (which is byte-identical to the baseline
`Step::UpdateContextSlot` arm): it is the typer's read guard interacting with a
newly-lifted body. Moving `guard::run` ahead of `narrow::run`, and treating the
narrowed int ops as type-sensitive, each failed to fix it, so neither was kept.
The repro is `scratch/tmpl/zip.js` (the harness includes concatenated in front
of the fixture) run through `./target/release/slag.exe`. The lift refuses the
step, with a comment pointing here, until that guard interaction is understood.

Verified: `cargo fmt --all --check`; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test
--workspace`; `sweep all` 48,633 at 100%; `sweep intl402` 3,365 at 100%; corpus
parity 0 (`node tools/corpus/bench.js`, mean-jitGap 12.18 on that run, the
full-corpus mean moves by several tenths between runs on a warm machine, so it
is quoted only with the parity row).

### MEASURED (2026-10-20): one cold `new` or `try` poisons a whole function's call path

The certified-callee lane (`call_slow` -> `certified_lane_inline`) refuses a
callee whose body *contains* `Step::Construct`, the `Args*` vector steps,
`Step::Call`, `EnterTry`, `TaggedTemplate` or `SuperCall`
(`CompiledBody::has_shared_vm_step_hazard`). The refusal is per body, not per
execution, so a step that never runs still sends every call to the interpreter
funnel. Measured on 1M method calls, the callee's own body varying and nothing
else:

| callee body (called as `assert.sameValue(i, i)`) | JIT ms | ns/call |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `if (a !== b) { return 0; } return 1;` | 13.8 | 13.8 |
| `if (a !== b) { throw a; }` | 13.8 | 13.8 |
| `if (a !== b) { throw new Error("bad"); }` | 164.7 | 164.7 |
| `if (a !== b) { var e = new Error("bad"); return e; }` | 171.9 | 171.9 |
| `try { if (a !== b) { return 0; } } finally {} return 1;` | 187.6 | 187.6 |

`JIT_HELPER_STATS` confirms the mechanism: the slow rows show `CallSlow` at
1,000,000 + warm-up (`helper 18`, ~7 per harness iteration) and
`JIT_LEAF_TRACE` reports `leaf-lookup-miss`; the fast rows inline. `throw a`
alone is fine, so it is the *`Construct`* (`new Error(...)`) and the `EnterTry`,
not the throw.

This matters far beyond the probe: `throw new Error(...)` is the canonical
defensive check, and a `try`/`finally` is ordinary code, so a great many real
functions are one cold-path step away from being 12x slower to call than their
bodies deserve. The fix is to make the hazard positional rather than existential,
admit the body and keep the steps that need `Vm::args`/`try_stack` on the
funnel (the compiled body can route a *step* back through the interpreter
machinery the way `Op::Intrinsic` does, or the lane can isolate `vm.args`/
`args_base_stack` lengths in `save_scratch` the way it already isolates
`var_ref_stack`/`class_stack`), but each of those touches the shared-state
contract §20.3/§21 of the `slag-jit` skill warn about, so it needs its own
slice with the sweep as the net, not a drive-by.

Repro: `scratch/c3/{throw_call,nothrow_call,new_only,throw_plain,try_only}`,
run with `./target/release/slag.exe --corpus scratch/c3/<name>`.

### MEASURED (2026-10-20): the certified lane admits try bodies and argument vectors

The previous entry measured a 12x call penalty for a body that merely contains
`Construct` or `EnterTry`. The certified-callee lane now admits both, by
isolating the two shared pieces of state they touch rather than refusing the
body:

- A callee with `handlers` (it owns a `try`) runs under the C3a control-state
  recipe: `Vm::is_control_free()` decides between the cheap `save_scratch` and
  `save_scratch_full` (which parks the caller's ~twenty control stacks on
  `saved_control`), and `clear_control_state` drops whatever the callee
  abandons on an abrupt exit before `restore_scratch` puts the caller's back.
  That is exactly what the interpreter's nested certified call already does, so
  the compiled lane now matches it.
- The `Vm::args`/`args_base_stack` pair is watermarked: the lane records their
  lengths before the run and truncates back if the callee left anything above
  them (a balanced run leaves the length alone, so the common call pays one
  compare). This is what admits `ArgsBase`/`ArgsPush`/`ArgsSpread`, `Call`,
  `Construct` and a tagged template, the hazard was never the vector itself,
  only a leak across a re-entry (a caller mid-`ArgsSpread` keeps its half-built
  vector below the watermark).

The gate is now two lists: `has_shared_vm_step_hazard` (the self-call lane,
unchanged) and `has_certified_lane_step_hazard` (the same list minus `EnterTry`
and the argument-vector steps). The self lane keeps the conservative gate
deliberately: giving `self_call_inline` the same plumbing cost
`calls/recursive_fib` 49.2 → 61-66 ms (16M self calls at ~0.7 ns each, the
tuple/extra local in a function that is otherwise inlined into `call_slow`),
and a self call cannot build a *fresh* vector for a different callee, so the
coverage lost there is small. Restoring the self lane's shape while keeping the
certified gate narrow put the row back at 48.5-53.2 ms (HEAD: 48.7-54.0).

Probes (1M method calls, `assert.sameValue(i, i)`, varying only the callee body):

| callee body | before | after | ns/call |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `if (a !== b) { throw new Error("bad"); }` | 164.7 | **59.0** | 59.0 |
| `if (a !== b) { var e = new Error("bad"); return e; }` | 171.9 | **59.4** | 59.4 |
| `try { if (a !== b) { return 0; } } finally {} return 1;` | 187.6 | **82.1** | 82.1 |
| `if (a !== b) { throw a; }` (a leaf, unchanged) | 13.8 | 13.5 | 13.5 |
| `if (a !== b) { return 0; } return 1;` (a leaf, unchanged) | 13.8 | 14.1 | 14.1 |

The try row lands at 82 ns rather than the lane's ~60 because the body pays
three try helpers per call (`EnterTry`/`ExitTry`/`FinallyEnd` are FFI calls with
a pending check each); that is the try representation's cost, not the lane's.
The remaining ~59 ns is the lane's own setup, a new `JitCallContext`, the
`ecma_functions` record resolution, the frame fill and the `vm.stack` carve,
and it is the C3 frame work's target (the leaf lane, which shares the caller's
ctx, is 14 ns).

Corpus: parity 0, mean-jitGap 11.99 (the full-corpus mean moves by tenths
between runs on a warm machine; `statements/try/completion-values` measured
377-414 ms across five runs of the same binary, so it is not a stable row).

Verified: `cargo fmt --all --check`; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test
--workspace`; `sweep all` 48,633 at 100%; `sweep intl402` 3,365 at 100%;
`--gc-stress` on `statements/try` and `Iterator` matches HEAD exactly (the one
try hang and the three zipKeyed hangs are pre-existing under the stress
deadline). Repro probes: `scratch/c3/{throw_call,new_only,try_only,throw_plain}`.

### FIXED (2026-10-20): the global store cell skipped the member-cell refresh

`c1`-era global store cells wrote the global object's property in place and
mirrored the JIT's global-value cell, but not the *read-side* member-value cell
(`agent.member_value_cells`). An in-place write does not bump the object's
generation (the slag-jit skill's §19 store discipline), so a later member read
