of the same name was served the pre-store value:

```js
realmA.calls = 0;                          // warms the member cell for realmA.calls
...
Reflect.construct(aGeneratorFunction, ["calls += 1;"], newTarget)();  // StoreIdent → global cell
realmA.calls                               // served the stale 0 from the member cell
```

`built-ins/GeneratorFunction/proto-from-ctor-realm-prototype.js` failed with
`Expected SameValue(«0», «1»)`, and it failed under `--jitless` too, the
interpreter's `try_global_cell_store` has the same gap. Both in-place store
paths (`Vm::store_global_value`, `Vm::try_global_cell_store`) and the compiled
`set_global_slot` helper now call `Vm::refresh_member_value_cell`, the same
discipline `JsObject::write_data_property_slot` follows.

Two traps made this expensive to find, both worth remembering:

- **A local `sweep all` can pass while CI's per-area sweep fails.** The fixtures
  are batched into fresh processes; a fixture that leaks per-`Agent` state (here
  a warmed member cell) only fails when its trigger lands in the *same batch*.
  `sweep all` split the pair, `sweep built-ins` did not. Reproduce with
  `--print-fixtures` to find the batch, then `--list <file>` with exactly that
  batch, a 32-fixture, ~10 ms repro instead of a 10-minute area sweep.
- **The failing assertion named the wrong suspect.** The value was right in the
  property and wrong in the cache, so every "which global did it write" probe
  came back clean; the store really did hit (`cell_store=true`). Instrument the
  *store's* branch and the *read path* that serves the assertion, not just the
  write target.

The compiling tier was also given the interpreter's `body.env_constant` guard
on the `LoadIdent`/`ResolveIdentStore`/`StoreIdent` cell paths (the run-entry
`globals_unshadowed` snapshot is only valid for a whole run in an env-constant
body), then that gate was **withdrawn**: an interleaved A/B on
`language/statements/for-in/head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration.js` (which is
env-changing and reads `Object`/`assert` through `LoadIdent`) put it at 720 ms
without and ~800 ms with, and it fixed nothing reproducible, the fixture above
was already green from the member-cell refresh alone. The interpreter keeps the
guard; the compiled tier's divergence (it may use the cell for a body whose
chain could later gain a shadowing binding, where the interpreter resolves) is
a known open item, recorded rather than paid for at 15% on the largest row.

Verified: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace`; and every area at
CI's batch size, `built-ins` 23,821, `language` 23,726, `annexB` 1,086,
`intl402` 3,365, all 100%.

Two things NOT attributable to this session, recorded so they are not

#### The bisect, closed

The fast batch repro makes the attribution exact instead of inferred:

| revision | built-ins batch 195 | 2-fixture pair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bc81db7d` (parent of `8e276655`) | 31 pass, 0 fail | 2 pass |
| `8e276655` (fast-path global stores) | 30 pass, **1 fail** | 1 pass, **1 fail** |
| `8e276655` + only the member-cell refresh | 31 pass, 0 fail | 2 pass |
| `HEAD` | 31 pass, 0 fail | 2 pass |

So the offending commit is `8e276655` and its *only* defect is the missing
read-side refresh: one disciplined write added to that tree turns the batch
green, with nothing else changed. The later commits (`c10e2f10` inlining the
certified store cell, `1fa40bb6` caching declarative slots) inherit the same
gap in their own in-place writers, which is why `HEAD` needs the refresh in
three places rather than one.

Reverting `8e276655` instead was measured and rejected: an interleaved A/B on a
5M-iteration `var += 1` loop (the shape that commit exists for) is **866-903 ms
at the parent versus 41.5-43.0 ms at the commit**, 20.7x. The corpus has no
global-*store* row (its `globals/*` are read-only), which is why the corpus
means showed the change as ~flat and why the regression hid there.

## FIXED (2026-10-20): a nested run on the caller's Vm clobbered `globals_unshadowed`

**Symptom.** Goats' `the_birds_mod_works` failed at `makeTerrain()` with
`SyntaxError: StoreIdent without a resolution` (44 cases, release only). The
standalone scene did not reproduce it; the mod-install path did.

**Cause.** `run_inner` recomputes `Vm::globals_unshadowed` at every activation.
The certified-callee lane runs a callee **on the caller's Vm**
(`run_certified_call_nested` -> `run_compiled_body_on`), and `VmScratch` did not
save that field. A callee with no ident names (or any shadowed chain) computes
`false`; after it returned, the caller's flag was `false` for the rest of its
run. The failing statement is `terrainMesh = rl.makeModel(...)`: its
`ResolveIdentStore` saw a clean chain and skipped the reference push, then
`StoreIdent` re-read the (now clobbered) flag, took the dynamic path and popped
an empty `var_ref_stack`. The `SLAG_STORE_TRACE` probe made it one line:
`resolve name=terrainMesh clean=true` immediately followed by
`store name=terrainMesh clean=false`.

This also explains the earlier `ctx_clean=true / vm_clean=false` mismatches: the
compiled tier reads its per-call `JitCallContext`, so it was unaffected; the
interpreter reads the shared `Vm` field and was not.

**Fix.** `VmScratch` now saves and restores `globals_unshadowed` (one bool, no
hot-path cost worth measuring), and both `StoreIdent` sites fall back to
`store_ident_value(..., true)` when the reference stack is empty: the resolve
skipped the push because the chain was clean then, so the global binding is the
target it meant. The internal `SyntaxError` is gone from both tiers.

**Gates.** New unit test
`ir::tests::a_nested_run_restores_the_callers_globals_unshadowed`; Goats
`the_birds_mod_works` 44/44 pass (release, linked to the local checkout);
`cargo test --workspace`; clippy `-D warnings`; test262 built-ins 23,821,
language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, all at 100%.

## LANDED (2026-10-20): function-site caches off SipHash

`instantiate_function*` makes three thread-local site lookups per closure
(`shared_source_info`, `shared_function_body`, `shared_params`) plus one agent
lookup (`shared_compiled_body`). All four used `std::collections::HashMap`'s
default SipHash over five-word tuple or pointer keys; a closure create is
~310 ns, so the hashing was a visible share. The four tuple caches now use a
combining `SiteHasher` (one rotate/xor/multiply round per word, an identity
hasher would collapse the key to its last field), and the pointer-keyed
`PARAMS_CACHE` and `Agent::compiled_bodies` use `MixHasher` (a splitmix64
finalizer: identity hashing would cluster the low bits of aligned pointers).

Interleaved same-binary A/B (release, 3 pairs):

| probe | before | after | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `e7` 300k closures, no call | 92.0-97.0 ms | 80.5-80.9 ms | **-13%** |
| `e5` 300k closures + one call | 130.2-138.3 ms | 117.2-118.5 ms | **-11%** |
| `cap_uncaptured` (captures a var) | 253.5-266.6 ms | 233.1-247.5 ms | -6.5% |
| `cap_let_drop` (fresh env per iteration) | 386.3-389.6 ms | 355.9-360.0 ms | -7.6% |
| `calls/closure_capture` (1M calls) | 34.5-35.1 ms | 34.3-35.5 ms | flat |

The for-in head-let corpus row stays inside its documented 590-820 ms band; the
pairs that separated read 582.6 -> 559.6 and 685.3 -> 545.7, so the row's share
is real but a single corpus run cannot price it. The full corpus could not
separate the slice either: **12.07 jit** on the pre-change binary, then
**11.54** and **12.52** on two runs of the final build (jl 4.07, 4.04, 4.20;
parity 0 throughout). The run-to-run spread is larger than the effect, so the
README's family table was left at its previous recorded run and the interleaved
probes above are the evidence.

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace`; test262 built-ins
23,821, language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, all 0 fail.

### Priced but not taken (2026-10-20 survey)

- **Per-iteration block env** (the for-in head-let shape): `env-new` ~10 ns,
  `block_declaration_instantiation` ~50-90 ns (two `Vec` allocations: the
  `bound_names` scratch and the env's `bindings`), `InitContextSlot`/leave
  ~10 ns each. Probe `Instant` pairs make exact attribution unreliable.
  Removing the `bound_names` Vec for a plain `Ident` is a small slice
  (~25 ns/env); an inline binding store would remove the other allocation.
- **Closure create is ~310 ns** even after Stages B+A: the remaining terms are
  the `ecma_functions` insert, the `Function` + `JsObject` boxes, and the
  batched property adoption. Stage D (record in the GC arena) remains gated by
  `.notes/closure-cost-plan.md`'s stop rule.
- **`eval` costs ~2.75 us/call** (`eval("")` 0.95 us; each extra token ~1.3 us)
  and the script-body cache already holds the compiled body, so the cost is the
  per-call instantiation/env setup, not compilation. `try/completion-values` is
  ~12% eval-bound; the rest is its try/finally machinery.
- **`arrays/typed_array`** is 11 ns/iter in the JIT (two element accesses +
  arithmetic) and 81 ns/iter in the interpreter (V8 `--jitless`: 20 ns).

## LANDED (2026-10-20): reuse the eval parse

`perform_eval` parsed the source on every call (`parse_script_utf16_eval`) and
only then hit the per-source compiled-body cache: the parse was the whole cost.
A 90-char eval source measured 9.8 us/call (`eval("1+1")` 2.75 us, `eval("")`
0.95 us), so `try/completion-values` (12 evals x 1423 iterations) was
parse-bound, not try/finally-bound.

A thread-local `EvalParseKey -> Rc<Program>` cache, keyed by the exact source
(materialised to a `Small`/`Flat` leaf so the untraced cache holds no GC edge),
the `EvalContext` flags (`in_function`/`in_method`/`allow_private`) and the
caller's private-name list. Parsing is realm-independent and the AST is plain
data (string literals are `Small`/`Flat`, BigInts have no heap edges).
`perform_eval` still bumps the template parse generation per evaluation, so a
cached parse presents a fresh template site exactly as a fresh parse would
(pinned by `script::tests::repeated_eval_keeps_a_fresh_template_object`; V8
also returns distinct template objects for two evals of the same tagged
template source).

Interleaved same-binary A/B (release, 3 pairs): `eval_try` (20k evals of the
90-char source) 202-205 -> **29-31 ms** (-85%, 9.8 -> 1.5 us/eval); 20k
`eval("1+1")` 53.6-55.5 -> 18.9-19.6 ms (-65%); the `try/completion-values`
corpus row 383.8-406.3 -> **206.0-207.7 ms (-47%)**. The remaining ~1.5 us is
the per-eval setup (env + declaration instantiation), not parsing. Corpus
`language` family mean (single runs) jit 9.94 -> 7.66, jl 8.51 -> 7.27; the
overall mean stays inside its usual noise band.

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (runtime 1056);
test262 built-ins 23,821, language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, 0 fail.

## LANDED (2026-10-20): stack sites without copying the source

The eval parse cache left `try/completion-values` at ~207 ms, and ablation
showed the rest was not eval setup: replacing its 12 `eval(...)` arguments with
constants left 1.35 ms, a non-throwing eval costs 1.5 us, and the `[].x.x`
eval that throws costs 7.7 us. Each caught throw builds an Error stack eagerly
(`define_stack`), and `frame_site` materialised
`syntax::SourceText::from_utf8(&source.to_string_lossy())`, a full `String`
copy of the source plus a units Vec and a line-starts Vec, for **every
frame**. With several caller frames whose source is the whole fixture, one
throw copied tens of KB.

`frame_site` now scans the source's own UTF-16 units (`line_column_at`),
matching `SourceText::line_column` exactly (CR, LF, CRLF, U+2028, U+2029; a
position at a terminator stays on the line it ends), with no allocation. A
differential test checks every offset of ten texts against `SourceText`.

Interleaved same-binary A/B (3 pairs): the throwing eval probe
112.7-122.9 -> 97.7-99.4 ms (-18%), the non-throwing probe 24.8-25.6 ->
22.2-23.4 ms (-9%), and the `try/completion-values` row **197.1-203.6 ->
95.9-100.5 ms (-51%)**, from ~4.8x node to ~1.2x. The corpus `language`
family mean (single run) read 8.27 against 7.66 before: the other two rows
moved inside their noise, so the isolated row is the evidence.

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace`; test262 built-ins
23,821, language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, 0 fail.

## LANDED (2026-10-20): capture chains shared per closure site

`EcmaFunction`'s `outer_chain` and `per_iteration_chain` are compile-time
layouts of the enclosing certified bodies and of the certified loop heads open
at a creation site. They were `Vec`s on the `CreateFunction`/`CreateArrow`/
`FunctionDeclInit` steps, and every execution of such a step deep-cloned them
into the new closure; for a per-iteration site that is a clone of
`Vec<(Vec<AtomId>, usize)>`, one allocation for the outer vector plus one per
head, per closure.

The fields are now `CaptureChain<T> = Option<Rc<[T]>>`, shared between the step
and every closure created from it. The `Option` is load-bearing: an ordinary
closure's chains are empty, and the first attempt (an unconditional `Rc<[T]>`)
regressed the plain-closure probe by ~10% (e7 median 79.1 -> 92.3 ms over 8
pairs), an `Rc` clone/drop pair costs more than copying a zeroed 24-byte
`Vec`. With `None` the empty case is a null check. Each field went 24 -> 16
bytes, so the record is **216 -> 200 bytes**.

Interleaved same-binary A/B (medians):

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `e7` 300k closures | 79.1 ms | 75.8 ms (-4%) |
| `e5` + one call each | 116.7 ms | 114.1 ms (-2%) |
| `cap_uncaptured` | 247.9 ms | 214.4 ms (-13%) |
| `cap_let_drop` | 365.9 ms | 358.9 ms (-2%) |
| for-in head-let row, 10 pairs | 543.0 ms | 485.5 ms (-11%) |

Nine of the ten for-in pairs improved; that row's creation sites carry a
non-empty per-iteration chain, so it is where the deep clone was actually
paid. Full corpus (3 interleaved pairs, sum of the 77 jit rows): 2663.7 /
2643.2 / 3061.2 -> 2964.0 / 2551.2 / 2614.1 ms; the corpus cannot separate the
change.

This takes `e7` below the closure plan's 85 ms stop gate, so Stage D is now
eligible (see `.notes/closure-cost-plan.md`).

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace`; test262 built-ins
23,821, language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, 0 fail.

## NULL (2026-10-20): the function record in the GC arena

Stage D of the closure plan, in its smallest form: `Agent::ecma_functions` kept its key and stored `Gc<EcmaFunction>` instead of the 200-byte record inline. The insert phase fell 100 -> 56 ns in the instrumented phase profile (same run, same timer overhead), and calls got cheaper, but the record became a GC box rooted by the map, every minor promotes it, and the root set grows with the registry.

Interleaved same-binary A/B, medians (8 pairs unless noted):

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `e7` 300k closures | 77.5 ms | 83.7 ms (**+8%**) |
| `e5` + one call each | 116-120 ms | 100-104 ms (-13%) |
| `cap_uncaptured` | ~220 ms | ~226 ms |
| `cap_let_drop` | ~376 ms | ~380 ms |
| for-in head-let row (4 pairs) | 540-558 ms | 916-1393 ms (**+70% and rising**) |

The call-path win is real and is about footprint: `ordinary_call` already borrows the record and copies five small fields, so what the handle removes is dragging a 200-byte value through the cache on every lookup (and a 200-byte rehash copy per grow). The for-in row shows the cost: its per-iteration closures turn the arena over, and every record is rooted and promoted before it is reaped.

Conclusion: the registry's value has to stay out of the GC's root set. The plan's Stage D proper (the record reachable only from its function object, no traced map) is a different measurement; it needs the record type reachable from `crux` and was not attempted. Do not retry the map-holds-a-handle form.

## LANDED (2026-10-20): NamedEvaluation folded into function creation

`f = function () {}` created the closure and then ran a `SetFunctionName` step, which redefines the fresh object's `name` through the generic define path: a `get_own_property_key` on "name", a placeholder check, and a `define_property` with a full descriptor. Measured against the same closure compiled through a comma expression (no NamedEvaluation), that step costs **~410 ns**, taking the loop from 78 to 211 ms per 300k closures.

The name is a compile-time fact (the assignment/declaration target), so it now rides in `Step::CreateFunction`/`Step::CreateArrow` and `register_function`/`instantiate_arrow` define it once, through the batched property adoption the creation already pays for. `compile_expr` reports the fold (`named_folded`) and the callers skip their `SetFunctionName` step. The fold only applies when NamedEvaluation does: `begin_named_initializer` is only called when the target is an identifier reference, so `(fn) = function () {}` stays unnamed (test262 `expressions/assignment/fn-name-lhs-cover.js` pins that) and the value's own parens are transparent (`f = (function () {})` is named).

**This also fixed a conformance gap.** The certified body's declarator path (frame slot or capture-context slot) never emitted `SetFunctionName`, so inside a function body `var g = function () {}` left `g.name` empty; only the uncertified and global paths did the naming. test262 has no fixture for a `var` declarator's name, so the suite stayed at 100%. V8 answers "g"; Slag now does too.

Interleaved same-binary A/B, medians:

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `f = function () {}` (hoisted var) | 211.5 ms | 86.6 ms (**-59%**) |
| `cap_let_drop` (assignment capture) | 368.0 ms | 245.4 ms (**-33%**) |
| `var f = function () {}` in a body | 78.1 ms | 86.6 ms (+11%) |
| `e5` (declarator + one call) | 119.0 ms | 126.6 ms (+6%) |
| unnamed control (comma expression) | 78.5 ms | 78.4 ms (flat) |
| for-in head-let row | 521.3 ms | 525.5 ms (neutral) |

The declarator regression is the price of the name it previously skipped: ~27 ns per closure, against ~410 ns for the step form. Full corpus (3 pairs, sum of the 77 jit rows): 2442.9/2371.2/2388.9 -> 2529.3/2379.8/2371.3 ms, neutral.

The ~27 ns residual is not explained by this measurement: the unnamed control pays the same property adoption (with an empty name) and is flat, so what differs is the non-empty name value, its handle allocation and the atom-to-string conversion. Caching that value per declaration site is the obvious next probe.

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 fail); test262 built-ins 23,821, language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, 0 fail.

### Follow-up (2026-10-20): the inferred name is resolved once per site

The fold above still resolved the binding's text per closure, `AtomId -> JsString` goes through the memoised `crux::lookup` (a thread-local borrow, a scan, and a clone), and `default_binding_display_name` built `JsString::from_utf8("*default*")`, nine encoded units, before it could reject the common case. The creation steps now carry the resolved `JsString` (resolved once per site, when the step is emitted), and the export-default check compares the slice against a `[u16; 9]` constant.

Interleaved same-binary A/B, medians (8 pairs): the named declarator probe 83.8 -> 81.5 ms (-2.7%; every pair improved), `f = function () {}` -1.3% (4 pairs). The named-versus-unnamed gap is still ~4 ms per 300k (~13 ns/closure), and this change does not explain it: with the lookup and the literal gone, what remains is inside creation with a non-empty `name`, the handle and the batched adoption. Chasing it further has not paid; the fold's win is 410 -> ~13 ns of overhead.

## LANDED (2026-10-20): generator states are reaped

`Agent::generators` maps a generator object's id to its state and is a traced root, and nothing ever removed an entry. A generator that was called and abandoned therefore left its state, the instantiated environment, the saved execution context, the arguments, the closure function, reachable forever. The table grows with every generator the program has ever created, so every collection scans all of them, and a loop that creates and drops generators is O(n^2) in collections.

Probes (interleaved same-binary A/B; `function* one() { return 1; }`):

| shape (200k unless noted) | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| create only (`one();`) | 21,696.6 ms | 282.2 ms (**-98.7%**) |
| create + one `next()` | 17,806.6 ms | 458.9 ms (**-97.4%**) |
| 20k create + next | 190.6 ms | 46.4 ms (-76%) |
| 2k create + next | 7.18 ms | 4.67 ms (-35%) |

The quadratic term is gone: 2k / 20k / 200k now scale linearly at ~2.3 us per generator (1.4 us of it is creation: a full `FunctionDeclarationInstantiation` per generator call).

Both generator tables are now `RefCell<HashMap<...>>` so the collection (which only has `&self`) can prune the entries whose generator object the sweep reclaimed, using the same swept-address list as the Array-iterator table. Each state records its object's address, the object is deliberately NOT referenced from the state, which is what lets it die, and a state borrowed at collection time is a generator executing across it, kept. A completed generator also drops its saved context, environment and arguments, since its body can never resume.

`call_generator` no longer `.cloned()`s the whole `EcmaFunction` record per call; it copies the fields it reads under a scoped borrow, like `ordinary_call`.

Cost: the resume path pays ~4% for the map's `RefCell` lookup (`control/generator_loop` 58.7 -> 61.3 ms; the probe 55.9 -> 58.5). That row holds one long-lived generator, so this fix does not help it: its ~61 ms is the resume machinery itself (~300 ns per `next()`), which is a separate target.

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 fail); test262 built-ins 23,821, language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, 0 fail.

## LANDED (2026-10-20): generator method dispatch is cached per prototype generation

Every `g.next()` went through `generator::dispatch_call`, which resolved `%Generator.prototype%` from the realm's intrinsic table (a RefCell borrow plus a SipHash of the name) and read `next`/`return`/`throw` off the prototype (three `JsString` conversions and three property lookups) before comparing the callee. That is per-call work to discover constants.

The three method values are now cached on the Agent as `(realm, prototype, generation, next, return, throw)` and revalidated by the prototype's generation, which bumps on any own-property change, so replacing a method invalidates the cache exactly (probe: after `proto.next = function () { return { value: 99 } }`, a call answers 99). The cached values are traced, so a method removed from the prototype stays alive while the cache names it.

Isolating the pieces first: a `next()` on an *already completed* generator (dispatch + result object, no resume) cost 197 ns; the body machinery added ~87. After the cache:

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `control/generator_loop` row | 62.8 ms | 49.4 ms (**-21%**) |
| completed-generator `next()` (200k) | 39.4 ms (197 ns/call) | 30.3 ms (151 ns/call) |
| resuming `next()` (200k) | 56.8 ms (284 ns/call) | 44.6 ms (223 ns/call) |

The remaining 151 ns of the completed path is the `{value, done}` result object (arena allocation plus the cached-shape adoption) and the state-table lookup; the row's remaining ~247 ns per resume is the resume machinery (context save/restore around the Vm run).

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 fail); test262 built-ins 23,821, language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, 0 fail.

## NULL (2026-10-20): builtin call entry, the capture env lane, typed-array elements

Three row-targeted investigations, each measured, none landed.

**Builtin call entry** (paid by every native method call, including the generator row). A bare `b.valueOf()` on a boolean costs **32 ns/call** against **9.8 ns** for a JS method call (`o.m()`) in the same loop shape, so ~22 ns is the entry plus the primitive-receiver member read. `call_inner` still resolved a builtin through the thread-local `BUILTIN_HANDLERS` get and then the `builtin_dispatch_cache` get, while the VM already has a direct-mapped verdict cell (`Agent::builtin_call_lookup`). Routing `call_inner` through that cell measured flat: `b.valueOf()` 6.52 -> 6.54 ms/200k, `[1].values().next()` 16.5 -> 17.1, the JS method 2.02 -> 2.06; reverted. The maps are not the cost.

**The capture env lane** (`calls/closure_capture`, still 30.9x). A closure that reads a captured variable is called through `leaf_call_env` (11 ns in the in-frame lane vs 30.7 ns with one context read, measured before the generator work), where the extra cost is the frame fill, the `body_context`/`lexical_env` swap and its restore around the leaf entry. `new_body_context` already returns early for a body that captures nothing and `leaf_lookup` is a direct-mapped cell, so the remaining ~19 ns is the swap protocol itself, the caller's machine code would have to install the environment inline to remove it. Not attempted.

**Typed-array elements** (`arrays/typed_array`, 21.2x). 2M iterations of `ta[k & 65535] = k & 255; s += ta[k & 65535];` = 11.4 ns per store+read pair: store alone 7.5 ns, read alone 5.9 ns (constant index saves 2.4 ns of the pair). Both are already fully inline, `JIT_HELPER_STATS` shows only the GC safepoint over the whole loop, and `SLAG_OPT=0` is 23% slower, so the optimizing tier is engaged. The CLIF shows, per access, a float -> uint -> float exact-integer check (ToIndex), a bounds check, the loaded value's tag check, a detached-buffer check and a property-flag test: the general element path, not a typed-array specialisation. The fix is an inline typed-array gate that skips ToIndex's round trip and the value tag checks, JIT emission work, not a tweak.

## NULL (2026-10-20): the typed-array view cell, bounded before it was written

A per-site cache of a resolved view (`data`, `byte_offset`, `array_length`, `element type`, validated by object id plus the buffer's detached/resizable flags) was the planned fix for `arrays/typed_array`. It was bounded first, and the bound is too small to justify it.

The gates already exist and are inline: `emit_typed_array_read_into` (all element kinds) and `emit_typed_array_store_inline` (Uint8), both declining to the general element path through the same fallback block. For 2M iterations of `ta[k & 65535] = k & 255; s += ta[k & 65535];`: store 7.5 ns, read 5.9 ns, pair 11.9 ns.

The bound comes from comparing the typed path with the **dense** one, which has the simplest geometry the engine has (an `array_dense` handle, a base pointer and a length):

| probe (2M iterations) | Slag | node |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| typed store + read | 23.9 ms | 1.1 ms |
| dense store + read | 18.9 ms | 1.6 ms |
| trivial `s += k` loop | 5.3 ms (2.65 ns/iter) | 1.2 ms (0.6 ns/iter) |

So caching the typed view's geometry can recover at most the typed-versus-dense difference, ~5 ms, 21% of the row, and only because dense is 11.8x node too. The dominant costs are shared by both paths: the per-access element dispatch (~6 ns per store+read pair over the loop floor) and the loop itself (2.65 ns/iteration against node's 0.6). Not implemented: an emitter change with a use-after-free surface (the cached `data` must still be revalidated against a possible detach every access) for a fifth of one row, while the same cost is paid by every dense-array row in the corpus.

## Analysis (2026-10-20): why the dense element path is 11.8x node

The typed row is 21x node; the dense equivalent, same loop, a dense `Array` instead of a `Uint8Array`, is **11.8x** (18.9 ms against node's 1.6 for 2M store+read pairs). So the gap is in the element path itself, not in the typed-array geometry, which is what the view-cell idea would have addressed.

Budget (2M iterations):

| part | ms | per access |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| loop floor (`s += k`) | 5.3 | 2.65 ns/iteration (node: 1.2 ms, 0.6 ns) |
| store alone | 17.9 | 5.9 ns/store |
| read alone | 10.9 | 2.4 ns/read |
| both | 18.9 | 9.5 ns/pair (node: ~0.2) |

The inline store gate is seven blocks: object tag, `array_dense` load, ToIndex (float -> uint -> float), `elem_len` bounds, hole probe, prototype byte, write barrier, the write, and the generation bump. Ablations, each built and measured:

| ablation | store | combined loop |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| hole probe removed | 17.9 -> 16.4 ms | unchanged |
| generation bump removed | flat | flat (18.8) |
| barrier split, so a numeric store never loads the elements box's GC header | flat | flat |

No single check dominates, which is the answer: the cost is the **dependent-load chain** (object -> slots box -> its fields -> elements buffer) plus ~15 branchy checks, against V8's map check and a store. The structural lever would be folding `elem_ptr`/`elem_len` into the object to cut one dependent load, but that grows every `JsObject`, and the arena's 16-byte size classes make it a whole-layout change (`slag-object-layout`). Not attempted.

## Analysis (2026-10-20): the counter loop, one non-numeric operand disables slot promotion

A bare `for (var k = 0; k < 2000000; k++) s += k` runs in 1.44 ms (0.72 ns/iteration, node-class: 1.2 ms), and its IR keeps both slots in registers, `b1(v18:f64, v22:int)` with `IntAdd` and no frame traffic. Add *anything else* to the function, even an unused `new Uint8Array(65536)` **after** the loop, and the same loop takes 5.2 ms (2.5 ns/iteration) with a `FrameLoad`/`FrameStore` per access. `SLAG_OPT=0` recovers 1.5 ms, so the optimizing tier is what loses it.

The gate is `pass::slots_unobserved`: promotion requires that no instruction other than `FrameLoad`/`FrameStore` touches `Heap::Slots`, and that no speculation guard exists. Two independent causes disqualify real bodies:

1. any op carrying the conservative world-effect set, `Call`, `Construct`, `ConstructArgs`, `MemberCellLoad`, …, i.e. any call anywhere in the body;
2. `narrow` inserts `GuardType` for a non-numeric operand (in the probe, `s + ta.length`), and a guard deopts: `emit_guard` mirrors the operand stack into the working region and resumes the interpreter at that step, which reads the frame.

Relaxing (1) was implemented and measured: no change, because (2) still disqualifies the body. Relaxing (1) is sound, a lifted body cannot expose its frame to a call (no `arguments` object: `Step::CreateArguments` has no lowering, so such a body never lifts; no direct `eval`: every call arm matches `direct_eval: false`), but it is only a prerequisite.

The fix is **Cut B** from `.notes/opt-per-op-overhead.md` §8, still unimplemented: `mem2reg` must publish the promoted slots, and the guard pass must store each live promoted slot back to its frame before the deopt branch (the flush splits the promoted region and the continuation reloads from the slot). Until then, every loop in a function that does anything non-numeric runs with a frame round trip per slot access, 3.5x on the same loop, and the floor under the whole `opcost` family.

## LANDED (2026-10-20): Cut B, frame slots stay promoted across guards

`pass::slots_unobserved` refused promotion to any body holding a guard or any
world-effect op, so a loop in a function that did anything non-numeric kept a
`FrameLoad`/`FrameStore` per slot access (the counter-loop analysis above).
Cut B removes both refusals and pays for them where they matter:

- `guard::run` now runs **before** `mem2reg`, so promotion sees every `GuardType`
  (from `narrow` and from `guard`) rather than only the ones that survive after it.
- The gate rejects only the fused declaration/loop-binding ops
  (`FunctionDecl`, `ForOfBindLocal`, `ForOfNextBindLocal`), which write a slot the
  pass cannot name. Calls and member accesses carry `Heap::Slots` conservatively
  but cannot observe the frame: a lifted body builds no `arguments` object and
  runs no direct `eval`.
- `mem2reg::insert_flushes` stores each promoted slot's reaching value back to the
  frame before every `Check`/`GuardType`/`GuardCallee`, because a failing guard
  resumes the interpreter at the next step and later steps read the frame.

Probe (`scratch/ab/l5`, 2M iterations of `s += k` plus a trailing
`new Uint8Array`, 5 interleaved same-binary pairs): **5.06 -> 1.48 ms**
(2.53 -> 0.74 ns/iteration), the bare-loop floor, i.e. the whole frame round
trip is gone.

Corpus (77 workloads, 3 interleaved same-binary pairs, idle host):
`mean-jitGap` 11.73 -> 11.45 (-2.4%), `mean-jlGap` 3.80 -> 3.92 (flat; the
jitless control), parity 0 mismatches. Concentrated rather than broad:
`arrays/index_loop` 18.4 -> 13.4 ms (-27%, the three before values 19.2/18.6/17.5
against 13.9/13.1/13.2), `language/expressions/template-literal/evaluation-order`
303.6 -> 295.5, and most rows flat. Runs taken while the host was at ~96% load
put the same delta at -3.7% and made individual families swing both ways; report
only interleaved pairs on an idle machine.

The flush is load-bearing. With `insert_flushes` disabled the probe returns
`"undefinedA1"` for `s + x + G` where `s` was promoted and `x` is a getter's
string, because the resumed interpreter reads the slot's initial `undefined`.
`opt_tier_flushes_a_promoted_slot_before_a_deopt` (crates/jit/src/lib.rs) is that
shape; it fails on the flush-disabled build and passes on the real one.

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 fail);
test262 built-ins 23,821, language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, 0 fail.

## LANDED (2026-10-20): a primitive string's member read is cell-served

A member read on a *primitive string* had no inline lane: `emit_member_cell_probe` (`compiler.rs`) and the opt tier's `MemberCellLoad`/`MemberGuard` both require `TAG_OBJECT`, so every `s.charCodeAt` / `s.slice` read fell to `get_member_name`, which reaches `get_primitive_member` → `current_realm()` → `intrinsics.string_prototype()` → `primitive_proto_data_get`. Measured on 1M iterations, a bare loop costs 0.54 ms and the same loop reading `s.charCodeAt` costs 32.1 ms: **31.6 ns per read**, of which the call adds only 6.3 ns. `.length` is cheaper (7.5 ns) because the helper has its own shortcut for it.

The fix is a string lane in both lowerers that consumes the same shared member-value cell the helper already populates. `JitCallContext::string_prototype_bits` snapshots the realm's `%String.prototype%`; the lane gates on `is_string(receiver)` (boxed String objects stay on the object path), loads the prototype's live `id` and `generation`, and serves `cell[(id ^ atom) & (MEMBERS-1)]` when id, name and generation match. The helper populates that cell on the first (cold) read via `primitive_proto_data_get`, and any mutation of the prototype bumps its generation, which invalidates the entry. `length` is excluded: it is an own virtual property of the string (never a prototype one), and the existing shortcut already covers it, routing it through the lane cost 2.2 ns/iteration before the exclusion.

The lane must hang off the object test, not precede it. Placing it first (`is_string` + the prototype load + a branch before `is_plain_object`) made plain-object reads pay it too: `o.d = i; s += o.d` went 42.1 -> 45.6 ms and `o.x += 1; s += o.x` 52.9 -> 56.2 ms over 4M iterations, a ~0.9 ns/iteration tax on every property access in the corpus. Branching `is_plain_object ? object-probe : string-lane` restores the object path to exactly the probe it had (measured back to 43.4/53.7).

`%String.prototype%` is the *intrinsic* (the value `ToObject` uses), not the reassignable `String.prototype` property, which is why a per-run snapshot is sound. Verified against node and the interpreter: `String.prototype = {}` leaves `"abc".foo` undefined in all three.

| row | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `strings/char_ops` (300k `charCodeAt`) | 11.20 ms | **3.33 ms** (-70%) |
| `opcost/string_charat` | 4.43 ms | **1.67 ms** (-62%) |
| `strings/search_slice` | 16.30 ms | **10.87 ms** (-33%) |
| `strings/split_join` | 65.87 ms | 63.13 ms (-4%) |
| `strings/coercion_concat` | 63.53 ms | 61.60 ms (-3%) |
| `opcost/prim_prop` (`.length`) | 1.73 ms | 1.73 ms (flat, by design) |

Families (5-pair interleaved same-binary A/B): `strings` mean-jitGap 12.27 -> 9.50 (-23%), the object rows flat. A subset corpus of the eleven touched and control rows sums 266.79 -> 251.43 ms (median of 7 interleaved pairs; five pairs land in 244.8-251.5 against a tight 264.0-273.3 before, the other two are host-load spikes). The full-corpus mean is only -3.3% on the day (median of 8 pairs, 11.45 -> 11.07): Windows Defender was scanning at 200% CPU throughout, and `mean-jlGap`, which this change cannot touch, moved 3.87 -> 4.17, so the full-corpus figure is not resolved here. The row and subset numbers are. Isolated probes: the read alone 32.1 -> 9.3 ms/1M, read+call 38.4 -> 11.8 ms/1M; `GetMemberName` helper calls in the read probe fall from 7,001,792 to 3,074 (one per repetition, from the cold path).

`opt_tier_string_member_read_follows_the_prototype` covers the invalidation: it warms the cell, reassigns `String.prototype.charCodeAt`, calls through it, restores it, and calls again. With the generation comparison disabled the test answers 101 where 111 belongs (the stale cell serves the original function).

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 fail); test262 built-ins 23,821, language 23,726, annexB 1,086, intl402 3,365, 51,998 pass / 0 fail.

## NULL (2026-10-21): the property store's cost is not in its lowering

`objects/warm_store` and `objects/compound_assign` are the largest remaining absolute gaps (35-48 ms against node's 2.3), so I decomposed them. 4M iterations, release, same machine:

| shape | slag | node |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `for (i) s = (s + i) \| 0` (bare) | 2.06 ms | 0.86 |
| `for (i) t = t + i` (f64 accumulator) | 2.92 ms | 2.30 |
| `for (i) n += o.d` (one read) | 9.79 ms | 0.86 |
| `for (i) o.d = i` (one store) | 25.0 ms | 0.92 |
| `for (i) o.d = 1` (constant store) | 23.4 ms | 0.92 |
| `for (i) o.d = i; o.e = i` (two stores) | 51.8 ms |, |
| `for (i) a[0] = i` (dense element store) | 13.5 ms | 0.97 |

**Correction to the earlier read figure.** A property read used in arithmetic costs ~1.9 ns, not the 6.3 ns quoted in the string-cell note: that probe's `| 0` was the cost, not the read (§ below). `s = (s + o.d) | 0` is 26.3 ms against `n += o.d`'s 9.79 in the *same* register-body lane.

**The store is invariant to its own lowering.** Four ablations, each built and run:

- Replacing the entire `emit_member_store` body with `is_plain_object` + one raw `store` to `in_fields` (no map probe, no deferred gate, no barrier, no cell refresh): **no change** (23.4-26.4 ms across runs).
- Removing the update arm's four-store value-cell refresh: no change.
- Removing the read's `MemberGuard` entirely (unsound, as a ceiling): no change (27.5 vs 27.7 ms).
- Two stores per iteration cost exactly twice one store (51.8 vs 25.0), so the cost is per store and lives in the loop, not in the gate.

A store whose emitted code is *ten instructions* and a store whose emitted code is *sixty* cost the same, so no amount of restructuring inside `emit_member_store` pays. The remaining hypotheses are outside the lowering: a Cranelift regalloc spill around the op (the disassembly reloads a spilled value before every back edge) or a micro-architectural effect on the store. Confirming either needs a profiler this host does not have, or a per-shape specialized code path that bakes the field offset in after a map check (V8's shape), a recompilation design, not a patch.

**Not landed (neutral):** threading the shape cell validated by `emit_shape_store_probe` into the update arm as block parameters, removing the duplicate map -> map_id -> cell derivation (~11 instructions, 3 dependent loads). The subset corpus summed 240.0 (HEAD) vs 242.1 ms (dedup), five interleaved pairs, unresolved. Reverted; the instruction count is not the bottleneck.

## LANDS (2026-10-21): the register lane's int op drops `canon` and `sextend`

`(s + o.d) | 0` costs 27.4 ms over 4M iterations against `n += o.d`'s 9.8, the bit op alone is ~4.1 ns. Its chain in the register lane's `emit_int_binary` was `fabs/fcmp/fcvt_to_sint_sat` -> `ireduce` -> the i32 op -> `sextend` -> `fcvt_from_sint` -> `bitcast` -> `canon`, i.e. two float<->int conversions plus a three-instruction canonicalization on the result.

Both tail pieces were redundant, and the optimizing tier's `call_int_binary` already says so in a comment: an integer-valued f64 in `[-2^31, 2^32)` can never carry the NaN-box tag prefix, so `canon` is the identity, and `fcvt_from_sint` takes the i32 directly, so the `sextend` is dead. Removed both; the register lane now emits what the opt tier always did.

Probes (4M iterations, 3 interleaved same-binary pairs): `s = (s + o.d) | 0` 27.4 -> **25.7 ms** (-6.5%, the three pairs disjoint: 27.1/27.3/27.8 vs 25.5/25.6/25.8) and `o.x += 1; s += o.x` 54.4 -> **52.8 ms** (-3.0%).

The corpus does not resolve it: the median `mean-jitGap` moves 10.75 -> 10.70 over three pairs, and families this change cannot touch moved by more than that (`calls` 9.99 -> 10.79, `control` 13.73 -> 14.50) on a host that varied ~10% during the run. Reported as an isolated win only.

**What is left of the 4.1 ns.** The remaining chain is the f64 -> i64 -> i32 -> i64 -> f64 round trip, about 11 cycles: `fcvt_to_sint_sat` and `fcvt_from_sint` are 4 cycles each and nothing on the path is redundant. Removing it needs the operand to already live in an i32 register, the int-plan (`BinStoreInt` / `IntRhs`), which currently fuses `s = (s + k) | 0` only when the RHS is an immediate, the counter, or an accumulator already proven `Int`. A member read is none of those, so `(s + o.d) | 0` cannot take the plan. Extending the plan to accept a guarded member read is the next cut, and it is a plan change rather than a lowering change. (`>>>` still does its `uextend` before `fcvt_from_uint`; same one-instruction removal, not measured.)

## LANDED (2026-10-21): the accessor scan stops allocating a String per chain link

Chasing the accessor cost turned up a per-read allocation on the hottest path in the engine. `ensure_deferred_namespace_evaluation_key` (called from `find_ecma_accessor` for **every prototype-chain link** of **every non-own-data member read**, and from `put_value`) tested the key before the cheap object-kind reject:

```rust
if crux::lookup(*id).to_string_lossy() == "then" { return Ok(()); }   // allocates
```

`to_string_lossy()` builds a UTF-8 `String` (and converts the whole key) for a comparison that only a *deferred module namespace* can care about. Reordering the existing kind test (`deferred_namespace_module(agent, obj).is_none()`) in front of the key test removes it from every ordinary read.

Probes (3 interleaved same-binary pairs, disjoint):

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `o.x` on a getter (1M, getter declared outside the loop) | 219.4 ms | **177.8 ms** (-18.5%) |
| `o.nope`, a property that does not exist (100k) | 18.2 ms | **10.8 ms** (-43%) |
| `o.a`, an own data property (control) | 5.55 ms | 5.53 ms (flat) |

The corpus moves in the same direction but does not resolve it on its own: the overall `mean-jitGap` is 10.88 -> 10.78 over three pairs, while **eight of the nine families improved** (language 7.60 -> 6.78, calls 10.58 -> 10.30, control 14.91 -> 14.68, arrays 10.08 -> 9.93, objects 9.33 -> 9.13, builtins 7.36 -> 7.23, strings 9.27 -> 9.10, globals 2.27 -> 2.17; opcost flat). A change that touches every non-data member read should move every family, which is what makes the family table the stronger evidence here than the corpus mean.

### Measured along the way (unchanged code, for the next reader)

A member read costs, over 1M iterations: **5.6 ns** for an own data property, **88 ns** for an accessor (after this fix; 110 before), and **105 ns** for a property that does not exist (after; 184 before). The accessor is 16x a data read because the member cell caches data properties only, a getter has to run, and the read re-enters `get_member_name` → `get_property` → `find_ecma_accessor` → `function::call` every time. A compiled method call with the same body (`o.m()` where `m` reads `this.a`) is 10.8 ns, so roughly 80 ns of the accessor cost is the helper chain rather than the getter itself. `RegExp.prototype.test` on `/[a-z]+/` against an 8-unit string is 396 ns and `exec` is 994 ns; `re.source` (a native accessor) 328 ns.

Two probe artifacts worth remembering: defining the getter *inside* the hot function changes what compiles and gave a bogus 683 ns figure, and `re.exec`'s 994 ns includes building the result array (`test` avoids it).

## LANDED (2026-10-21): own accessors skip the chain walk, and `test` stops cloning the state

Two small cuts out of the accessor/regexp investigation.

**Own accessors.** `get_property`'s plain-object fast path looked the property up, accepted only a `Data` kind, and dropped the accessor case on the floor, so `find_ecma_accessor` looked the *same* property up again and then walked the chain. An own accessor is authoritative (nothing on the chain can shadow it), so the getter now dispatches straight from the descriptor the fast path already found.

**`test`'s receiver.** `regexp_receiver` clones the whole `RegExpState` per call, the source `JsString` and a heap `String` of flag text, because the clone is what releases the `Agent` borrow. `test` builds no result array, so it needs only the compiled `Rc<Regex>` and the `Copy` flags: `regexp_match_parts` returns exactly those, and `regexp_builtin_match` takes them instead of the state. `exec` still takes the full state (its result array reads `source`).

Medians of seven interleaved same-binary pairs:

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `o.x` own accessor (1M) | 167.1 ms | **155.4 ms** (-7.1%) |
| `re.test` on `/[a-z]+/` (100k) | 37.91 ms | 37.34 ms (-1.5%) |
| `re.test` on `/a/` (100k) | 16.72 ms | 16.19 ms (-3.2%) |
| `re.test` with three capture groups (100k) | 90.75 ms | 89.82 ms (-1.0%) |
| own data property (control) | 5.53 ms | 5.60 ms (flat) |
| missing property (control) | 10.26 ms | 10.52 ms (flat) |

The regexp win is small because a flagless regex's `flags_text` is the empty `String`, and cloning an empty `String` does not allocate, the clone was cheap for exactly the shape the corpus uses. It still removes the clone for flagged regexes.

Corpus: unresolved, 11.04/10.63/10.73 -> 10.93/10.64/11.08 mean-jitGap, families mixed on a host varying ~10%. Only the probe medians are quoted.

**What is still open, and is the largest thing found this session.** An own accessor read is 155 ns against **10.8 ns** for a compiled method call with the same body (`o.m()` where `m` reads `this.a`). A getter that returns a *constant* costs the same as one that reads `this.a` (156 vs 154 ns), so the whole gap is the invocation path, not the body.

An earlier draft of this note blamed a missing JIT entry; that was wrong. `ordinary_call` holds no `agent.jit_hook` reference, but it calls `run_compiled_body`, which calls `crate::jit::run_jit_body`, machine code *is* entered. The gap is that a Rust-initiated call builds the per-call scaffolding: `take_vm` from the pool, `setup_certified_frame`, a ~40-field `JitCallContext` plus a `lookup_info` in `run_jit_body`, then `return_vm`'s full reset. A compiled call site instead reuses the caller's live context and carves the callee's frame inside the caller's own working buffer. See `.notes/rust-initiated-call-plan.md`.

## LANDED (2026-10-21): accessors and setters take the leaf lane

`get_property`/`put_value` dispatched an accessor through `crate::function::call`, which goes `call_inner` -> `ordinary_call` -> `run_compiled_body` and builds the whole per-call scaffolding. `call_callback` (what every builtin uses for a user callback) tries `builtins::function::try_leaf_call` first, which runs a leaf body through the pooled-Vm `do_call_fast` path, and only then falls back to the same `call`. The accessor sites used the plain `call`, so the cheap lane was never tried.

All seven sites in `context.rs` (three getter dispatches, two setter dispatches, the reference-get and reference-put getter/setter) now use `call_callback`. A non-leaf accessor falls back to exactly the same `call` as before.

Probes (3 interleaved same-binary pairs, disjoint):

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| getter returning a constant (1M) | 146.2 ms | **98.3 ms** (-31%) |
| getter reading `this.a` (1M) | 153.2 ms | **112.0 ms** (-27%) |
| own data property (control) | 5.55 ms | 5.42 ms (flat) |

Corpus (3 interleaved pairs): median `mean-jitGap` 10.97 -> 10.72 (-2.3%), with the families that read accessors most moving furthest, builtins 8.36 -> **7.43** (-11%), strings 10.18 -> **9.28** (-8.9%), language 8.02 -> **7.29** (-9%), calls 10.90 -> 10.34 (-5%). `mean-jlGap` fell too (3.85 -> 3.80), which is expected: the interpreter's accessor dispatch went through the same `call`.

An own accessor read is now 110 ns against 9.2 ns for a compiled method call with the same body. The remaining cost is `try_leaf_call`'s own `take_vm` + `do_call_fast` + `return_vm`, and the non-leaf fallback. The reusable-context slice in `.notes/rust-initiated-call-plan.md` still applies to that remainder.

## LANDED (2026-10-21): a builtin's callback loop reuses one leaf Vm

Every caller-supplied callback a builtin dispatches went through `function::call_callback` -> `builtins::function::try_leaf_call`, which takes a pooled `Vm` (`Agent::take_vm`), runs the leaf, and returns it (`Agent::return_vm`, whose contract is a full `Vm::reset`, ~45 field stores and ~25 stack clears, because the pooled Vm must not trace the finished run's stale state). A `forEach` over four elements therefore paid four take/reset pairs where one Vm could serve the whole loop.

`builtins::function::CallbackVm` holds a Vm across the loop: `with(agent, |agent, leaf| ...)` creates the guard, `leaf.call(agent, callee, this, args)` reuses the Vm, and the Vm returns to the pool once, after the body (on the error path too). Reuse needs only `Vm::rebind` between calls because a successful leaf run already restores every persistent field it touched, `run_inline_leaf` truncates the value stack to the call site and `run_leaf_regs`/`run_leaf_body` restore `leaf_frame_base`/`offset`, `body_context`, `lexical_env`, and (on the step path) `ip`, `strict`, `chain_short`, `loop_counter`, the array-index stack and `call_args`. A Vm taken from the pool is otherwise clean, and the register lane only writes `acc`, `loop_num` and `loop_counter`, none of which a caller reads. On an error the Vm goes back through `return_vm`'s full reset, since an unwind may leave the stack past the call site.

The same change also stops re-deriving the leaf entry. `try_leaf_call` resolved the entry and then called `do_call_fast`, which re-ran the whole call-site gate and did a *second* `leaf_lookup`. `Vm::run_leaf_entry` is `fast_call_core`'s leaf arm without that: the caller's entry goes straight to `try_jit_leaf` / `run_inline_leaf` (keeping `do_call_fast`'s termination check).

Converted: `builtins/array.rs` (`forEach`, `map`, `filter`, `some`, `every`, the `find`/`findLast` pair, `reduce`/`reduceRight`), `builtins/typed_array.rs` (the same set), `builtins/keyed.rs` (`Map`/`Set.prototype.forEach`), `builtins/iterator.rs` (`Iterator.prototype`'s eager `every`/`some`/`find`/`forEach`/`reduce`, including `call_predicate`). `Iterator.prototype.filter`'s per-`next()` predicate and `flatMap`'s recursion stay on `call_callback`, one call per invocation, nothing to hoist.

Interleaved, alternating-order A/B (10 rounds, median; order swaps every round, results written per binary):

| row | base | new | delta |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `opcost/array_for_each.js` | 28.66 ms | 25.39 ms | **-11.4%** |
| `opcost/map_for_each.js` | 26.37 | 23.43 | **-11.1%** |
| `opcost/typed_array_for_each.js` | 29.63 | 27.48 | **-7.3%** |
| `opcost/array_for_each_js.js` (control) | 3.60 | 3.50 | -2.6% |
| `arrays/hof_methods.js` (6 rounds) | 24.71 | 22.50 | **-8.9%** |

Probes on `scratch/ab/re2` (8 rounds, alternating, median): `[1,2,3,4].forEach(cb)` 28.36 -> **25.85 ms** (-8.8%), `map(cb)` 43.56 -> **39.68** (-8.9%), `[1].forEach(cb)` 10.94 -> 10.87 (-0.6%), `forEach(Math.abs)` 40.60 -> 41.21 (+1.5%). The one-element row and the native-callback row are flat, which is exactly the shape of the change: there is one callback per builtin invocation to amortise, and a non-leaf callee never enters the lane.

**Measurement trap, twice.** A first pass ran the base binary then the new one in every round and reported -7..-11% on *every* converted row, but also on rows the change cannot touch, and the alternating-order run kept only the converted rows. A second attempt wrote both binaries' output into the same pair of files, so each file held half of each binary and every delta collapsed to ~0. The design that is evidence: one output file per *binary*, order swapped every round, median over >=6 rounds. A fixed order is not an A/B on this host.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 failed); the four sweeps at `--batch 32 --timeout 15 --recheck-timeout 15`, `built-ins` 23,821, `language` 23,726, `annexB` 1,086, `intl402` 3,365, all 100% (51,998); corpus parity 0 mismatches; the four lane probes under `--gc-stress --gc-verify --nursery-stress` exit 0.

What is left in this lane: a native callback (`forEach(Math.abs)`) is still ~400 ns per builtin invocation and never enters the leaf lane at all (the `FunctionKind::EcmaScript` gate), and a leaf callback is still ~2x a compiled call site because the JIT leaf entry builds a fresh call context per invocation, the reusable-context slice in `.notes/rust-initiated-call-plan.md`.

## LANDED (2026-10-21): `RegExp.prototype.test` runs the engine capture-free

`test` calls the engine's match half and keeps only `.is_some()`, but the matcher always allocated the capture buffer: `Matcher::new` -> `Caps::new(groups)` is a `Vec` per call, its undo trail grows on every capture a repeat owns, and `search` moves that `Vec` out as the `Match` the caller then drops. A counting allocator in a scratch crate priced it: `/a/` on `"a"` was 2 allocations (376 bytes) and 84 ns per `search_at`, `/(a)(b)(c)/` 4 allocations and 271 ns, while the JS-level `re.test("a")` measured 158 ns, so roughly half of `test` was engine time and half the builtin's own protocol.

A pattern with no backreferences never *reads* a capture (that is the same `backref_free` condition the repeat memo already relies on), so the boolean lane runs with `Caps::disabled()`: `set`, `reset` and `clear_owned` become no-ops and the trail stays empty. `engine::exec_end`/`search_end` are the two entry points, `Regex::match_end_at`/`search_end_at` expose them, and the runtime's `regexp_exec_protocol` now owns the `lastIndex` protocol for both `test` and `exec`, the read, the sticky attempt, the leftmost search and the write, so the two callers cannot drift apart (the read is unconditional and precedes the global/sticky check; `failure-lastindex-access.js` pins it). `search`'s position loop moved into a shared `search_loop` for the same reason.

The first cut of this forgot `clear_owned`, which indexes `caps.values` to clear a repeated atom's captures, with no backreferences the buffer is still *written*, and `/(a)+/.test("aaa")` panicked on the empty `Vec`. `boolean_lane_agrees_with_the_capture_lane` now cross-checks `search_end_at`/`match_end_at` against `search_at`/`exec_at` at every start position for repeated, nested, named and lookaround captures, backreferences, alternation and the `i`/`u`/`s`/`m`/`iu` flags.

Engine cost with the counting allocator (same scratch crate): `/a/` **84 -> 64 ns** and 2 -> 1 allocations, `/(a)(b)(c)/` **271 -> 178** and 4 -> 1, `/(a)+/` 306 -> 256, `[a-z]+/` on 8 chars 329 -> 310 (its cost is the per-choice `Rc<[Task]>` snapshot, not the capture buffer).

JS A/B on `scratch/ab/re3` + `scratch/ab/re`, 8 interleaved rounds with the order swapped every round, medians:

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `/a/.test("a")` (100k) | 16.11 ms | **13.74 ms** (-14.7%) |
| `/a/.test("b")` (no match) | 15.27 | **13.14** (-14.0%) |
| `/a/y.test("a")` (sticky) | 19.33 | **16.39** (-15.2%) |
| `r_a.js` (`/a/`, the size probe) | 16.28 | **13.68** (-16.0%) |
| `/zzz/.test(8 chars)` | 15.60 | **13.40** (-14.1%) |
| `/(a)(b)(c)/.test("abc")` | 88.88 | **83.59** (-6.0%) |
| `/[a-z]+/.test(8 chars)` | 36.22 | **34.55** (-4.6%) |
| `re.exec` (unchanged lane) | 95.82 | 97.35 (+1.6%) |
| `re.lastIndex`, `re.source`, plain call, bare loop |, | flat |

**Measurement trap, third time this session.** The first A/B of this change reported 0.0% and sent me looking for a phantom (a marker build proved the builtin was reached and the change was worth -13%). The script wrote each binary's output by *position* (`base`/`new` files) instead of by binary, so with the order swapped every round each file held half of each binary. Output files must be named after the binary; the round order is what alternates.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 failed; `regexp` 39); sweeps `built-ins` 23,821 + `language` 23,726 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0.

Left in the matcher: `tasks` is still a `Vec` allocated per call and every choice point snapshots the forward path into a fresh `Rc<[Task]>`, which is why a repeat-heavy pattern still allocates 6 times and runs at ~35 ns per character. Eliminating that needs the task stack to be reusable across calls (it borrows the program, so a caller-owned scratch cannot name its lifetime without restructuring `Task` around indices).

## LANDED (2026-10-21): a native callback runs its own closure, not the general call

`forEach(Math.abs)` was 400-500 ns per builtin invocation, 1.5x a *JS* callback through the same lane, and the reason was not the callback machinery but `call_inner`: for a crux-native builtin it looks the id up in the thread-local handler registry (`builtin_handler`) and then in the agent's `builtin_dispatch_cache`, both `HashMap`s, before finally running `native(&this, args)`; `function::call` adds the `with_agent` window around all of it. A per-element callback paid that per element.

`builtins::function::try_builtin_call` asks the agent's direct-mapped `builtin_call_lookup` cell instead, the same verdict `fast_call_core` already uses, and runs the registered `Handler` or the function's own crux-native closure. `Other` (an unregistered or not-yet-memoized dispatch, which the general path resolves and memoizes) and a multi-realm run both fall back to `call`, and a termination request is still observed before dispatch, as in `call_inner`. Re-entrancy needs no special case: a host callback marked re-entrant may run JS, and the nested run takes its own Vm through `call_inner`, which is what the general path does for it today.

Probe order matters. The lane is tried *after* the leaf probe: with the native probe first, every JS callback paid an extra `FunctionKind` load on the callee's heap record and the JS rows moved +2..+9% while the control moved +3.5%. Leaf-first leaves the JS callback path exactly as it was and costs a native callee one failed `EcmaScript` gate.

12 interleaved rounds, order swapped each round, medians:

| row | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `[1].forEach(Math.abs)` (100k) | 14.77 ms | **7.10 ms** (-52.0%) |
| `[1,2,3,4].forEach(Math.abs)` | 50.83 | **11.92** (-76.6%) |
| `[1,2,3,4].map(Math.abs)` | 52.64 | **23.86** (-54.7%) |
| `[1,2,3,4].forEach(cb)` (JS callback, control) | 26.11 | 26.30 (+0.7%) |
| `Map.prototype.forEach` | 23.37 | 24.56 (+5.1% median, +1.2% min; the bare-loop control moved +4.4%) |
| typed-array `forEach` (JS callback) | 29.77 | 28.98 (-2.7%) |

That is ~127 ns -> ~30 ns per native callback. `.call`/`.apply` with a native target take the same lane (`Math.max.apply(null, xs)`).

Correctness probe (`scratch/ab/natcheck.js`, exits 0 in jit, jitless and under `--gc-stress --gc-verify --nursery-stress`): a native callback that coerces runs `valueOf`; a coercion that throws propagates out of the builtin; arguments are forwarded unchanged (`["10","10","10"].map(parseInt)` gives `[10, NaN, 2]`); `reduce(Math.max)` is `NaN` because reduce passes the index and the array too; `filter(Boolean)`, `some(Number.isFinite)`, `Map`/`Set` forEach, `parseInt.call`, `"abc".charCodeAt.call`, `Array.from(arr, Math.sqrt)`.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 failed); sweeps `built-ins` 23,821 + `language` 23,726 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0.

## LANDED (2026-10-21): the current-agent slot is a `Cell` (and two nulls around the callback lanes)

`crux::function::with_agent` records the live agent for the duration of a call, and its already-current path, the one every nested call takes, was a `RefCell` borrow plus a compare. A scratch crate timing `with_agent(p, || black_box(1))` against a bare closure over 20M iterations: **2.88 -> 2.11 ns per call** after `CURRENT_AGENT` became a `Cell<*mut ()>` (bare closure: 0.38 ns). The payload is `Copy` and nothing ever holds a borrow across the read, so `get`/`replace` are the whole surface.

End to end that is at the noise floor (12 interleaved rounds: `[1,2,3,4].forEach(Math.abs)` 12.20 -> 11.92 ms, the JS-callback rows flat, control -0.1%), which is what 0.8 ns per callback predicts. The isolated number is the evidence; the change is strictly less work on a path every Rust-initiated call walks.

**The window cannot be dropped**, only made cheaper. It is what makes a native callback's object coercion work: `to_number` on a heap value consults `current_agent()` and re-enters through `ecma_call`, and a callback lane cannot prove a window is already open (the same lane is reachable from `context.rs`'s accessor dispatch, which is not always under a VM run).

**NULL: deciding the callback lane once is slower for JS callbacks.** Replacing the leaf-then-native probes with one `callback_lane(callee)` -> `Leaf | Builtin | General` decision should have removed a gate from both lanes. Measured: `array_for_each` **+4.4% and +5.5%** in two runs, `typed_array_for_each` **+5.5% and +7.3%**, with the bare-loop control at **-0.7% and +0.2%**, while `nat4_forEach` improved 10%. Marking the lane decision `#[inline]` did not recover it. The extra call/enum return costs the leaf path more than the removed gate saves. Reverted; the leaf probe stays first and a native callee pays one failed `EcmaScript` gate.

**NULL: `Map.prototype.forEach`'s iteration body is not slow.** The `+5..9%` medians seen earlier in the session were drift, with the same JS callback and four entries it measures 24.4 ms/100k against `Array.prototype.forEach`'s 26.2, and its min moved +1.2%. The per-entry `HashMap` lookup, `borrow()` and `entries.get(i).cloned()` together cost less than one array element read plus its callback, so there is nothing to fix there.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 failed); sweeps `built-ins` 23,821 + `language` 23,726 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0; the native-callback correctness probe exits 0 under `--gc-stress --gc-verify --nursery-stress`.

## LANDED (2026-10-21): `generator.next()` dispatches in place

`control/generator_loop.js` was the corpus's worst *relative* gap (23.4x node) and 200k `g.next()` calls cost ~200 ns each. The generator machinery itself was not the problem: an *exhausted* generator, where `next()` only builds `{value: undefined, done: true}`, cost almost as much (~170 ns), so the money was in the call dispatch.

`%Generator.prototype%.{next,return,throw}` were not in any `handler_for` table, so a generator method call fell all the way through `fast_call_core`: the registered-handler probe missed, `is_eval_function` ran (an intrinsics hash of `"%eval%"` per call), and the call *withdrew* its frame (`PendingCall::Function`); the driver then re-dispatched through `call_inner` -> `builtin_handler` (another hash) -> `builtin_dispatch_cache` (a third) -> `builtin_dispatch_at` -> `generator::dispatch_call`'s identity match -> the handler.

`generator::handler_for` and `async_generator::handler_for` now register those six functions (the three generator methods and their async-generator twins). That is exactly what `dispatch_call` resolved, reached one layer earlier: `fast_call_core`'s handler arm runs it in place, with no frame withdrawal, no eval-identity hash and no chain walk. Nothing changes for a shadowed `next` (the registry is keyed by the function's own id) or for a `.call`/`Reflect.apply` on the intrinsic (those still resolve through the chain).

12 interleaved rounds, order swapped each round, medians:

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `g.next().value` in a compiled loop (200k) | 40.57 ms | **27.49 ms** (-32.2%) |
| `g.next()` without reading `.value` | 45.00 | **26.86** (-40.3%) |
| `next()` on an exhausted generator | 33.85 | **16.17** (-52.2%) |
| `yield` of a constant | 40.83 | **27.14** (-33.5%) |
| corpus `control/generator_loop.js` | 44.65 | **30.88** (-30.8%) |
| plain compiled call / object-literal controls | 1.13 / 0.46 | 1.12 / 0.46 (flat) |

What remains in a `next()` is ~137 ns: ~20 ns dispatch (now the handler cell), ~15 ns the `agent.generators` lookup plus its `Rc` clone, ~20-30 ns the `{value, done}` object, and ~60 ns of suspend/resume, the last of which is another Rust->JIT entry per resume, i.e. the parked `.notes/rust-initiated-call-plan.md` problem.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 failed); sweeps `built-ins` 23,821 + `language` 23,726 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%, which is what exercises the async-generator twins (the corpus has no async workloads); corpus parity 0.

## LANDED (2026-10-21): for-in enumerates a plain object's own keys in one pass

`language/statements/for-in/head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration.js` is the corpus's largest row (~500-660 ms of a ~2.5 s total) and the first thing worth knowing about it is that **it has no dominant cost**. Measured by ablating the amplified body (100k calls, per body):

| piece | per body |
| --- | ---: |
| empty body (the call) | 3.9 ns |
| `var fns = {}` | 34 |
| `Object.create(null)` | 95 |
| 3 stores on that fresh object | 131 (44/store; a warm store is ~6) |
| for-in enumeration of the fresh 3-key object | ~720 |
| 3 capturing closures in the for-in | ~1480 |
| 3 calls to those closures | ~357 |
| the 6 `assert.sameValue` calls and their readers | ~2300 |

(≈5.1 us per body; node does 0.54 us.) The closure half decomposes further: a closure costs **262 ns** with a non-captured or function-scope-`var` capture, but **~490 ns** when the captured binding is per-iteration (a body `let` is worse still, ~770 ns). A call to a *fresh* closure costs **119 ns**, to a *capturing* one ~260 ns, and to a stable one **4.5 ns**, the leaf cache is per function id, so a new closure misses it every iteration.

This part fixes the enumeration. `own_property_keys` followed by `get_own_property_key` per key walks the property vector twice, and `for_in_key_levels` then hashed every key into a `HashSet` for a dedup that a single-level chain cannot need. `JsObject::own_string_props` reads the stored vector once and returns each string key with its enumerability; the runtime consumes it directly, and the duplicate list is built lazily (never for a one-level chain, linear up to 32 keys, a set past that so a wide object cannot go quadratic). The exotic-key kinds (proxy, string, index-based, host, module namespace) keep the exact per-kind loop, including the namespace live-binding read.

12 interleaved rounds, order swapped each round, medians: the corpus row **-3.6%** (472.2 -> 455.2 ms; min -2.3%), and the isolated shape it is dominated by, a fresh `Object.create(null)` with three keys, enumerated 100k times, **-14.3%** (67.2 -> 57.6 ms). Controls: a 500-key object over a cached enumeration -1.4%, a three-level prototype chain -0.7%, the generator rows flat.

**What this row still needs, in order.** (1) Closure creation is ~35% of it; the plan's Stage B is already implemented (`shared_source_info`), so what is left is the 408-byte record (Stage A) *and* the per-iteration capture surcharge, which is roughly twice the record's share, measure the env side first. (2) `Object.create(null)` at 95 ns and a cold property store at 44 ns are allocation costs on a fresh dictionary object. (3) A fresh-closure call at 119 ns against 4.5 ns for a stable one: the leaf cache is keyed by function id, so every iteration's new closure pays a full `ecma_functions` lookup and entry fill. None of these is a single-line fix; this note exists so the next session starts from the numbers rather than re-deriving them.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (38 suites, 0 failed); sweeps `built-ins` 23,821 + `language` 23,726 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0.

## NULL (2026-10-21): seeding the leaf cache at closure creation is a wash

The for-in row's remaining call cost is *cold* calls to newly created closures, so the obvious fix was to seed the leaf cache at creation: a fresh function id misses the 256-entry cell, and the miss path (`ecma_functions` lookup + entry rebuild + cell write) is what a warm call does not pay.

Measured first, before touching the row: a call to a closure created in the same iteration is **129 ns**, against **42.6 ns** for a warm call in a megamorphic site (`calls/closure_capture`: 64 closures called 1M times). Seeding the cell in `register_function`, where the `ir`, strictness and environment are already in hand, cuts that to **~71 ns** (`e1`: create + call 138 -> 122 ms per 300k, -11.3%; `e3` create + store + call -8.5%; `e4` -7.0%), but it taxes *every* closure creation: create-only went 86.8 -> 91.6 ms per 300k (**+5 ns per closure**, the cell write plus an `Rc` clone and the evicted entry's drop). 12 interleaved rounds: `calls/closure_capture` +0.4%, `calls/method_call` +0.6%, `construct_churn` +1.0%, `recursive_fib` -0.3%, and the for-in row **+1.6%** . The tax is paid by every closure; the win only by one that is called immediately. Reverted.

The measurement also kills the premise. For a *capturing* closure the seed recovers only ~10 ns of the 243 ns cold call (`c3`: create + call 167 -> 157 ms per 300k), so the miss path is not what makes a fresh capturing call expensive, the leaf cache stores everything it needs. What remains is the per-call setup the warm path avoids: `calls/closure_capture` proves a capturing closure's *steady-state* call is 42.6 ns (that is the certified-callee lane / leaf run with the callee's env already cached), while a callee that is new every iteration re-enters the slow call with a fresh `environment`. That is the parked Rust-initiated-call problem in `.notes/rust-initiated-call-plan.md`, not a cache-hit problem, and it is worth ~730 ns of the for-in row's 5.1 us per body (three cold capturing calls), pursue it there, not here.

So the numbers to carry forward: **closure creation 262 ns** (490 when the captured binding is per-iteration), **cold call to a fresh closure 129 ns** (243 if it captures), **warm megamorphic call 42.6 ns**, **stable inlined call 4.5 ns**. The gaps between the last three are the JIT's call lanes, and none of them is a lookup that a cache would fix.

## LANDED (2026-10-21): a leaf Vm returns to the pool without the full reset

`.notes/rust-initiated-call-plan.md` sized the accessor/callback lane's largest single block as the `take_vm`/`return_vm` round trip, and named the *reset* half of it: `Agent::return_vm` calls `Vm::reset`, ~45 field stores and ~25 `Vec::clear`s, because the pool is a GC root and must not trace a finished run's state. That full reset is only necessary for a run that might have left the Vm dirty. A *successful* leaf run restores every persistent field it touches, the value stack to the call site, `leaf_frame_base`/`offset`, `body_context`/`lexical_env`, and on the step/JIT paths `ip`, `strict`, `completion`, `chain_short`, `loop_counter`, the array-index stack and `call_args`, so after one, only a handful of fields can still be dirty: the register lane's `acc` (a GC value) and its two counters, the frame base, the global cached for the compiled fast path, and the short-lived stacks.

`Vm::clean_after_leaf` clears exactly those and `Agent::return_leaf_vm` pools the result; the error path keeps `return_vm`'s full reset, because an unwind can leave the value stack past the call site. `take_vm`'s contract is unchanged: everything it does not re-point is still at `reset`'s values.

| `forEach(cb)` over 4 elements | 25.35 | **23.90** (-5.7%) |
| `forEach(cb)` over 1 element | 10.81 | **9.93** (-8.1%) |
| `map(cb)` over 4 elements | 38.95 | **36.69** (-5.8%) |
| `forEach(Math.abs)` (native, control) | 12.48 | 12.48 (flat) |
| data property / compiled call / missing property (controls) |, | flat |

Also 12 interleaved rounds on the callback rows alone:  `array_for_each` -5.7%, `map_for_each` -4.7%, `typed_array_for_each` -7.7%. The full corpus, 6 interleaved rounds of medians: **2282 -> 2262 ms (-0.85%)**, best rows `array_for_each` -9.5%, `json_stringify` -5.4%, `closure_capture` -5.3%, `object_keys` -4.7%, `typed_array_for_each` -3.6%, `map_for_each` -3.5%; worst `template-literal/evaluation-order` +3.2%, `array_to_sorted` +3.0%, `regexp_test` +2.8%, `hof_methods` +2.5%, `for_in` +2.2%. Every "worst" row is one this change cannot reach (no leaf call on its path), so those are binary-layout noise, not a regression, the rows that *do* call the lane all move the right way.

This is not the whole of the plan's block: the remaining half is the *take* side (pop + `rebind`, and the JIT's ~31-field context build, which Option A measured as worthless on its own). Reusing the caller's live Vm would still remove the pool pop, and that is still gated behind the `get_member_name` contract change.

## LANDED (2026-10-22): a tagged template is scanned for closure captures

The previous entry left ~450 ns unexplained on the compiled tagged-template path
of `language/expressions/template-literal/evaluation-order.js`. Instrumenting
`ir::tagged_template` settled that first: the step itself is cheap.

| phase (per call, timer included) | ns |
| --- | ---: |
| `is_callable` | 24.8 |
| `get_template_object` | 26.7 |
| the three stack pushes | 26.6 |
| `do_call_fast` (+ pending completion) | ~117 |

Each delta carries one `Instant::now`, so the step is roughly 120 ns of real
work, and a tagged template in a compiled loop measures **182 ns/iteration**
against **9 ns** for a plain call of the same closure (`f`). The step is not the
row's problem.

What was: **the containing function was never certified**, so every call ran the
AST env path. `JIT_DUMP_STEPS` diagnostics showed `bench` (the timed function)
at 22 steps, `certified=false`, and never entering `run_jit_body` at all, while
the same `bench` without the tagged template in its nested body was 15 steps and
certified. The conclusion is `analyze_scope`'s closure walkers: `collect_captures`
is the prepass that decides which bindings a closure captures (and therefore
which get context slots), and `closure_expr_allows` walks a nested closure's
body. Both had `ExprKind::TaggedTemplate { .. }` as a leaf, the prepass
returned `true` (skip it), the closure walk returned `false` (bail the body).
`FastScopeScan::expr`, the main scan, already walked the tag and the
substitutions (Cut 78), so the two disagreed.

The prepass skipping it was a **correctness bug**, not just a pessimisation: a
binding captured only through a tagged template was left in a frame slot the
closure cannot reach.

```js
function f() { var x = 41; return (t => x)`a`; }
f();   // ReferenceError: "x" is not defined   (node: 41)
```

Both walkers now treat the construct as what it is, a call whose first argument
is the template object: the tag is a callee-like reference and the substitutions
are ordinary expressions. The closure walk keeps the `Call` arm's direct-`eval`
rejection for a tag named `eval`.

12 interleaved rounds, order swapped each round, medians:

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| the corpus row | 269.68 ms | **203.88 ms** (-24.4%) |
