## PROFILE (2026-10-22): the for-in row, decomposed

`language/statements/for-in/head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration.js` is still the
corpus's largest row: **493 ms** (4.93 us per amplified body) against node's
54 ms. The previous session's guess, that its timed `bench` is uncertified, is
wrong: `bench` certifies (15 steps) and `__t262Body` runs on the certified-callee
lane (`run_certified_call_nested`), never through `ordinary_call`. The cost is
spread over three mechanisms, measured here by ablation on one binary.

Each probe is the row's own shape with one piece removed, 100k body calls,
medians of a clean build (no in-process timers, an `Instant::now()` left in the
hot helper cost 1 us/body and read as a 28% row regression):

| probe | ns/body |
| --- | ---: |
| full body, the row's six `assert.sameValue` reduced to a one-line `sameValue` | 4849 |
| same, without the six asserts | 3328 |
| same as that, without the for-in and its closures (`Object.create(null)` + 3 stores) | 1477 |
| for-in, 3 closures capturing a function-scope `var` | 2698 |
| for-in, 3 closures capturing the per-iteration `let` head | 3850 |
| `for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)` with 3 capturing closures | 2734 |
| `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)` with 3 capturing closures (control) | 1939 |
| 3 capturing closures in one body, no loop | 1270 |
| 3 non-capturing closures in one body, no loop | 749 |
| 1 capturing / 1 non-capturing closure | 728 / 268 |

Derived, which is what matters:

| piece | cost | share of the row |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| six asserts (each `sameValue` + its reader, incl. `fns.a()` calls) | 1521 ns | ~31% |
| three per-iteration environments (for-in head) | 1152 ns (384 each) | ~24% |
| three closures at the non-loop rate | 1270 ns (~423 each) | ~26% |
| `Object.create(null)`, three stores, for-in enumeration | ~1477 ns | ~30% |
| capture premium, per closure (a captured binding vs none) | ~173 ns | inside the above |
| capture-context setup, per call of a body that captures anything | ~370 ns | inside the above |

The shares overlap because the pieces nest; they are the right sizes to choose a
target from, not a sum.

**The per-iteration environment is the most concentrated fixable block.** The
`for (let …)` and `for-in (let …)` head copies go through `per_iteration_env`
(`crates/runtime/src/jit.rs`), which per iteration allocates an `EnvRecord`
(a ~104-byte arena box for `DeclarativeEnv`, whose `bindings` is a
`RefCell<Vec<(JsString, Binding)>>`), grows a heap `Vec` for one binding,
copies the name, and fills a five-field `Binding`. The interpreter's
`Step::PerIteration` does the same inline. Nothing about the storage is needed
here: these envs are `context_transparent`, the loop addresses them by slot
index (`LoadPerIteration { depth, index }`, `set_slot`), and a closure created in
the body reads the head through its static context chain. A slot-array
representation for this variant would remove the name clone, the `Binding`, and
the `Vec` allocation per iteration.

**Not GC.** `--nursery-threshold 262144` against 8192 moves neither the row nor
the closure probes, so the cost is allocation and teardown, not collection.

Two things to keep in mind. The per-iteration copy costs 384 ns per iteration
for a for-in head but 265 for a `for (let i = …)` head (`g3 - g4`); the two forms
emit the same `PerIteration` helper, so the difference is the env it copies
*from*, and it is unexplained. And the assert share (1521 ns for six) is a
`sameValue` call plus a reader call each, `fns.a()` on a closure created in the
same iteration, so it moves with the closure work rather than separately.

Next, in order: (1) the per-iteration env's storage (above); (2) `EcmaFunction`
Stage A from `.notes/closure-cost-plan.md` plus the capture-context setup, which
between them are the other ~26%+; (3) the asserts, which are the largest single
share but decompose into three fresh-closure calls that (1) and (2) also reach.

## LANDED (2026-10-22): a declarative environment carries its rare state lazily

The PROFILE entry above sized the per-iteration environment by reuse: copying it
costs 315 ns per iteration, and nothing about the copy is needed beyond a slot
array. Before writing that variant, the record sizes said something simpler was
wrong:

| type | bytes |
| --- | ---: |
| `EnvRecord` (the box every env allocates) | 160 |
| `DeclarativeEnv` | 112 |
| `Binding` (one entry) | 80 |
| `JsString` | 48 |

A per-iteration environment holding ONE binding therefore allocated a 160-byte
arena box plus a 128-byte binding vector, both traced. Half of `DeclarativeEnv`
was two `RefCell<Vec<..>>` that ordinary scopes never touch:
`disposable_resources` (`using`) and `annex_b_functions` (Annex B block
hoists). They now live behind one lazily allocated `Box<EnvExtras>`:

| type | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `DeclarativeEnv` | 112 | **64** |
| `EnvRecord` | 160 | **112** |
| `FunctionEnv` | 152 | **104** |
| `GlobalEnv` | 128 | **80** |

`Trace for DeclarativeEnv` mirrors `RefCell`'s own rule (a cell borrowed
mid-collection aborts the sweep rather than panicking). The public surface is
unchanged: every outside reader already went through `add_`/`has_`/`drain_`
methods, so only `env.rs` moved.

Measured, 10-12 interleaved rounds with the order swapped each round
(`slag-base-env.exe` = the previous commit):

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| the for-in row | 522.14 / 878.95 ms | 507.54 / 857.20 ms (-2.5%) |
| per-iteration-env probe (3/body) | 389.08 ms | 366.56 (-5.8%), flat on a later, 2x slower machine state |
| `Object.create(null)` + 3 stores, no envs | 326.01 | 320.36 (-1.7%) |
| 3 capturing closures, no loop (control) | 126.93 | 130.36 (+2.7%, within this host's noise) |

The full corpus was inconclusive on this host at this time: -0.71% and +1.83%
across two 6-round runs, with single rows swinging +150% in one run and reading
flat when re-tested in isolation (24 interleaved runs each), the disk reached
100% mid-session and the machine's absolute times drifted ~13% between runs. The
change is landed on the sizes above and on the two probes it can reach, not on a
corpus total.

What this does NOT do: it does not remove the binding vector, which the reuse
ablation showed is ~148 of the 315 ns, so the slot-array variant from the PROFILE
entry is still the way to reach the rest. It also leaves `Binding` at 80 bytes
for a value plus four flags.

## PROFILE (2026-10-22): a function expression in an object literal costs ~450 ns extra

Found while decomposing the for-in row's asserts and confirmed on minimal probes
(100k body calls, medians of one binary):

| probe | ns/body |
| --- | ---: |
| `var f = function () { return 1; };` (control) | 310 |
| `var o = {}; o.a = function () { return 1; };` | 414 |
| `var o = { a: 1 };` (control) | 94 |
| `var o = { a: f };` (closure created first, then stored) | 340 |
| `var o = { a: function b () { return 1; } };` (named, no inference) | 769 |
| `var o = { a: function () { return 1; } };` (anonymous) | 839 |
| `var o = { a: () => 1 };` | 593 |

Two separate costs, both in the literal path (`ir::compile_object`):

1. An **anonymous** function/arrow value disqualifies the whole literal from
   `Step::ObjectFast` (`fast_object_names` bails on
   `is_anonymous_function_definition`), so every property takes an
   `ObjectBegin`/`ObjectInitName` step and the closure gets its name from a
   post-hoc `set_function_name` (an own-property lookup plus a redefining
   `define_property`). Anonymous vs named in the same literal: 839 vs 769.
2. Even the batchable form pays ~340 ns over the control, because the closure is
   still created through the general `CreateFunction` step and then defined
   per-key.

The fix would be named evaluation at *creation*, thread the property key into
`CreateFunction`/`CreateArrow` (the way `pending_class_name` already threads a
class's inferred name) so the function is created with its final `name` and the
literal can take `ObjectFast`. Not measured; no corpus row uses the pattern
(two files contain `: function (` and neither evaluates it in a loop), so this is
a real-world win rather than a corpus one.

## MEASURED (2026-10-25): what the security audit cost

66 commits landed between `883af3dd` and `8bc1f77b` for the audit. Re-measured
both binaries, three interleaved corpus rounds per binary and three micro-suite
rounds per binary:

| harness | `883af3dd` | `8bc1f77b` | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| corpus mean JIT gap | 10.40x | 10.76x | +3.5% |
| corpus mean interpreter gap | 3.69x | 3.88x | +5.1% |
| micro-suite JIT column |, |, | flat (16/16 within 1%) |
| micro-suite interpreter column |, |, | +8-16% on 11 of 16 |

The V8 total itself drifted +3.1% between the two corpus runs, so ~+2.2% of the
JIT number is real. The interpreter number is not drift.

Bisected on four rows with eight checkpoint builds. Two commits carry the JIT
damage: `8d0bebf2` (execution-context stack and function records into
AgentRoots) took `opcost/map_for_each` 21.7 -> 25.4 ms, and `cbafcd42` (IC caches
into AgentRoots) took it on to 29.9 and `calls/closure_capture` 34.6 -> 38.5.
The interpreter damage is spread across the whole AgentRoots refactor
(`typed-array write` 25.99 -> 29.69 in steps at `d08a165b`, `8d0bebf2`,
`2c4e4f9b`).

The mechanism is indirection: every traced table moved behind
`Agent::roots: Rc<AgentRoots>`, so a hot read is now pointer -> large struct ->
`RefCell` where it was one inline field, and `Agent::ecma_function` is a
`Ref::filter_map`. On a 4-9 ns call lane that is 50-100% of the lane.

The recovery plan, the family table, and the pre-existing queue are in
`.notes/perf-plan.md`. The README's performance section now carries these
numbers at this commit.

## LANDED (2026-10-25): an object-literal method no longer blocks scope certification

`FastScopeScan::expr` returned `false` for every `Method`/`Get`/`Set`, so any body containing `{ m() {} }` was uncertified and ran the environment path. The capture prepass (`collect_expr_captures`) already walked those closures through `closure_allows`; the main scan did not. Walk them the same way (plus the computed key through `property_name`), and add the matching `key_captures` helper to the prepass so the two walkers agree on the capture set, a closure inside a computed key would otherwise have been laid out as a frame slot it cannot reach.

The `for (using ...)`/`for (await using ...)` head also needs a bail in the `For` arm (matching `for-in`/`for-of`): a `using` binding registers a disposable resource the certified frame slot has no machinery for. The old unconditional method bail had masked it; without the fix four `statements/using` + `statements/await-using` fixtures regressed.

| probe | uncertified | certified |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `{ m() { return 1; } }` in a 200k loop (corpus) | 19,272.7 ms | **8,421** |

This is only the certification step. The certified body still ran interpreted (the optimizing-tier lift refuses `ObjectMethodName`; the per-step pass lowers it) and still leaked the home object, so the real win is the next entry.

## LANDED (2026-10-25): a method's home object is a GC leak

`EcmaFunction::trace` traced `home_object`. Every function record is a permanent Agent root (`ecma_functions`), and for a method the home object is the object literal whose method property is the closure itself, the record's root formed an uncollectable cycle. Every method ever created pinned its object literal, its closure, and the closure's properties: a 200k-iteration `{ m() {} }` loop grew `live` to 803k and every minor GC scanned all of it.

The fix is the pattern `environment` and `resolving_promise` already use: the record keeps the typed `Value` for reads, the `Function` box carries an erased `GcAny` edge traced only while the box is reachable, and `EcmaFunction::trace` stops visiting it. The `home_object` field stays on the record so the super machinery reads it unchanged; only the GC edge moved.

| metric | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `{ m() {} }` 200k loop (corpus) | 8,421 ms | **117.4** |
| `live` at the end | 803,477 | **9,825** |
| `swept` over the run | 200,001 | **996,845** |
| minor pause | 13,981 us | **41 us** |

The probe now lands at ~585 ns/iteration, faster than the `{ m: function () {} }` control (145 ms, unchanged; it has no home object) and level with the cost of creating any closure. The two commits together are 164x on the probe (19,272.7 ms -> 117.4 ms).

## LANDED (2026-10-25): the leaf cache is a `Cell` table of `Copy` records (P1 R2)

Slice 4h moved the leaf cache into `AgentRoots` behind a `RefCell`, and priced
the borrow it added at +6.3% `per-iteration` / +4.5% `construct churn`. The
option that slice left on the table is taken here: `LeafEntry` is `Copy`, so
the table is `Box<[Cell<Option<LeafEntry>>; 256]>`, a hit is one load plus an
identity compare, and there is no borrow flag and no `Rc` refcount bump.

The `Rc<CompiledBody>` became a borrowed `*const CompiledBody`
(`LeafEntry::body`). The lifetime argument is not "the function record owns it",
records are reaped, but the stronger one `shared_compiled_body` gives:
every body a leaf record can name was inserted into
`AgentRoots::compiled_bodies` when it was compiled, that table is never cleared
or evicted, and it is the cache `EcmaFunction::ir` is cloned from. The leaf
cache is a sibling field of it inside the same roots allocation, so the body
outlives the record and the eviction. The JIT's cold consult is the one place
that still needs an owner (the cache pins the bodies it compiles), so
`lookup_info_leaf` re-derives the record's `Rc` by id, only until the body's
`jit_info` fast pointer is set; a warm body returns before the lookup, and the
sticky not-compilable mark returns null without one.

The traced env edge is unchanged: the collector copies each cell out
(`Cell::get`) and traces it, exactly as 4h's `Copy` verdict arrays do.

Interleaved A/B against a binary from `HEAD` (`ed04170c`), order flipped each
round, medians of 7 rounds (`--bench`, interpreter):

| row | before | after | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `per-iteration` | 11.601 ms | **10.812 ms** | **-6.8%** |
| `construct churn` | 20.036 ms | **19.317 ms** | **-3.6%** |
| `function calls` | 31.539 ms | **30.812 ms** | -2.3% |
| `closure capture` | 36.363 ms | **35.827 ms** | -1.5% |

That recovers the measured 6.3% / 4.5%. The other rows are inside the
suite's own spread (`bare loop` +5.2%, `string concat` +2.9% both ways).

The callback lanes gained more than the plan predicted, because they read the
cache per element: corpus medians of 5 alternating rounds (jit column):

| row | before | after | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `opcost/typed_array_for_each` | 30.805 ms | **26.382 ms** | **-14.4%** |
| `opcost/array_for_each` | 29.669 ms | **26.174 ms** | **-11.8%** |
| `opcost/map_for_each` | 28.367 ms | **25.357 ms** | **-10.6%** |
| `opcost/array_to_sorted` | 39.899 ms | **38.191 ms** | -4.3% |
| `calls/direct_leaf` | 13.272 ms | **12.898 ms** | -2.8% |
| `calls/closure_capture` | 41.888 ms | **41.548 ms** | -0.8% |

`global_leaf_cells` and `slot_leaf_cells` were deliberately left as `RefCell`s:
4h measured the global-callee lane that hits `global_leaf_cells` at 0%, and the
`Copy` record already removed their entry clone (`calls/method_call` +1.1%,

## NULL (2026-10-25): the call lanes' `Ref::filter_map` record read is below the noise floor (P1 R3)

R3's premise was that `Agent::ecma_function`'s `Ref::filter_map` remap is a per-call cost on the lanes the corpus blames. It is not: reading the record under a plain `table.borrow()`, and, in a second shape, merging `construct_inner`'s two record reads into one, measures inside the noise floor on every lane that touches it. Reverted.

The lanes were probed directly rather than inferred. `fn_call`, a non-leaf ordinary call (`function callee(o) { try { return o.x + 1; } catch (e) { return 0; } }`, 300k iterations, ~77 ns/call), and `cb_nonleaf`, a builtin-invoked JS callback whose body calls a helper, so it is not a certified leaf and every element goes through `function::call` -> `call_inner` (8-element `forEach`, 100k rounds, ~345 ns/element). Both are in `scratch/ab/r3/`.

A 15-round alternating A/B against the R2 binary, with an A/A control (the R2 binary against a copy of itself) for the floor:

| lane | statistic | R2 -> R3 | A/A control |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| `cb_nonleaf` | median | +2.0% | -4.1% |
| `cb_nonleaf` | min | +1.6% | -0.9% |
| `fn_call` | median | -3.6% | -2.2% |
| `fn_call` | min | -1.6% | -1.0% |

The control's own 4% median spread on `cb_nonleaf` is larger than the effect, so the median column resolves nothing; the min-based comparison is the usable one, and its floor is ~1%. Against that floor the restructured version (fields read in place under one plain borrow, no closure, no `Option<tuple>` return, which the first shape paid for) is -0.3% / -0.6%, i.e. flat, and the `--bench` suite measured every row inside +/-2% min (`construct churn` +0.8%, `function calls` -0.1%, `closure capture` -1.0%).

So the cost is not the guard: `Ref::filter_map` on a `Ref` that is about to be dropped is a few instructions on a 77-345 ns call. The useful part of this attempt is the floor itself, an A/A control is mandatory before reading a 2-4% delta on this machine, and `cb_nonleaf`'s ~345 ns/element is where the callback lane's money is (the leaf callback row is ~260 ns/element), not in the record read. Profiling that lane is the next step, not more indirection work.

## LANDED (2026-10-25): the leaf cache caches the negative verdict, the non-leaf callback lane's per-element record lookup

The callback lane the corpus never shows: `Array.prototype.forEach` with a callback that is *not* a certified leaf (`sink += helper(x)`), so `call_callback` -> `try_fast_call` -> `try_leaf_call` misses and the general `function::call` runs. On 8 elements × 100k rounds that is ~334 ns/element against ~130 for the leaf callback. Instrumenting the lanes (temporary `SLAG_LANE_STATS` counters, removed) showed the miss path re-did `ecma_functions.get`, a pooled `Rc` deref, a `RefCell` borrow and an id hash, on **every element**, because `leaf_lookup` only cached positive records.

The fix is the negative verdict the embedding notes named: the cache cell is now `LeafCacheCell::{Empty, NotLeaf(id), Leaf(entry)}`. A record whose `leaf_inline` is false fills `NotLeaf`, and the next probe answers from the cell. Soundness is registration order, not generation: `leaf_inline` is written once by `set_compiled`, which runs before `register_ecma_function` inserts the record, ids are never reused, and `reap_dead_functions` clears the cell (both variants) with the record. An absent record is still not cached, only an existing record's verdict is.

Measured on the lane itself (7 probes × 15 alternating rounds, medians and mins, against the R2 binary; A/A control on the same probes: −4.1% median / −0.9% min on the noisiest row):

| probe | before (min) | after (min) | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `p3` callback calls a global (`sink += helper(x)`) | 263.192 ms | **226.109 ms** | **-14.1%** |
| `p4` same, no capture | 250.232 ms | **209.189 ms** | **-16.4%** |
| `captured_call` callback calls a captured local closure | 256.879 ms | **216.532 ms** | **-15.7%** |
| `member_call` callback calls `Math.abs` | 289.242 ms | **249.468 ms** | **-13.8%** |
| `global_read` callback reads a global, no call | 259.588 ms | **218.927 ms** | **-15.7%** |
| `p2` leaf callback (control) | 100.672 ms | **101.023 ms** | +0.3% |

Results are identical on every probe (4400000 / 3600000 / 13200000), so this is not a semantic shortcut. The corpus does not move, all 36 `opcost` and 6 `calls` rows are inside ±1.1% min except `json_stringify`, whose own A/A control (two copies of the same binary) spans +1.2% min / +5.1% median, i.e. the row is unmeasurable at this sample size. That is the point: no corpus row has a non-leaf callback, which is why the lane had never been priced.

## NULL (2026-10-25): the interpreter's IC cells have no recoverable indirection left (P1 R4)

R4's question was whether the interpreter's cell access is still the residual after R1, and its stated fix was "read them through the same `&roots`, not change their storage". Read against the code, the answer is no on both counts.

The hot read path is `member_cell_get` -> `member_cell_warm_probe`, and its first probe is one `Cell::get` on `AgentRoots::member_value_cells` (`agent.rs:849`, a `[Cell<MemberValueCell>; MEMBER_CELLS]`) with three compares on the 32-byte record (`ir.rs:5671`). That is already borrow-free, the audit's `RefCell` never survived on this path, so the only cost 4h added is one dependent load: `agent.roots` (an `Rc<AgentRoots>`, so the inner pointer is a load) instead of the pre-audit inline field. The neighbouring caches never left `Agent` at all: the slot cache (`member_cells`, `agent.rs:1818`) and the chain cache (`member_chain_cells`, `agent.rs:1843`) are plain inline arrays, zero indirection, and they are the ones a prototype or method read resolves through. The second value table, `global_value_cells` (`agent.rs:863`), has the same one-load shape.

Removing that load has exactly one shape, thread a run-held `&AgentRoots` (an `Rc::clone` local, per R1) through `run_inner_inner` and every cell helper, and it buys ~0.3 ns per access (one dependent L1 load on a 32-byte-hot line). The rows that could show it are the small cell-read ones, and their own A/A control (two copies of the same binary, 11 alternating rounds) gives `obj_prop` +1.3% median on a 0.639 ms row, `element_read` +0.3% on 0.652, `dyn_key_read` +0.0% on 0.918. At 100k reads the removable work is ~5% of a 6.4 ns read, but it is a load, not work: there is nothing to delete, and the diff to make `agent.roots` resolve further up the stack is the whole dispatch. INLINING the tables back into `Agent` would remove it and is what M-1 forbids.

So this is closed as structurally verified rather than measured-then-rejected: the audit's cost on the cell path is one dependent load, which is the minimum `AgentRoots`-owning-the-traced-tables permits. The stop rule's remaining instruction, profile the dispatch instead of more indirection work, is where P1 leaves off; the callback lane's next target is the general call machinery around a certified body (`with_agent`, context push/pop, `take_vm`/`return_vm`, `run_jit_body`'s per-call setup), now ~180 ns/element after the negative-verdict win.

## NULL (2026-10-25): the certified-callee nested lane does not pay for a builtin-invoked callback

After the negative-verdict win, a certified (non-leaf) callback still costs ~180 ns/element in the general funnel. The obvious collapse is the lane the interpreter's own call steps and the JIT's `certified_call` helper use: `Vm::run_certified_call_nested`, which runs the callee as a nested activation on the caller's Vm and skips `call_inner`'s pooled-Vm take/reset. `CallbackVm::call` was extended to try it (stage the args, `run_certified_call_nested`, truncate) before falling back to `crate::function::call`. It is **slower**, measured same-binary:

| probe (min) | lane off | lane on | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `p3_nonleaf` (calls a global) | 232.476 ms | 238.206 ms | +2.5% |
| `p4_nonleaf_nocapture` | 214.738 ms | 220.400 ms | +2.6% |
| `captured_call` | 227.432 ms | 231.308 ms | +1.7% |
| `global_call` | 233.706 ms | 237.235 ms | +1.5% |
| `member_call` | 257.339 ms | 264.560 ms | +2.8% |
| `global_read` | 228.956 ms | 231.984 ms | +1.3% |
| `p2_leaf_capture` (control) | 105.243 ms | 103.025 ms | -2.1% |

**The method is the durable part.** The first pass compared two binaries and read +3.3–4.8% on the non-leaf rows, but the leaf control row, whose path the patch does not touch, moved +2.3% too, so the comparison was measuring build layout, not the lane. Rebuilding one binary with an `SLAG_CB_NESTED` gate and A/B-ing the *same* binary with the env set and unset removed that confound and resolved the effect to ~2%. For a 1-3% change, that is the experiment to run first: same binary, env gate, alternating rounds. The gate and the lane are both reverted.

What it rules out: the funnel's cost is not the pooled-Vm round trip. `save_scratch`/`restore_scratch`, the explicit `ExecutionContext` push and `run_compiled_body_on(frame_prepared)` cost at least what `take_vm`/`return_vm` do on a pooled Vm, and the shared body run (`run_jit_body` + the compiled code) is paid by both. So the ~180 ns is the body run plus activation bookkeeping, not the Vm lifecycle, and no further "collapse the chain" edit on this lane is worth trying.

## LANDED (2026-10-25): an anonymous function in an object literal is named at creation

The 2026-10-22 PROFILE entry priced `{ a: function () {} }` at ~450-530 ns over the same closure as a plain variable, split between two costs: an anonymous function/arrow value disqualified the whole literal from `Step::ObjectFast` (so every property took an `ObjectInitName` step), and the closure was created nameless and then renamed by a post-hoc `SetFunctionName` (an own-property lookup plus a redefining define). Both are gone.

`fast_object_names` now rejects only an anonymous **class** value (its name goes through `pending_class_name`, which this path does not fold); `compile_object`, in both the `ObjectFast` arm and the static-key step arm, threads the property key into `CreateFunction`/`CreateArrow` through `begin_named_initializer`, the mechanism the `var f = function () {}` form already used. The step arm's `ObjectInitName { set_name }` becomes `anonymous && !named_folded`, i.e. false exactly when the fold happened. A computed key keeps the post-hoc naming (its text is only known after `ToPropertyKey`, which must run before the value), and `__proto__` is excluded (it is not a NamedEvaluation, it sets the prototype).

15 alternating rounds, medians and mins, against the previous binary:

| probe (100k bodies) | before | after | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `{ a: function () {} }` | 81.397 / 76.053 ms | **40.361 / 38.573** | **-50.4% / -49.3%** |
| `{ a: () => 1 }` | 66.403 / 63.452 ms | **39.133 / 37.629** | **-41.1% / -40.7%** |
| `var f = function () {}` (control) | 33.644 / 32.325 | 33.467 / 31.863 | -1.4% min |
| `{ a: function b () {} }` (control) | 51.566 / 48.553 | 50.478 / 48.560 | 0.0% min |
| `var f = ...; var o = { a: f }` (control) | 40.599 / 38.899 | 40.727 / 38.776 | -0.3% min |
| `{ a: 1 }` (control) | 4.785 / 4.684 | 4.790 / 4.587 | -2.1% min |

After the change the literal costs create-closure + create-object: 38.6 ms against 31.9 + 4.6. The arrow row is now cheaper than the function-expression row, matching the control ladder.

Correctness was diffed against node across 13 shapes, the `ObjectFast` batch, the step path forced by a computed key / a duplicate key / `__proto__`, a certified loop body, shorthand, a numeric key, a string key, a parenthesized value, anonymous class, and the `name` own-property attributes from `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, all identical. Found while doing it, and **not** part of this change: `{ __proto__: fn }` does not set the prototype in Slag at all (the proto-setter arm matches an object/null value only, and a function value is neither), so `Object.getPrototypeOf(o) === fn` is false where node says true. The previous binary behaves identically, so it is pre-existing and unrelated.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites, 0 failed); sweeps `language` 23,726 + `built-ins` 23,821 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0 (77 rows).

## LANDED (2026-10-25): a per-iteration environment stores its slots inline

The PROFILE entry of 2026-10-22 left the per-iteration copy at ~200 ns, of which the binding vector's allocation was ~150: the copy built a whole `DeclarativeEnv`, an arena box plus a `Vec<(JsString, Binding)>` with one 80-byte entry, its name cloned and its value read out of the previous env *by name*, for bindings that are always the same head names in the same order.

`EnvRecord` now has a `PerIteration` variant (`env.rs`). It stores the head names once per loop in an `Rc<[JsString]>` and the values inline, in head order (`[Cell<Option<Value>>; 2]`), so a copy per iteration is `Rc::clone` + two `Cell::get`/`Cell::set` and allocates nothing. The values are always the `push_initialized_binding` shape (initialized, mutable, not deletable), which is why bare slots suffice. Anything outside that shape, a head with more than two declarations, a sloppy assignment creating a name, goes to an `extra` table with the declarative record's semantics, so the name-addressed surface (`has_binding`, `get_binding_value`, `set_mutable_binding`, `delete_binding`, …) is total. The record is 88 bytes, under the 104-byte `FunctionEnv` the box already sizes to, so `EnvRecord` and its arena slot are unchanged.

The copy is by slot only when the source is the same loop's previous record (`names_match` guards it); otherwise it falls back to the name-addressed copy, which is the loop-entry case (the capture context) and the bytecode path's first iteration. Besides the allocation this removes the per-head name comparison, which only existed because the copy addressed the previous env by name.

Because the record is context-transparent by construction, `context_env` now returns a two-variant `ContextEnv` (declarative or per-iteration) exposing `slot_value`/`slot_mutable`; `is_context_transparent` and the snapshot writer normalize the new variant (a snapshot rebuilds it as an ordinary declarative record). The Annex B function-declaration path in `eval.rs` had been asking `has_binding` only on a declarative env; it now asks on a per-iteration env too, which is where a declaration shadowed by a loop head is actually visible.

Measured with two binaries built from HEAD (`scratch/ab/slag-head.exe`, a cache hit) and the working tree, alternating the order each round. The host was under load from an unrelated process, so the mins are the numbers to read; the medians drifted with it.

| probe | before | after | min |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| per-iteration-env probe (3 envs/body, 100k bodies) | 475.3 ms | **420.8** | **-11.5%** |
| `language/statements/for-in/head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration.js` | 563.4 ms | **508.4** | **-9.8%** |

The ablation that prices the whole remaining machinery (skip the per-iteration env entirely) still measures ~-33% on the probe, so what is left is the arena box itself, one live record per iteration is what per-iteration bindings are. There is no second allocation left to remove.

Correctness: 12 semantic shapes diffed against node (for-in and `for` heads with closures, two and three head declarations, a const for-of head, nested capturing loops, a closure writing its own iteration's head, `eval` reading the head by name, a sloppy assignment creating a name in the body, a block capture, `break`, `delete` on a head), all identical. New tests: `env.rs` covers the slot copy's independence and the name fallback for a mismatched head (mutation-checked: forcing `names_match` to `true` fails it); `jit/src/lib.rs` covers the surplus-name/overflow path and the by-name read through `eval`.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites, 0 failed); sweeps `language` 23,726 + `built-ins` 23,821 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0 (77 rows, `mean-jitGap=11.26`, `mean-jlGap=3.93`).

## LANDED (2026-10-25): the capture context is a slot record too

The PROFILE entry above priced the capture-context setup at 310 ns per call for one captured name and 510 for three, and named the reason: `ScopeInfo::new_body_context` built a `DeclarativeEnv` per call and, per captured binding, ran `create_mutable_binding` (a duplicate scan over the binding vector, a `Vec` push, a name clone) followed by `initialize_binding` (a second scan by name). Name-addressed work for bindings the compiler addresses by index, `context_names` order, `context_const`, `context_param`, `context_tdz` are all static.

`PerIterationEnv` is now `SlotEnv` (`env.rs`) and serves both sites: a shared `Rc<[SlotSpec]>` layout (the name and the mutability/strictness of each slot) plus a value table (`[Cell<Option<Value>>; 2]` inline, one heap array beyond that). The per-iteration path is unchanged in shape, its layout is built once per loop from the step's head names, and the capture context gets its layout from `ScopeInfo`, built once when the body is certified (`context_layout`), so a call is now an `Rc` clone plus the value table plus one store per initialized slot: no name clone, no vector, no scans, and nothing name-addressed on the hot path.

One record type, two uses, distinguished by data rather than by variant: `context_transparent` is true for a per-iteration copy (a certified body's closures resolve past it) and false for a capture context (it *is* the context). Everything else the same code: the layout's `mutable`/`strict` carry a captured `const`'s immutability and strictness (a sloppy write to it still throws), an unset slot is the TDZ, and `extra` stays the total fallback for a name the layout does not describe. `EnvRecord::Slot` replaces `PerIteration`, `ContextEnv` gains `Slot`, `has_this_binding`/`get_this_binding` read the reserved `this` binding out of the same table, and the snapshot writer normalizes the record to a declarative one.

Measured with two binaries (`scratch/ab/slag-slot.exe` = before, `slag-capture.exe` = after), alternating order, 8 rounds, mins:

| probe | before | after | min |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `language/statements/for-in/head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration.js` | 498.08 ms | **448.68** | **-9.9%** |
| the same row, re-measured on the final tree (6 rounds) | 497.28 | **441.85** | -11.1% |
| `p0` the row's shape, 100k bodies | 402.71 | **373.78** | -7.2% |
| `p19` one capturing closure, uncalled | 114.89 | **105.41** | -8.3% |
| `p20` three capturing closures, uncalled | 192.44 | **174.94** | -9.1% |
| `p15` three capturing closures + calls | 233.55 | **221.09** | -5.3% |

The row's delta is larger than the isolated setup deltas, and it is not GC pacing: the same comparison with `--nursery-threshold 262144` is -10.0%. What it is instead: in this shape the body's capture context holds the loop head, so the per-call record was a `DeclarativeEnv` *plus* a one-binding vector, and both the allocation and the two scans per call were paid 100k times per run.

Correctness: 11 capture shapes diffed against node (a captured var written by a closure and observed after return, a captured `let`'s TDZ, a strict write to a captured `const`, `eval` writing a captured var, a captured param with `arguments`, an env-path arrow capturing `this`, two-level nesting, `delete` on a captured var, a loop closure capturing both the head and a body `let`, a late write, a block `let`). New tests: `env.rs` pins the capture context's const/TDZ semantics (mutation-checked: dropping the spec's strictness fails it) and the overflow table's order and laziness; the per-iteration tests and the `SlotEnv` size invariant still hold.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites, 0 failed); sweeps `language` 23,726 + `built-ins` 23,821 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0 (77 rows, `mean-jitGap=10.15`, `mean-jlGap=3.86`).

## CORRECTION (2026-10-25): the "null-prototype store" was a leaf/non-leaf artifact

The PROFILE entry above reads `Object.create(null)` + 3 stores as 88 ns per store against 20 ns into `{}` (`p8 - p16`), and listed that as a target. **That delta is not the store.** `p16` (`var o = {}` + 3 stores) is a body with no calls, so it is a *leaf* and its calls run on the in-place lane; `p8` reaches `Object.create(null)`, which makes the body non-leaf. The two probes therefore differ by the whole non-leaf activation, not by the property write.

Probes that hold everything else fixed (`scratch/ab/nullproto/*`, 100k bodies, min of 5-7):

| probe | ns/body |
| --- | ---: |
| `function body() { return 1; }`, leaf | 5 |
| `… { noop(); return 1; }`, one user call, body non-leaf | 55 |
| `… { Math.abs(1); return 1; }` | 84 |
| `… { Object.create(null); return 1; }` | 110 |
| `… { var o = {}; return 1; }`, leaf, one object | 47 |
| `… { var o = {}; o.a = 1; return 1; }`, one fresh define | 88 |
| `… { var o = { a: 0 }; o.a = 1; return 1; }`, in-place update | 107 |
| `… { var o = { a: 0, b: 0, c: 0 }; return 1; }`, literal batch (3 props) | 105 |

So a call in a body costs **~50-105 ns more per invocation** than a leaf body's (the leaf lane skips the execution-context push, the Vm round trip and the frame re-alloc, by design), and the property write itself is ~41 ns for a fresh define, ~19 ns for an in-place update, ~19 ns per property when the literal batch defines it.

The null-prototype premium does exist, but it is small and it is not in the row's favour. With both bodies non-leaf and one call each (`r1` returns `{}` from a callee, `r2` returns `Object.create(null)`): 416 vs 522 ns/body, i.e. **~35 ns per store**. And the row's actual shape prefers the null prototype, because the for-in enumeration over it skips the prototype-chain consult:

| the row's body | ns/body |
| --- | ---: |
| `Object.create(null)` + 3 stores | **3509** |
| `{}` + 3 stores | 4023 |
| `{ a: 1, b: 1, c: 1 }` | 3888 |

Nothing to change here: the row already uses the faster shape, and the store path it exercises is ~41 ns per fresh define, not 88. The remaining targets on this row are the ones the (now corrected) decomposition points at, closure creation (~42% of it, and already stop-rule-gated for its arena stage), the for-in enumeration, and the non-leaf activation.

## PROFILE (2026-10-25): closure creation and for-in begin, by phase

Both blocks were profiled with a temporary per-phase accumulator (env-gated `SLAG_PROF`, `Instant` pairs accumulated and printed every 10k calls; `e7` = 300k `var f = function () { return 1; }`, for-in over a fresh 3-key `Object.create(null)` object, 100k loop entries). The timers inflate the absolute numbers, `e7` is 305 ns uninstrumented and ~470 ns under eleven `Instant` pairs, so read the shares, not the levels. The instrumentation is reverted.

### Closure creation (`register_function`)

| phase | ns |
| --- | ---: |
| `shared_source_info` (enclosing-source walk + slice hash + cache lookup) | **75** |
| `shared_function_body_with_key` | 29 |
| `shared_params` | 26 |
| setup (strictness/realm/context reads) | 24 |
| the `EcmaFunction` literal + name/params clones | 26 |
| `Function::new_with_prototype` + `set_environment_edge` | 64 |
| `shared_compiled_body` | 31 |
| `agent.register_ecma_function` (the record insert) | **121** |
| `set_compiled` | 25 |
| `set_function_properties_batched` | 44 |

`register_ecma_function` is the record copy into `Agent::ecma_functions`, the block `.notes/closure-cost-plan.md` measured at 97 ns together with `store_construct_patterns` and whose alternatives (a boxed value, a `Vec` slab) were rejected on measurement. Stage D remains gated by the plan's stop rule (`e7` = 91.4 ms for 300k, above the 85 ms threshold).

`shared_source_info` is the one block here that the plan did **not** account for: it runs per closure, and per closure it walks the execution-context stack for the enclosing source, clones that text, **hashes the function's source slice**, and probes a thread-local cache. All of that is fixed per creation *site*, the node address, span and realm are the same every time, but it is recomputed 300k times for `e7`. The fix is to carry the site's `Rc<SourceInfo>` in the `CreateFunction`/`CreateArrow`/`FunctionDeclInit` step payload (built once when the body is compiled, traced from the compiled body the way `ScopeInfo::context_layout` is), so creation only clones an `Rc`. Worth ~70 ns per closure: roughly 210 ns/body on the for-in row (three closures), and it grows with the size of the function's source text, since the hash is over that slice.

### for-in begin (`for_in_begin`)

| phase | ns |
| --- | ---: |
| `ToObject` + `as_object` | 26 |
| the enumeration-cache probe | 26 |
| `for_in_key_levels` | **279** |
| `for_in_cache_put` | **134** |

Uninstrumented context (100k bodies, mins): a fresh 3-key null-prototype object **970** ns/body, the same object with no keys **412**, a *shared* 3-key object (cache hit) **196**, a shared empty object **188**, a fresh 3-key plain object **1308** (the extra level costs 338).

So a cache miss costs ~780 ns and a hit ~8 ns; the miss is `for_in_key_levels` plus the cache build. Inside those two phases, for a 3-key object:

- `JsObject::own_string_props` **materializes a vector-free object** (`materialize_properties`), then builds three `Vec`s (`indices`, `strings`, and the copied `keys`) and sorts the index keys.
- `key_value` makes a **`Handle::new` GC box per key** (`Value::String`), plus a `crux::lookup` memo scan.
- `for_in_cache_put` builds a chain-snapshot `Vec`, wraps it in an `Rc`, **copies the key list** (`keys.to_vec()`) and wraps the copy in a second `Rc`, although `for_in_begin` already wraps the original in an `Rc` for `ForInState`. Five allocations where three would do, and one copy of the key list that the cache and the loop could share.

Next, in order: (1) share the key-list `Rc` between `ForInState` and the cache entry, and skip the chain-snapshot allocation for a single-link chain; (2) have `for_in_key_levels` push straight into its result from the object (no materialize, no `indices`/`strings` staging, sort only when an index key is present); (3) the closure `SourceInfo` in step payloads.

## LANDED (2026-10-25): a for-in begin caches one key list, and a short chain inline

The PROFILE entry above put `for_in_key_levels` at 279 ns and `for_in_cache_put` at 134 ns per loop entry over a fresh 3-key null-prototype object, and named the reason: the miss path built the key list, then **copied** it into the cache (`keys.to_vec()`), wrapped the copy in a second `Rc` while `for_in_begin` was already wrapping the original, and snapshotted the prototype chain into a `Vec` behind another `Rc`.

Three changes:

- `for_in_cache_put` now takes the shared `ForInKeys` and stores it, so the cache and the running `ForInState` hold one list (the JIT helper, the interpreter's `ForInBegin`, and the bytecode path all construct it once).
- The chain snapshot is a `ForInChain`: up to two links inline (a null-prototype object is one, a plain object over `Object.prototype` two), one `Rc` beyond that. Probing copies the inline pair, so no allocation on either side.
- `JsObject::own_string_props` builds one result vector instead of three: only array-index keys are staged (they enumerate first, ascending, and an ordinary object rarely has one); the string keys already sit in insertion order and go straight in.

Measured with two binaries, alternating order, 7 rounds, mins:

| probe | before | after | min |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| fresh 3-key null-prototype object | 97.07 ms | **88.22** | **-9.1%** |
| fresh 0-key null-prototype object | 42.86 | **38.67** | -9.8% |
| fresh 3-key plain object (two links) | 129.42 | **106.55** | **-17.7%** |
| shared 3-key object (cache hit) | 20.41 | 20.65 | +1.2% (noise) |
| the for-in corpus row | 450.88 | 465.77 | +3.3% min / -0.6% median, noise |

The row does not move because it is dominated by closure creation and calls, not enumeration; the probes that isolate the enumeration are 9-18% faster, and the plain-object shape (the one ordinary code enumerates) benefits most because its two-link chain is now inline.

Enumeration order was diffed against node across eight shapes (index keys before strings, literal order, non-enumerable and symbol keys skipped, prototype chains, a shadowed prototype key, delete during enumeration, null prototype).

## LANDED (2026-10-25): a creation site resolves its source texts once

The phase profile above measured `shared_source_info` at 75 ns per closure, per closure it walked the execution-context stack for the enclosing text, cloned that text, **hashed the function's own source slice**, and probed a thread-local cache, all of which are fixed for a creation site.

`Step::CreateFunction` and `Step::CreateArrow` now carry an `OnceCell<Option<Rc<SourceInfo>>>`. The first creation resolves it (in the creating frame's context, the same context the old per-creation resolution used, and the frame that carries the text) and stores it; every later creation from that site is a `OnceCell::get` plus an `Rc` clone. `Some(None)` is stored too, so a source-less site is not re-walked. `instantiate_function_expression_with_source` / `instantiate_arrow_with_source` take the resolved value; the old entry points delegate with `None`, so every non-step caller (the tree-walker, modules, snapshots, `new Function`, class members) is unchanged. `Step::FunctionDeclInit` still resolves per creation, a declaration is created once per evaluation, not per loop iteration, and it was left for a follow-up.

Measured with two binaries, alternating order, 7 rounds, mins:

| probe | before | after | min |

| `e7` 300k closures | 92.31 ms | **77.97** | **-15.5%** (305 → 260 ns each) |
| `e5` the same, called | 134.56 | **119.27** | -11.4% |
| `p14` 3 closures/body, no loop | 147.90 | **128.26** | -13.3% |
| `p19` one capturing closure | 110.91 | **101.69** | -8.3% |
| the for-in corpus row | 459.61 | **427.16** | **-7.1%** |

`e7` is now **below** the 85 ms stop rule in `.notes/closure-cost-plan.md` (77.97), so that plan's arena-record stage (Stage D) is no longer blocked by it, a later session can re-open it. `Function.prototype.toString` and error stacks were diffed against node for anonymous, named, and block-bodied closures and arrows created in a loop.

## LANDED (2026-10-25): a function declaration reuses its site's source texts too

The `Step::CreateFunction`/`CreateArrow` source cell left one creation path on the old per-creation resolution: `Step::FunctionDeclInit`, which is the hot one for declarations, a body-level `function inner() {}` instantiates its closure on **every call** of the enclosing body, so the enclosing-text walk and the slice hash ran per call.

The variant now carries the same `OnceCell<Option<Rc<SourceInfo>>>`, filled at the three emit sites (a block-level declaration, a statement-position one, and the hoisted body-level one) and read by both the interpreter arm and the JIT's `create_function_decl`; those go through `instantiate_function_with_resolved_source`, which already existed. That completes the pattern, every step-based creation path resolves once per site.

## LANDED (2026-10-25): for-in enumerates a vector-free object from its map

The residual in `for_in_key_levels` was `JsObject::own_string_props`: it called `materialize_properties` first, rebuilding the property vector of a **vector-free** object from its map (one allocation, a descriptor walk, and a state change that pushed later stores onto the slower `map_set` scan), then staged the keys in a vector of its own, and `key_value` boxed each key.

`JsObject::for_each_own_string_prop` visits the keys in place and reads a vector-free object straight from its map: a written descriptor is an own property (a presize hole is not), and the descriptor ordinal order is creation order, because `define_fresh` materializes before any fill that would land out of order. It serves the whole enumeration or **declines before visiting anything** (`false`), and `for_in_key_levels` then falls back to `own_string_props` (an object with an array-index key, where the map order is not the spec order, and every exotic object).

That decline ordering is load-bearing and cost a regression: the first version checked each key as it visited and returned `false` when it reached an index key, so a vector-authoritative object with `p2, p4` before `0, 1, 2` had the strings visited, declined, and the fallback emitted them again, test262's `statements/for-in/order-simple-object` caught it. The vector path now scans for an index key before the first visit; the unit test pins both the order and the "no partial visit" invariant.

Two binaries, alternating order, 7 rounds, mins:

| probe | before | after | min |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| fresh 3-key null-prototype object | 86.24 ms | **75.99** | **-11.9%** |
| fresh 3-key plain object | 107.16 | **89.33** | **-16.6%** |
| the for-in corpus row | 408.21 | **397.26** | -2.7% |

Across this session's three for-in changes the fresh 3-key null-prototype enumeration is 97.07 -> 75.99 ms (-21.7%) and the plain-object one 129.42 -> 89.33 (-31%).

## NULL (2026-10-25): boxing the function record into the arena is a regression

A second attempt at Stage D (`.notes/closure-cost-plan.md`), this time as the minimal change the 2026-10-20 measurement left open: `AgentRoots::ecma_functions` becomes `RefCell<IdMap<Handle<EcmaFunction>>>`, `register_ecma_function` allocates the record with `Handle::new(data)` inside the mutable borrow (so a `--gc-stress` collection aborts the sweep rather than collecting the record before its entry makes it reachable), and `ecma_function`/`ecma_function_mut` return a copied handle instead of a borrow guard. The rationale was that creation becomes one bump allocation plus a small insert, and reads become a pointer dereference with no 300-byte copy.

Two binaries (`slag-enum3.exe` = HEAD `82470a1d`, `slag-staged.exe`), alternating order, 7 rounds, mins:

| probe | before | after | min |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| the for-in corpus row | 396 ms | **715** | **+80.6%** |
| `p14` 3 closures/body, no loop |, |, | +19.5% |
| `d1` body-level declaration |, |, | +20.2% |
| `e7` 300k closures |, |, | +11.8% |
| `e5` the same, called |, |, | **-10.7%** |

Only the called probe improved; everything dominated by *creation* regressed, which is the opposite of the hypothesis.

`--gc-trace` on the for-in row gives the mechanism. Inline record (`before`): `live=6921`, **one** major collection, minor pauses averaging **101 µs**. Arena box (`after`): `live=307009`, **two** major collections with **9.7 ms** and **19.3 ms** pauses, minor pauses averaging **56 µs**. The box is traced from the map, so every record is promoted out of the nursery on its first minor and retained until `reap_dead_functions` removes its entry; the old generation fills and the majors are paid. The inline `IdMap` insert, by contrast, frees the replaced record synchronously, the allocator does the work the collector now has to do, and it does it at the 300k-closures scale where it is cheapest.

A second cost the small-value steady state hid: `IdMap` reallocates roughly three times more often with a 304-byte value than with an 8-byte handle.

**Plan-level conclusion.** Stage D cannot be "the same `IdMap`, but boxed", that shape is strictly worse. It has to move the record onto the `Function` object as a traced field (V8's JSFunction → SharedFunctionInfo), so the record dies with its object and the table becomes only an id→function index (not an owner that promotes every record). That is a different, larger change and remains unmeasured.

The experiment is reverted (`crates/runtime/src/agent.rs`, `crates/runtime/src/function.rs` restored to `82470a1d`).

## PROFILE (2026-10-25): the non-leaf activation, and the inline splice's feedback starvation

The last row target from the 2026-10-25 decomposition is the non-leaf activation (a call inside a body costs ~50-105 ns more per invocation than a leaf body). Measured at `82470a1d` (binary `befb0e02`), 100k iterations, min of five runs, both modes:

| probe | JIT | jitless |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `o2` the loop calls a leaf body | 4.93 ms (4.9 ns/call) |, |
| `o5` the loop calls a body that calls a leaf | 5.73 ms (**57 ns/call**) | 24.0 ms (**240 ns/call**) |
| `o4` the loop calls a body that calls `Math.abs` | 8.94 ms (**89 ns/call**) |, |

So the JIT's certified-call lane is ~52 ns above the leaf lane, and the interpreter's is ~235. The two lanes were read rather than guessed at:

- **JIT** (`certified_lane_inline`, `crates/runtime/src/jit.rs:2235`): one `ecma_functions` probe and an `Rc` clone, the `CertifiedInlineInfo` validation, `save_scratch`/`restore_scratch` (~25 saved scalars plus four stack truncations each way), a 7-field env swap, a `vm.stack` carve plus a per-slot frame fill, **a whole ~430-byte nested `JitCallContext` built field by field**, `jit_depth` inc/dec, and the compiled entry.
- **Interpreter** (`Vm::run_certified_call_nested`, `crates/runtime/src/ir.rs:7790`): the same list plus `new_body_context`, an `ExecutionContext` push/pop, and `run_compiled_body_on` -> `run_jit_body`, which builds a *second* per-run context.

The lane is ~100 stores of per-activation state. The one structural idea, reuse the caller's `JitCallContext` in place instead of building a nested one, is worse: 20 fields differ (so 20 saves + 20 sets + 20 restores, 60 stores) to replace a 38-field construction. Only two fields are outright redundant (`vm.current_function`/`vm.body_context` are re-stored by `run_compiled_body_on` after the nested lane already set them), worth ~2 ns. **No single removable block; the lane is not the next lever.**

### Why the call rows cannot be closed by the call lane anyway

`calls/direct_leaf` (2M iterations) is 12.0 ms = **6 ns per iteration** against V8's 1.1 ms = 0.55 ns. V8 inlines the callee into the loop; Slag's leaf lane is already ~5 ns/call, so the row's gap is inlining, not the lane.

`SLAG_INLINE`'s splice cannot supply it. `sites_from_feedback` (`crates/jit/src/opt/pass/inline.rs:48`) reads `CompiledBody::feedback`, which only the **interpreter's** `observe_*` steps write (`crates/runtime/src/ir.rs:2234`). Cut 69 compiles a loop body on its **first consult** (`lookup_info_compiles_loop_bodies_on_the_first_consult`), i.e. before it has run a single interpreted iteration. A call site inside any loop body therefore has no feedback, `IcState::Specialized` is never reached, and `sites_from_feedback` returns `None` for every site. Verified, not inferred:

- `SLAG_FEEDBACK=1` over the whole `calls` family reports **2 sites / 6 hits**, with six workloads, that is the non-loop bodies only.
- `SLAG_FEEDBACK=1 SLAG_INLINE=1` on `direct_leaf` reads 12.2-12.3 ms against 12.0-12.3 ms default: no movement.
- The splice machinery is also weak where feedback *does* exist: a straight-line hot body whose call is its block's last instruction (`z3`) reports one inlinable site and moves only 11.58 -> 10.89 ms (-6%), so the pass is not yet a complete answer even with a site map. Open question, not a conclusion.

A lazy-compile policy does not fix this shape either: a benchmark loop body is one activation, so there is no "next entry" at which a feedback-driven recompile could happen. Closing `calls/*` needs a call site inside a compiled loop body to be inlinable **without** feedback, either static resolution (a `CallFast` whose callee slot is written once by a `FunctionDeclInit` in the same body and never otherwise, and whose callee is a capture-free leaf, so no guard is needed) or true OSR plus compiled-code feedback. The first is the smaller change and reuses the existing `Callee`/splice machinery; it is the next session's candidate, not this one's.

Probes: `scratch/ab/calllane/`, `scratch/ab/inl/`, and `scratch/ab/nullproto/{o2,o4,o5}` (git-ignored).

## NULL (2026-10-25): mid-block splicing, a latent miscompile in the splice, and why the box guard cannot inline fresh closures

The queued static-inline item was started with the piece that does not need new analysis: `try_inline` no longer requires the call to be its block's last instruction, so the ubiquitous `s += f(x)` shape can splice. The instructions after the call move to the continuation block. Unit-tested (`splices_a_call_that_is_not_its_blocks_terminator`, verified IR), and the whole-corpus measurement under `SLAG_FEEDBACK=1 SLAG_INLINE=1` first read `calls/recursive_fib.js` **49.8 -> 3.16 ms (-93.6%)**. That number is **withdrawn: it was a miscompile** (the bench value changed from 656700 to 42900).

### The latent bug the shape exposed

The splice guarded the assumed callee with `Op::GuardCallee`, whose failure path is a *deopt*: it mirrors `inst.args[2..]` (the call's operands) into the working region and resumes the interpreter at the call step. For a mid-block call that stack is wrong, the step's operand stack also holds every value the enclosing expression already evaluated (`fib(n-1)` in `fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`, `s` in `s += f(x)`), so the interpreter resumed with a truncated stack and produced a different program. Verified four ways: the deopt trace shows the guard firing (`jit-deopt step=17 depth=3`, 3,856 times), the budget bisect puts the break between 16 and 24 (the third expansion level), `SLAG_OPT=0` computes the right value (no splice), and the under-limit builds all compute it too.

The guard is only sound when nothing else is live at the step, which is exactly what the old last-instruction restriction happened to guarantee. So the splice now emits **no deopt at all**: `Op::CalleeEq` (a new pure IR op, one `icmp Equal` on the bits) plus a `Term::Branch` to a fallback block that performs the ordinary call and jumps to the continuation. Correct for any shape, and a spliced body stays deopt-free, which keeps it eligible for the certified-callee lane.

### Why it still does not pay

With the guard sound, the corpus (5 interleaved rounds, per-row minimum, flags on vs off, parity 0 across all 77 rows):

| row | off | on | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `calls/recursive_fib.js` | 60.08 ms | 56.32 | -6.3% |
| `calls/method_call.js` | 62.87 | 58.92 | -6.3% |
| `calls/direct_leaf.js` | 13.33 | 12.53 | -6.0% |
| `opcost/array_indexof.js` | 2.15 | 2.05 | -4.8% |
| `objects/warm_store.js` | 39.30 | 37.43 | -4.7% |
| `objects/spread_assign.js` | 137.66 | 154.82 | **+12.5%** |
| `opcost/regexp_test.js` | 35.48 | 40.41 | **+13.9%** |
| `strings/split_join.js` | 63.77 | 75.18 | **+17.9%** |
| `opcost/json_stringify.js` | 90.40 | 108.86 | **+20.4%** |
| `strings/coercion_concat.js` | 66.35 | 79.94 | **+20.5%** |
| `opcost/object_keys.js` | 45.52 | 56.36 | **+23.8%** |

The guard compares the callee against a box baked at **compile time**. A closure created per invocation of the enclosing function (the common shape, `fib` inside `bench`) never matches after the first invocation, so the site takes the fallback from then on, and the fallback is not cheaper than the leaf lane the site already had. That is the whole regression: the feature pays only where the callee identity is stable across invocations (a top-level function, a long-lived closure), and loses where it is not.

So the feedback/box-guard design cannot deliver this. The sound path is the one this session queued: a call whose callee slot is written once by a `FunctionDeclInit` in the same body and never otherwise is *provably* the closure that step creates, so the splice needs no guard and no feedback. That still needs (a) the callee's `CompiledBody` at the caller's compile time, from the declaration's AST through the same `shared_function_body`/`shared_compiled_body` keys the runtime uses, and (b) a scope-aware proof that the slot is not reassigned. Both are unbuilt.

State: the mid-block splice and the deopt-free fallback are landed behind the same `SLAG_INLINE` gate (off by default, so no behaviour change); the box-guard path remains measurably mixed and must not be enabled without the static analysis.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites, 5,843 passed, 0 failed); sweeps `language` 23,726 + `built-ins` 23,821 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0 (77 rows, flags on and off).

## LANDED (2026-10-25): a declared callee splices with no check at all

The NULL above ended on the blocker: the box guard cannot inline a closure created per invocation, so the splice needed the callee's identity proven at compile time. It is now proven from the body's own steps, and the splice needs **no comparison and no feedback**.

`CompiledBody::declared_calls` holds `(call step, declaration step)` pairs, computed by `compile_body`. A call qualifies when all of these hold:

- its callee is a frame slot (`CallFastSlot`/`CallFastSlotStore`);
- exactly one `FunctionDeclInit` in the body writes that slot, so no other declaration, block-level or a reused slot, shares it;
- that declaration is one of the **hoisted body-entry** ones `compile_body` emits before any statement, so it dominates every call;
- the declared name is never assigned (`collect_script_assigned`: `var f = …`, `f = …`, `f++`, a for-of head), the only thing that could overwrite the closure after the init;
- the callee, compiled from the declaration through the same `shared_function_body`/`shared_params` keys `register_function` uses, is a certified leaf that reads no environment (`leaf && !leaf_uses_env`).

Every test is conservative, a body that does anything unusual is left unspliced. `resolve_declaration` builds the record exactly as `register_function` does (name from the atom, site-shared params/body, the declaration's own `"use strict"` OR the enclosing body's, the step's chains) and compiles it through `compile_body`, so the IR the splice clones is the IR the closure runs; `a_declared_callee_resolves_to_the_runtime_body` asserts the two bodies agree on step count and frame layout.

The splice then jumps straight into the cloned body, no `Op::CalleeEq`, no fallback call, so the body stays deopt-free.

Measured, two binaries (same HEAD with `SLAG_INLINE=0`), 5 interleaved rounds, per-row minimum, all 77 rows' results identical:

| row | off | on | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `calls/direct_leaf.js` | 12.29 ms | **5.87** | **-52.2%** |
| every other row |, |, | within ±3% (this host's noise) |

`node tools/corpus/bench.js` (one interleaved round, all four engine/mode combinations, `mismatches 0`): the `calls` family gap is 9.09x (the README records 9.57x) and the `direct_leaf` row is 6.70x (10.47x), on a 12.0 -> 7.7 ms row. The overall gap reads 10.45x, inside this host's noise band, so the family table is left at its recorded commit.

Seams: `SLAG_INLINE` is now **on** by default (`=0` disables it, the same-binary A/B used above). The feedback-recorded (guarded) sites moved behind their own `SLAG_INLINE_FEEDBACK` switch, default **off**, because they are measured mixed, a closure created per invocation never matches the compile-time box, so those sites pay a comparison and then the fallback call (+24% on `object_keys` in the NULL above).

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites, 5,844 passed, 0 failed); sweeps `language` 23,726 + `built-ins` 23,821 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0 (77 rows, splice on and off).

## CORRECTION (2026-10-25): the assignment collector missed `for-in`/`try`/`switch` bodies

The declared-callee proof above reads `collect_script_assigned` as "the declared name is never assigned". That collector treated `ForIn`, `Try`, `Switch`, `ClassDecl`, `With` and `UsingDecl` as no-ops, so a body that reassigned its callee inside one of those statements could still be recorded as a declared site, a latent wrong-program bug in a feature that had just been enabled by default. Found by writing the refuse-shapes test: `for (var k in { a: 0 }) { f = function () {}; }` before the callee's loop still produced one site.

It had not miscompiled in the shapes tried by hand (a caller with `for-in`/`try`/`switch` did not reach the splice, verified by running both the stale-body and the throwing variants), but "it did not fire" is not a proof, and the site list is a compile-time claim.

The collector now walks all of them: a `for-in` head's target and body, a `switch` discriminant and every case, `try`/`catch`/`finally`, a class declaration's name, a `using` declaration's bindings, and a `with` body (conservatively). Over-approximating is always sound for a never-assigned check, and the collector also feeds the script epilogue's write-back set and the `CallFastGlobal` fuse, where a larger set is conservative in the same direction.

`declared_sites_skip_a_callee_the_body_reassigns` pins it: the unassigned shape yields exactly one site, and `=`, a braced `for-in` body, a bare `for-in` head, `switch`, `try`, and a write from a nested closure each yield zero.

**Context-slot callees: not pursued.** Extending the proof to a *captured* declaration would allow a call whose callee lives in the capture context. Two things make it a bad trade: such a call is not fused (the compiler emits a separate `LoadContextSlot` and a generic `Call`, so the step list does not name the slot at the call), and the shape that motivated it, `fib`'s own recursion inside `bench`, resolves its declaration from an **enclosing** body, which a body-local analysis cannot see at all. That recursion is already served at run time by the G21 self-call lane. Nothing is left for a context-slot splice to buy.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites, 5,846 passed, 0 failed); sweeps 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0 (77 rows, splice on and off), and `calls/direct_leaf.js` still 5.78 ms.

## PROFILE (2026-10-25): the two ~15x rows, `objects/warm_store` and `control/generator_loop`

Both were taken as targets because they sit at ~15x node. Both turn out to be bounded by their design, not by a missing fast path, and the measurements below are the evidence.

### `objects/warm_store`: the store is the guard set, and node's number is elimination

The row is `o.d = i; s += o.d;` over 4M iterations on one stable object. Ablations (JIT, 4M iterations, min of three):

| probe | ms | per iteration |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| bare loop (`s += i`) | 3.04 | 0.76 ns |
| the row's read only (`s += o.d + i`) | 9.92 | **1.7 ns per read** |
| the row's store only (`o.d = i; s += i`) | 25.40 | **5.6 ns per store** |
| the row | 36.59 | 9.1 ns |

`JIT_HELPER_STATS` shows `set_member_name` **once** and `set_member_slot` **zero** times: the store is entirely inline after the first iteration (the shape-cell hit → the deferred field-update gate), so the 5.6 ns is the generated gate itself, the `member_map_cells` probe, the `props_deferred` bit, the written/writable/inline-ordinal checks, the barrier check (young receiver or non-heap value) and the not-global check, then the field write plus the four-store value-cell refresh (the no-bump discipline). ~45 instructions with several dependent loads.

One redundant step was tried and is a NULL: `emit_member_store` probes the shape cell, then `emit_deferred_update_store` re-derived the same map id and cell address. Passing the probe's cell through measured **-1.7% on the store probe (26.41 -> 25.42 ms min) and -0.2% on the row**, Cranelift was already CSE-ing the repeated loads, so it was reverted rather than kept for unmeasurable code.

node's 2.3 ms is 0.58 ns for store+read+add, which is not a cheaper store: the object does not escape the function, so it eliminates the store, the read and the loop. Slag has no escape analysis, and a guarded store + a cache-served read cannot be made 10x cheaper by shaving instructions. This row moves only when the tier can eliminate the access, not when the access gets faster.

### `control/generator_loop`: the resume machinery, not the loop side

200k `g.next()` calls cost ~170 ns each, and the loop side is **not** where it goes. The row's shape puts `bench`'s own locals in the capture context (a nested function declaration), so its body is refused by the optimizing tier on one step, `UpdateContextSlot`. Moving the generator to the script scope makes that body lift cleanly (only the generator's own `Yield` refuses), and the row then reads **34.14 -> 33.16 ms (-2.9%)**, so the per-step member read and call dispatch are worth ~3%, and the remaining ~165 ns per `next()` is the resume path: the handler dispatch, the `agent.generators` lookup, the `{value, done}` object, and the suspend/resume (a fresh Rust -> JIT entry per resume, `.notes/rust-initiated-call-plan.md`). That matches the 2026-10-21 note's ~137 ns with drift.

Lifting `UpdateContextSlot` would therefore buy ~3% on this row, and it is not free: an earlier session lifted it and `built-ins/Iterator/zip/basic-longest.js` failed under `sweep all`, recoverable only by `SLAG_GUARD=0`/`SLAG_TYPER=0`, a typer read-guard bug on a newly-lifted body, unaffected by reordering the passes or widening the guard's type-sensitive set. A 3% row is not worth that class of compiler bug until the guard bug is understood.

Both rows are left as they are. What they need is named: `warm_store` needs inlining/escape analysis (or a compiled store cell keyed by object id, which the interpreter already has and the JIT deliberately does not read); `generator_loop` needs a cheaper resume entry, not more lifting.

## NULL (2026-10-25): a compiled object-keyed store cell buys 0.3%

The `warm_store` note above says the store is ~45 instructions of gate. The obvious response is to give the compiled store the interpreter's L1a cell, an object-keyed `(id, name) -> (generation, field)` record, so a warm store skips the map probe, the `props_deferred` bit and the written/writable/ordinal checks and is one guarded field write plus the value-cell refresh. That was built: a `MemberFieldCell` table on `AgentRoots` (16 direct-mapped entries, `#[repr(C)]` for the compiled probe), a `member_field_cells` pointer in `JitCallContext`, a probe ahead of the shape probe in `emit_member_store`, and a record on the two warm arms (a value write changes none of the recorded fields, so a hit never re-records). The read ABI (`MemberValueCell`) was left untouched, and the field ordinal is re-checked against `INLINE_FIELDS` so a stale cell falls back rather than writing out of bounds.

It measures **nothing**: 5-round interleaved mins against the same HEAD, the store probe 24.92 -> 24.84 ms (**-0.3%**) and the row 35.45 -> 35.26 ms (**-0.5%**), both inside this host's A/B floor. The instruction count was not the limit: the store's ~45 instructions are several independent L1 load chains, and the CPU already overlaps them; the new probe is *also* a load chain, so removing 25 instructions and adding 10 changes nothing. Reverted rather than kept: it is a new table, a new ctx field and a new recording discipline for no measurable effect.

What this leaves: the row is not instruction-bound and not gate-bound. Its 8.9 ns per iteration is a latency chain (the store's probe feeds the value-cell refresh, which feeds the next read) plus the loop's float-carried counter, and node's 0.58 ns is escape analysis. A store cell would matter only if the probe chain were shortened by more than the new probe costs, i.e. by hoisting it out of the loop, which is the guard-as-IR-op work, not a cell.

## PROFILE (2026-10-25): the `UpdateContextSlot` lift's guard-pruning miscompile, narrowed

The `control/generator_loop` note above prices lifting `UpdateContextSlot` at ~3% and refuses it on a known miscompile. The repro is still live and was narrowed this session.

Lifting it (ContextLoad -> UpdateValue -> ContextStore, exactly the `UpdateLocal` shape over the helpers, `stack_delta` +1) makes `built-ins/Iterator/zip/basic-longest.js` fail: *"Expected arrays to contain the same values at index 1"*. Attribution, each a filtered sweep over `Iterator/zip`:

| switch | result |
| --- | --- |
| none (lifted) | **FAIL** |
| `SLAG_GUARD=0` (read-guard *pruning* off, guards still emitted) | pass |
| `SLAG_TYPER=0` (no guards emitted) | pass |
| `SLAG_UNBOX=0`, `SLAG_INLINE=0`, `SLAG_WIDEN=0`, `SLAG_MEM2REG=0` | **FAIL** |

So it is `guard::run`'s pruning, not the guard's emission and not the new ops. The IR diff of the failing body (dumped with `JIT_DUMP_IR=1`, pruned vs `SLAG_GUARD=0`) shows pruning removing two `GuardType`s whose results only feed call arguments, and, with each of them, a `FrameStore(v36) slot7` that `mem2reg` had emitted *before* that guard as the promoted-slot materialization (`slot7` is never loaded by the IR, so once the guard goes the store looks dead and DCE removes it). The suspicion is therefore in the interaction, not in the lift: either a materialization that a *later* resume still needs, or `narrow`'s numeric-slot proof (which reads the guard) surviving a step whose guard is then removed. Not proven; the micro-reductions tried so far (a captured counter read through an array) compute correctly.

Not landed. The lift stays refused with its comment pointing here until the interaction is understood; it is a ~3% row and a wrong-value bug is not a trade.

Gates for this commit: docs only, plus the two reverted experiments; the tree's code is the commit that passed fmt/clippy/40 suites/51,998 sweeps.

## FIX (2026-10-26): the `UpdateContextSlot` lift, and a leaf record keyed on a recycled box

The lift is landed. The `built-ins/Iterator/zip/basic-longest.js` failure it exposed is not the guard-pruning / DCE interaction the earlier profile suspected: `SLAG_GUARD=0` and `SLAG_TYPER=0` only decided whether the body stayed compiled. With the optimizing tier off (`SLAG_OPT=0`) the failure persisted, and `--jitless` passed, so the per-step JIT's call lane had it too.

Root cause: `LeafCallRecord` identified a callee by its NaN-boxed `Value` bits, i.e. the `Function` box address. The GC recycles boxes. A probe recorded the numbers padding closure's compiled entry at an address, that closure died, a different padding closure (`function () { return undefined; }`) was allocated at the same address, and the machine-code gate matched on the prefix, the payload, `code_gen` and the epoch, so the call ran the dead callee's entry. The fixture's `expected` array then held `100 + j` where it should have held `undefined`. The closure-creation trace showed one box-bits value with two different function ids over a short run.

Fix: the record carries the callee's stable `Function::id`, and the in-frame hit path, the only machine-code path that jumps straight to a cached entry, loads the id from the box and compares it. The load is safe there because a nonzero cached entry names a compiled ECMAScript leaf, never a builtin or a non-function. The fill and env helpers (`record_matches`) and the certified lane already keyed on the function id, so they were not the hole.

Tests: `a_leaf_record_rejects_a_recycled_box` (runtime) pins the identity discriminator; `lifts_update_context_slot` replaces the refusal test; the three `installed_jit_*` cache-reuse tests still count a handful of probes, so the extra check does not defeat the cache.

Gates: fmt; clippy `-D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites, 5,847 passed, 0 failed); sweeps 23,726 + 23,821 + 1,086 + 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0 (77 rows, mismatches 0).

### Measured (2026-10-26): the lift, and the id check

Two release binaries (`68c54706` and this tree), 7 interleaved rounds per family, per-row minimum: `control/generator_loop.js` **34.08 -> 33.00 ms (-3.2%)**, the parked estimate. The other `control` rows are flat (for_in +1.0%, nested_loops +0.1%, switch -0.3%, try_catch +1.2%). The `calls` family read -0.4% to +3.6% across two 7-round passes, so the check itself was measured with a same-binary gate (a temporary `SLAG_LEAF_NO_ID` switch, since removed): `direct_leaf.js` +0.0%, `method_call.js` +1.6%, `closure_capture.js` +1.4%, `construct_churn.js` +0.5%, `apply_call.js` -0.9%, against an A/A floor of +-1.4% on those rows. The larger two-binary deltas are code layout, not the check.

### AUDIT (2026-10-26): no second instance of the box-identity class

The guarded feedback splice looks like the same trap: `Op::CalleeEq` compares the callee against a compile-time box constant (`InlineTarget::Guarded::callee_box`). It is sound, because the feedback store retains the first callee as a `Value` and `CompiledBody::trace` traces that store, so the box cannot be recycled while the code that names it exists (I5c-2c-ii in `.notes/optimizing-tier-impl.md`). Everything else keys on something stable: the certified and leaf lookups on `Function::id`, the member/global cells on object ids and generations, the call-site monomorphism log on the permanent shared-body pointer, and the self-call gate on two live values. `LeafCallRecord` was the only instance.

That is the next slice, because it needs no JIT-entry work and every `next()` pays it.

The profile above put ~82 ns of every `next()` in the driver, not the resume, so the first slice took the cheapest part of it: the `AgentRoots::generators` table used the default `HashMap` (SipHash) for a single-`u64` key, and `GeneratorResume` read the flag under one borrow and then took a second for the run. ## LANDED (2026-10-26): the engine reports why bodies are not compiled, and PGO measured

Two of the pillars in `.notes/bottleneck-method.md` are now real.

### The counters

`JIT_HELPER_STATS` printed `helper <index> <count>`, which is unreadable without
the enum order to hand. The compiler now records `Helper::name()` beside the
increment it emits, so the dump is `helper <index> <count> <name>`. The name
array lives in `HelperCounts` beside the counts, is written only when the
instrument is on, and is filled by both emitters (`compiler.rs` and
`opt_lower.rs`).

`SLAG_JIT_REPORT` is a new census: every body the compiler refuses, one row per
`(tier, reason)` with body and step counts, then the compiled and deopt totals.
`tier=opt` means the optimizing tier refused and the baseline tier compiled it
anyway; `tier=none` means no tier produced code. A lift refusal is named from
the body's blocker census, so a row reads `SwitchTest` rather than `step`.

`tools/opcount.sh` runs every workload in its own process (a `--corpus` run
sums all rows into one process, so it cannot attribute) and prints the rows as
TSV, ready to sort or diff between builds.

Reading it turned up three placeholder names in `step_name`: the compound
member stores and the two LICM hoist guards were all reported as the generic
`step`, so five rows came out with an empty reason. They are named now. Those
five are the hoist guard, which the lift refuses on purpose (it models the
guard as an always-miss, a measured pessimization), so the census now says that
instead of leaving a blank.

20 of 77 rows have at least one body the optimizing tier refuses:

| row | blocker | steps |

### The generator row, by count

`JIT_HELPER_STATS` on the 200k `next()` probe, per iteration:

| helper | per iteration |
| --- | ---: |

So a `next()` is one member-name read, one general call, two context loads, one
