### PGO: measured, and large

Method: `-Cprofile-generate`, train by running the 77-row corpus plus the
scratch probes once, `llvm-profdata merge` (the copy bundled with the
toolchain), rebuild with `-Cprofile-use`. Both builds are the release profile
(`lto = "thin"`, `codegen-units = 1`); the only difference is the profile.

7 interleaved rounds over the full corpus, per-row minima:

| | ms | |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| no PGO | 2114.2 | |
| PGO | 1697.3 | **-19.72%** |

- mean per-row ratio **0.8905**, median **0.9246**;
- twelve rows improve 24-36% (`hof_methods` -35.8, `typed_array_for_each` -35.0,
  `map_for_each` -33.0, `spread_assign` -31.5, `num_valueof` -31.3,
  `array_for_each` -30.1, `construct_churn` -28.8, `generator_loop` -28.4,
  `for-in/head-let` -26.8, `array_slice` -26.3, `json_stringify` -24.7);
- the worst row is +0.5% (`nested_loops`); seven rows are within +0.2%.

The A/A control is what makes this a measurement rather than a layout wobble:
two non-PGO builds of the same source, same 7 rounds, give total **+0.33%**,
mean ratio 0.9969, worst row +2.8%. Build-to-build noise is an order of
magnitude smaller than the PGO delta at the total, and a third of it per row.

Two honest limits:

- the profile was trained on the corpus, so part of the gain is fitting the
  benchmark. The next measurement is to train on Goats (and one tsc run) and
  evaluate *there*, before this is wired into the release build;
- PGO changes layout, so it cannot be mixed into an A/B of another change. It
  lands as its own change, with its own before and after, and the profile
  becomes a build input that is regenerated when the corpus changes.

Not wired in yet. The experiment is reproducible in about ten minutes: two
builds and one training pass.

--workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites,
5,847 passed, 0 failed); sweeps `language` 23,726 + `built-ins` 23,821 +
`annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%; corpus parity 0 (77 rows,

### PGO: validated off the training set

The -19.7% above was trained on the corpus it was measured on. Retrained with
`opcost` (36 of the 77 rows) held out entirely, then measured:

| rows | total | mean ratio |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| held out (36 `opcost` rows) | 356.8 -> 315.5 ms, **-11.56%** | 0.9598 |
| trained on (41 rows) | 1725.5 -> 1411.3 ms, -18.20% | 0.8993 |
| all 77 | 2082.2 -> 1726.9 ms, -17.07% | 0.9276 |

Roughly two thirds of the effect survives on code the profiler never saw, which
is what branch layout doing its job looks like; the rest is the profile being
tuned to the rows it was gathered from. Three held-out micro rows get worse
(`array_indexof` +19%, `array_fill` +11%, `array_reverse` +11%), all of them
~2 ms rows where layout is close to a coin flip.

`tools/pgo.sh --train` reproduces the whole thing: instrumented build, training
over the given workloads, `llvm-profdata merge`, optimized build. It writes the
profile to `target/pgo.profdata` and the binary to `target/pgo/release/`, and
leaves `target/release` alone. A second run reproduced -19.67%, so the recipe is
stable.

Not made the default. PGO moves layout, so it cannot be mixed into an A/B of
another change; it roughly doubles the build; and the profile is a build input
that has to be regenerated when the corpus moves. Adopting it is a decision
about the project's reported numbers, not only about speed.

## PROFILE (2026-10-26): PGO is a diagnostic, and it says 71% of our hot code never runs

PGO stays off by default (decided: a customer build, not the shipped one). But
its size is itself information: `-Cprofile-use` only changes branch weights,
layout and inlining choices, so a 17-20% win means the static shape of the hot
code disagrees with the dynamic path.

The profile that `tools/pgo.sh --train` already produces can be interrogated
directly, with no new build and no sampler:

```
llvm-profdata show --all-functions --counts target/pgo.profdata
```

Per function it prints the instrumented block counters. A block whose count is
zero is code that is laid out inside a function the workload *does* enter, and
never runs.

**Headline, over the whole corpus: of 155,677 static blocks in the 17,106
functions the workload enters, 110,341 never execute (70.9%).** That is the
mismatch PGO is paid to fix.

Read the table as "hot static code", not as call counts: a block's count is its
entries, so a loop's blocks count once per iteration. That matters below, where
it is what exposes the finding.

| entries | blocks | never run | function |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 987,910,221 | 4 | 0% | `Vec::resize` |
| 765,549,553 | 11 | 27% | `Value::kind` |
| 549,830,384 | 19 | 26% | `Vm::chain_cell_read` |
| 462,436,650 | 39 | 56% | **`crux::string::lookup`** |
| 459,553,639 | 54 | 44% | **`crux::string::intern`** |
| 433,601,239 | 13 | 46% | `JsString::from_utf8` |
| 429,178,417 | 76 | 61% | `jit::call_slow` |
| 396,186,576 | 62 | 35% | `Vm::get_member_name` |
| 362,378,618 | 54 | 46% | `JsObject::ordinary_property_lookup` |
| 307,521,852 | 245 | 78% | `Heap::collect_minor_inner` |
| 265,488,602 | 129 | 77% | `jit::certified_lane_inline` |
| 185,137,525 | 21 | 57% | `heap::with_heap_cell` closure |
| 136,139,354 | 32 | **94%** | `heap::maybe_stress_collect` |
| 109,775,244 | 29 | 83% | `Vm::context_chain_env` |
| 104,306,192 | 49 | 82% | `CompiledBody::has_lane_step_hazard` |

### Finding 1: the atom memo is a 64-entry linear scan on the hottest path

`crux::string::lookup` (AtomId to JsString) and `crux::string::intern` (the
reverse) are the second and third hottest engine functions by block entries, and
44-56% of their blocks never run. The blocks that do run are a loop:
`memo.iter().rev().find(...)` over a per-thread `Vec` with `MEMO_CAP = 64`,
under a `RefCell` borrow, cloning the `JsString` on every hit.

Block entries are iteration counts, which is exactly the evidence this table
gives: 462M entries in `lookup` is not 462M calls, it is calls times the scan
length. The memo was added because the interner takes a global lock and
copies; it converted that into a linear search of up to 64 entries, and the
search is now one of the three hottest code paths in the engine.

The fix is small and local: a direct-mapped cell keyed by the atom id
(`id % N`, validated by comparing the id) for `lookup`, which turns the hit path
into one compare and a refcount bump, and a keyed direct-mapped cell for
`intern` (hash the units, compare the candidate). Both keep the existing
fallback, so a miss costs what it costs today. This is the single change the
profile argues for most strongly.

### Finding 2: the cold half of hot functions can be outlined by hand

The functions with the worst cold share are not big dispatch functions where
cold code is expected; they are small predicates and accessors on the hot path:

- `heap::maybe_stress_collect` at **94% cold**, 136M entries. Its fast path is
  one TLS flag read; everything else (the collector call, the TLS accessor
  internals) is inline in it, and is entered for every allocation in a stress
  run and never otherwise.
- `Vm::context_chain_env` 83%, `CompiledBody::has_lane_step_hazard` 82%,
  `jit::certified_lane_inline` 77%, `collect_minor_inner` 78%, `call_slow` 61%.

Outlining those arms into `#[cold] #[inline(never)]` helpers is the hand
version of the transformation PGO chooses, and unlike PGO it needs no profile at
build time. It is a batch job, not a single change: one outlined branch will not
move a corpus total, so it should be judged on the sum of a set, with the
block-count table in this entry as the work list.

### What this changes about the plan

PGO is priced now and stays on the shelf. The method it justified (counters,
then this) produced two candidate changes that are structural rather than
incremental: the memo scan, and a cold-outlining pass over a named list. Both
are measurable without a stopwatch, the first by the memo's own hit path and the
second by the block counts in this table moving.

### REVERTED (2026-10-26): the atom memo is not the cost

The entry above named the atom memo as the change the profile argued for most
strongly: `crux::string::lookup` scanning a 64-entry `Vec` in reverse per
identifier read. Implemented it as a direct-mapped table (one slot per atom id,
and one per FNV hash of the units for the other direction), probed and
overwritten. **Reverted.**

7 interleaved rounds, corpus per-row minima: total 2110.9 -> 2090.7 ms (-0.96%).
Re-run at 11 rounds: -1.12%. Nothing of it came from the paths the memo serves:

| row | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `opcost/obj_prop` (member read) | 0.61 | 0.61 (+0.4%) |
| `globals/declarative_read` (identifier reads) | 2.44 | 2.44 (+0.2%) |
| `globals/nested_read` | 2.44 | 2.45 (+0.3%) |
| `calls/method_call` | 54.56 | 54.51 (-0.1%) |

The rows that did move are unrelated to interning and reproduced across both
runs: `array_fill` -11.8%, `object_keys` -4.3%, `json_stringify` +9.5%. That is
the binary's layout shifting under a small code change, and with a reproduced
9.5% regression on one row it is not worth its risk.

### The inference was wrong, and the profile said so all along

The claim was: a block count is an entry count, so 462M entries in `lookup` means
calls times scan length, therefore the scan is a top-three cost. The premise is
right; the conclusion is not, because nothing in `sum(blocks)` separates "many
calls" from "a deep loop".

The profile carries the entry block's count, which is the call count. Dividing
gives blocks per call:

| function | entries | entry-block | blocks/call |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `crux::string::lookup` | 462,436,650 | 36,116,894 | 12.8 |
| `crux::string::intern` | 459,553,639 | 17,939,370 | 25.6 |
| `Vm::chain_cell_read` | 549,830,384 | 69,296,259 | 7.9 |

So the memo scan is real (about five and ten iterations per call, not one), but
it is also only ~2% of the work once the surrounding call is counted, and the
measurement above says replacing it moves nothing. 36M calls across the training
set also says most of that path is identifier binding at compile time rather than
the runtime read loop, where the cost is amortised.

The rule for the next reading of this table: never rank a function by
`sum(blocks)`. Divide by the entry block first. A ratio near 1 is a hot straight
line; a large ratio is a loop, and then the question is whether that loop is
where the time goes, which counts cannot answer.

### REVERTED (2026-10-26): lifting `!=`/`!==` promotes two bodies into a slower tier

The refusal census listed `Binary` as the blocker on three rows. `binary_op`
refused `NotEqual`/`StrictNotEqual`, so a body containing one `!==` (for example
`x !== 0` in a test262 helper) lost the optimizing tier entirely. Implemented
`!=`/`!==` as the equality op plus `Op::Not` (both equality ops answer a
canonical Boolean, and `Op::Not` on a `Bool` is a bit flip), inside
`emit_binary`, which covers both `Step::Binary` and `Step::BinaryImm` (`x !== 0`
arrives as the immediate form). **Reverted.**

It works: `Binary` disappears from the census for
`template-literal/evaluation-order` and `statements/try/completion-values`, and
both bodies compile.

It is slower. Corpus total 2287.4 -> 2306.9 ms (+0.85%), and the two rows that
changed are the two worst rows in the run:

| row | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `statements/try/completion-values` | 116.23 | 121.41 (+4.5%) |
| `statements/for-in/head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration` | 456.06 | 471.48 (+3.4%) |

Those are exactly the rows whose bodies moved tier, so the attribution is not in
doubt.

The negated comparison is not the cause. `JIT_DUMP_IR` shows `v10:bool =
Not(v9)` over `v9:bool = StrictEq(...)`, which takes the bit-flip path. Nor is
the body's own `if (!compareArray(...)) throw ...`: both builds report 17,060
`unary_slow` calls for this row, one per invocation and equal to its
`load_context` count, so the optimizing tier and the per-step tier materialise the
same Boolean there. What makes the optimized body slower is therefore elsewhere
in the tier, and it is not determined here.

Two things follow.

1. **"Refused" is not automatically a problem.** The census names bodies that did
   not get compiled; it cannot say whether a body is faster compiled, and these
   bodies are not: two of the three are 3-5% slower optimized, and the third is
   flat. Ranking refusals by weight is fine as a way to pick candidates, but the
   tier choice needs its own measurement per row.

2. **`unary_slow` has no breadth.** Only three rows in the corpus call it at all
   (`for-in/head-let` 600k, `template-literal` 500k, `try/completion-values`
   17k), so the boolean-materialisation theory that started this thread is not a
   lever, whatever the tier does.

Reverted to the pre-change tree; `target/release` was rebuilt from it, and the
`Binary` refusals are back in the census.


## NULL (2026-10-26): lifting the LICM hoist guard does not pay

The refusal census named `HoistGuard` on six corpus rows, and the skill's
section on the guard said the lift was the follow-up that would recover the
hoist. It was implemented behind `SLAG_OPT_HOIST=1` (default off), measured,
and reverted. It is correct: the probe runs the interpreter's own code, and
`SLAG_HOIST_TRACE=1` reports `hit=1` on all 1628 entries of both probes on
`objects/own_read`. `JIT_HELPER_STATS` shows no per-iteration helper call in
the guarded loop.

It is slower. Same binary, flag on vs unset, one process per row, 7 interleaved
rounds, per-row minima:

| row | off (ms) | on (ms) | change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| objects/own_read | 3.191 | 10.686 | **+235%** |
| globals/nested_read | 2.663 | 3.707 | +39% |
| globals/object_read | 2.696 | 3.644 | +35% |
| globals/declarative_read | 2.687 | 3.616 | +35% |
| objects/proto_read | 52.99 | 55.66 | +5% |
| opcost/obj_prop | 0.6514 | 0.6312 | -3% |
| opcost/baseline (control) | 0.0842 | 0.0874 | +4% |
| objects/warm_store (control, no guard in the body) | 40.07 | 38.49 | -4% |

The two control rows bound the run-to-run floor at about 4%, so only `obj_prop`
is flat and the rest are real regressions. `warm_store`'s code cannot change
with the flag, which is what makes that 4% a noise reading rather than a win.

### Why: the optimizing tier's scalar loop, not the guard

`JIT_DUMP_IR` on `objects/own_read` shows the guarded copy exactly as
intended: the guard hoists `o.a` and `o.b`, the preheader computes their sum
once into a hidden slot, and the loop body is `s += hoisted`. The loop is six
IR ops, no calls, no member reads.

The baseline tier's fused loop for the same body keeps BOTH the counter and the
accumulator in f64 registers (the raw-f64 pass), so its per-iteration body is
two `vaddsd` plus a compare and a branch. The optimizing tier keeps `s` in a
frame slot (a load and a store per iteration) and lowers `Add` on two untyped
`Value`s to the generic tag-checked sequence, because the hoisted value is only
proven to be a non-object primitive, not a Number. `own_read` is 0.8 ns per
iteration on the baseline tier and 2.7 ns on the optimizing tier.

The emitted fast path, counted from `JIT_DUMP_CLIF`'s disassembly:

| per iteration | baseline tier | optimizing tier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| instructions | 7 | 32 |
| accumulator | f64 register | frame load + frame store |
| operand typing | proven Number (raw-f64 pass) | two tag checks, NaN canonicalisation, select |
| loop test | `vucomisd` + branch | tagged Bool materialised, then compared to `false` |
| fallback | none | `call_indirect` to the generic binary helper |

That is the 3.3x, and it is not a defect in the guard: the guarded copy IS the
six-IR-op loop above, and its lowering is what costs 25 extra instructions.
The same conversion is even emitted twice in the lowered test
(`fcvt_from_sint` of the counter at two separate value ids).

So the guard works and the hoist is real; what it exposes is that the
optimizing tier's loop is the slower of the two for this shape. That is the
same conclusion the `!==` null reached from the other side: a body promoted to
the optimizing tier got slower.

### The corpus-wide tier map

Same binary, `SLAG_OPT=0` (baseline tier only) vs default, 5 interleaved
rounds, whole corpus in one process, per-row minima. Total 3257.9 (opt) vs
3480.1 (base), so the optimizing tier is a net **-6.4%**, but the win is
concentrated and several rows go the other way:

| row | opt | base | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| objects/destructure | 4.64 | 171.17 | -97% |
| arrays/typed_array | 18.83 | 29.88 | -37% |
| objects/warm_store | 43.79 | 50.52 | -13% |
| calls/closure_capture | 51.55 | 56.87 | -9% |
| strings/coercion_concat | 105.24 | 87.27 | **+21%** |
| objects/proto_read | 71.08 | 62.01 | +15% |
| opcost/array_for_each | 40.25 | 35.48 | +13% |
| control/generator_loop | 47.80 | 42.64 | +12% |
| opcost/json_stringify | 137.06 | 124.99 | +10% |

Roughly a third of the 77 rows are 5% or more faster on the baseline tier. The
tier is chosen statically (the optimizing tier whenever the lift accepts), so
those rows pay the wrong choice.

### What this makes the next target

Not the hoist, and not a tier heuristic guessed from row names. The measured
difference is inside the optimizing tier's loop: a loop-carried JS binding
stays in a frame slot and its arithmetic stays generic, while the baseline
tier's fused loop registers and types both accumulators. Making the optimizing
tier's loop do the same is the change that would pay on `own_read`, the four
`globals` rows, `proto_read`, and the rows above that lose to the baseline.

The experimental code was reverted, so the tree carries no 3.3x path. Gating
the switch to a safe subset does not rescue it: the only rows whose guard could
be admitted under `numbers=true` are refused first by an outer `numbers=false`
guard, so the subset is a no-op. This note is the specification for
re-deriving the lift once the loop is competitive.

The type proof the loop needs is already available: `own_read`'s step-14 guard
is `numbers=true` and establishes the invariant operand's type at loop entry,
and the optimizing tier ignores it. Consuming that proof (typing the hoisted
slot, then letting the slot fixpoint type the accumulator) is the next slice to
price; typed loops in the same tier already run at 0.8 ns per iteration.

## NULL (2026-10-26): re-derived the hoist guard with `numbers=true` typing — correct, still does not pay

Re-derived the reverted `SLAG_OPT_HOIST` faithfully (an `Op::HoistGuard` helper,
the three-copy lift, and a `narrow` change that trusts a `Number`-declared
`FrameLoad`), measured it, and reverted the guard modelling again. The
`numbers=true` typing works — the fast copy's `FrameLoad` of the RHS-result slot
is now `Number` (`v12:num = FrameLoad() slot5`) — but `own_read` reads 9.16 ms vs
2.92 ms default (+213%), the same pessimization.

The root cause is one layer deeper than the note above assumes. The three-copy
hoist shares the accumulator frame slot `slot1` across the fast/read-only/general
copies; the read-only and general copies store non-Number values to it, so
`narrow`'s global per-slot fixpoint types `slot1` Unknown and `mem2reg`'s global
`non_heap_slots` refuses to promote it. The fast copy's accumulator stays
`v11:? = FrameLoad() slot1` + a generic `Add`, whatever the RHS slot's type is.

"Type the hoisted-slot `FrameLoad`" is therefore necessary but NOT sufficient:
it types the RHS sum, not the loop-carried accumulator. A distinct fast-copy
accumulator slot does not rescue it either — its copy-in `s_fast = s` reads the
contaminated `slot1`, so `s_fast` stays Unknown. The fix needs a per-block type
lattice (the accumulator is Number only on the fast-copy path) feeding a
per-block `mem2reg`, or a bytecode change that tracks the accumulator's pre-loop
value as a Number.

Kept: the `narrow` change (`is_numeric_inst(FrameLoad)` trusts a
`Number`-declared `FrameLoad`) plus its regression test, as the named
prerequisite.

## LANDED (2026-10-27): `Object.assign`/spread copy own string data properties without materializing

The second-largest absolute-excess row, `objects/spread_assign` (119.6 ms
against node's 23.2), is almost entirely `Object.assign({}, o)` over a
3-property fresh object literal. Probes (200k iterations, one row per
`--corpus`): a manual `p.x=o.x; p.y=o.y; p.z=o.z` is **35 ms**, `Object.assign`
is **101 ms**, so the builtin copy costs ~500 ns/call against ~175 ns for the
same three defines. `Object.keys` on the same object is 104 ms, so the shared
cost is the enumeration.

Two changes, both in the own-property copy:

- **The descriptor's value.** For an ordinary source, `get_own_property_key`
already returned `PropertyKind::Data { value, .. }`; the loop re-read the value
with a generic `[[Get]]` (`get_property_key`/`get_key`), a second lookup. Use
the descriptor value for a data property, keep the generic get for an accessor
(the receiver matters) and for every non-ordinary source (a proxy, module
namespace, or host object's `[[Get]]` is not its descriptor). -5.8% on the row.
- **The key list.** `own_property_keys` -> `ordinary_own_property_keys` calls
`materialize_properties` (a vector-free object becomes a `properties` vector)
and builds three `Vec`s plus a clone per key. `JsObject::own_string_data_keys`
returns the keys straight from the map descriptors when the object is a
vector-free ordinary object with only string, non-index keys, and `None`
otherwise (a symbol or index key must enumerate in its own position, and an
accessor-bearing vector is not this shape) so the caller falls back to the
generic list. The result is still a snapshot, so a destination `[[Set]]` that
runs user code cannot invalidate the iteration. `object_assign` and
`copy_data_properties` (object spread) both take it.

Measured, 5 interleaved corpus rounds, per-row minima, against the
descriptor-value-only tree: total **-0.61%**, `objects/spread_assign`
**-19.90%** (112.5 -> 90.1 ms); controls flat (`opcost/baseline` -0.30%,
`objects/warm_store` +0.09%). Cumulative on the row from before the pair:
117.3 -> 90.1 ms (**-23%**), and `Object.assign` itself 101 -> 78 ms.

Corpus after both: `mean-jitGap` **10.51 -> 10.26**, `mean-jlGap` 3.74 -> 3.84
(the jitless column is load-sensitive; the change is on the shared builtin, so
it serves both tiers), `mismatches=0`. Gates: fmt, `clippy -D warnings`,
`cargo test --workspace` all green.

Lead for the next slice: `Object.keys` still pays the same
`own_property_keys`/materialize path (104 ms for 3 keys), and
`ordinary_own_property_keys` still builds three `Vec`s. `own_string_data_keys`
is the non-materializing enumeration it could share.

## LANDED (2026-10-27): `Object.keys` enumerates an ordinary object without the per-key lookup

`Object.keys`'s `enumerable_string_keys` called `own_property_keys` (the
`materialize_properties` + three-`Vec` path) and then re-read each key's
descriptor for its enumerability. An ordinary object's enumerability is already
on the stored property, and `Object.keys` never calls `Get` (its
`EnumerableOwnProperties` kind is `key`), so no user code can run between keys to
change a later one: the snapshot is sound. It now takes `own_string_props`,
which yields `(key, enumerable)` for the string keys in spec order from one
vector. `Object.values`/`entries` keep their per-key re-read, because they do
call `Get`.

Separately, `ordinary_own_property_keys` gained a fast path for the common shape
(no array-index, no symbol key), where the stored order is already the spec
order: one pass builds the answer instead of staging `indices`/`strings`/
`symbols` and merging. The exotic order keeps the general path.

Measured one row per process, 7 interleaved rounds, minima: `opcost/object_keys`
**43.8 -> 36.0 ms (-17.7%)**, `builtins/object_keys` (keys+values+entries)
**58.7 -> 52.8 ms (-9.9%)**, and `opcost/json_stringify` -4 to -5% on the
whole-corpus pass. A whole-corpus run moved its controls (`objects/warm_store`
+3.9%, the 0.1 ms `baseline` +5% on a 0.005 ms absolute), so the corpus-total
delta is not separable from layout; the isolated rows are the measurement.

Gates: fmt, `clippy -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`; test262 language
23,726 + built-ins 23,821 + annexB 1,086 + intl402 3,365 at 100%; corpus parity
0. `Object.keys` semantics diffed against node across index order, symbols,
non-enumerable, getters (which `Object.keys` does not invoke), primitives,
arrays, `Map`, and a proxy.

## LANDED (2026-10-27): `Object.values`/`entries` read the descriptor value, not a second `Get`

`object_values` and `object_entries` re-read each key's descriptor (required:
`EnumerableOwnProperties` re-reads enumerability so an earlier key's getter can
hide a later one) and then called the generic `Get` for the value, a second
lookup. An ordinary object's own data property already carries its value in the
descriptor `get_own_property_key` returned, so it is used directly; an accessor
still runs `get_property`, and a namespace, proxy or host source always takes it
(its `[[Get]]` is not its descriptor). The per-key descriptor re-read is
unchanged, so the getter-mutates-a-later-key cases still see the mutation.

Measured one row per process, 7 interleaved rounds, minima: `builtins/object_keys`
(keys+values+entries) **51.7 -> 45.1 ms (-12.7%)**. Cumulative on that row from
before the enumeration work: 58.7 -> 45.1 ms (-23%).

Gates: fmt, `clippy -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`; test262 language
23,726 + built-ins 23,821 + annexB 1,086 + intl402 3,365 at 100%; corpus parity
0. `values`/`entries` diffed against node across index order, symbols,
non-enumerable, a getter that deletes a later key, a getter that makes a later
key non-enumerable, a setter-only property, primitives, arrays, `Map` and a
proxy.

## LANDED (2026-10-27): `Object.keys` boxes its keys in the enumeration, not a second pass

`enumerable_string_keys` returned `Vec<JsString>` and `object_keys` re-mapped it
into a `Vec<Value>` with a `Handle::new` per key, an intermediate allocation and
a second pass. The helper now boxes as it enumerates and returns the
`Vec<Value>` directly (`Object.keys` is its only caller), under the same
stress-suppression window, renamed `enumerable_string_key_values` to match.

Measured one row per process, 7 interleaved rounds, minima: `opcost/object_keys`
**35.8 -> 31.0 ms (-13.4%)**, `builtins/object_keys` 45.0 -> 42.3 ms (-6.1%).
Cumulative on `opcost/object_keys` from before the enumeration work: 43.8 ->

## PROBE + SCOPE (2026-10-27): the scalar pass is worth 5.8% (all `destructure`); the next slice is a mutable field

Before scoping the escape-analysis frontier, the existing pass's reach, same
binary, `SLAG_SCALAR=0` vs on, 5 interleaved rounds, per-row minima: corpus total
2118.4 -> 1995.2 ms (-5.81%), `objects/destructure` 120.5 -> 3.6 (-97.0%), and the
other allocation rows flat (`object_alloc` and `array_alloc` both ~0, `construct_churn` +0.65%,
`array_slice` +0.37%, `warm_store` +0.06%).

The refusal census is no longer allocation: 11 first-blocker steps across the
corpus (`Yield`, `RunRegBody`, `RegExpLiteral`, `no return`, `HoistGuard`,
`FusedLoop`, `CatchBind/EnterTry/Exit`, `CallApply`,
`Break/SwitchDisc/SwitchTest`, `Binary`, `AssignMemberName(compound)`), 106 bodies

`JIT_DUMP_IR` on `objects/warm_store` shows a provably non-escaping `NewObject`
in a frame slot, read and written across the loop through
`MemberStore`/`MemberCellLoad`/`MemberGuard`. Two exact reasons the pass misses
it: the slot forwarding is block-local (the store is in the preheader, the loads
in the loop body), and it only replaces a field read with the literal's
*constant*, not with a later store's value. The scoped slice (cross-block slot
forwarding, store-to-load forwarding for a virtual member, dead-object removal)

(construct/method inline first) and `array_slice` (builtin inline first) are out
of its reach by mechanism, not by effort.

## LANDED (2026-10-27): the scalar pass elides a non-escaping object's mutable field, and re-types its accumulator

The `.notes/escape-scope.md` slice, implemented. `opt/pass/scalar.rs` gains
cross-block slot forwarding (a slot stored once in the entry block aliases the
object at every load; the entry dominates every reached block), store-to-load
forwarding for a virtual object's named field in its own block (a preceding
`MemberStore(root, atom, v)` is the value; a computed `ElementStore` to the
root bails), and dead-member-store removal. `escaping_literals` now allows a
`MemberStore` whose *receiver* is the object (a write to its own field is not an
escape; a store that uses the object as the value still escapes).

The second half was the bigger win, and it is a pipeline fact the module doc
missed: `narrow` and `mem2reg` run *before* `scalar`, so a guard whose result is
`Unknown` poisons the accumulator's `Add` and the store that feeds the
accumulator's slot, and `mem2reg` refuses to promote a slot with an `Unknown`
store. Once `scalar` substitutes a typed value for the guard's result, the body
can be typed, so the pipeline now re-runs `narrow` and `promote_frame_slots`
after `scalar`, but only when scalar actually changed the body. The result is
that `s += o.x` becomes a raw f64 `vaddsd` (`JIT_DUMP_CLIF`) instead of a generic
tagged `Add`.

Measured, 5 interleaved corpus rounds, per-row minima, against the previous
commit: total 2053.3 -> 2015.4 ms (**-1.85%**); `objects/warm_store` 34.7 -> 9.3
(**-73.1%**), `objects/compound_assign` 43.9 -> 28.1 (**-36.0%**),
`objects/destructure` 3.6 -> 2.6 (**-28.0%**); controls flat (`opcost/baseline`
-0.07%). The same-binary seams agree: `SLAG_SCALAR=0` vs on is 34.6 -> 9.3
(-73.1%) on `warm_store` and 44.1 -> 27.9 (-36.6%) on `compound_assign`. Corpus
parity 0 (77 rows), `mean-jitGap` 10.26 -> 10.12, the `objects` family 8.99 ->
6.26.

A new test, `opt_tier_scalar_replaces_a_mutated_literal_field`, pins the
`warm_store` shape: the object created before the loop, a field written and read
inside it, the tier matching the interpreter, and `REPLACED` advancing.

Gates: fmt, `clippy -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`; test262 language
23,726 + built-ins 23,821 + annexB 1,086 + intl402 3,365 at 100%.

The `compound_assign` win is the re-type, not elision: its IR keeps the object
(the `MemberStore` keeps it alive) but the arithmetic becomes f64. That says the
re-type (typing an accumulator a guard poisoned) is a broad lever independent of
the object, and is the mechanism the "consume the `numbers=true` proof" note was
reaching for.

## NULL (2026-10-27): re-typing after inlining is a wash

The re-type above is enabler-driven: `scalar` substitutes a typed value for a
guard's `Unknown` result, which is what lets `narrow`/`mem2reg` type the
accumulator. `inline` clones typed callee IR but leaves the *call result*
`Unknown`, so extending the re-type's gate to `scalarized || inlined` was
measured (5 interleaved corpus rounds, per-row minima) at **+0.71%** on the
corpus total, with mixed per-row movement (`calls/closure_capture` -3.5%,
`calls/direct_leaf` -5.7%, `builtins/json_roundtrip` +4.7%, the for-in row
+3.1%), i.e. layout. Reverted; the gate stays `scalarized`, and the reason is in
a comment at the gate.

## LANDED (2026-10-28): a loop-carried field becomes a header phi, and the object is elided

`objects/compound_assign` (`o.x += 1; s += o.x` in a loop header) read the field
before storing it, so the scalar pass had no preceding store to forward, declined,
and left the object allocated: 30.4 ms against a ~3 ms floor.

`promote_loop_carried_field` (`opt/pass/scalar.rs`) now runs after `one_pass` in
the same fixed point. For a non-escaping literal object, a header that is its own
back-edge with exactly one entry predecessor, and the field's `MemberCellLoad`
followed by a `MemberGuard` then a `MemberStore` in that header, it pushes a block
parameter, appends the literal on the entry edge and the stored value on the
back-edge, substitutes the guard's result with the parameter, and drops the store,
the load, the guard, the slot store and the literal. The lowered body is:

```
b1(v25:f64, v29:?):
  v9 = Add(v29, v8)          ; the field, no cell probe, no guard
  v15 = Add(v14, v9)         ; s += field
  FrameStore(v15) slot2
  v22 = Add(v25, 1)          ; the counter
  branch v24, b1(v22, v9), b2(v22)
```

Measured on the row, 7 interleaved rounds, per-row minima: 30.86/30.92/30.92/
31.95/31.57/33.34/31.07 -> 12.93/12.42/13.00/13.05/13.13/13.22/12.80, i.e. 30.40
-> 12.11 ms (**-60.2%**). The same-binary seam (`SLAG_SCALAR_LOOP=0`, 5 rounds)
agrees: 30.86 -> 11.98 (**-61.2%**), every off round 30.86-32.38 and every on
round 11.98-13.01, a total separation. Corpus parity 0/77. Three `bench.js` runs
of the one binary read `mean-jitGap` 9.73 / 10.25 / 10.53 (the metric's own
run-to-run spread is that wide; the previous commit measured 10.12), the
`objects` family 5.64 / 5.33 / 5.27 against 6.26.

**Attribution.** A same-binary seam is the only honest A/B here, and it needed a
new one: `SLAG_SCALAR=0` disables the whole pass. With `SLAG_SCALAR_LOOP=0`, an
IR-diff of all 77 rows (per row, one process, `JIT_DUMP_IR=1`, interned-string
addresses normalised) leaves exactly ONE row whose IR differs, `compound_assign`.
Everything else the seam "moved" (up to -9.6% on `slice_concat`) is noise: the
same row spanned 20.14-22.78 ms across rounds. A before/after *build* comparison
had suggested +6.7% on `calls/direct_leaf` and +5.6% on
`language/expressions/template-literal/evaluation-order`; those rows' IR is
byte-identical, so that was layout, not the pass.

**Two bugs the gate caught.** (1) The refusal "no guard op in the body" was
checked before, and then the promotion looked for a `MemberGuard` to strip, so it
could never fire. Corrected: `only_these_sites` requires the body's ONLY guard op
to be the `MemberGuard` being removed (a surviving guard is a deopt point, and a
deopt resumes the interpreter with the frame, where the elided object no longer
is) and every other reference to the object to be a frame access of the three
sites. (2) `find_member_store_after` used `bool::then_some((i, inst.args[1]))`,
which evaluates its argument eagerly and indexed `args[1]` on instructions with no
args; the workspace test suite panicked on it (`installed_jit_hoists_invariant_
member_reads_...`). Now `then`.

A new test, `opt_tier_scalar_promotes_a_loop_carried_field`, pins the shape (note:
the same field update in a `while` body does not lift at all, `AssignMemberName
(compound)`, so the test uses the `for` form).

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`; test262
language 23,726 + built-ins 23,821 + annexB 1,086 + intl402 3,365 at 100%.

**What is left in the row.** The header parameter is `Unknown`, so the three `Add`s
keep their tag checks and `s` stays a frame slot. The next slice types the carried
value `Number`: the entry value is a numeric literal and the back-edge value is a
numeric-preserving arithmetic op over the carried value, so by induction it is a
Number on every iteration (a Number op Number cannot produce a String). That is
the same lever the `warm_store` re-type used, one level up.

## LANDED (2026-10-28): the carried field is typed Number, and `narrow` learns a block parameter's type

The promotion above left the header parameter `Unknown`, so the row kept three
tag-checked `Add`s and a frame slot for the accumulator: 12.1 ms against a ~3 ms
floor. Two changes close it.

**The carried type is proved, not guessed.** `carried_type` types the parameter
`Number` when the value entering the loop is numeric and the back-edge value is
a numeric-preserving arithmetic op (`+ - * / % ** unary- ToNumber`) whose other
operands are numeric. That is an induction: a Number op Number is a Number, so no
String can appear through the cycle, whatever the op would do to a non-Number.

**`narrow` seeds its numeric lattice from a block parameter's declared type.**
A parameter has no defining instruction, so the sweep in `value_numerics` could
never give it a flag and every operand reaching a loop through a parameter was
non-numeric. The declared type is the claim the IR already makes and every
lowering already reads it as the operand's register class, so the lattice adding
it is not a new claim.

The lowered body is three pure f64 adds with the accumulator as a parameter and
no frame traffic at all:

```
b1(v25:f64, v29:f64, v30:f64):
  v9:f64 = Add(v29, v8)       ; the field
  v15:f64 = Add(v30, v9)      ; s
  v22:f64 = Add(v25, v8)      ; the counter
  v34:num = Canon(v22)
  v24:bool = Lt(v34, v23)     ; v23 is `n`, still Unknown (a function parameter)
  branch v24, b1(v22, v9, v15), b2(v22, v15)
```

Measured, 7 interleaved corpus rounds, per-row minima, against the previous
commit: `objects/compound_assign` 12.05 -> 3.02 ms (**-74.9%**, and 30.4 -> 3.0
over the session, 10x), `objects/warm_store` 9.56 -> 3.06 (**-68.0%**),
`objects/destructure` 2.77 -> 1.04 (**-62.6%**). Corpus total 2328.8 -> 2330.5 ms
(+0.07%, flat: three rows out of 77). `bench.js` gap: `compound_assign` 1.22x,
`warm_store` 1.24x, `destructure` 1.29x, the `objects` family 5.27x -> 4.18x,
overall `mean-jitGap` 10.12 -> 10.00 (two runs of the one binary: 10.04 and
10.00), `mean-jlGap` 3.76, parity 0/77.

**The seeding is the broader half.** `warm_store` and `destructure` were not
touched by the promotion at all; their accumulators were already in the loop. The
operand that kept their `Add` non-numeric was the loop counter, a `Type::Int`
block parameter. This is the mechanism the 2026-10-20 note "the counter loop, one
non-numeric operand disables slot promotion" was measuring.

**Attribution.** An IR diff of all 77 rows between the two binaries leaves
exactly three rows whose IR differs (`compound_assign`, `warm_store`,
`destructure`). So the movers the timing A/B also showed on `template-literal/
evaluation-order` (+5.9%) and `try/completion-values` (+5.4%) have byte-identical
IR and are build layout, not this change.

**Discipline note: `objects/warm_store` is no longer a usable control row.** It
was the second control in the protocol; two successive changes have moved it
(34.7 -> 9.3 -> 3.1). Choose the second control per change and prove it was not
touched with the IR diff, keeping `opcost/baseline` (flat at 0.083 ms here) as
the invariant one.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`; test262
language 23,726 + built-ins 23,821 + annexB 1,086 + intl402 3,365 at 100%.

**What is left in the row.** `n` is a function parameter, so `Lt(Canon(i), n)`
keeps a tag check and a `Canon` per iteration, and both `n` and the counter make
the loop test the only tagged work left. A function's parameter types are the
next broad lever: `Type::Int`/`Number` seeds exist now, but nothing types an
argument at the call site.

## PROBE (2026-10-28): the inline splice is starved by the tier-up policy, not by its sites

`opcost/method_call` runs `s = (s + obj.m(k)) | 0` for 100k iterations at 1.3 ms
and V8 does it in ~0.03 ms. The IR shows why the body cannot be fixed by typing:

```
b1(v28:int):
  v8:num = BitAnd(v28, v7)          ; k = i & MASK
  v9:? = FrameLoad() slot2          ; s, a frame slot
  v11:? = MemberCellLoad(v10) atom644
  v12:? = MemberGuard(v10, v11)
  v15:? = Call(v10, v12, v8) 19     ; not spliced, so `call_slow`
  v16:? = Add(v9, v15)              ; Unknown, tag-checked
  v18:? = BitOr(v16, 0)             ; Unknown
  FrameStore(v18) slot2
  CompletionStore(v18)              ; a write per iteration
```

The callee is a closure literal in the same body (`var obj = { m: function (x)
{ return x + 1; } }`), so a splice would turn the whole loop into
`s = (s + k + 1) | 0` in registers. It does not splice, and `SLAG_INLINE=0` moves
this row by only 2%, so the pass is not attempting it.

**Why the site is missing.** `sites_from_feedback` needs a recorded call site, and
`SLAG_INLINE_TRACE` (new, see below) shows the store holds NO `Call` record for
this body at all. The recorder (`Vm::record_call_site`) is only reached from the
interpreter's step dispatch, and `JitEngine::consult` compiles a body with a loop
on its **first** consult, deliberately: *"a loop body compiles on the first
consult - it runs once with many internal iterations, so a pure count would
never promote it"* (`runtime/src/jit.rs`). So a loop body never executes an
interpreted step, so it never records a call site, so the splice never fires for
exactly the bodies where it would pay.

That also explains the 2026-10-25 note "`SLAG_INLINE_FEEDBACK=1` helps nothing in
the corpus": the feedback store is empty by construction, not because the splice
is unprofitable. Measured here: `SLAG_FEEDBACK=1 SLAG_INLINE_FEEDBACK=1` on this
row is 1.29 ms against the default's 1.28 ms, and the IR is unchanged.

The recording mechanism is fine elsewhere: sweeping the corpus with the probe on,
a 144-step row records ~9,961 calls per site, so the interpreter path works; only
loop bodies starve.

**And where it can fire, it does not pay.** The same sweep with
`SLAG_FEEDBACK=1 SLAG_INLINE_FEEDBACK=1` changes the IR of exactly ONE of the 77
rows, `calls/recursive_fib` (the guard-split splice the pass emits for a
recursive callee: `CalleeEq` then either the spliced body or the real call). That
row measures 55.1/56.1/56.7/58.4/67.9 ms against the default's
51.0/51.8/52.0/53.6/59.4, i.e. it loses. So the earlier "`SLAG_INLINE_FEEDBACK=1`
helps nothing in the corpus" is right for the rows it reaches and wrong about the
reason: the rows that would profit never get a site.

**Cost of the naive fix.** Letting a loop body run interpreted once before
compiling would feed the splice, and the corpus harness would not notice (it
times the minimum of several calls). But a program whose main loop is in a
function called once pays a whole interpreted run: this row's interpreter column is
9.7 ms per call for 100k iterations (~97 ns/iteration), so a 10M-iteration loop
would pay about a second. That is not a trade to make blindly, so it is left as a
design decision rather than landed here.

**A static alternative.** The callee is a closure literal in the caller's own
body, so the splice could be proved instead of measured: forward the member read
`v11` to the literal's field value, guarded by `CalleeEq` against that value.
`one_pass` declines today because the object escapes as the call's *receiver*,
which is correct (the callee can write `this.m`), so the proof needs the callee
body: no store to that atom, then the forwarding is sound. That is the next
slice, and it needs no feedback at all.

Instrument added: `SLAG_INLINE_TRACE=1` prints the site count per compiled body,
each recorded site's state/hits/first id, and each resolver lookup's outcome.
Compile-time only, so it costs nothing when unset.

## LANDED (2026-10-28): the splice's static route, and the re-type after inlining

The PROBE above found the splice starved: a loop-bodied caller is compiled on its
first consult, so it never runs an interpreted step, so it never records a call
site, so `sites_from_feedback` is empty for exactly the bodies where the splice
would pay. This lands the route that needs no feedback.

**`sites_from_creations`** derives a splice target from the IR: a `Op::Call`
whose callee operand is a `NewClosure` value, directly or through a frame slot
stored exactly once in the entry block. The slot argument is the one
`slot_aliases` already makes (an entry-block store dominates every reached
block, and a captured binding lives in a context slot, not a frame slot); a body
that writes a slot without naming it (`FunctionDecl`, `ForOfBindLocal`,
`ForOfNextBindLocal`) refuses every slot. The site is `InlineTarget::Created`,
which splices with no comparison at all: the call's callee operand is provably
the closure being spliced.

**`resolve_created`** builds the closure exactly as `register_function` builds it
for that step (shared body/params, `body_is_strict(..) || step.strict`,
`ThisMode`), compiles it, and accepts it only if `leaf && !leaf_uses_env`, the
same gate `resolve_declaration` uses. `spliceable` then requires a value-returning
body whose only slot reads are its inputs.

**The re-type after inlining now pays, and is on.** `narrow`/`mem2reg` were
gated on `scalarized` because a 2026-10-27 measurement found the `inlined` half
a wash (+0.71%). That measurement was vacuous for the same reason the feedback
splice was: inlining fired on almost no body, so the gate was measuring noise.
A splice replaces a call whose result was `Unknown` with the callee's arithmetic,
which is exactly the value the re-type needs. Two things had to be fixed to make
it land:

- The continuation parameter is created with the call's result type (`Unknown`)
  and `narrow` reads a parameter's *declared* type, so a value crossing the
  splice's block split stayed untyped. The re-type now runs
  `normalize_param_types` -> `narrow` -> `mem2reg` twice, because the edge
  argument is only typed by the `narrow` in the round before the one that reads
  the parameter.
- With that, `objects/warm_store`-style promotion happens through a spliced call:
  the accumulator leaves its frame slot and the loop is f64 registers.

Measured on `opcost/js_call` (`var g = function (x) { return x + 1; }; s = (s +
g(i)) | 0`), one row per process, 7 interleaved rounds, per-row minima, all three
configurations of ONE binary:

| config | ms | |
|---|---:|---|
| `SLAG_INLINE_CREATED=0 SLAG_RETYPE_INLINED=0` | 0.88 | before |
| splice only (`SLAG_RETYPE_INLINED=0`) | 0.63 | -28.6% |
| both (default) | 0.53 | **-40.1%** |

Corpus, 7 interleaved rounds, per-row minima, `SLAG_INLINE_CREATED=0` vs default:
total 2190.8 -> 2187.4 ms (-0.16%, i.e. flat: two rows of 77),
`opcost/js_call` 0.788 -> 0.514 (**-34.9%**), `opcost/array_for_each_js` 3.686 ->
3.348 (**-9.2%**). An IR diff of all 77 rows between the two modes leaves
exactly those two rows changed. The re-type's own marginal, `SLAG_RETYPE_INLINED`
0 vs 1, is -17.4% on `js_call`, about -5% on `array_for_each_js` and -3% on
`calls/direct_leaf` (the third row its IR reaches), and its corpus-wide effect is
inside the noise floor.

New test, `opt_tier_splices_a_closure_the_body_creates`, pins the route with the
`inline::CREATED` delta (a global counter, like `scalar::REPLACED`).

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`; test262
language 23,726 + built-ins 23,821 + annexB 1,086 + intl402 3,365 at 100%.

**What is left in the row.** 5.3 ns/iteration against node's ~0.3 (which is V8
having made the loop nearly free). The spliced region is its own block pair
(`b1 -> b4 -> b3`) because the splice splits the block at the call, and the
continuation's raw-f64 result is canonicalized back with a `Canon` per iteration
(`unbox` put `v31` in an f64 register while `s`'s add still reads a `Value`
word). Merging the callee's single block into the caller's, or teaching `unbox`
that a raw value may feed a raw operand, is the next slice; the block split also
shows up as the loop's only remaining branches.

## LANDED (2026-10-28): the member-call splice, guarded by a callee comparison

`opcost/method_call` is the shape the PROBE above could not reach: the callee is
a member read of an object the body built (`var obj = { m: function (x) { return
x + 1; } }; obj.m(k)`), so `closure_of_callee` cannot say the operand *is* a
`NewClosure` value, and the object escapes as the call's receiver (the callee may
write `this.m`), which is what stops the scalar pass from forwarding the read.

The splice does not need the forwarding. The site is proved by a runtime
comparison instead: `CalleeEq(callee_operand, literal_value)`, where the literal
value is the closure the body's own `NewClosure` created. The `MemberGuard`
before it has already established that the cell's value is the receiver's field,
so the comparison asks exactly "is this still the closure we created?" and a
field written since takes the ordinary call. That is sound with no escape
analysis and no feedback, and it is invocation-local: comparing against the
SSA `NewClosure` value rather than a baked box is what makes it work for a
closure created per call (a `Guarded` site's baked box never matches a fresh
closure, which is what the 2026-10-25 note on that site class was seeing).

The lowered loop:

```
b1(v28:int):
  v8:int = BitAnd(v28, v0)         ; k
  v9:? = FrameLoad() slot2         ; s
  v11:? = MemberCellLoad(v10) atom644
  v12:? = MemberGuard(v10, v11)
  v35:bool = CalleeEq(v12, v1)     ; is obj.m still the closure we created?
  branch v35, b4(), b5()
b4():
  v34:f64 = Add(v8, 1)             ; the callee body, inlined
  v37:num = Canon(v34)
  jump b3(v37)
```

Measured on the row, one process, 7 interleaved rounds, minima: 1.19 -> 0.68 ms
(**-43.0%**). Corpus, 5 interleaved rounds, per-row minima, `SLAG_INLINE_CREATED=0`
vs default: total 2170.1 -> 2154.1 ms (**-0.74%**), `opcost/method_call` 1.172 ->
0.668 (-43.0%), `opcost/js_call` 0.778 -> 0.588 (-24.4%), `opcost/
array_for_each_js` 3.650 -> 3.304 (-9.5%). An IR diff of all 77 rows leaves
exactly those three changed, so the +10.4% the same A/B showed on
`calls/closure_capture` is noise: its IR is byte-identical.

New test, `opt_tier_splices_a_member_closure_with_a_callee_guard`, writes the
field mid-loop so the guard's fallback is observable, and checks the tier
against the interpreter across three invocations (each with its own closure).

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace -D warnings`, `cargo test --workspace`; test262
language 23,726 + built-ins 23,821 + annexB 1,086 + intl402 3,365 at 100%.

**Still open in these rows.** The spliced region sits in its own block pair and
its raw-f64 result crosses the continuation as `Canon`; the continuation's
parameter joins with the fallback call's `Unknown`, so the accumulator only
promotes when the fallback path is absent (`js_call` it does, `method_call` it
does not). Typing a splice's result from the callee's return value would close
that, and it is the same missing piece as typing a function's parameters.

## FIXED (2026-10-28): the inline-path re-type must not run on a scalar-only body

The two commits above share one regression that their own same-binary seams could
not see, because the seam (`SLAG_INLINE_CREATED`) disabled the splice and not the
re-type: `objects/compound_assign` 3.0 -> 45.9 ms, `objects/warm_store` 3.1 ->
34.9, `objects/destructure` 1.0 -> 116.4. Those are the three rows the earlier
scalar work had just fixed, and the cause was the re-type block, not the splice.

Running `normalize_param_types` *before* `narrow` demotes the loop counter's
`Int`: the enum join over the entry seed and the back-edge widens it to
`Number`, `loop_counter` still fuses the increment into `IntAdd`, and `IntAdd`
then has a `Value`-word operand. The lowering refuses that, so the whole body
falls back to the baseline tier, which is the 15-100x in the numbers. With
`SLAG_UNBOX=0` the malformed IR is visible directly (`b1(v25:num)` feeding
`v22:int = IntAdd(v25, v34)`).

The re-type is now two paths: a `scalar`-only body keeps exactly the historical
`narrow` then `mem2reg` round, and only an `inline`-only body gets the
`normalize` -> `narrow` -> `promote` loop twice. Re-measured, same binary,
5 interleaved rounds, per-row minima:

| row | seam off | seam on | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `objects/compound_assign` | 2.884 | 2.887 | restored (was 45.9) |
| `objects/warm_store` | 2.921 | 2.921 | restored (was 34.9) |
| `objects/destructure` | 0.986 | 0.984 | restored (was 116.4) |
| `opcost/method_call` | 1.175 | **0.666** | -43% |
| `opcost/js_call` | 0.770 | **0.587** | -24% |
| `opcost/array_for_each_js` | 3.638 | **3.291** | -10% |

The lesson for the protocol: a same-binary seam only attributes the code it
actually gates. A change to a *shared* pipeline stage needs its own switch, and
here the two `objects` rows that `opcost/baseline` cannot see were the evidence.

## LANDED + NULL (2026-10-28): the exact creation site needs no comparison, and in-place splicing loses

Two changes to the creation-site splice, one landed and one not.

**LANDED: the expected value is the operand when the operand is the closure.** The
member route compares the callee operand against the literal's value, and that was
being applied to the *exact* routes too: a `var g = function () {}` call's operand
is a `FrameLoad` of the slot that holds the closure, so the recorded expectation
(the closure) never equalled the operand (the load) and the splice emitted a
`CalleeEq` that can never fail, on top of splitting the block. `closure_of_callee`
now returns the *operand* when the operand is the closure or the slot's single
store (no comparison at all, the slot proves it) and the literal's value only for
the member route. `opcost/js_call` 0.53 -> **0.49 ms**, `opcost/method_call`
unchanged at 0.67, `objects/compound_assign` unchanged at 2.90.

**NULL: splicing a single-block callee in place.** The continuation block is what
forces the call result's `Unknown` type onto a parameter and then a `Canon` at the
representation boundary, so the obvious next step was to skip it: a callee whose
IR is one block with no parameters and a value return can be copied into the
caller's block at the call site, with its return value substituted for the call's
result. Measured on `opcost/js_call`: **0.93 ms against 0.49**, i.e. worse than
not splicing at all.

The cause is a latent fragility that the block-splitting splice happened to
dodge. Removing the continuation changes which values `normalize_param_types`
joins, `narrow` demotes the counter's entry `Const 0` to `Number`, `loop_counter`
still fuses the increment into `IntAdd`, and the body's CLIF then mixes an
`i64` `Value` word with an `i32` constant: `JIT_DUMP_CLIF` reports "opt assemble
failed", the optimizing tier refuses the body, and it runs on the baseline tier.
That is the same failure mode as the re-type regression above, from the other
direction: **`loop_counter` can emit a body the Cranelift verifier rejects**
whenever the counter parameter is not typed `Int`, and nothing checks it.

So in-place splicing is not landed. The fix that makes it (and any future
pipeline reordering) safe is for `loop_counter` to type the counter cycle itself:
it has already proved the counter is int32 (an int32 entry constant, `i ± c`
increments, an int32 bound), so it can set the parameter, the entry constant and
the increment to `Int` rather than relying on `normalize_param_types` to derive
that from a seed `narrow` may have demoted. That is its own slice, with the
`js_call` row as its falsifier (expect the in-place splice to then reach about
0.3 ms, and `opt assemble failed` to disappear from `JIT_DUMP_CLIF`).

## PROBE + NULL (2026-10-28): the element-read rows are a dependent-load chain, not a gate

Attacking the `opcost` element/intrinsic rows (element_read 15.9x, element_write
10.4x, obj_prop 28.3x, prim_prop 30.1x, array_at 55.1x) needed a decomposition
first, so a scratch copy of the `element_read` workload was split three ways
(100k iterations, one row per process):

| loop body | ms | |
|---|---:|---|
| `s = (s + arr[k]) \| 0` (the row) | 0.655 | |
| `s = (s + k) \| 0` (no element read) | 0.102 | arithmetic + counter + frame slot |
| `s = (s + 1) \| 0` (a constant) | 0.063 | counter + frame slot only |

So the arithmetic and the loop's own machinery are 0.06-0.10 ms of 0.655: **the
`Op::ElementLoad` ladder is 5.5 ns of the 6.5 ns per iteration.** The ladder is
`emit_dense_element_read` (`opt_lower.rs`): object tag test, `obj_ptr` compute,
load `array_dense`, then the key gate, load `elem_len`, bounds, load `elem_ptr`,
address, load the element, hole test. Four dependent L1 loads
(`array_dense` -> `elem_ptr` -> element) plus a length load, 4-5 branches.
V8 with PACKED_DOUBLE elements does elements-pointer -> element: 3 levels, no
hole test and no element tag test, because elements-kind feedback supplies what
we re-check per access. That is the whole gap, and none of it is a slicing
target: matching it means hoisting the array descriptor (which is loop-invariant
for a `var arr` read in a loop) and an element-kind proof.

**NULL: the i32 element key.** The one part that looked removable was the
canonical-index gate (`fcvt_to_uint_sat` + `fcvt_from_uint` + 2 `fcmp` + `band`),
which exists because a key arrives as a `Value` word. `narrow` drops an int32's
proof when its only use is a key (`restrict_int_to_arith_use` treats a key as a
"boundary" use), so the index is always a double. Keeping the proof and taking
the raw i32 in the dense arms (an unsigned widening makes a negative index out of
range, so the bound check still rejects it) is sound and was implemented both
halves. Measured with `SLAG_INT_KEY=0` as the seam, 5 rounds each:
`element_read` 0.628-0.654 on vs 0.622-0.655 off, `element_write` 0.377-0.399 vs
0.377-0.399, `dyn_key_read` 0.865-0.903 vs 0.863-0.910, `array_at` 1.070-1.122 vs
1.073-1.134. Every row is inside its own noise: **the gate is not where the time
is.** Reverted.

Two findings worth keeping from the attempt:

- `Type::Int` in this IR is ambiguous — sometimes an i32 register, sometimes a
  `Value` word merely *known* to hold an int32 (the `narrow` slot proof types a
  `FrameLoad` that way). Keying a lowering decision on it produced
  `uextend.i64 <i64>` and "jit codegen error: Verifier(...)" on every
  typed-array fill. The register class must be read from the CLIF value
  (`builder.func.dfg.value_type(v) == types::I32`), which is exact.
- The register body's member-read arms (`LeafOp::GetMemberNameLocal`,
  `LeafOp::GetMemberComputedLocal`) never apply the typer's read guard, and
  cannot: a deopt inside a register run resumes at the run's start step, so the
  guard would re-execute the run's side effects. So the register-lane rows
  (`obj_prop`, `prim_prop`, `element_write`) get no value typing at all, which is
  why they sit at 28-30x.

**The leaf exemption is worth keeping, measured.** `SLAG_TYPER_LEAF=1` (the new
seam that lets the typer's read guard reach a leaf body) changes the IR of
exactly one corpus row and costs `calls/construct_churn` **58 -> 110 ms**: a
guard marks a body `deopts`, and every machine-code inline lane refuses such a
callee. The exemption stays; the seam stays as its test.

## NULL (2026-10-28): "type the counter cycle" is not expressible, and in-place splicing loses twice

Two attempts from the same follow-up.

**NULL 1: `loop_counter` typing the cycle it proved.** The idea: after proving the
counter int32, set the parameter and the seed constant to `Type::Int` so
`normalize_param_types` could not widen them back to `Number`, and refuse the
fusion when a use needs a `Value` word (a key, a call argument, a return). It
works structurally — the typed-array `fill` body that produced "jit codegen
error: Verifier(...)" now assembles — but the use rule rejects a fusion that was
previously *correct*: `opcost/element_write` (`arr[k] = i`, the counter stored as
an element value) went **0.375 -> 0.45 ms (+20%)**, in every round of both
binaries, because the counter lost its int cycle and `unbox` put it in a raw f64
register with two `Canon`s per iteration. Corpus total otherwise flat. Reverted.

**The finding behind it.** `Type::Int` on a *block parameter* does not make it an
i32 register: block parameters are `i64` in CLIF, so the annotation only means
"the `Value` word is known to hold an int32". That is why `uextend.i64 <i64>`
fired when I read the type to decide the key register class, and why typing a
param or a seed cannot move a counter into an i32 register at all. Only a
*producing instruction* (`IntAdd`, a bit op with an int result, `Const` with an
`Imm::Int`) yields an i32 CLIF value. So the counter's int cycle is decided by
which instructions produce it, not by the types on it — and the only lever that
changes the producers is `loop_counter` itself, which is already fusing them.
The remaining risk (the seed's `Const` staying `Number` while the param gets
`Int`) is what the "narrow then promote, once" ordering avoids, which is why the
re-type split in `pass/mod.rs` is the actual guard.

**NULL 2: in-place splicing, for a second reason.** Re-tried on top of the
`loop_counter` change (so the counter cycle was valid): `opcost/js_call`
**0.577 ms against 0.510** for the block-splitting splice, with no codegen
error. The in-place IR keeps the accumulator and the `|0` in `Number` words
(`b1(v25:int, v31:num)`, `v15:num = BitOr(...)`) where the block-splitting CFG
promotes them to i32 in the continuation (`v32:int`, `v15:int`) — the block
boundary is what gives `narrow`/`mem2reg` a parameter whose declared type it can
derive from a single incoming value. Removing the block removes that, and the
`Canon` per iteration comes back. Reverted; the continuation block is load
bearing, not overhead.

## METHOD (2026-10-28): rank by recoverable time, cross with tier and interpreter, then ablate

Everything the last three sessions chased was chosen from `mean-jitGap`, and that
metric gives a row where V8 does 0.02 ms the same weight as a row where it does
80 ms. So a 0.6 ms `opcost` row at 55x outranked a 452 ms row at 8.6x, and the
work went into the 0.6 ms row. `tools/corpus/where.py` replaces the ranking with
absolute recoverable time (`slag - node`) and adds the two discriminators the
ratio table cannot show:

- **tier**: what `SLAG_OPT=0` (the baseline tier) does with the same row. A row
  the optimizing tier is *slower* on is a tier-selection bug, and it is visible
  in ms. Twenty rows are, totalling **-14.29 ms** of corpus time
  (`try/completion-values` -4.6, `spread_assign` -3.5, `template-literal -1.6`,
  `closure_capture` -1.0). For scale: the best win of the last session, splicing
  a member call, was worth 0.5 ms of absolute time.
- **jl**: the *interpreter* gap. Both engines interpret the same work, so V8's
  optimizer cannot flatter it. `gap_jl` near `gap_jit` means the deficit is in
  shared runtime machinery; `gap_jl` far below it means V8's optimizer removes
  work we do.

The ranked head (one `bench.js` run, 3 interleaved tier rounds):

| recover | share | slag | node | gap | jl gap | tier | verdict | row |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 400.0 | 22.0% | 452.6 | 52.6 | 8.6 | 7.5 | -0.47 | runtime | `language/.../for-in/head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration` |
| 173.0 | 9.8% | 200.8 | 27.8 | 7.2 | 6.5 | -1.64 | runtime | `language/.../template-literal/evaluation-order` |
| 67.6 | 4.4% | 91.4 | 23.8 | 3.8 | 3.0 | -3.49 | runtime | `objects/spread_assign` |
| 64.8 | 4.0% | 83.0 | 18.2 | 4.6 | 4.8 | +0.58 | runtime | `opcost/json_stringify` |
| 62.5 | 3.4% | 70.8 | 8.3 | 8.5 | 7.3 | +0.94 | runtime | `strings/split_join` |

The two biggest rows are **28% of the corpus**, both `runtime`, and both
indifferent to the tier (0.5% and 0.8%): their cost is not in the optimizing
tier, and no amount of opt-tier specialization moves them.

**Then ablate the row's own workload**, per component, on both engines and both
modes, one process per variant (`tools/corpus/ablate.sh`). Components are read
off as deltas, and the `jl` columns are the ones to trust. For the head-let row
(simplified asserts, 100k body calls, closures over a `for (let x in obj)` head):

| variant | slag jit | slag jl | node jit | node jl | jl gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| as written | 337.5 | 476.0 | 26.0 | 65.5 | 7.3 |
| no assert/read/call block | 278.2 | 301.4 | 25.0 | 55.0 | 5.5 |
| no closures (`fns[x] = x`) | 147.3 | 163.1 | 24.4 | 35.4 | 4.6 |
| no `for`-in (unrolled) | 188.2 | 324.8 | 12.8 | 37.8 | 8.6 |
| empty body, 100k calls | 0.41 | 2.26 | 0.02 | 1.49 | **1.5** |

Per-component cost in our *interpreter*, and against V8's interpreter:

| component | slag | node | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 300k closures (`for`-let capture) | 138 ms (460 ns each) | 19.6 ms (65 ns) | **7.0x** |
| 900k member reads + calls | 175 ms (194 ns) | 10.5 ms (12 ns) | **16.7x** |
| fresh object + 6 stores + 3-iteration `for`-in | ~160 ms | ~5 ms | ~10x (residual) |
| 100k calls to an empty body (frame machinery) | 2.26 ms | 1.49 ms | **1.5x** |

So: **calls and frames are near V8 (1.5x). Closure creation is 7x. Property
reads, calls, and fresh-object defines are 10-17x.** The corpus' largest rows are
made of exactly those three, and the `jl` column says the gap is in the runtime,
not in what the optimizing tier does with it. V8 then gets a further 2.6x on
these rows from inlining and escape analysis (`node_jl / node_jit` = 2.5-4.3),
which is the second-order prize and the reason a jit-only comparison overstates
how far ahead V8's *runtime* is.

**Work order (absolute recoverable time, `jl`-verified):**

1. **Closure creation with a per-iteration capture**: 460 ns against V8's 65 ns,
   and the component of 28% of the corpus. `register_function`'s phase split was
   measured in 2026-10-25 as "diffuse, at its architectural floor" — that
   conclusion was reached when the row was ranked by ratio. At 250 ms it is the
   largest single item in the project and the floor claim needs re-deriving
   against V8's 65 ns, not against our own previous version.
2. **Property read/call on a fresh ordinary object**: 194 ns against 12 ns. The
   member-value cell is per-shape and a fresh object pays its fill; V8's IC is
   per-site and pays a map compare.
3. **Fresh-object property defines and `for`-in enumeration**: ~160 ms of the
   same row.
4. **Tier selection**: 14.29 ms, free, twenty rows where the baseline tier wins.

Numbers 1-3 also explain the second row (`template-literal/evaluation-order`:
70k closures + calls) and the third (`spread_assign`: defines).

## PROFILE (2026-10-29): closure creation, by phase, on a clock that can see it

`register_function` plus its instantiation prelude is **280-300 ns per closure**
against node-jitless's **9 ns** on the same shape (30x). Three `scratch/lcf/clo`
probes, one process each, `--corpus` minima:

| variant | slag jl | node jl | per closure |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `e-closure-nostore` (`g = function(){return i;}` in a 300k loop) | 85.5 ms | 4.57 ms | **280 ns** vs 9 |
| `a-var-closure` (+ `fns.x = g`) | 94.0 | 6.55 | 313 vs 22 |
| `c-closure-free` (the loop alone) | 5.2 | 1.72 | 17 |

Not GC: at 3,000 and 30,000 iterations the per-closure figure is 301 and 313 ns,
the same as at 300,000.

`SLAG_CLOSURE_PROFILE=1` (new, permanent, cycle-counter based) splits it. Two
things had to be fixed before the split was worth reading, and both are now in
the skill's measurement protocol:

- `std::env::var_os` costs **142 ns** on Windows. An env-gated instrument that
  reads its switch per call is the largest term it measures: the first version
  reported a 142 ns "call prologue" that was entirely the switch read. Cache the
  gate.
- `Instant::now()` costs ~30 ns here, more than most phases. The cycle counter
  (`_mm_lfence(); _rdtsc()`) costs ~13 ns per mark. Even so its *absolute* scale
  under-reads, non-uniformly.

So the phase table is calibrated against an ablation, not trusted as seconds.
`SLAG_CLOSURE_SKIP=props` (same binary) skips `set_function_properties_batched`:
the row goes 99.5 -> 85.9 ms, i.e. **45 ns**, where the timer read 19 ns. The
timer under-reads by **2.4x** on this path; the ratios below are rescaled by it.

| phase | timer | calibrated |
|---|---:|---:|
| registry insert (`ecma_functions`) + `store_construct_patterns` | 46 | **~112** |
| `Function::new_with_prototype` + the `[[Environment]]` edge | 40 | **~97** |
| `set_function_properties_batched` | 19 | **45** (ablation) |
| instantiation prelude (source-info, body cache, params cache) | 13 | ~31 |
| `shared_compiled_body` + `set_compiled` | 10 | ~25 |
| `EcmaFunction` construction, setup, trailing | 4 | ~10 |

The interpreter's own creation step (`running_context` + `site_source_info` +
`stack.push`) rounds to zero on every clock tried, so the cost is inside the
instantiation, not around it.

**Two thirds of a closure is the record insert and the object allocation.** For
reference V8 does neither: one bump allocation of a ~40-byte `JSFunction` whose
`SharedFunctionInfo` is per-site and already on the AST node, and `length`/`name`
live on the SFI rather than being defined per closure.

### NULL (2026-10-29): the record is not size-bound at 200 bytes

`EcmaFunction`'s `name: Option<JsString>` was 48 of its 200 bytes, and `JsString`
is 48 bytes because of its inline small-string form. It is a property of the
declaration SITE, not of the closure: the only reader is `compile_body`'s
`function_name` (Cut 46 self-tail-call recognition), once per site. So the field
was dropped and the name passed into `compile_body` instead (record 200 -> 152,
and one fewer 48-byte clone per closure and per call).

Measured on two interleaved binaries, 7 pairs, minima:

| probe | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `a-var-closure` | 94.4 ms | 93.4 ms |
| for-in head-let row | 741.4 ms | 748.3 ms |

Flat. That is a useful answer rather than a disappointment: the insert's cost is
the `HashMap` probe/growth machinery and the allocation churn around it, not the
value copy. The earlier `Box<EcmaFunction>` regression (52 -> 128 ns/insert) reads
the same way from the other side. The change is kept because it is a strict
simplification, and recorded here so nobody re-runs the size experiment.

### What this redirects

The next closure slice is not "shrink the record further". It is to stop paying a
map insert per closure: the record reachable from its function object, with the
table a non-owning id -> function index. Every `IdMap`-roots-the-record form is
measured worse (Stage D, twice: +70% and +80.6% on the head-let row from
promoting each record on its first minor), so the shape that remains untested is
exactly the one `closure-cost-plan.md` names. That is a larger change than a
slice: it needs the record traced from `crux`'s function object and an id ->
function path for the API, stack traces, snapshots and feedback.

The cheaper half is the allocation: `Function::new_with_prototype` makes TWO
arena allocations (the `JsObject`, ~528 B, and the `Function` box) and resolves
the canonical empty map through a thread-local `Vec` scan per create
(`canonical_empty_map`). A per-realm cached empty map for
`%Function.prototype%`, used with the existing
`ordinary_object_create_with_map`, removes the TLS access, the `mark_prototype`
call and the scan from every closure.

### LANDED (2026-10-29): the function-kind empty map is cached per kind

`Function::new_with_prototype` called `canonical_empty_map(Some(proto))` on
every closure. Even on a cache hit that is a thread-local heap-cell access, a
`mark_prototype` flag test and a linear scan of the empty-map `Vec`. A
function's `[[Prototype]]` is one of six realm intrinsics, so the map the
`ordinary_object_create` implied is constant per kind: it is now cached in
`AgentRoots::function_empty_maps` (traced, so a collection between creates
cannot free the shape) and the object is built on it with the existing
`ordinary_object_create_with_map`. The first resolution still runs
`mark_prototype` through `canonical_empty_map`, so the elements protector sees
the link before any object can record a clean-chain verdict against it.

Same-binary A/B, 7 (probe) and 5 (row) interleaved pairs, minima:

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 300k closures, `--jitless` | 94.87 ms | **91.52 ms** (-3.5%) |
| for-in head-let row | 755.3 ms | **746.0 ms** (-1.2%, faster in all 5 pairs) |

Per closure that is about 11 ns of a ~290 ns create. Corpus `mean-jitGap`
9.46 -> 9.36 over 77 rows, `mismatches=0`. The in-engine phase read
(`function-object`) went 55.2 -> 49.4 raw ticks, i.e. the timer sees about 40%
of the real move, consistent with its 2.4x compression.

The remaining half of that phase is the allocation itself: `init_ordinary`
writes every field of a ~528-byte `JsObject`, and the `Function` box is a
second arena allocation. That is the structural item, not a scan.

## PROFILE (2026-10-29): the corpus's #1 row decomposed, and it is calls

Closure creation was the assumed headline of the for-in head-let row. It is
not: it is 12% of the row. The row's body (`__t262Body`, 100k iterations per
`bench()` call) decomposes as follows, `ablate.sh` on amplified one-component
variants (`scratch/lcf/hl2`, 1000 bodies per call, `--jitless` column, per
body):

| variant | jl µs/body | delta | per operation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `e-empty` (`Object.create(null)` + 3 defines + a 3-key for-in) | 0.83 | | |
| `c-noclos` (+ 3 `fns[x] = 1` stores) | 1.41 | 0.60 | **199 ns/store** |
| `b-nostore` (closures instead of stores) | 2.14 | 0.73 | **245 ns/closure** |
| `d-noassert` (the real body minus the 6 `assert.sameValue` calls) | 2.74 | | |
| `a-full` (the real body) | **7.18** | **4.44** | **740 ns/assert** |

So the six assertion statements are **62% of the row** and calls are its single
largest term. Everything the last two sessions optimised here (closure creation,
defines, stores) is 30% combined.

The calls are also 3-8x node wherever they are. Per-call, same harness:

| call shape | jl ns/call | jit ms |
|---|---:|---:|
| `add(1,2)` where `add(a,b){return a+b}` | **92** | 0.097 |
| `o.m(1,2)`, `m` the same body, read off a literal object | 106 | 0.115 |
| `add(1,2)` where `add` also has `if (a===b) throw ...` | **301** | 0.438 |
| `A.same(x, y)` with the same throw, called as a method | 358 | 1.176 |
| 3 string args to the same `add` | 166 | 0.357 |

Two mechanisms, both verified in the engine rather than inferred:

1. **The optimizing tier refuses any body containing `throw`.**
   `SLAG_JIT_REPORT=1 JIT_DUMP_STEPS=1` on the two `add` shapes prints
   `opt-blockers: Throw` for the throwing one and nothing for the plain one.
   The blocker is one line, `block_successors` in
   `crates/jit/src/opt/lift/mod.rs` (`Step::Throw { .. } => Err(Unsupported::Step("Throw"))`):
   a `throw` block has no successor because the lift has no throwing terminator.
   The interpreter still treats the body as a leaf (`steps_are_leaf` does not
   exclude `Throw`), which is why the jl cost is 3x rather than 30x, but it
   falls to the **step-path** leaf instead of a register leaf.
2. **A leaf body with a branch is a step-path leaf**, so each call dispatches
   its steps instead of running one register run. That is the 92 -> 301 ns
   jump in the interpreter, and it is the same shape: `return a + b` is one
   register run, `if (...) throw ...; return a + b` is not.

For real code this matters more than the fixture: every validation helper,
parser and assertion path in the wild is "compare, throw on failure, return".
The engine makes each of those callers pay 3x in the interpreter and refuses
their callees entirely in the optimizing tier.

**The next slice, in order of value:**

1. Lift `Step::Throw` in the optimizing tier (`Term::Throw` + the lowerer's
   throw control, mirroring the baseline compiler's `throw_control`). It is one
   `block_successors` arm plus a terminator, and it un-refuses a whole class of
   bodies. Verify with `SLAG_JIT_REPORT` that the `Throw` blocker disappears and
   with the throw/unwind fixtures.
2. Make a branching leaf lower to register ops with a branch (`if` + `throw` is
   the minimal case), or at least stop marking such a body a leaf so it takes
   the general lane rather than the step-path leaf.
3. Only then revisit closure creation, which is 12% of this row.

Measured along the way, for the next reader: a `for...in` over a 3-key literal
object is ~790 ns/iteration (`l-leaf-forin` 1.345 µs against `j-leaf` 0.554 for
the same six calls); a `throw` in a callee costs +209 ns/call even though it
never executes (`h-throw` 3.10 µs against `i-nothrow` 2.14 over 9 calls); and a
member read costs ~14 ns on top of a leaf call (`o-method-num`).

### LANDED (2026-10-29): the optimizing tier lifts `throw`

A lifted body has no handler (`Step::EnterTry` has no lowering), so a `throw`
in one always escapes. That makes it the simplest terminator in the tier, and
the lift had it as the *only* refused terminator: `block_successors` gave a
`throw` block no successor. Now it lifts as `Term::Throw(value)` (which the IR
already had, and which `cse`/`dce` already walked), and the lowerer raises the
value through `Helper::ThrowControl` and returns.

`throw_control` is the right entry point rather than a new "set the pending
error" helper, for two reasons learned by reading rather than guessing.
`throw_machinery`'s escaping arm is what closes an active for-of iterator
(spec 14.7.5.6) and disposes the scopes' `using` resources (spec 9.4.3,
nesting a SuppressedError on a throwing disposal); a bare pending-error write
would skip both. And it scans `try_stack` against the *current* body's handler
table, which for a lifted body is empty, so every enclosing frame is skipped and
the throw escapes exactly as it must. The `ip` argument is 0: with no handlers
there is nothing for `throw_machinery` to match it against.

Measured, same-binary interleaved, minima:

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| for-in head-let row, jit | 377.7 ms | **368.8 ms** (-2.4%) |
| whole corpus, jit | 1970.7 ms | 1963.8 ms (-0.35%, inside the noise floor) |
| `control` family | 98.9 ms | 98.8 ms (flat) |

`SLAG_JIT_REPORT` no longer prints `opt-blockers: Throw`. A probe of the shape
(`add(a,b){ if (a===b) throw ...; return a+b }`, 6 calls per body) reads
0.438 -> 0.393 ms compiled. That is a 10% move and not the 4x the per-call
interpreter figure suggested, because the *baseline* tier already ran such a
body well; the gain is in the tier the body now lands in, not in a broken lane.

One thing this deliberately does NOT do: mark the body `deopts` so the
machine-code inline lanes refuse it. That looks necessary and is not: the
in-frame leaf tail already checks the ctx's pending byte after the call
(`emit_leaf_result_tail`), so a throwing callee propagates through an inlined
caller exactly like a throwing slow path. Making it `deopts` instead measured
0.393 -> **1.246** ms, worse than not compiling the body at all.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites); test262 `language` 23,726 + `built-ins` 23,821 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 = 51,998 at 100% (`--timeout 15 --recheck-timeout 15`); corpus 77 rows `mismatches=0`.

**Item 2 of the previous note stands and is now the larger half:** a branching
leaf body is a *step-path* leaf, not a register leaf, which is the 92 -> 301 ns
per-call figure in the interpreter. That is untouched here.

## NULL (2026-10-29): whole-body register segmentation is not a drop-in

A branching leaf body (`add(a,b){ if (a===b) throw ...; return a+b }`) is a
*step-path* leaf, not a register leaf, because `lower_leaf_ops` accepts only
left-leaning straight-line shapes. That is the 92 -> 301 ns per-call figure in
the interpreter (see the 2026-10-29 row decomposition above).

The tempting shortcut is to reuse the machinery that already exists:
`lower_leaf_ops_segmented` + `apply_register_runs` split a *loop body* into
maximal straight-line runs, each replaced by one `Step::RunRegBody`. Extending
that to the whole body when `leaf_ops` is `None` looked additive (compute
`leaf_ops` first, so a body that already has the whole-body form keeps it, and
move `declared_calls` after the collapse so its step indices are the final
ones; the per-loop call already runs during `compile_statements`, before
`declared_calls` is computed).

It compiles and it is **wrong**: the corpus probe dies with
`TypeError: Uncaught exception`, i.e. a step read a stack slot the run never
