left. `lower_leaf_ops_segmented`'s accept rules are written for a loop body,
where the runs are bracketed by loop machinery; over a whole function body a
run can absorb steps whose value-stack effect the surrounding step-path code
still depends on (a statement completion, a `Push` feeding a non-lowerable
step). Reverted; the tree is unchanged.

**What the next attempt needs.** Either restate the run invariant for a whole
body — a run may only absorb a step sequence that leaves the value stack
exactly as those steps would — or teach the register *leaf* executor to branch
(`LeafOp::Jump`/`JumpIfFalse` with op-index targets, patched from a
step->op map, only when the shadow stack is empty at the branch and the target
step emits an op). The second is the design the skill's mirror list already
describes and costs the full seven-place `LeafOp` mirror; the first is cheaper
only if the invariant holds, which is what this attempt assumed and did not
prove. Measure before building either: the win is interpreter-only
(`leaf_ops` feeds the interpreter's leaf lanes; the JIT compiles steps).

## PRICED (2026-10-29): per-call cost, all four shapes

Before building anything on the "calls are 62% of the row" finding, the four
call shapes were priced against node on the same harness (per call, `ablate.sh`
minima, 6000 calls per run):

| shape | slag jl | node jl | slag jit | node jit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| register leaf `add(a,b){return a+b}` | **99** | 70 | **16** | 50 |
| branch leaf `if (a===b) return 0; return a+b` | **146** | 75 | 19 | 57 |
| non-leaf `mid(a,b){return add(a,b)}` | **304** | 124 | **80** | 88 |
| method read + register leaf `o.mid(a,b)` | **107** | 73 | 19 | 49 |

Two conclusions that change the plan, and both were cheap to get:

1. **The JIT is at or ahead of node on every one of these shapes** (16 vs 50,
   19 vs 57, 80 vs 88, 19 vs 49). The per-call cost in the ranked column is
   not where the corpus gap lives.
2. **Both of the remaining "call" items are interpreter-only.** The branch-leaf
   penalty is +47 ns jl and +3 ns jit; the non-leaf penalty is +205 ns jl and
   +64 ns jit. So the 62%-of-row finding is a description of the *interpreter*,
   which matters for `--jitless` and as the machinery diagnostic, not for the
   headline.

That reorders the remaining work: the 8.6x on the row under the JIT is not
per-call, it is that the fixture makes ~3 non-leaf activations per assertion
statement, and both we and node pay real per-activation cost for those.

### NULL (2026-10-29): branch-capable register leaves, blocked by the completion wrappers

The design was built and works up to one step: `LeafOp::Jump`/`JumpIfFalse`/
`JumpIfTrue` over op indices, patched from a step->op map, accepted only when
the shadow stack is empty at the branch, the target step emits an op, and the
executor turned from `for op in ops` into an index loop. It compiles and the
engine runs.

It never fires, and the reason is the step list. `function add(a,b){ if (a===b)
return 0; return a+b; }` compiles to

    ResetCompletion, LoadLocal 0, LoadLocal 1, StrictEqual, JumpIfFalse(8),
    Push(0), Return, Jump(8), NormalizeCompletion, LoadLocal 0, LoadLocal 1,
    Add, Return

so a guard clause is *bracketed* by `ResetCompletion` and `NormalizeCompletion`,
and the branch target IS the `NormalizeCompletion` step. Braces around the
`if` body add a `ListBegin`/`ListEnd` pair on top. None of those lower to a
register op, so `lower_leaf_ops` still returns `None` and the body stays a
step-path leaf. Making it fire means deciding that statement-completion
machinery is a no-op inside a register leaf body, which is a semantic claim
about completion values, not a mechanical change - exactly the "when in doubt,
a body stays on the step path" rule in the bytecode-vm skill.

The step lists above are the artifact: the next attempt starts from them, not
from re-deriving what a guard clause compiles to. Reverted; `crates/` is
unchanged.

### NULL (2026-10-29, second attempt): the register form cannot carry a branch yet

Re-attempted the branch-capable register leaf, this time with the completion
wrappers understood. Two findings, one of them load-bearing.

**The `Return` rule was the first blocker, and relaxing it is sound and ready.**
`lower_step`'s `Step::Return` arm refused any return that was not the body's last
step, which is every multi-path body. `ReturnAcc` ends the register run, so the
ops emitted for the steps after it are reachable only through a jump that targets
them; dropping the `index + 1 != total` guard is correct on its own.

**The real blocker is the shadow stack at the branch.** With the branch ops in,
the wrapper skipping in and the target resolution working, `lower_leaf_ops` still
returns `None` - and tracing every other return point in the function left the
branch guard as the only one that can fire. So at

    LoadLocal 0, LoadLocal 1, Binary(StrictEqual), JumpIfFalse(8)

the compile-time operand stack is NOT empty when the branch is reached: the
register binary consumes its right operand and leaves the left one as a re-readable
shadow entry (the op re-reads it from the frame). A branch with a live shadow would
need the two paths to agree about that entry, which the flat op array has no phi
to express - the guard is right to refuse.

Fixing it means changing the binary lowering so a condition leaves the shadow
empty, which is a change to the register op contracts (`BinReg`/`BinImmLocal` and
the operands' re-read semantics), not a slice on top of them. Reverted again;
`crates/` is unchanged.

The design that is now known to work up to that point, for the next attempt:
`LeafOp::Jump`/`JumpIfFalse`/`JumpIfTrue` over op indices, the executor as an
index loop, targets resolved after the array is built to the first step that
emits an op (skipping the completion wrappers `lower_step` already treats as
no-ops), gated on an empty shadow at the branch, and the `Return` guard relaxed.

## NULL (2026-10-29): the "tier-selection cluster" and the `calls/*` pessimization are both mirages

`where.py` reports `gap` (slag_jit/node_jit) and `jl_gap` (slag_jl/node_jl), and
three rows looked like the optimizing tier was hurting:

    gap 28.3, jl_gap 4.4   calls/closure_capture
    gap  7.4, jl_gap 2.6   calls/method_call
    gap 13.2, jl_gap 6.6   control/generator_loop

`jl_gap` is not "jitless versus jit". It is slag-jitless over NODE-jitless. So a
low `jl_gap` next to a high `gap` says the *interpreter* is closer to node's
interpreter than the compiled engine is to node's compiled engine: it is a
statement about node's optimizer, not about our tier choice. Measured directly
(`--corpus` minima over three runs, whole `calls` family):

| row | jit | jitless | ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `closure_capture` | 38.4 ms | 123.1 ms | **3.2x faster compiled** |
| `method_call` | 53.6 | 172.8 | 3.2x |
| `apply_call` | 30.3 | 100.4 | 3.3x |
| `recursive_fib` | 46.0 | 496.2 | 10.8x |
| `direct_leaf` | 5.75 | 78.8 | 13.7x |
| `construct_churn` | 55.1 | 134.0 | 2.4x |

There is no JIT pessimization on any of them, and `SLAG_OPT=0` changes
`closure_capture` by 6% and `method_call` by nothing. The 28.3x is node's
optimizer inlining `fns[i & 63](i)` (node_jit 1.4 ms against its own
node_jitless ~28 ms, a 20x optimizer win); no tier switch reaches it. The item
that would is the one the notes already name: a callee resolved *inside a
compiled loop body*, which needs either a call-site IC for a computed callee or
OSR plus compiled-code feedback, because `sites_from_feedback` is empty for
exactly those bodies.

**Tier selection is not a lever either.** Corpus-wide, three interleaved runs:
the optimizing tier is **1966.7 ms** and `SLAG_OPT=0` is **2236.6 ms**, so the
optimizing tier is 13.7% faster overall. A per-row oracle could still recover the
~14 ms the earlier note measured across 20 rows, but no static rule finds it, and
0.7% does not pay for the machinery.

Both were worth the twenty minutes: they remove the two largest remaining
candidates from the board with numbers rather than impressions.

## PROBE (2026-10-29): the empty-feedback claim holds, and the real cost is the env-carrying leaf

Ran the confirmation the previous note asked for. `SLAG_FEEDBACK=1` over three
single-row corpus dirs (a named global leaf called in a loop, an
8-way computed callee, a monomorphic computed callee) reports **0 sites, 0
hits on all three**, and `SLAG_INLINE_TRACE=1` reports
`0 site(s) of 21 step(s), feedback=false` for the loop bodies. So the claim is
stronger than the earlier note: a call site inside a loop body records no
feedback at all, named or computed.

That is not what makes those rows slow, though. Per call (ablate minima, count
divided out):

| probe | jit ms | per call | node jit | per call |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| named global leaf `inc(i)`, 2M | 15.28 | **7.6 ns** | 82.0 | 41 |
| `fns[3](i)`, monomorphic computed, 2M | 19.88 | 9.9 | 84.6 | 42 |
| `fns[i&7](i)`, poly computed, no capture, 2M | 27.07 | 13.5 | 86.8 | 43 |
| `fns[i&7](i)`, **capturing** callee, 1M | 26.58 | **26.6** | 1.18 | **1.2** |
| the same with `base` captured too, 1M | 31.38 | **31.4** | 1.44 | 1.4 |

Two readings:

1. **The computed-callee penalty is small** (13.5 vs 7.6 ns). It is not what
   `calls/closure_capture` pays.
2. **A leaf that reads a captured binding costs 2x a plain leaf** (26.6 against
   13.5 ns), and that is exactly the row's shape: every callee captures. In the
   interpreter the same step is 85 -> 127 ns, so the lane is not an interpreter
   artifact either.

So the scoped target is the *env-carrying leaf lane* (`leaf_uses_env`, the
`leaf_call_env` helper and the `body_context`/`lexical_env` swap), where 13-18 ns
per call is paid to install an environment that is almost always the same one the
callee was created with. Node's 1.2 ns is inlining, which is the optimizer
project; the env lane is runtime work and is the cheaper half.

Also worth recording: `a-named-leaf` at 7.6 ns/call against node's 41 ns means
the *leaf call lane itself* is already 5x faster than node's compiled call. The
gap on `calls/*` is concentrated in the capturing shape, not in calls as such.

## INSTRUMENT (2026-10-29): a RIP sampler, and what it says the gap is made of

Every ranking instrument this project had was an *external* one: total time
per row, a tier seam, or a hand-instrumented phase timer. None of them could
answer "which function is the engine running", which is why the last sessions
priced components one at a time and still could not see the whole. This adds
the missing one.

### The sampler

`SLAG_SAMPLE=<interval-µs>` starts a watchdog thread in the CLI
(`crates/cli/src/sampler.rs`). It suspends the engine thread on the interval,
reads `Rip` from the thread `CONTEXT`, resumes, and records
`rip - module_base`. At exit it prints to stderr:

    profile samples <n> outside <m> (<pct>%)
    profile 0x<rva> <count> <share>
    profile end

The binary does no symbol handling. `tools/profile.py` turns the offsets into
functions with the artifacts the release build already writes: the PE unwind
directory (`llvm-readobj --unwind`) for exact `[start, end)` ranges and the
PBD's publics (`llvm-pdbutil dump -publics`) for names. It caches the table
next to the binary. `--group` aggregates by `crate::module`, `--top N` by
function.

Two attribution traps, both hit and fixed while building it:

1. **A public symbol has no size.** Letting `llvm-symbolizer` resolve an
   address directly attributes every address after the last public symbol to
   that symbol: `Vm::setup_frame` (a 4.4 KB function) swallowed 5 MB of code
   and appeared as the engine's #1 cost at 7.27%. Resolve the address to its
   unwind range first, then name the range by the public at its start. That
   moved `setup_frame` to 1.24% and deleted a phantom 2.1% entry
   (`assign_super_computed`, a helper no workload calls).
2. **Build with `debug = false` has publics for about half the functions.**
   327 unnamed ranges remain (33% of samples); each is labelled `local near
   <nearest preceding named function>`, which is honest but only a hint.

Validated against rows whose profile is obvious: `opcost/baseline` is 90%
outside the image (compiled code), `opcost/regexp_test` is topped by
`regexp::engine::Matcher::match_at`, `opcost/json_stringify` by
`builtins::json::dispatch_call`, `builtins/map_churn` by
`builtins::keyed::dispatch_construct`.

### The measurement that reframes the goal

Same binary, one `--corpus` pass, 77 rows, all four modes agreeing
(`mismatches=0`):

| | total ms |
| --- | ---: |
| slag jit | 2085.4 |
| slag jitless | 5320.4 |
| node jit | 727.0 |
| node jitless | 1758.7 |

So the **total-time gap is 2.87x**, and each engine's optimizer is worth the
same: slag's jit/jitless ratio is **2.55x**, node's is **2.42x**. The 9.7x
`mean-jitGap` headline is a mean of per-row ratios, so it is dominated by rows
where V8 folds the loop to nothing; it is not a statement about the engine.
**The deficit is the runtime, at about 3x, and it is inherited equally by both
tiers.** Optimizer work (inlining, escape analysis, better IR) cannot close
it: at parity per tier, a perfect optimizer would only reach node's *current*
number by fixing the primitives.

### Where the 2085 ms goes (self time, corpus-wide, 63332 samples)

| share | subsystem |
| ---: | --- |
| 37.8% | [jit/native code] (outside the image; our own compiled bodies) |
| 9.0% | `runtime::jit` (the helper mirror) |
| 8.2% | `runtime::builtins` |
| 8.1% | `runtime::ir` (VM, frames, dispatch) |
| 6.1% | `crux::object` |
| 5.8% | `crux::heap` (allocation + GC) |
| 4.8% | `crux::string` |
| 3.7% | `runtime::function` (closure creation) |
| 2.2% | `core::slice` (sort) |
| 1.7% | `crux::map` (shapes) |

It is **flat**: no function exceeds 2.2%, and the top ten together are under
15%. There is no hot spot to fix; there is a uniform tax. That is the single
most important thing this instrument says, and it is why every "find the one
big win" session has ended in a NULL.

Top named functions: `Heap::collect_minor_inner` 1.99,
`jit::call_slow` 1.98, `string::lookup` 1.51, `Heap::alloc` 0.95,
`JsString::from_utf8` 0.91, `map::Map::find` 0.85, `dense_index_define` 0.84,
`string::intern` 0.70, `JsString::as_slice` 0.70.

### Per row, where time concentrates

The aggregate is flat but individual rows are not, and that is where a slice
can be proven:

`objects/spread_assign` (115 ms) is **40% property machinery**:
`Map::find` 8.10, `JsObject::set_with_receiver_key` 7.99,
`define_property_or_throw` 7.16, `Map::get_or_create_child` 5.07,
`get_own_property_key` 3.79, `define_fresh` 2.20, `canonical_numeric_index`
2.13, `string::lookup` 3.90. The define path per new key is a linear
`Map::find` over the current shape's descriptors plus an FxHash transition
lookup keyed on `(PropertyKey, MapAttrs)`, which is where the 45 ns measured
for a fresh-object define (`.notes` 2026-10-29, `scratch/storecost`) comes
from.

`calls/recursive_fib` is 67% `jit::call_slow` and 29% compiled code, i.e. the
self-call lane plus the callee's work and nothing else.

`calls/method_call` is **85% compiled code**: the splice removed the runtime
entirely. A row like that has no runtime slice to take, which is the target
state for the others.

`builtins/object_keys` is 28% native / 24% `crux::object` / 21% `crux::heap`.

`language/.../head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration` (477 ms, the #1 row) is
`runtime::jit` 14.9, native 14.6, `runtime::ir` 10.9, **`runtime::function`
10.8**, `crux::object` 6.7, `crux::string` 6.6. The 10.8% in
`runtime::function` is closure creation, consistent with the 12% the ablation
found, and it is the largest named term on the row.

### Why "make one thing faster" is not the plan

At 2.87x total and a uniform tax, a 10% corpus move needs roughly 200 ms, which
is more than the entire `crux::string` family. The realistic shape is three to
five slices of 30-60 ms each, each verified on the row it touches with a
same-binary seam, and each recorded here.

### Negative: `-C target-cpu=native`

The bottleneck note lists it as an untried, knowledge-free lever. Measured:
two builds of the same tree with and without it, 5 interleaved whole-corpus
rounds, per-row minima: **base 2251.1 ms, native 2328.9 ms (+3.46%)**. Row
deltas ranged from -21% to +44% on rows the flag cannot plausibly affect.
Even if the flag helps somewhere, this machine cannot resolve it against the
build-to-build layout effect, so it is not shippable on this evidence. Keep
the generic target.

### Negative: two builds of identical source differ by 3.5%

The same run is also the cleanest measurement yet of the layout confound:
`b-named` style row-level swings of -21..+44% and a 3.46% whole-corpus move
between two binaries whose *source is identical* (only the codegen target
differed). Any slice landing under ~4% must be proven with a **same-binary**
seam, not a before/after build pair. This raises the bar for the "small
slices" strategy and is why the sampler exists: it picks targets by share, and
the seam proves them.

### SCOPED (not started): the compiled define takes a shape-cell path

The define probe (`scratch/def/three.js`, 600k defines, 46.5 ms) is the
clearest concentrated profile in the corpus:

| share | function |
| ---: | --- |
| 11.2% | the general `[[Set]]` routine (anonymous, calls `put_value`, `get_prototype_of`, `define_fresh`, `Map::find`, `field_offset`) |
| 10.6% | `Map::get_or_create_child` (FxHash transition lookup) |
| 9.9% | `Map::find` (linear descriptor scan) |
| 4.9% | `Map::field_offset` (a **second** linear scan of the same vector) |
| 3.1% | `JsObject::define_fresh` |
| 2.4% | `get_own_property_key` |
| 2.2% | `with_heap_cell` |

So one new-key define performs two full descriptor scans plus a hashed
transition lookup, and the batch literal path already proves a cheaper define
exists: `{a:1,b:1,c:1}` costs 22 ns/field against 44 for three incremental
defines.

The slice is to let a compiled named store take the shape-cell path for a
**missing** key as well as a present one: probe `(map id, name)` for a
`(child map, offset)` pair, and write through `in_fields` with a map bump,
guarded by (1) the receiver is extensible, (2) it is a plain ordinary object
(no proxy/indexed/arguments kind), (3) the prototype chain is clean (no setter
for the key, the same chain-clean gate the constructor fill already needs),
and (4) the shape cell's `count` still matches the map. Any guard failure
declines to today's path. The cell already exists for present keys
(`emit_shape_store_probe` / `emit_deferred_field_store`), so the work is the
decline logic and the guard set, not a new mechanism.

Expected: 46 -> ~20-25 ns per define, which is 20-25 ms on
`objects/spread_assign`, ~25 ms on the #1 row's three stores, and part of
`calls/construct_churn`. Correctness surface is the whole [[Set]] semantics,
so it must land behind the full four-sweep gate, with fixtures for a prototype
setter, a non-extensible target, a frozen field, and an accessor on the chain.

## LANDED (2026-10-29): the fresh-object define drops one transition hash and two descriptor scans

The scoped slice above, implemented in three parts, all inside the define path
`fast_fresh_store` -> `define_fresh`:

1. **A one-entry transition hint on the map.** `Map::get_or_create_child`
   hashed `(PropertyKey, MapAttrs)` on every fork. A shape gains the same next
   key on every object that carries it (a constructor's fields, a literal's
   keys), so `Map::last_transition` caches the last `(key, attrs) -> child` and
   the steady state is two compares. The `transitions` map stays
   authoritative; the hint is only a memo.
2. **`define_fresh` writes the field at the ordinal it already knows.** The
   transition appends the descriptor at the parent's descriptor count, so the
   fresh key's offset is known before the fork. The old code then called
   `map_set`, which re-resolved the key in the child map with another scan.
3. **`fast_fresh_store`'s post-define cache fill scans once.** It called
   `field_offset` (scan) and then `find` + `descriptor_at` (a second scan) on
   the same map for the same key. One `find` answers both.

Measured, 7 interleaved rounds, per-row minima, pre-change binary against
post-change binary:

| probe | pre | post | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `scratch/def/three.js` (`{}` + 3 defines, 200k bodies) | 35.85 ms | **31.58 ms** | **-11.9%** |
| `objects/spread_assign` | 95.64 | **90.74** | **-5.1%** |
| whole corpus (77 rows) | 1963.7 | **1952.0** | **-0.60%** |

The hint alone, same-binary seam (`SLAG_DEFINE_HINT=0`), same protocol: 32.92
-> 31.93 ms on the define probe (**-3.0%**), so parts 2 and 3 are the other
~9%. Re-profiled after the change, `Map::get_or_create_child` falls from 10.6%
to 2.9% of the probe and `field_offset` from 4.9% to 2.8%.

The corpus number is small because most rows do not define incrementally: the
defining rows are `spread_assign` (-5.1%), `json_roundtrip` (-2.2%) and
`array_slice` (-2.5%), and the rest is inside the layout noise. The define is
still 3 scans and a helper call away from the batch literal's 22 ns/field, so
another slice exists, but it needs the ordinal threaded from the pre-check
through `define_fresh` and back (this change stopped at the two provably
redundant scans).

**Soundness of the untraced hint (the non-obvious part).** `last_transition`
holds a `Handle<Map>` and is not visited by `Map::trace`. That is sound for two
reasons, both checked rather than assumed: the heap is a **non-moving**
mark-sweep (`Gc<T>` derefs straight to an individually boxed payload, and
`JsObject::map` is a `Cell<Option<Handle<Map>>>`, which the collector could not
rewrite), and the child is **reachable anyway** through `transitions`, which is
traced and which no code ever removes an entry from. The GC's invariant is
reachability, not uniqueness. If a future change ever removes a transition
entry, it must clear the hint.

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets
-- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites, 0 failed); test262
`language` 23,726 + `built-ins` 23,821 + `annexB` 1,086 + `intl402` 3,365 =
51,998 at 100% (`--timeout 15 --recheck-timeout 15`); corpus 77 rows
`mismatches=0`.

### LANDED (2026-10-29, same day): the ordinal threaded through the define

The note above stopped at the two provably redundant scans. The third was a
*double proof* of the same fact: `fast_fresh_store` proved the key absent by
scanning (`field_offset`), `define_fresh` proved it again (`map.find`), and the
cache fill resolved it a third time (`find`).

Now the caller hands the define what it already resolved
(`FreshKey::{Absent, At(ordinal), Unknown}`) and the define hands back where
the value landed (`FreshDefine::{Declined, NoMapSlot, At { slot, writable }}`),
so:

- an undescribed key skips `define_fresh`'s scan entirely (`Absent`);
- a presize hole fills at the ordinal the caller already found (`At`);
- the cache fill takes the reported ordinal and writability instead of
  scanning, and a vector-only define reports `NoMapSlot` so the caller has no
  slot to cache (the three-state result is why the return type is not a bool:
  "declined" and "defined without a map slot" must not be conflated).

Measured the same way (7 interleaved rounds, per-row minima, pre-change
binary): the define probe **36.07 -> 30.47 ms (-15.5%)** for both slices
together (the hint and the two scan merges alone were -11.9%, so this half is
about -4%), `objects/spread_assign` 94.68 -> 89.59 (-5.4%),
`builtins/json_roundtrip` -3.0%, `control/generator_loop` -5.4%. The corpus is
**1960.7 -> 1953.5 (-0.37% for this half, -0.97% against the pre-change
binary)**, which is honest: only the rows that define incrementally move, and
the rest of the swing is the layout noise the sampler commit measured.

**The trap this half walked into, and the test that caught it.** Treating
`Map::field_offset == None` as "the key is absent" is wrong: a
non-default-attributes define, a dictionary-mode object, and a key past
`INLINE_FIELDS` are all *undescribed but present* — they live only in the
property vector. `installed_jit_member_store_respects_non_writable` failed
(50 instead of 10) because a `writable: false` property was redefined as a
fresh writable field. The map describes exactly the keys whose field mirrors
the value; undescribed means "not map-served", never "not present". The
fallback to `get_own_property_key` is load-bearing.

Gates: same four as above, all at 100%, plus `--gc-stress --gc-verify` on the
define probe.

### LANDED (2026-10-29, same day): a computed string key takes the fresh-store path too

Both slices above were invisible to the corpus's biggest defining shape,
because `fast_fresh_store` began with

    let PropertyKeyName::Name(atom) = key else { return Ok(false) };

and a computed store arrives as `Key(PropertyKey)` — the key already converted
by `assign_computed_plain`'s `to_property_key`. But `member_reference` maps
*both* forms to `PropertyKey::String(atom)`, so the acceptance test was pure
conservatism: a computed key that converted to a string atom is the same store
as the named form. It now goes through `name_atom`, which already existed for
exactly this normalization.

That one test change is the session's largest win, because the corpus's #1 row
is `fns[x] = function () { return x; }` — three computed-key stores per body,
100k bodies:

| row | before | after | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `language/.../head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration` | 408.67 ms | **365.24 ms** | **-10.6%** |
| `opcost/object_keys` | 32.74 | 31.45 | -3.9% |
| `strings/concat_loop` | 9.99 | 9.46 | -5.3% |
| whole corpus | 1957.9 | **1916.3** | **-2.12%** |

(7 interleaved rounds, per-row minima; re-run 1947.6 -> 1903.2, -2.28%.) The
#1 row is now 365 ms against node's 54.8, i.e. the row that was 21% of the
recoverable time has moved 10.6% in one change.

**Two rows that "regressed" are the layout noise, and the workload says so.**
`control/generator_loop` read +6.9% in the first pass and +5.8% in the second,
but its source contains no computed property store at all (`s += g.next().value`
is a *read*), so the change cannot reach it. `calls/closure_capture` likewise
(+1.1%, no stores). This is the +-44% single-row build-to-build swing the
sampler commit measured, and it is why a row-level claim needs the workload's
shape as well as the number.

Gates: the four sweeps at 100% (51,998), `cargo test --workspace` 40 suites,
corpus `mismatches=0`.

Cumulative for the three define-path slices, 7 interleaved rounds, per-row
minima, against the binary the session started from: **corpus 2057.6 ->
1986.4 ms (-3.46%)**, with the #1 row **-13.2%** (458.26 -> 397.65, run-to-run
absolute levels vary; the paired delta is the reading) and `spread_assign`
-8.2%. The define probe is -15.5% over the same range. Nothing is left to
reclaim here by trimming: the remaining define cost is the runtime helper round
trip, so the next step in this area is a machine-code define, not another scan.

## PROFILE (2026-10-29): the two remaining big blocks, priced and reasoned

Both were followed up as asked; the answer for both is "the mechanism is known
and it is not a cheap slice". Numbers first, then the reasoning, because the
reasoning is what saves the next session.

### `runtime::function` on the #1 row (12.3% of the row)

`SLAG_SAMPLE=50`, the row alone (544 ms under the sampler, so shares are
slightly inflated toward sampling overhead):

| share | entry | what it is |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 7.23% | `local near runtime::function::is_constructor` (0x140a3fa70, 4232 B) | **`register_function`** |
| 2.31% | `instantiate_function_with_resolved_source` | the statement/expression form's prelude |
| 1.32% | `local near instantiate_dynamic_function` | its prelude |
| 0.73% | `owning_realm` | per-create realm resolution |
| 0.37% | `shared_accessor_body` | |

The 4232-byte anonymous function was identified by its callees
(`Gc::new`, `JsObject::define_fresh`, four `Rc::drop_slow` sites,
`drop_in_place<JsString>`, `raw_vec::handle_error`), which is the closure
record build: allocate the function object, define the boilerplate
properties, drop the shared inputs.

**Reachable? No new lever.** This is the same mechanism the project has
attacked four times: record size 200 -> 152 (flat), boxing the record into the
arena (+70%, then +80.6%), `IdMap<Handle<EcmaFunction>>` (+80.6%), Stage D
twice. The profile shows *what* it spends the time on (a `Gc::new` plus the
boilerplate defines) and nothing about *how* to make it cheaper that the
earlier measurements did not already rule out. The four `Rc::drop_slow` call
sites in its callee list are not evidence of churn: the sampler recorded no
samples in `drop_slow`, so those are cold arms, not per-create frees.

### `runtime::jit::call_slow` (56.6% of `calls/recursive_fib`)

`SLAG_SAMPLE=50`, the row alone: **56.6% `call_slow`, 9.7% `load_context`**,
29.1% compiled code, and essentially nothing else. The row is ~1.3M recursive
calls in 60 ms, so **~46 ns per call**, of which ~26 ns is the self-call lane
and ~4 ns is a second helper (`load_context`, because `fib` reads its own name
from the enclosing function's scope) — against node's ~5 ns per call.

`self_call_inline` per call does, in order: four guards; `save_scratch` (a
17-field `VmScratch`); `vm.stack.resize(base + buf_len, Undefined)` (a ~25-slot
memset, `JIT_STACK_SLACK` 16 + `JIT_INLINE_HEADROOM` 4 + frame);
`vm.stack.reserve`; the frame fill; `install_nested_frame`; `jit_depth += 1`;
the indirect entry call; and the same restores. Every one of those is
load-bearing: the scratch fields are what a caller mid-`switch`, mid-append or
mid-deopt would have read by the nested body, the memset is what keeps
`vm.stack` a valid root array for the conservative scan, and the nested frame
is what a helper's `frame_get` addresses.

**So the only real lever is to stop calling a helper at all** — a native
self-call: the compiled body calls its own entry with a freshly carved frame
and a depth guard, exactly as V8 does. That needs `vm.stack`'s ptr/len/cap in
the ctx so machine code can bump the length, plus an inline frame fill, the
depth check, and the write-back. It is a frame-protocol change, not a slice,
and its ceiling is `recursive_fib`'s 41.7 ms of recoverable time — about **1%
of the corpus**. Priced at that, it is the wrong next investment.

### What this says to do instead

The corpus self-time map is flat (no function over 2.2%), the two biggest
recoverable rows are 30% of the total, and after today's define work the #1
row's remaining mass is: 16.9% compiled code, 14.5% JIT helpers, 13.1%
`runtime::ir`, 12.3% closure creation, 7.4% heap (of which 4.8% is
`core::slice::sort` — the GC's sorted live-set search, not user sorting).
Four of those five need structural work. The one that does not is the GC's
live-set lookup, which is a *sort plus binary search per allocation* and shows
up as `heapsort` in every allocation-heavy row; that is the next thing to
price.

### NULL (2026-10-29): skipping the major GC's dead set does not pay, and that is the finding

The `heapsort` in the #1 row (4.78%) is `dead.sort_unstable()` in the
collector. The sweep itself never reads that list — it re-walks the arena on
mark bits — so the list exists only for the GC-4 compaction hook, and the major
path built it (a full `for_each_live` walk plus a sort) even when the hook was
the no-op the agent passes when `has_weak_structures()` is false. Gating it on
`precise`, which is exactly the caller's request for the set, looked like free
money.

Measured: **corpus 1887.5 -> 1906.5 (+1.01%)**, re-run **1892.8 -> 1896.6
(+0.20%)** — a wash at best, and the #1 row (where the 4.78% lived) moved only
-1.91% on its own. Reverted.

**Why it could not have worked: `precise` is effectively always true.** The
agent passes `has_weak` for it, and `has_weak_structures()` counts
`stack_traces` — which any `Error` construction populates. So the dead set is
built on essentially every major collection of a real run, the gate never
fires, and the flat measurement is the gate not firing rather than the work not
mattering. The lead that remains is upstream of this: make a transient stack
trace not force a precise dead set, which is a GC-semantics question (what a
stale stack word may keep alive), not a slice — and the minor path's own skip
(31% of a pause, recorded in its comment) suggests it is worth asking.

**Correction to the note above:** the suggestion that `heapsort` is "a sort plus
binary search per allocation" was wrong and is replaced by what is written
here: it is the collector's dead-set sort, at most once per collection.

## LANDED (2026-10-29): the wasm compiler emits native v128 instructions, 6.6x on a SIMD loop

Wave 5 carried `V128` as a Cranelift `I128` and lowered every vector op by
calling runtime helper mode 70, which re-enters the interpreter's
`simd_exec`. V8 does the opposite in both wasm tiers: the op *is* the machine
instruction (`i8x16.add` → `Add(V16B)` on NEON, `paddb` on x64). On x64 the
helper costs a call, two spill stores, a load, and a dispatch back into the
interpreter's lane loop, per op.

**Fixture.** `crates/wasmtest/fixtures/simd-native-loop.wast`: 2M
iterations over exactly the ops that had no native arm: `i32x4.mul`,
`i16x8.splat`+`i16x8.add`, `i32x4.shl`, `i32x4.gt_s`, `v128.bitselect`,
`i32x4.replace_lane`, `i8x16.bitmask`, plus an extract to consume the
result. Expected value `-1857128295` cross-checked against Node v24.12.0
(V8). The older `simd-loop.wast` covers only `i32x4.add` + `v128.xor`,
which were already native, so it cannot see this work.

**Method.** Same-binary seam, `SLAG_WASM_SIMD_NATIVE=0` restores the helper
path (`compile.rs::simd_native()`, cached in a `OnceLock`, because the raw
`var_os` read is ~140 ns and cannot sit on the per-op path). Seven
interleaved rounds, alternating order, per-row minimum and median. Two
controls (`simd-loop`, `leaf-loop`) run in the same driver so a machine-wide
drift cannot be read as a win.

| row | compiled | helper | interpreter |
|---|---|---|---|
| simd-native, before any lowering | 219.17 | 217.65 | 1031.41 |
| simd-native, after | **35.74** | 235.58 | 1142.09 |
| simd-loop control | 11.70 → 13.31 | - | - |
| leaf-loop control | 13.60 → 15.61 | - | - |

Same-session A/B: **35.74 vs 235.58 ms, 6.59x**. The compiled row is now
31x the interpreter row (1142.09 / 35.74). Both controls moved +14% between
the two sessions, and the helper row moved +8% with them, which is why the
before/after columns above are not directly comparable; only the A/B row
is. This is the NULL register's lesson repeating: layout and machine state
move a row more than most optimisations do.

**What the corpus caught that the unit test did not.** The first cut mapped
the shift opcodes through `sub - 0x6b` as `0 => shl, 1 => ushr, 2 => sshr`,
but the wasm block order is `shl, shr_s, shr_u`, so arithmetic and logical
right shift were swapped. The differential test passed because it only used
shift count 5 on a value whose bytes were all small enough that `shr_s` and
`shr_u` agree; `simd_bit_shift.wast` failed 31 commands, and `simd_splat`
2 (the `…_operand` shapes that splat then shift). The test now runs counts
0, 1, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 15, 16, 17, 32, 33 over a `0xAA…` pattern for all four
shapes. Treat every per-shape opcode table as needing its own arity check:
the same class of bug hit the `i64x2` comparison table earlier in this work.

**Gates.** `wasmtest equiv waspec/test/core` → 254 suites, 0 diverged,
8264/8264 functions compiled; `equiv waspec/test/core/relaxed-simd` → 7
suites, 0 diverged; `cargo test -p wasm --features compile --lib` (125),
`cargo test -p wasm --lib` (44), `cargo test -p wasmtest`,
`cargo test -p runtime --lib` (1079); workspace clippy and `cargo fmt
--check` clean.

Plan reference: `.notes/wasm-plan.md` §10.3.

## LANDED (2026-10-29, same day): native float v128 arithmetic, 18x on a float loop

Follow-up to the entry above. The integer set left the `f32x4`/`f64x2`
family on the helper: sixteen opcodes in one interpreter dispatch
(`fp_arith_binop`, which calls `values::exec_num` once per lane). All sixteen
now lower: add/sub/mul/div, min/max, and pmin/pmax.

**Fixture.** `crates/wasmtest/fixtures/simd-native-float.wast`: 2M
iterations of eight `f32x4` and eight `f64x2` ops over two loop-carried
accumulators, clamped by `min`/`max` so the sequence can never reach a NaN or
an infinity (a NaN result would make the expected value engine-specific).
Expected value `-1996488704` cross-checked against Node v24.12.0.

| row | compiled | helper | interpreter |
|---|---|---|---|
| simd-float | **56.13** | 1017.18 | 2508.56 |
| simd-native (integer probe, re-run) | 32.87 | 221.90 | 1050.07 |
| simd-loop control | 12.51 | - | - |
| leaf-loop control | 13.99 | - | - |

Same-binary A/B: **56.13 vs 1017.18 ms, 18.1x**; the compiled row is 44.7x
the interpreter row. The integer probe re-measured at 6.75x, consistent with
the 6.59x recorded above, and both controls stayed flat, so the float ratio is
not a machine-state artifact. The 18x is larger than the integer 6.75x because
each op here is a serially dependent FP instruction with a five-instruction
canonicalization, while the helper pays the full per-op dispatch plus a
`exec_num` call per lane.

**What the float work needed that the integer work did not.**

- `values::exec_num` canonicalizes every float result (`canon32`), so the
  native path must too. `0 * inf`, `inf - inf` and `0 / 0` produce a NaN from
  non-NaN operands, and x86's default quiet NaN for those has the **sign bit
  set** (`0xFFC00000`), while the canonical one is `0x7FC00000`. The test
  covers all three shapes for exactly this reason.
- add/sub/mul/div mask on `isnan(result)`; min/max mask on
  `isnan(a) || isnan(b)`, because the ordered pick would otherwise return the
  non-NaN operand (which is Cranelift's own `fmin`/`fmax`, i.e. IEEE 754-2019
  `minimum`/`maximum`, not wasm).
- min/max tie-breaking is the OR of the bit patterns for min and the AND for
  max: an equal pair differs only for `-0`/`+0`, and the OR keeps the negative
  sign for min while the AND keeps the positive one for max.
- pmin/pmax take a plain ordered comparison and return `a` in the unordered
  case, with no canonicalization at all: the interpreter returns the raw
  operand bits there.
- `fcmp` on a vector yields an **integer** vector (`i32x4`/`i64x2`), so every
  mask needs a `bitcast` to the lane type before the bitwise select; the
  verifier rejects the mix.

**Gates.** `wasmtest equiv waspec/test/core` → 254 suites, 0 diverged,
8264/8264 functions compiled; `simd` → 59 suites, 0 diverged; `relaxed-simd`
→ 7 suites, 0 diverged. `cargo test -p wasm --features compile --lib` (126),
`-p wasm --lib` (44), workspace clippy, `cargo fmt --check` clean. The new
`v128_native_float_arith_matches_the_interpreter` runs all sixteen opcodes
over canonical/payload/signaling NaN, `±0` pairs, infinities, and
overflow/underflow shapes.

## LANDED (2026-10-29, same day): native float unops and `i8x16.swizzle`, 21x

Third cut of the same work. This closes the rest of the unary float family
(`abs`, `neg`, `sqrt`, `ceil`, `floor`, `trunc`, `nearest` for both shapes)
and `i8x16.swizzle`.

The NaN split matters more here than anywhere else in the family: the
interpreter routes `abs`/`neg` through `f32_bitop`, a pure mask on the pattern
that **preserves a NaN payload**, but routes `sqrt` and all four rounding
forms through `f32_unop`, which canonicalizes. The lowering matches that
split exactly: `band`/`bxor` against a sign-bit mask for `abs`/`neg` (straight
on the raw 128-bit pattern, no lane bitcast needed), and
`sqrt`/`ceil`/`floor`/`trunc`/`nearest` followed by `canonical_float`.

`i8x16.swizzle` uses Cranelift's portable `swizzle`, whose semantics are the
spec's, including reading zero for an index past 15. On x64 it lowers to
`paddusb` with `0x70` plus `pshufb` (so `16..=127` saturates into the
zeroing region); without SSSE3 Cranelift falls back to a libcall. The same
caveat applies to the rounding forms: they are `roundps`/`roundpd` only with
SSE4.1, and a per-lane libcall otherwise, so on a target without SSE4.1 the
helper would win. `native_isa` uses `cranelift_native::builder()`, which
enables the host's features, so the measured path is the good one.

**Fixture.** `crates/wasmtest/fixtures/simd-native-unop.wast`, 2M iterations
of a non-negative, finite chain (`abs` before every `sqrt`, clamp after), so
no NaN can appear and the expected value is exact: `2139095055` from Node
v24.12.0. It looks like a NaN bit pattern only because the result sums raw
lane bits; the loop itself never produces one.

| row | compiled | helper | interpreter |
|---|---|---|---|
| simd-unop | **63.74** | 1358.30 | 2956.54 |
| simd-float (re-run) | 55.64 | 1012.95 | 2547.40 |
| simd-native (integer, re-run) | 32.40 | 221.10 | 1048.25 |
| simd-loop control | 11.96 | - | - |
| leaf-loop control | 13.43 | - | - |

Same-binary A/B: **63.74 vs 1358.30 ms, 21.3x**; the compiled row is 46.4x the
interpreter row. The two earlier probes re-measured at 18.2x and 6.8x with the
controls at 11.96/13.43 against the 11.70/13.60 baseline, so the machine was at
nominal speed and the numbers are comparable across the three entries.

**Gates.** `equiv waspec/test/core` → 254 suites, 0 diverged, 8264/8264
functions compiled; `simd` → 59 suites, 0 diverged; `relaxed-simd` → 7 suites,
0 diverged. `cargo test -p wasm --features compile --lib` (127, including the
new `v128_native_float_unop_and_swizzle_match_the_interpreter`, which covers

zero, and swizzle indices of 16, 127, 128 and 255), `-p wasm --lib` (44),

## LANDED (2026-10-29, same day): native v128 conversions, 16.5x

Fourth and last cut of the SIMD lowering work: the ten conversion opcodes
(`i32x4.trunc_sat_f32x4_s/u`, `f32x4.convert_i32x4_s/u`,
`i32x4.trunc_sat_f64x2_s/u_zero`, `f64x2.convert_low_i32x4_s/u`,
`f32x4.demote_f64x2_zero`, `f64x2.promote_low_f32x4`).

These do not share one shape, because the Cranelift primitives do not line up
with the wasm lane counts:

- The four-lane pairs are direct: `fcvt_to_sint_sat`/`fcvt_to_uint_sat` into
  `i32x4`, and `fcvt_from_sint`/`fcvt_from_uint` out of it. The x64 backend
  accepts `fcvt_to_*_sat` **only** at 32-bit lanes, which is why the f64 forms
  cannot use it.
- `f64x2.convert_low_i32x4_s/u` widens the low two lanes with
  `swiden_low`/`uwiden_low` and converts the i64 lanes; x64 fuses that pair
  into `cvtdq2pd` (signed) and an `unpcklps`/`subpd` pair (unsigned).
- `i32x4.trunc_sat_f64x2_s/u_zero` and demote/promote go per lane
  (`extractlane`, scalar op, `insertlane` into a zeroed result), because
  Cranelift's `fpromote`/`fdemote` require the same lane count and there is no
  `f32x2` type to bridge 128-bit to 64-bit float vectors.
- The NaN asymmetry in the interpreter decided the canonicalization:
  `F32DemoteF64` returns `canon32`, so demote canonicalizes, but
  `F64PromoteF32` returns the widened payload untouched, so promote must not.
  The differential test carries a payload NaN through both to pin it.

**Fixture.** `crates/wasmtest/fixtures/simd-native-convert.wast`, 2M
iterations of three closed round trips (`f32x4` through
`trunc_sat`/`convert`, `f64x2` through `trunc_sat_*_zero`/`convert_low`, and a
demote/promote pair), all integral and bounded so the expected value `-913309696`
from Node v24.12.0 is exact.

| row | compiled | helper | interpreter |
|---|---|---|---|
| simd-convert | **48.49** | 802.18 | 1843.48 |
| simd-unop (re-run) | 63.14 | 1347.87 | 2987.99 |
| simd-float (re-run) | 55.28 | 1019.45 | 2542.43 |
| simd-native integer (re-run) | 32.06 | 219.78 | 1038.35 |
| simd-loop control | 12.08 | - | - |
| leaf-loop control | 13.37 | - | - |

Same-binary A/B: **48.49 vs 802.18 ms, 16.5x**; the compiled row is 38.0x the
interpreter row. All three earlier probes reproduced in the same run (6.9x,
18.4x, 21.3x) and the controls sat on the 11.70/13.60 baseline, so the machine

## LANDED (2026-10-29, same day): native integer lane groups and relaxed ops, 31.7x

Fifth cut. This closes the integer families and the half of relaxed SIMD whose
deterministic choice is a lowering that already existed.

Integer side:

- `min_s`/`min_u`/`max_s`/`max_u` at 8, 16 and 32 bits map to Cranelift's
  `smin`/`umin`/`smax`/`umax`, which accept vectors.
- Saturating add/sub map to `sadd_sat`/`uadd_sat`/`ssub_sat`/`usub_sat`, and
  `avgr_u` to `avg_round` (`(x + y + 1) // 2`).
- `narrow_i16x8_s/u` and `narrow_i32x4_s/u` map to `snarrow`/`unarrow`. Both
  concatenate their two operands with the first in the **low** lanes, which is
  exactly the wasm order, so no swap is needed. `unarrow` is the signed-input,
  unsigned-target form (`narrow_*_u`), not `uunarrow`.
- `extmul_{low,high}_{s,u}` widen that half of both operands and multiply, so
  each is three CLIF ops (`swiden_*`/`uwiden_*` plus `imul`). The opcode block
  starts at `0x9c`, not `0x9b`: `0x9b` is `i16x8.avgr_u`. That is why the
  tables were checked against `simd.rs::exec_int_binop` rather than against a
  remembered spec list.
- The 12 `extend_{low,high}_*_s/u` forms are one widening instruction each.

Relaxed side, all reusing existing lowerings: `relaxed_swizzle` (the MVP
`swizzle`), the four `relaxed_trunc` forms (the saturating conversions),
`relaxed_laneselect` (bitselect), and `relaxed_min`/`relaxed_max` (the spec
min/max). Left on the helper: `relaxed_madd`/`relaxed_nmadd`, whose interpreter
choice computes the product and sum in f64 and rounds **once**, which is not
`fmul` then `fadd`; and `relaxed_q15mulr`/the dot products, which have no
Cranelift instruction.

**Fixtures.** `simd-native-int.wast` and `simd-native-relaxed.wast`, 2M
iterations each. The integer probe chains saturating adds, min/max, the
average, the narrows, the extends and extmul at all three widths, with the

## DECIDED + LANDED (2026-10-29, same day): relaxed madd/nmadd go two-rounding, 8.2x

`relaxed_madd`/`relaxed_nmadd` may be computed fused or with two roundings; the
spec accepts either. The interpreter computed them in **f64** and rounded once,
which is neither: for `f32` lanes it behaves like a fused multiply-add with an
extra-wide intermediate. No `fmul` then `fadd` can match that bit for bit, so a
native lowering and the interpreter could not agree without a decision.

**The decision:** two roundings, meaning the product is rounded to the lane
width before the add. That is an allowed result, it matches what the hardware
`mul` plus `add` produce, and it lets both paths be the same two instructions.
The interpreter (`simd.rs::exec_relaxed`) now does the arithmetic in the lane's
own width and canonicalizes with `canon32`/`canon64`; the compiled path emits
`fmul` then `fadd` (or `fsub` for nmadd) and canonicalizes with the same
helper as the rest of the float family.

The corpus cannot tell the two choices apart: `relaxed_madd_nmadd.wast` wraps
its expectations in `either(...)` and its `_cmp` cases only check determinism.
So the choice is pinned in a unit test instead:
`v128_native_relaxed_matches_the_interpreter` asserts the exact bits for the
classic distinguishing triple (`x = 1 + 2^-22`, `y = 1 + 2^-15`,
`z = -(1 + 2^-15 + 2^-22)`), which is `0` with two roundings and `2^-37`
when fused. That assertion is what stops a future tightening from silently
changing the answer.

**Fixtures.** `simd-native-madd.wast`, added to the relaxed probe as well, and
parameterised so every product and sum is exact (a factor of two, a half, or a
quarter) and therefore identical under either behaviour. That keeps the Node
comparison meaningful even though V8 may choose fused: expected `-2142240768`
from Node v24.12.0, and the combined relaxed probe keeps its `-2147483633`.

| row | compiled | helper | interpreter |
|---|---|---|---|
| simd-madd (isolated) | **28.34** | 231.65 | 887.88 |
| simd-relaxed (all 14 ops) | **73.55** | 788.39 | 2416.29 |
| simd-int (re-run) | 58.15 | 1851.17 | 3720.82 |
| simd-convert (re-run) | 49.10 | 768.15 | 1810.69 |
| simd-unop (re-run) | 63.21 | 1353.64 | 2949.12 |
| simd-float (re-run) | 55.50 | 1036.07 | 2511.85 |
| simd-native integer (re-run) | 32.53 | 216.57 | 1037.40 |
| simd-loop control | 12.22 | - | - |
| leaf-loop control | 13.69 | - | - |

Same-binary A/B: **28.34 vs 231.65 ms, 8.2x** for the isolated madd pair, and
the combined relaxed row at 10.7x. The smallest of the seven ratios, which is
what the dependency chain predicts: the four madd ops sit on a serial
accumulator, so the native form adds `fmul`, `fadd` and a compare/select of
latency where the helper added a call.

**A caveat worth recording:** adding the four madd ops to the relaxed probe
moved that row from ~60 ms to ~74 ms compiled (helper ~718 to ~788). The
compiled path grew more than the helper because the row is latency-bound, not
throughput-bound; the isolated row is the per-op number and it is 8.2x ahead.
Reading the mixed row as a per-op cost would understate the win.
