**Second correction to the same claim.** `iadd_pairwise` exists, and the x64
backend carries special cases for **exactly** the four `extadd_pairwise`
shapes and for `i32x4.dot_i16x8_s`, so all five lower from ordinary CLIF that
the backend recognises:

| wasm | CLIF | x64 |
|---|---|---|
| `extadd_pairwise_i8x16_s` | `iadd_pairwise(swiden_low, swiden_high)` | `pmaddubsw` |
| `extadd_pairwise_i8x16_u` | `iadd_pairwise(uwiden_low, uwiden_high)` | `pmaddubsw` |
| `extadd_pairwise_i16x8_s` | `iadd_pairwise(swiden_low, swiden_high)` | `pmaddwd` |
| `extadd_pairwise_i16x8_u` | `iadd_pairwise(uwiden_low, uwiden_high)` | `pmaddwd` + fixup |
| `dot_i16x8_s` | `iadd_pairwise(imul(widen, widen), imul(widen, widen))` | `pmaddwd` |

The operand order matters for the pattern to match: `iadd_pairwise` fills the
low half of its result from its first operand, and the wasm op's lanes are in
that same order, so the widened low half is passed first.

**Fixture.** `crates/wasmtest/fixtures/simd-native-pairwise.wast`, 2M
iterations cycling through all five ops, with each stage narrowed back with
saturation so the lanes stay bounded. Expected `89195929` from Node v24.12.0.

| row | compiled | helper | interpreter |
|---|---|---|---|
| simd-pairwise | **24.82** | 442.06 | 1485.42 |
| simd-popcnt (re-run) | 30.64 | 418.34 | 1267.26 |
| simd-loop control | 11.89 | - | - |
| leaf-loop control | 14.01 | - | - |

Same-binary A/B: **24.82 vs 442.06 ms, 17.8x**, and the compiled row is 59.9x
the interpreter row, the widest interpreter gap of the ten probes. That is
consistent with what the helper does here: each of these ops loops lanes and
performs a widening multiply or a saturated add per lane, which is exactly the
texture `pmaddwd` replaces.

**Gates.** `equiv waspec/test/core` → 254 suites, 0 diverged, 8264/8264
functions compiled; `relaxed-simd` → 7 suites, 0 diverged. `cargo test -p wasm
--features compile --lib` (130, with the five ops added to the integer lane
differential test), `-p wasm --lib` (44), workspace clippy and `cargo fmt
--check` clean.

What is left: `i16x8.q15mulr_sat_s` and its relaxed form (relaxed 0x111),
which have no pattern-recognised CLIF shape and would need a hand-built
widen/multiply/shift/narrow sequence.

## MEASURED (2026-10-29, same day): `q15mulr_sat_s` by hand, 2.4x

The last op, and the first one that really is a hand-built sequence. The
interpreter computes `sat_i16((a*b + 0x4000) >> 15)` per lane in i64; there is
no CLIF shape the backend recognises, so the lowering widens both operands
(`swiden_low`/`swiden_high`), multiplies, adds the `0x4000` rounding constant,
arithmetic-shifts by 15, and lets `snarrow` perform the saturation. Nine
vector ops. The relaxed form (0x111) aliases the same kernel, which is also
what the interpreter does.

The saturation edge is the interesting one and it lands correctly:
`a = b = -32768` gives `(2^30 + 0x4000) >> 15 = 32768`, which `snarrow`
clamps to `32767`, matching the interpreter's `clamp(-32768, 32767)`.

**Fixture.** `crates/wasmtest/fixtures/simd-native-q15.wast`, 2M iterations of
the multiply-and-add pair, which converges to a small fixed point. Expected
`-70185836` from Node v24.12.0.

| row | compiled | helper | interpreter |
|---|---|---|---|
| simd-q15 | **18.29** | 43.74 | 436.32 |
| simd-pairwise (re-run) | 24.82 | 442.06 | 1478.49 |
| simd-loop control | 11.29 | - | - |
| leaf-loop control | 13.06 | - | - |

Same-binary A/B: **18.29 vs 43.74 ms, 2.4x**. The lowest ratio of the eleven
probes by a wide margin, and the reason is legible: the helper does eight lane
iterations of a cheap i64 multiply, add, shift and clamp, so there is little
per-op work to remove, while the native form costs nine instructions. It is
still a win, and it removes the last integer op from the helper, but a hand-built
sequence does not buy what a single instruction does. The compiled row is still
23.8x the interpreter row, so the difference is real rather than noise.

**Gates.** `equiv waspec/test/core` → 254 suites, 0 diverged, 8264/8264
functions compiled; `relaxed-simd` → 7 suites, 0 diverged. `cargo test -p wasm
--features compile --lib` (130, with `q15mulr_sat_s` and the relaxed form
added to the differential tests), `-p wasm --lib` (44), workspace clippy and
`cargo fmt --check` clean.

With this, every SIMD op the interpreter supports in the compiled subset now
has a native lowering; the helper remains only as the `SLAG_WASM_SIMD_NATIVE=0`
fallback and for the relaxed dot product.

## LANDED (2026-10-29): the JIT cache evicts by use, and only the overflow

The client's remaining complaint is a latency outlier, not a throughput gap:
average frame time is vsync-bound at 60, but an explosion drops it to 40-45 for
a while, and after the program has been running a while the drops stop. A
warm-up signature. This is the third visit to the JIT body cache
(`.notes/frame-cost-profile.md` §4b/§7.1 item 2 is the first, 2026-09-16), and
this time the defect is in the policy rather than its size.

**Two defects, both in `crates/jit/src/lib.rs`.**

1. *The recency signal was dead.* `JitCache::lookup` bumped an entry's
   `last_used`, and eviction ordered by it. But `lookup` is only reached while
   `CompiledBody::jit_info` is unset: as soon as a body compiles, the runtime
   stores the info pointer in the body and every later call returns it
   directly (`runtime::jit::lookup_info`'s `known > 1` arm), so the cache never
   sees a warm call again. `last_used` therefore ordered entries by *last
   compiled*, and "least recently used" was really "least recently built" —
   it evicted exactly the bodies that had been running longest.
2. *Eviction removed half the cache in one insert.* A single new body at the
   cap removed `len - evict_to` entries, i.e. 512 of 1024. One body arriving
   during an explosion cost the program 512 bodies' compiled code, each of
   which then had to re-earn the 16-consult threshold (Cut 69's anti-thrash
   rule), so the next ~16 frames ran an eighth of the scene interpreted.

Together they read exactly as the client reports: a burst of new bodies (the
explosion) crosses the cap, the FIFO-ordered mass eviction takes the startup
scene bodies, those bodies run interpreted for the threshold window, fps falls,
and once the core set has recompiled nothing overflows again until the next
novel body appears.

**The change.**

- `CompiledBody::jit_used` (`Cell<u32>`, saturating) is bumped by the compiled
  call path (`note_body_use` in `runtime::jit`, called from both
  `lookup_info` and `lookup_info_leaf` warm arms) — the only place that can see
  a warm call. The cache reads it as the eviction key.
- Eviction removes `len - cap + 1` entries, the overflow only.
- Counters are halved once per `cap` evictions (one full cache turnover), not
  per eviction. Halving per eviction was the first cut and it was wrong: a
  count of 10 lost to the compile-order tie-break after four inserts, which
  `cache_keeps_a_warm_core_when_new_bodies_arrive` caught.
- Ties (nothing recorded since the last decay) fall back to compile order,
  which is the old behaviour and is the right one when there is no evidence
  either way.
- `SLAG_JIT_CACHE_CAP` overrides the capacity in one binary, so a client can
  price the policy in its own scene; `SLAG_JIT_REPORT` now prints
  `jit evicted N` beside `jit compiled N`, and `compiled >> evicted` is the
  signature of a working set that does not fit.

**Measurement.** Four new unit tests pin the policy (`cache_evicts_an_unused_
body_not_a_warm_one`, `cache_keeps_a_warm_core_when_new_bodies_arrive`, plus
the two existing ones re-expressed for the overflow-only rule); the old
`cache_evicts_least_recently_used_bodies` still passes unchanged, which is the
check that the fallback ordering is intact.

The counter's cost, priced on the thinnest compiled rows (isolated rows, one
process each, 7 interleaved rounds, before/after binaries, per-row minima):

| row | before | after | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `opcost/baseline` (control) | 0.077822 | 0.077909 | +0.11% |
| `opcost/js_call` | 0.499879 | 0.498497 | -0.28% |
| `opcost/method_call` | 0.662969 | 0.665134 | +0.33% |
| `opcost/obj_prop` | 0.602842 | 0.601984 | -0.14% |
| `opcost/element_read` | 0.619358 | 0.612937 | -1.04% |
| `opcost/element_write` | 0.375457 | 0.379098 | +0.97% |
| `opcost/prim_prop` | 1.553183 | 1.576633 | +1.50% |
| `calls/direct_leaf` | 5.701800 | 5.729990 | +0.49% |

Every row is inside its own noise and the signs disagree, so the extra Cell
update is not measurable even on the 0.5 ms call row. Corpus total, 3
interleaved rounds: 1958.3 vs 1969.1 ms minima (-0.55%, and the change cannot
make the corpus faster — eviction never runs with 77 rows). `node
tools/corpus/bench.js`: `n=77 mean-jitGap 10.16 mean-jlGap 3.78 mismatches=0`.
Sweeps 23,726 / 23,821 / 1,086 / 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%.

**Not established.** The client's frame-level win needs a client run: on for a
while, watch `SLAG_JIT_REPORT=1`'s `jit evicted` line (a steady-state ring of
compiles and evictions means the body set genuinely exceeds the cap, and
`SLAG_JIT_CACHE_CAP=4096` is the one-line test), and read `rl.getTime()` across
an explosion. If `evicted` stays at zero, the drop is not the cache and the
next suspects are the first-compile burst (an explosion body compiling at depth
0 in the frame it first runs) and the GC's reaction to the particle burst.

## The loop-carried accumulator is the cost, not the read (measured 2026-10-30)

The corpus's op rows are `s = f(<read>) | 0` in a bare loop, and they sit at
10-30x node. A probe of the three shapes that make one up (100k iterations,
isolated rows, 3 runs each, per-row min) localises the gap precisely, and it is
not the read machinery:

| shape | slag | node |
|---|---:|---:|
| `s = (s + k) | 0` (fused int lane, no read) | 0.77 ns | 0.21 ns |
| `s = s + o.x` (read through the L1a cell, untagged add) | 2.90 ns | 0.30 ns |
| `s = (s + o.x) | 0` | 6.00 ns | 0.21 ns |

The fused int lane proves the ceiling: when the accumulator lives in an i32
register the whole iteration is one add plus the loop test (0.77 ns). The read
adds 2.1 ns because its result is `Unknown`, so the slot it is stored into is
not promotable (`non_heap_slots` refuses an `Unknown` store: a promoted slot
leaves the frame and the GC would lose a live heap value) and the accumulator
round-trips the frame slot every iteration. The `| 0` alone costs 3.1 ns, and it
is **loop-carried latency**, not throughput: `fadd` -> `cvttsd2si i64` ->
`ireduce` -> `bor` -> `cvtsi2sd` -> next `fadd` is ~16 cycles in a chain that no
amount of ILP can overlap. V8's number is not a better read; it is that `s`
never leaves an i32 register.

So the lever is a *type* on the read, and the payload that pays is **int32**, not
`Number`: an exact int32 read makes `narrow` type the whole RMW `Int`, the slot
becomes promotable, `fuse_wrapping_arith` collapses `(s + x) | 0` into one
`IntAdd`, and the loop becomes the 0.77 ns shape above.

**Landed: an int32 read guard on a register body's element read.** A register
body lifts its reads through `emit_reg_body`, which bypasses the step-path typer
guard entirely, so the guard is emitted there: the first element read whose value
feeds the same body's arithmetic combine and whose write-back is truncated
(`(s + a[k]) | 0`, `(s + a[k]) & mask`) becomes `Op::GuardType` typed `Int`. Its
lowering checks `f64(i32(x)) == x` (one round trip, and false for a fraction, a
NaN, and every value the saturating conversion clamps) and deopts otherwise. The
IR on `opcost/element_read` becomes:

```
b3(v41:int, v49:int):            ;; i, s
  v15:int = BitAnd(v41, v14)     ;; k = i & MASK
  FrameStore(v41) slot2          ;; the deopt materialization
  FrameStore(v49) slot3
  FrameStore(v15) slot4
  v18:? = ElementLoad(v16, v15) step33 counter2   ;; arr[k], guarded
  v19:int = GuardType(v18) step33 counter2
  v23:int = IntAdd(v49, v19)     ;; the whole (s + arr[k]) | 0
  v38:int = IntAdd(v41, v37)
  v40:bool = Lt(v38, v39)
```

`opcost/element_read` 0.613 -> 0.292 ms (-52%, jitGap 15.8 -> 7.6), repeated on
three isolated runs. `s = s + a[k]` without the truncation is unchanged (0.259 ->
0.263): the guard is gated on the truncation precisely because there the loop
still carries a `Number` and the guard only buys a deopt branch plus the flush
(+19% when the gate was absent).

Three traps this cost, all now in the code as comments:

- **A guarded read must not run the general helper.** The guard is after the
  merged read value, so a receiver the inline lanes decline would run
  `get_member_computed` and *then* deopt, firing a getter twice when the
  interpreter re-runs the body. `Op::ElementLoad` therefore carries the guard's
  resume state (`Imm::Guard`) and its `slow` arm deopts instead of calling the
  helper. Only the dense, typed-array and validated-cell lanes reach the value.
- **A deopt out of a compiled fused loop must re-publish `Vm::loop_counter` and
  `Vm::loop_num`.** The compiled run keeps the counter in its frame slot (the
  `FastLoopHead` stores it) and Route B's accumulator in another, while the
  interpreter's register executor and its `PushAcc`/`PopAcc`/`BinStoreNum` steps
  read the `Vm` fields. `emit_guard` now writes both from the frame slots on the
  deopt path (`Imm::Guard` carries the two slot indices, `u32::MAX` = none).
  Without it a deopt inside a fused loop resumes with a stale counter and the
  loop runs zero times (found by probe: `Object.create(arrayProto)` with own
  elements, which declines every iteration).
- **The in-lowering deopt needs a frame-materialization point.** `mem2reg`
  flushes a promoted slot into its frame word before every guard so the resumed
  interpreter sees it; a deopt hidden inside `Op::ElementLoad`'s lowering has no
  IR op boundary, so `mem2reg` now treats a guarded `ElementLoad` as a deopt
  point too, and dedups a flush run (the read and its following `GuardType` are
  two adjacent deopt points over one frame, which cost a second triplet of stores
  until the dedup).

`deopt_probe.js` (scratch, not committed) covers fractional elements, strings,
holes, a getter counting its calls, a prototype element, i32 overflow,
`2^32`-scale doubles, NaN/Infinity, a loop starting at 7, and a fresh-array
literal receiver; all ten agree across jit, jitless and node.

**Measured NULLs this pass.**

- Type a slot's `x | 0` as `Number` when at least one operand is a Number (sound
  by spec: mixing a Number with a BigInt throws, so only a Number can flow on and
  the result of a bit op on Numbers is integral). `opcost/js_call` 0.507 ->
  0.930 ms, `opcost/method_call` 0.66 -> 1.36: the claim makes the `+` a raw-f64
  op and the unbox pass then inserts a `Canon` on the loop-carried path. Reverted
  with the reason recorded at `narrow::is_numeric_inst`.
- Guarding a read that feeds an untruncated `s + a[k]`: +19% (see above).

**Also landed in the same pass, each measured on isolated rows.**

- `to_int32`/`to_uint32` take an in-range fast path: the interpreter's `| 0` was
  doing two `fmod` calls (`rem_euclid`) per operand. `mean-jlGap` 3.79 -> 3.45.
- `binary_inline` handles the bitwise/shift operators on two Numbers, so a
  register body's `x | 0`/`x & m` no longer calls the general evaluator.
- The optimizing lift accepts the remaining register-body leaf ops that are
  read-only arithmetic: `GetMemberName`/`GetMemberComputed` with the accumulator
  as receiver (`os[i & 1023].w`, `strs[k & 3].length`), `UpdateAcc`, `UpdateReg`,
  `BinRemConst`, the depth-0 context and per-iteration reads and combines, and
  the accumulator-receiver computed store. `objects/many_objects_read` 19.3 ->
  13.5 ms (-30%), `opcost/prim_prop` 1.61 -> 0.88 ms (-45%), and the 42 bodies
  of `builtins/json_roundtrip` that refused on `RunRegBody` now compile.
- An int-key dense element read: `narrow` keeps a proven-int32 element key `Int`,
  so the dense lane bounds-checks it with one unsigned compare instead of the
  f64 canonicalization. `s = s + a[k]` 0.406 -> 0.259 ms (-36%).

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo test
--workspace`, four sweeps 23,726 / 23,821 / 1,086 / 3,365 = 51,998 at 100%,
corpus parity 0.

**Not established.** The corpus mean does not resolve this work: two runs of the
same binary gave `mean-jitGap` 8.18 and 9.58 in this session, because the mean is
a mean of 77 ratios against node times that round to 0.0 ms on the op rows. The
row-level numbers above are the measurement; the mean is reported only as
`n=77 mean-jitGap 8.98 mean-jlGap 3.46 mismatches=0`. The guard reaches exactly
one corpus row (`opcost/element_read`) because the other truncated-RMW rows are
refused by the hoist guard (`opcost/obj_prop` and the `1.7x`-shape `own_read`
family), and the hoisted read lowers as a plain slot load.

**Next, in order.** Model `Step::HoistMemberGuard`/`HoistGlobalGuard` in the
optimizing lift (a probe op returning a bool, lowered to the same member-cell
validation the interpreter step runs, feeding the existing fused-test terminator),
which unblocks 6 rows and would let the int32 guard reach `obj_prop`'s shape; then
the same guard on the *named* read; then Route B's int lane admitting a guarded
read (`IntRhs::Element`), which is where V8's `i32` accumulator actually lives.

## The hoist guard, modelled: `opcost/obj_prop` 0.61 -> 0.043 ms (measured 2026-10-30)

The optimizing tier refused every body with a loop-invariant read hoist
(`Step::HoistMemberGuard`), so six rows ran the per-step tier. The reason for the
refusal was honest: the lift modelled the guard as always-miss, which runs every
read per iteration (+571% on `own_read` when measured). The fix is to model the
probe, but the interesting part is what the probe has to be.

**The probe.** `Op::HoistProbe` (`Imm::Hoist`) validates the value-operand slots
and every hoisted read, materializes the hit's values into the hidden slots, and
answers a bool; the existing fused-test terminator branches on it (a miss jumps to
the compiler's general loop, unchanged semantics). The reads go through one new
helper, `hoist_member_probe`, which runs the interpreter's own
`member_cell_warm_probe`.

That the probe must *warm* is not incidental: the warm probe falls back to the
map-keyed read, and the value cell is cold on the first pass because this is the
program's first read of the property (a synthetic row reads `o.x` only inside the
loop). A version that only validated the id-keyed cell missed every time and
`obj_prop` stayed at 0.61 ms. Being *stricter* than the interpreter is safe
(a miss takes the general loop); being *looser* would hoist a non-invariant read,
so the probe never runs user code and never accepts a value the interpreter's
guard would reject.

**The gate.** A guarded copy pays only where the body's accumulator becomes an
int32. The probe therefore requires a read to be an exact int32
(`f64(i32(x)) == x`) iff a register body in the guarded region loads its hidden
slot into a truncated read-modify-write, and the lift accepts the body only when
*every* hoisted read meets that test. Without the gate `own_read`
(`s += o.a + o.b`) goes 2.9 -> 15.2 ms: the copy is a generic `Value`-word
read-modify-write, where the per-step tier's fused int lane was 0.73 ns/iter.

**The counter's type, and why it mattered more than the read.** With the probe
hitting, `obj_prop` was 0.61 -> 0.367 ms and then stalled: at 10M iterations it
was still 36.6 ms (3.7 ns/iter) with a three-op IR loop. The loop counter's phi
was typed `Number`, so `loop_counter`'s fused `IntAdd` increment round-tripped
`i32 -> i64 -> i32` every iteration (and the lowering had to convert it, or the
verifier rejected the `iadd` widths). The cause is in `normalize_param_types`'s
join, which is the *last* word on a promoted parameter's type: a counter's
preheader init is `Const 0`, `narrow` demotes it to `Number` (its only uses are
the loop test and the header edge), and the join of `Number` and `Int` is
`Number`. The join now answers `Int` when *every* incoming value is an `Int` or
an integral in-range constant, `resolve` converts a `Value` word into an `Int`
parameter, and `IntAdd`/`IntSub`/`IntMul` convert a `Value`-word operand rather
than emitting a mismatched `iadd`. `obj_prop` at 10M: 36.6 -> 4.3 ms (0.43
ns/iter, which is the fused lane's own floor).

Measured, isolated rows, repeated:

| row | before | after | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `opcost/obj_prop` | 0.610 | 0.043 | -93% (jitGap 27.8 -> ~2.0) |
| `opcost/obj_prop`, 10M iterations | 62.9 | 4.3 | -93% |
| `opcost/element_read` (read guard) | 0.613 | 0.292 | unchanged by this pass |
| `objects/own_read` (gated out) | 2.90 | 2.96 | flat |

Corpus, 3 interleaved rounds against the previous binary: `mean-jitGap` 9.56 /
10.96 / 9.47 vs 9.11 / 9.23 / 7.18, `mismatches=0`. The whole-directory run is
not usable for row-level attribution here (one run showed `head-let` +79 ms and
`spread_assign` +22 ms; isolated, both overlap their own spread), which is the
same allocation-context artifact the corpus note above records.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo test
--workspace`, four sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0.

**Still refused, in order of value.** `Step::HoistGlobalGuard` (the global/`Env`
counterpart: the same probe over the global-value cell, which is the
`globals/declarative_read`/`nested_read`/`object_read` family) and the
`opcost/obj_prop` shape with a *non*-int32 invariant (the read then stays a
`Value` word and the probe gate declines it). The typed key insight from the read
guard carries over: the payload that pays is int32, not `Number`.

## The global hoist guard, modelled: neutral, because the read is not the cost (measured 2026-10-30)

`Step::HoistGlobalGuard` is now modelled like the member one: the same
`Op::HoistProbe`, one helper (`hoist_global_probe`, exactly the interpreter's
`try_global_cell_read`), plus the `globals_unshadowed` gate an env-resolved read
needs, and the same fused-lane gate that refuses a guarded copy which would
replace the per-step tier's `BinStoreNum`/`BinStoreInt` lane.

It is a **NULL**: `globals/declarative_read` 2.50 -> 2.46 ms, `nested_read` 2.53
-> 2.50, `object_read` 2.45 -> 2.46, `hoisted_local` 2.54 (still refused, see
below), each isolated and repeated. Keeping it anyway: it removes a refusal
without a regression, so real code reading a warm global in a loop compiles.

The reason there is nothing to win is the useful part. All four rows sit at the
same 2.5 ns/iter, including `hoisted_local`, which deliberately reads the value
into a local *before* the loop and so has no global read in its body at all. The
read is already free in `declarative_read` (its declarative binding misses the
global-value cell, so the guard takes the general loop, and the row's number is
identical to the hoisted control). **The globals family is floor-bound on the
loop body itself**, `s += i * 3 + k` at 2.5 ns/iter against node's 0.6, not on the
binding.

Measured NULL, and a reverted one: lifting the negated comparisons
(`StrictNotEqual` -> `StrictEq` + `Not`, `NotEqual` -> `Eq` + `Not`) is correct
and unblocks bodies that hold a `!==`, but it also lets a body whose loop runs
the per-step tier's fused lane compile into a generic `Value`-word loop:
`globals/hoisted_local` (`s += i * 3 + k`, which the plan keeps in `Vm::loop_num`)
goes 2.54 -> 3.55 ms. Reverted, with the reason at `emit_binary`. The lesson is
the same one the member hoist taught: **this tier must not take a body from the
fused lane**, and today the only defense is refusing the steps that would let it.

Gates: fmt, clippy, workspace tests, four sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0
(`n=77 mean-jitGap 8.97 mean-jlGap 3.31`).

**Next.** The globals rows need the arithmetic loop, not the read: `s += i * 3 + k`
should be `f64` in registers with the `i * 3` folded into a strength-reduced
induction variable, which is a real loop-optimization slice (and the same shape
shows up in `control/nested_loops`). The cheaper approach is to teach the
optimizing tier the Route-B `BinStoreNum` recipe (`rhs_recipe`'s counter-imm
forms) so a compiled body can keep the fused lane's accumulator instead of
losing it.

## FIXED (2026-10-30): the member hoist lost its fused-lane gate, `own_read` 3.0 -> 9.4 ms

Refactoring the hoist arm into the shared `hoist_probe` emitter dropped the
fused-lane refusal from the *member* arm (only the global one kept it), so
`objects/own_read` compiled into a generic `Value`-word copy of
`s += o.a + o.b`. Its loop runs the per-step tier's `BinStoreNum` lane at 0.73
ns/iter, and the compiled copy costs 2.5: 2.99 -> 9.44 ms isolated, repeated,
`mismatches=0` throughout (it is a slowdown, not a miscompile). Both arms now
refuse a guarded copy whose region runs `BinStoreNum`/`BinStoreInt`/
`BuilderAppend`; `obj_prop` keeps its win because its body has no fused lane.

The way this was caught is worth recording: the row was measured "flat" in the
commit that introduced it, because that measurement compared against a binary
from the *previous* commit rather than a rebuild of the current tree. Build the
binary from the tree you are about to commit, then measure.

Measured after the fix, isolated: `own_read` 2.99 ms, `obj_prop` 0.042 ms,
`hoisted_local` 2.60 ms. Corpus `n=77 mean-jitGap 8.90 mean-jlGap 3.47`,
parity 0. Sweeps 51,998 at 100%.

## Speculative Number guards on a register body's slot operands (measured 2026-10-30)

`globals/hoisted_local` (`s += i * 3 + k`, with `k` a local copied from a global
`const`) sat at 2.5 ns/iter against node's 0.6, and the read was not the cost.
The cost was one unknown operand: `k`'s slot has no type proof, so
`Add(i * 3, k)` stayed a `Value` word, which kept the loop-carried accumulator
unknown too. Nothing downstream could lower to f64, and the accumulator stayed in
the frame instead of a register.

A register body now asserts `Number` on the slot operand of an arithmetic combine
(`Op::GuardType` typed `Number`, deopting on a non-Number) when every op before it
in the body is numeric-shaped (`numeric_chain`: the counter, a numeric constant,
a slot read, or an arithmetic combine of those). The guarded value types the
chain, the chain types the accumulator's store, and the loop becomes:

```
b1(v20:int):
  v6:f64 = Mul(v20, v5)          ;; i * 3
  v8:num = GuardType(v7)         ;; k, one tag check per iteration
  v9:f64 = Add(v6, v8)
  v11:f64 = Add(v21, v9)         ;; s, loop-carried in a register
  v18:int = IntAdd(v20, v17)
```

Measured, isolated, repeated: `globals/hoisted_local` 2.60 -> 1.23 ms (-53%,
jitGap 4.4 -> ~2.1); `globals/declarative_read`/`nested_read`/`object_read`
unchanged (2.5-2.6); `objects/own_read` 2.99 (the fused-lane refusal keeps it in
the per-step tier, where it is faster); `opcost/obj_prop` 0.042 unchanged.

Why the gate matters, and why the guard is *not* applied to the loop-carried
accumulator: an accumulator guard must re-run every iteration (`s` changes), which
measured as no better than the fused lane it replaced; the operand guard runs on a
value that is loop-invariant, and typing *it* is what unlocks the rest. A
pre-loop guard on the accumulator is the cleaner form of the same idea and is the
next step.

Also landed with it: the negated comparisons (`!==`/`!=` as `StrictEq`/`Eq` plus
`Not`), which the lift had refused outright - that refusal was what kept these
bodies (the parser desugars some loop shapes into one) in the per-step tier.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo test
--workspace`, four sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0, deopt probes agree with
node. Corpus `mean-jitGap` 8.73 / 9.12 / 8.83 across three runs (the spread is the
known machine-state noise; the row numbers above are the measurement).

## LANDED (2026-10-30): a `++` counter is a Number, and a loop slot is promotable

`control/nested_loops` was 29.2 ms against node's 3.1 (9.4x). It was not the `%`:
three of its four defects were about how the body *types*, and only one was about
the remainder.

The IR showed the inner loop entirely in `Value` words:

```
b2():  v8:? = FrameLoad slot2 ; v9:? = Add(v30, v8) ; v11:? = Mod(v9, v10)
```

1. **`Op::UpdateValue` was absent from the numeric lattice** (`narrow`). `j++`
   lifts to `Op::UpdateValue` (`ToNumeric(x) ± 1`), which is the generic form for
   any loop whose head the `for`-fusion does not recognize, so the slot stored it
   was never proven a Number, so every read of `j` was `Unknown`, so `i * 31 + j`
   and the accumulator were too. Typing it (operand numeric -> result numeric, and
   the same in `rewrite`) is what made the chain numeric.
2. **`mem2reg`'s "definitely assigned" analysis computed the least fixpoint.**
   `store_reach` initialized `reach_out` to `false` and iterated upward, so a loop
   header with a back edge stayed "not store-reached" forever: the back edge's
   `out` depends on the header's own `in`, and the cycle never receives a `true`.
   Every loop-carried accumulator in the corpus was therefore unpromotable. It is
   a forward must analysis, so it now starts from `true` and shrinks (the greatest
   fixpoint), over reachable blocks only (an unreachable block has no definition
   for `rename` to substitute, and `apply` would drop its loads).
3. **`retype_phis` needed a fixpoint.** A promoted loop has several phis feeding
   each other (the header and the latch both carry the accumulator), all created
   `Unknown`, and `join(Unknown, t)` is `Unknown` — so one round left the cycle
   untyped and the newly promoted accumulator was *worse* than the frame slot it
   replaced (21.4 vs 20.4 ms). It now joins from `Never` (the identity of `join`)
   and iterates.
4. **`loop_counter::prove` only knew `Add`/`Sub`.** The inner counter's
   `UpdateValue` was refused, so `j` stayed a Number word with a `Canon` and an
   `is_double` branch per iteration. It now admits `UpdateValue` (delta 1/-1),
   synthesizing the wrapping op's constant. `x--` rewrites to `IntAdd(x, -1)`.

`%` itself: `unbox` now feeds a raw f64 into `Mod` (the lowering reads the bits as
f64 and canonicalizes a raw operand only on its helper fallback, which runs once
rather than the `Canon` it replaced running every iteration), and
`opt_lower::call_mod_int` skips an operand's integrality and i32-range guards when
the IR already types it `Int`. Two traps: the raw-operand guard in the binary arm
is keyed on `known`, which is false for `Mod` by construction, so it bailed
`opt:raw-float-boundary` and the row silently ran the baseline tier; and the
`IntAdd` rewrite must *append* the delta operand when the instruction being
rewritten (`UpdateValue`) had only one.

Measured, isolated (`scratch/nl`, one row per process, minima of 3):

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `control/nested_loops` | 29.18 ms | **13.92 ms** (-52%) |
| the same loop with `+ 7` in place of `% 7` | 16.66 | **4.89** |
| the same loop with `& 7` | 16.71 | 9.39 |

So the body itself went from 4.1 to 1.2 ns/iteration (node is 0.76), and the
remainder is now the single largest term at ~2.2 ns: `srem` is Cranelift's
`checked_srem_seq` (an `idiv` plus its overflow checks). Strength-reducing a
`% <constant>` to a reciprocal multiply is the next lever for it, and it is a
codegen feature rather than a typing one.

Corpus: total 2085.4 -> **1910.9 ms** against node 722.2, so the headline gap is
2.87x -> 2.65x; `mean-jitGap` 8.45 / 8.52 across two runs, parity 0, `control`
family 12.19x -> 11.39x. The promotion alone is worth -4.3% (same-binary seam:
`SLAG_MEM2REG=0` totals 1997.2 ms). `SLAG_MEM2REG_TRACE=1` prints each slot's
allow/promote verdict, which is how the analysis fix was found.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo test
--workspace`, four sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0.

## PRICED, NOT TAKEN (2026-10-30): constant-divisor `%`, and the env-leaf lane

Two candidates that were queued as "the next lever" turned out to be worth about
0.2% each once priced, so neither was taken. The numbers, because the next reader
will propose both again.

**Constant-divisor `%` strength reduction.** Nearly free to measure: keep the
4M-iteration `nested_loops` shape and swap only the operator.

| body | ms | ns/iter |
|---|---:|---:|
| `s += (i * 31 + j) + 7` | 4.79 | 1.20 |
| `s += (i * 31 + j) & 7` | 9.06 | 2.27 |
| `s += (i * 31 + j) % 7` | 13.87 | 3.47 |

So the entire remainder is 1.2 ns/iter above a bit op, and a perfect magic-multiply
reduction (Cranelift's `srem` is a `checked_srem_seq`, an `idiv` plus its overflow
tests) saves at most 4.8 ms on the row and nothing else in the corpus. That is
0.25% of the total for a hand-rolled signed division with an `INT_MIN` correction,
so it stays in the queue behind anything that moves a family.

**The env-leaf lane.** The lane is 26.6 ns per call against 7.6 for a named global
leaf, and the obvious suspect is `leaf_lookup` plus `new_body_context`. It is not:
`leaf_lookup` is a direct-mapped `Cell` hit (hash, one load, one id compare) and
`new_body_context` returns `None` immediately for a leaf. Caching the closure's
`[[Environment]]` in `LeafCallRecord` would save that comparison and nothing else,
at the cost of holding an untraced GC handle in a record whose identity check is
the only thing keeping it live. The 19 ns is the two-field `body_context` /
`lexical_env` swap plus the per-capture `load_context` call (a second capture adds
4.8 ns), and neither is removable without giving compiled code an inline context
slot read, which is a storage decision, not a slice.

## NULL (2026-10-30): `new_in_place` for the `Small` string concat

`JsString::concat`'s tiny-result path built the `Small` value on the stack and
passed it to `Gc::new`, which copies the (enum-sized) value through another stack
temp into the arena. The `Rope` and `ConsString` paths below it already use
`Handle::new_in_place` for exactly that reason, so converting the `Small` path
looked like free money on the most frequent allocation in the engine.

Measured on a 300k-iteration `s += (q + q).length` loop and on the isolated
`strings/coercion_concat` row: 11.52 / 11.27 / 10.47 ms against 12.33 / 11.52
before, and 66.32 / 65.90 against 66.4. Inside the row noise, and the loop's three
control probes (`t = q`, `q.substring`, `q.repeat`) all moved UP, which is a layout
shift. Reverted. `Gc::new`'s self time is the heap borrow, the RefCell flag and the
`young` push, not the copy.

### What that loop's profile does say

`SLAG_SAMPLE=200` on a 10M-iteration `s += (q + q).length` script:

| share | function |
|---:|---|
| 20.3% | `JsString::concat` |
| 15.4% | `Gc::new` |
| 11.5% | `collect_minor_inner` + `scan_regions` |
| 2.2% | `Heap::alloc` |
| 2.0% | `as_slice` |

Per operation, same loop: `q + q` 32 ns, `q.substring(0, 2)` 51, `q.repeat(1)` 88,
`q.charCodeAt(0)` 10, `q.length` 7. `--gc-trace` puts the whole minor cost at
1.6 ms of the 11.4 (74 minors, 22 us each), so allocation is ~25 ns and GC ~5 ns
of the 32. A bump allocation of 48 bytes is not inherently 25 ns, but nothing in
the allocator is individually large: `Heap::alloc` is 2.2% and `Gc::new` is the
borrow plus bookkeeping. The gap to node's ~10 ns is spread across five terms,
which is the same "portfolio, not a big win" conclusion the corpus-wide profile
gives.

## MEASURED (2026-10-30): the string builtins are allocation-bound, and two censuses come back clean

Chasing the `strings` family, and the two censuses that would have found another
systemic defect like the `UpdateValue` / `store_ref` pair. Neither census found
one, which is the useful part.

### The per-operation costs

300k-iteration loops, isolated, one row per process:

| operation | ns/iter | note |
|---|---:|---|
| `s += 1` | 0.6 | the loop floor |
| `s += q.length` | 7.4 | a member read |
| `s += q.charCodeAt(0)` | 10.3 | a builtin call, no allocation |
| `s += (q + q).length` | 39 | one small-string box |
| `s += q.substring(0, 2).length` | 51 | one `Sliced` node |
| `s += q.repeat(1).length` | 88 | one `Flat` node |

`q.substring` against `q.charCodeAt` is the same dispatch, a `to_number` on two
arguments, and one allocation. So the allocation is ~30 ns of it, and the family's
gap to node is not in any builtin's code.

`String.prototype.split` of a comma string, linear fit over 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 pieces
at 200k iterations each (329 / 481 / 830 / 1321 ns): **187 ns fixed per call plus
71 ns per piece**. The fixed part is two `to_string` calls, `array_create` and the
`Vec<JsString>`; the per-piece part is one box plus one `dense_index_define`
(15.6% of the isolated split profile) plus a 48-byte copy into and out of the
`Vec<JsString>` intermediate. `join` on the same array is 487 ns.

### Why it is ~30 ns

`size_of::<JsString>()` is 48 bytes (`SLAG_CLOSURE_PROFILE=1` prints it), so with
the 16-byte `GcHeader` a one-character string is a **64-byte box, exactly one cache
line**. The arena is streamed, so essentially every allocation is a cold-line miss
on top of the bookkeeping. The 10M-iteration concat profile splits the cost as
`JsString::concat` 20.3%, `Gc::new` 15.4%, minor GC 11.5%, `Heap::alloc` 2.2%; no
single term is dominant, and `--gc-trace` puts the collector at only 1.6 ms of the
11.4 (74 minors at 22 us). So the lever is box *density*, not the allocator, the
collector, or any builtin: the enum's size is set by the four `flat:
OnceCell<Arc<[u16]>>` variants (48 bytes with a 24-byte `OnceCell`), not by
`SMALL_STRING_CAP`.

### Census 1: untyped arithmetic in the optimizing tier

`JIT_DUMP_IR` for every corpus row, counting `v?:? = <arith>(`. Eleven rows have
any left, the worst being `opcost/array_alloc` (45 across 40 bodies, all cold), and
the two biggest rows (`head-let` 363.7 ms and `template-literal` 190.8 ms) have 8
each in their `assert` helper bodies. The lattice now types the hot loops, so there
is no second `UpdateValue`-sized typing gap to find.

### Census 2: bodies that do not reach the optimizing tier

`JIT_DUMP_CLIF` for every corpus row: **zero `opt-lower bail`** (the silent
fallback into the baseline tier that cost 21 -> 28 ms on `nested_loops` before it
was noticed), and ten lift refusals total, all accounted for: two `HoistGuard` (the
deliberate `region_uses_fused_lane` refusal), `AssignMemberName(compound)`,
`RegExpLiteral`, `NoReturn` (an empty body), a `FusedLoop` in `search_slice`'s cold
200-iteration builder loop, and four unnamed `Step("step")` bodies whose blockers
the `opt-blockers` listing does not separate. Tier coverage is not where the
remaining time is either.

## LANDED (2026-10-30): `split` boxes each piece once, straight into the result array

The split path built a `Vec<JsString>` of pieces and then handed it to
`array_from_list`, which called `items.iter()` and `item.clone()` for each one:
every piece was copied into the vector, copied back out of it, and boxed with a
third copy, plus a `Vec` growth and a second pass. The pieces are boxed once and
defined into the (stack-rooted) result array as the scan produces them, which is
what the existing GC argument already required, so the intermediate vector was
pure overhead.

Measured on `s.split(",")` at 200k iterations, 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 pieces (before
peeled from the landed commit's binary, after from this one):

| pieces | before ms | after ms |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 65.8 | 47.1 |
| 4 | 96.3 | 59.9 |
| 8 | 166.0 | 96.0 |
| 16 | 264.2 | 172.2 |

Linear fit: **71 -> 45 ns per piece, 187 -> 147 ns fixed** per call. The isolated
`strings/split_join` row (one process, minima of 3) goes 61.9 -> 55.4 ms (-10.6%,
gap 7.70 -> 7.03), and a split + assign + join microbench 78 -> 55 ms.

The corpus total cannot resolve this: a re-run minutes later moved node's own
total 722.2 -> 740.5 ms (+2.5%), and per-row node deltas of +9.5% and -10% on rows
this change cannot touch, so the pair is inside the documented noise. Parity 0.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo test
--workspace` 5860 pass, four sweeps 51,998 at 100%.

## LANDED (2026-10-30): the compound member store lifts, and that is what unblocks the call splice

`calls/method_call` was 55.2 ms and the helper census showed `leaf_call_fill` once
per call: `counter.inc(i)` never spliced. The interesting part is why, and it was
not the splice. `inc` is `this.value += x`, and `Step::AssignMemberName` with a
compound op was the last refused member store in the lift, so the CALLEE body could
not lift at all. A callee with no lifted IR is not a splice candidate, so the only
route left for the call site was the leaf-call fill lane at 28 ns/call.
`SLAG_INLINE_TRACE=1` showed `resolve Created { create_step: 1 } -> ok` next to an
IR dump that still contained `Call`, which is what pointed at the callee.

The lift now models the read-modify-write: the parser leaves `[object, old, value]`
on the stack, the step applies `compound_binary(op)` to `old` and `value`, and the
result goes through `Op::MemberStore` (the same validated store the plain form
uses, so a setter still fires and the helper's nullish check is unchanged). The
logical assignments stay refused: their store is conditional on the old value and
the step carries no flag for which arm ran, so a faithful lift needs a new step
field, not a lowering. The computed compound store stays refused too: the step
converts the key once for both halves and `Op::ElementStore` would convert it
again, which is observable for an object key.

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `calls/method_call` | 55.2 ms | **27.4 ms** (-50%) |
| its gap to node | 6.87x | 3.46x |
| `leaf_call_fill` per run | 14,000,000 | 0 |

Corpus total 1910.9 -> **1880.4 ms** against node 730.6, so 2.65x -> **2.57x**
(session start 2085.4 / 722.2 = 2.87x). Parity 0.

The general lesson, worth checking first next time a call row will not splice: the
splice needs the CALLEE to lift, and a refusal inside the callee presents as "no
site" in the caller. The refusal census names it.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo test
--workspace` 5860 pass, four sweeps 51,998 at 100%.

## NULL (2026-10-30): the prototype-method splice route, and where `construct_churn` actually goes

`calls/construct_churn` lifts all three bodies and still reported `0 site(s)`,
because `sites_from_creations` bails on any body holding a `FunctionDecl`
(`single_closure_slots` returns `None`, since a declaration writes a frame slot
the IR does not name). So `function Item() {}` plus `Item.prototype.sum =
function () {}` disabled EVERY creation route, including the ones that never read
a slot.

A route was built and measured: an atom the body installs a closure at in its
entry block, matched against a call whose callee is a member read of that atom,
behind the existing `CalleeEq` guard (sound without any proof of the chain: a
shadowing instance property or a later prototype write makes the guard miss). It
works. `resolve Created { create_step: 3 } -> ok`, the `Call` disappears from the
IR, and `leaf_call_fill` goes from 1 per iteration to 0.

It does not pay, because the row is construct-bound, not call-bound. Same window,
500k iterations, four ablations:

| shape | ms | per iteration |
|---|---:|---:|
| `s += new Item(i).sum()` | 63.9 / 62.9 | 126 ns |
| `s += new Item(i).x` | 46.5 / 48.2 | **94 ns, all construct** |
| `s += one.sum()` (spliced) | 17.0 / 16.6 | 33 ns, all call |
| `var o = new Item(i); s += o.x + o.y` | 47.4 / 47.8 | 95 ns |

So the construct is 94 of the 126 ns and the call is 32. Removing the call
entirely is worth at most 25%, and in practice nothing: the leaf-call lane was
already rebuilding the frame and calling the entry, and the spliced body pays the
same two member reads. Route-firing against route-blocked in adjacent windows was
57.1 against 57.9 ms median. Corpus-wide the route adds exactly ONE site (11
`resolve` lines in total, 4 of them `-> none`), so it was reverted rather than
landed as a heuristic in the inliner.

**Machine-state caveat.** The corpus run in the same window moved node's own total
730.6 -> 889.3 ms (+21.7%) and the same reverted source measured
`construct_churn` at 71-75 ms where it had measured 57-59 minutes earlier. Every
number above is a within-window pair; the absolute milliseconds in this entry are
not comparable with other entries.

**`calls/closure_capture` is not a splice target either.** `fns[i & 63](i)`
selects among 64 closures, so no static proof names the callee, and the site is
correctly megamorphic. It runs the env-leaf lane at 30 ns/call: the bodies capture
`base` and `k`, so each call pays the two-field `body_context`/`lexical_env` swap
plus a `load_context` helper per capture, whose real cost is the cache miss on the
closure's env box. That is the lane priced at 26.6 ns earlier today; making it
cheaper needs an inline context-slot read in machine code (env layout offsets as
compile-time constants), which is a storage project, not a slice.

**The lead this leaves.** A fresh-object construct is 94 ns against node's ~20 for
a two-field constructor, and it is the largest single per-operation cost measured
today. The journal already prices the pieces (the fresh-receiver chain read, the
defines, the FFI construct cascade), so the next step there is a decomposition, not
a guess.

## MEASURED (2026-10-30): the ninth property

The construct decomposition asked for. Field count is the dose, one row per
process (the corpus runner shares an allocation context inside a directory), 500k
iterations, minima of 2-3, object escaping into `arr[i & 63]` so nothing is
scalar-replaced:

| properties | literal, ms | per object | `new F()`, ms | per object |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 | 59.4 | 119 ns | 183 | 366 ns |
| 8 | 63.1 | 126 | 213 | 426 |
| 9 | **211.1** | **422** | **405** | **810** |
| 10 | 238.1 | 476 | 482 | 964 |
| 12 | 328.3 | 657 | | |

Two cliffs, and only one of them is expected:

- The step from 8 to 9 properties is **+296 ns for a literal and +384 ns for a
  construct**, then ~40 ns per further property. It is not the literal lowering:
  both lengths take the same `object_fast` helper and the same helpers per
  iteration, so the cost is inside the shared create.
- `object_fast_create` adopts `INLINE_FIELDS` (8) keys into the in-object field
  region and then defines the tail through `create_data_property_key`. The 9th
  key's descriptor ordinal is 8, so its property-vector position is 8, and the
  vector must be positionally aligned with the descriptor ordinals (the L1c
  transition discipline), which materializes the vector and copies the eight
  in-object fields into it. That transition, once per object, is the ~115 ns;
  each key past it is one generic define at ~40 ns.

Priced and rejected on the spot: the composite shape cache was keyed on the WHOLE
key list, so a literal longer than `INLINE_FIELDS` re-forked its 8-key head with
one `get_or_create_child` per key on every evaluation. Keying it on the
vector-free head instead changed nothing (211.1 before, 223.9 after), because the
one-entry transition hint already makes each fork step a hit; reverted.

The obvious lever, raising `INLINE_FIELDS` to 16, is already in the journal as a
measured loss on box size. The remaining option is to let the tail define pad the
vector with holes instead of copying the in-object fields, since every reader of
an ordinal below `INLINE_FIELDS` reads `in_fields` (`JsObject::write_data_property_slot`
branches on exactly that). That changes what `properties` means for its other
consumers (`materialize_properties`, the key enumerators), which is why it is a
project and not a slice.

Also recorded here because it is the same row family: a bare construct with no
fields is 98 ns against an empty literal's 62, so the construct machinery alone is
~36 ns, and `new Item(i)` with two fields plus a prototype method call is 126 ns
(`calls/construct_churn`'s per-iteration cost at that window).

## LANDED (2026-10-30): `SmallProps` gains a `base` (inert), the first step of the suffix store

`.notes/property-vector-base.md` scopes the ninth-property cliff: the property
vector must be positionally aligned with the descriptor ordinals, so an object
growing past `INLINE_FIELDS` materializes its in-field head into the vector once
(measured +296 ns for a literal, +384 for a construct).

This lands the plumbing only: `SmallProps` carries the descriptor ordinal of its
first entry, plus `ordinal_len()` (the positional length, which differs from the
entry count once a base exists) and `get_ordinal()`. Two call sites move to them,
both identities while `base` is 0: `map_field`'s above-cap arm and
`map_transition_aligned`, whose question is "does the vector cover every
descriptor ordinal", not "does it hold that many entries".

The change is inert by construction, so the evidence is the invariants rather than
a time delta: `base` is 0 at every construction site, `get_ordinal(o)` is then
`slice().get(o)` and `ordinal_len()` is `len`. A unit test
(`small_props_ordinals_shift_by_the_base`) drives a non-zero base through both
accessors so the semantics are pinned before the define path uses them. The
9-key probe keeps its cliff with the same ratio (lit9/lit8 3.17 against 3.34;
the absolute milliseconds of that run are a faster window than the entry above).

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo test
--workspace` 5861 pass, four sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0
(`mean-jitGap` 8.31).

## LANDED (2026-10-30): the property vector is a suffix store, the ninth property stops copying the head

`define_fresh`'s "fresh key on a full map" arm now starts the vector at ordinal
`INLINE_FIELDS` instead of materializing it, so an object that grows past the
in-object field cap keeps its head in `in_fields` and puts only the tail in the
vector. `SmallProps` needed no new field (`base` landed inert earlier today), and
`materialize_properties` folds a suffix in front of the head it rebuilds from the
map.

The label, in the journal's probe shape (500k iterations, one row per process,
objects escaping into `arr[i & 63]`, minima of 3, base and new interleaved):

| row | before | after | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8-key literal | 51.6 ms (103 ns) | 49.4 (99) | -4% |
| 9-key literal | 154.9 (310) | **68.0 (136)** | **-56%** |
| 9/8 ratio | 3.00 | **1.38** | |
| 8-field construct | 195.5 (391) | 189.5 (379) | -3% |
| 9-field construct | 343.7 (687) | **228.1 (456)** | **-34%** |
| 9/8 ratio | 1.76 | **1.20** | |

A new corpus row carries it: `objects/wide_literal` (a 12-key literal loop,
86.2 -> 74.7 ms, node 10.6 in the same window). Corpus-wide the change is free,
`mean-jitGap` 8.21 for the base binary against 8.18 and 8.23 in two after-windows
(78 rows, parity 0, so the two after-values are the spread), and every other row
is inside its own window's noise: `builtins/object_keys` +2.4% in one pairing and -1% in the next
(the row alone spans 41-47 ms on this machine), the five `control` rows and
`calls/construct_churn` (-1.4%) within a couple of percent either way.

The first cut failed two fixtures, both for-in enumeration of a many-key object,
and both were the same defect: `for_each_own_string_prop`'s vector-free arm
skipped `offset >= INLINE_FIELDS` outright, which was sound only while a deferred
object could not describe a tail ordinal. It now serves the tail from the vector.
Three more sites needed the same treatment, and they are the audit's answer for
the next reader of this state:

- `define_fresh`'s duplicate-of-a-mapped-key arm wrote the value through
  `map_set`, which mirrors nothing at or above the cap, so an in-place redefine of
  a tail key silently dropped the write (`get_ordinal_mut` now serves it).
- `drop_map`, the three paths that clear the map to enter dictionary mode, must
  complete the vector first: a suffix store's head is described only by the map.
- `sync_map_after_define`'s alignment probe read a vector POSITION
  (`properties.get(descriptor_count())`) where the invariant is about an ORDINAL;
  with a base the two differ, so it could transition a map onto the wrong entry.

Serving enumeration from the map is what keeps the cost out of the rows that
enumerate a deferred object repeatedly: the walk originally built a `Property` per
key, and it now hands the caller `(key, enumerable)`, which is all an enumerator
reads.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo test
--workspace` 5861 pass, four sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0.

## LANDED (2026-10-30): a number's spelling goes into the concat, not through a box

`concat_primitive`, the `Add` fast path for a string next to a plain primitive,
boxed the primitive's spelling and then boxed the concat, so `"value=" + i` paid
two allocations and a template substitution paid one per operand. The integer
spelling now goes straight into the result buffer:
`crux::number::integer_units` writes the decimal into a caller's stack buffer
(the same fast path `small_integer_string` used, now shared by both), and
`JsString::concat_units` / `concat_units_left` build the result once, as an inline
`Small` when it fits.

| shape (300k iterations, one row per process, minima of 3) | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `"value=" + i` | 28.5 ms (94.9 ns) | 18.2 (60.8) |
| `"value=" + i + ":" + (i * 2)` | 64.8 (216) | 51.2 (171) |
| `strings/coercion_concat` | 60.8 | 48.4 (**-20%**) |

The other four `strings` rows are flat in the same window (-1.4% to +1.5%).
Node's `"value=" + i + ":" + (i * 2)` is 25.9 ns, so that row is ~6.6x where it
was ~8.3x. Both tiers gain: `binary_slow` (the JIT's non-numeric `Add`) and the
interpreter funnel through `apply_binary`, which shows in the corpus jitless gap
(3.40 -> 3.36 in the same run).

What is left in the shape is the ALLOCATION COUNT. The chain still builds one box
per `Add` (three here) and node builds one string. Measured: a `Small` box is
~30 ns (`q + q` is 27.6 ns over the loop floor, `i + ""` 40 ns, of which the
spelling itself is well under 10), so fusing the chain into a single box is worth
another ~90 ns per iteration on this row. That is the next slice: the pieces are
already `Value`s in registers, so it is a lowering peephole (an `Add` spine whose
seed the typer proves a string) plus one runtime helper that sizes the buffer
exactly and fills it.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, 5861 tests, four
sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0 (`mean-jitGap` 8.57 in a slow window).

## LANDED (2026-10-30): a concat chain builds one string, not one per `+`

With a number's spelling going straight into the concat (the previous entry),
what is left in `"value=" + i + ":" + (i * 2)` is the ALLOCATION COUNT: one box per
`Add`, where node builds one string. The optimizing tier now folds a left-leaning
`Add` spine into a single `ConcatChain` helper call, so the chain is assembled
into one box.

The peephole is in the lowering, not the IR: `opt_lower` defers an `Add` whose
left operand the typer proved a `Type::String` (the only way the lattice assigns
it is a string constant) and keeps folding `Add`es on its pending result, up to
eight pieces. Every such `Add` is a concatenation by definition (one operand is a
string, so the result is one) and the intermediate strings are unobservable, so
the fused call is exact: `crates/runtime/src/expr.rs::concat_chain` spells the
integral numbers into a stack buffer, sizes the result exactly, and writes one
`Small` (no buffer allocation at all when it fits) or one `Flat`; a piece that is
an object, a Symbol or a fractional number takes the general per-piece
`ToPrimitive`/`ToString` path. The pieces ride in a `stack_slot` array in the
JIT frame, which the conservative scan already covers, and the helper is
classified as disturbing the leaf-eligibility epoch (its general path can run
user code).

| same-binary pair, one row per process, minima | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `strings/coercion_concat` | 49.0 | **38.9 (-21%)** |
| the other four `strings` rows | | -0.7% to +0.4% |

Against the window before the number spelling landed, `coercion_concat` is 61 ->
38.9, so the row is ~5.1x node where it was ~8.0x.

Measured, not assumed: the fusion is worth less than the box it removes. Folding
three boxes into one saved 37 ns/iteration, not the ~60 the box price predicted,
so the helper's own cost (the call, the per-piece tag dispatch, the exact-size
fill) is ~20 ns of it. Two shapes are outside it: a body the lift refuses (the
same chain in an interpreter-run body still pays per-`Add` boxes), and a piece
that is not an integral number.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, 5861 tests, four
sweeps 51,998 at 100% (plus `built-ins --filter String/* --gc-stress`, 1223
fixtures), corpus parity 0.

## MEASURED (2026-10-30): the builtin callback lane, decomposed

The four HOF rows (`opcost/array_for_each`, `map_for_each`, `typed_array_for_each`,
`arrays/hof_methods`) are one mechanism at ~20 to 26 ms each: a builtin iterating
a collection and calling a JS callback per element. The corpus already carries the
control: `opcost/array_for_each_js` performs the same four calls directly from JS
and runs at 7 ns per element, while `array_for_each` runs the same four through
`Array.prototype.forEach` at 60 ns.

Split by collection length (100k calls per row, `small.forEach(cb)`):

| length | ns/call | slope |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 107 | |
| 2 | 151 | +44 per element |
| 4 | 240 | +44 |
| 8 | 461 | +55 |
| 16 | 782 | +40 |

So roughly **65 ns per `forEach` call plus 42 ns per element**. The per-element
figure is the one that matters: a JS loop calling the same closure with the same
three arguments (`myEach(small, cb)`, the JS equivalent) is 20.5 ns per element
compiled, so ~22 ns of the 42 is the Rust lane's own scaffolding.

Ablation (throwaway build, `SLAG_CB_SKIP` bitmask, bit set = that work skipped;
minima of 2, baseline 69.0 ns per element):

| skipped | ns/element | |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| nothing | 69.0 | |
| `globals_unshadowed` (context read + name scan) | 64.7 | **-4.3** |
| the `global` field's per-call clear in `clean_after_leaf` | 69.2 | 0 |
| `with_leaf_run`'s TLS push/pop | 67.2 | -1.8 |
| the `stack.reserve` up to `stack_cap` | 68.5 | -0.5 |
| all four | 62.1 | -6.9 |

Landed from it: `globals_unshadowed` is now computed only when the body names an
identifier, which a leaf body never does (the check existed "for uniformity only"
because `steps_are_leaf` excludes the reference machinery). That is -3.5% on
`forEach(cb)` and `forEach` over four elements in a same-binary pair, both rows
under a JS loop that pays the same call.

**The named next slice** is the remaining ~19 ns/element, and it is all
`run_jit_leaf`'s per-call setup: the `stack.resize` of the frame plus working area,
the per-slot frame-init loop, `bind_this_value`, `lookup_info_leaf`, the region
pointer, and `clean_after_leaf`'s twelve stores. The TLS registration and the
`reserve` are not it (measured above), and neither is the body: `--jitless` costs
the same as the JIT on this row (25.2 against 24.0 ms), because the scaffolding,
not the body's tier, is what dominates. The structural fix is a callback lane that
reserves the frame segment once for the loop and rewrites only the parameter slots
per element, which is a change to the leaf-call entry rather than a trim.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, 5861 tests, four
sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0 (`mean-jitGap` 8.32).

## NULL (2026-10-30): gating the `%String.prototype%` snapshot, and where the leaf prologue actually runs

Following the callback-lane decomposition, the same argument the file already
makes for `has_call_apply`/`has_call_intrinsic` applies to
`JitCallContext::string_prototype_bits`: only a `Step::GetMemberName` site loads
it, yet every compiled run snapshotted it (a realm read plus a handle clone). The
gate was built (`CompiledBody::has_member_name`, the `CertifiedInlineInfo` mirror,
three ctx sites) and measured:

| row | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `small.forEach(cb)` (4 elements) | 23.82 | 23.44 (-1.6%) |
| the same, second pairing | 22.89 | 22.63 (-1.1%) |
| `calls/direct_leaf` | 5.77 | 5.72 (-0.8%) |
| `calls/recursive_fib` | 46.26 | 46.26 (0) |

Reverted: a field, a mirror entry and five gated sites for under one nanosecond
per element is not a trade worth carrying. The useful part is what the two
unchanged rows prove: **a compiled-to-compiled leaf call never enters
`run_jit_leaf`**. The caller's machine code invokes the callee's entry directly
(the in-frame lane), so `run_jit_leaf` and its ~35-field `JitCallContext` build
are on the RUST-initiated call path only: a builtin's callback loop, a native
handler, `apply`/`call`, an argument-vector call.

That bounds the callback-lane work precisely. The ~19 ns per element left in

callback entry that keeps one context and one frame segment for the whole loop.

## LANDED (2026-10-30): a keyed-collection call hashes its receiver id once

`Map.get`/`has`/`set`/`delete`/`size` and the `Set` twins each did two lookups
into the agent's identity table: `map_of`/`set_of` ran `has_map`/`has_set` (a
`contains_key` on the object id) for the brand check, then the body looked the
SAME id up again for the data, cloned the `Rc`, and borrowed it. The table entry
IS the brand (a live record for the id means the receiver is a Map the brand
check accepts), so both the compiled intrinsic helpers
(`map_get_fast`/`set_has_fast`/`map_set_fast`) and the nine hot builtins now do
one lookup, via `map_data_of`/`set_data_of`. That also removes nine `.unwrap()`
calls from the receiver path, replacing them with the same TypeError the brand
check raises.

| row | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `opcost/map_get` | 3.13 | **2.83 (-9.6%)** |
| `opcost/set_has` | 3.10 | **2.85 (-8.1%)** |
| `builtins/map_churn` | 29.24 | **27.14 (-7.2%)** |
| `builtins/set_churn` | 39.64 | **38.52 (-2.8%)** |

Both halves are in the numbers above: the fast-path folding alone was -6.3% /
-1.8% / -10.2% / -7.6%, and the builtins' own bodies added another -1.1% /
-1.3% on the churn rows.

The remaining ~28 ns for one `Map.get` on a 1024-entry map (node: 3) is not the
table walk or the key hash, which are now single identity-hashed probes. It is
the call lane around them, and it is the same wall as the callback rows: a builtin
invocation from compiled code pays the general-path scaffolding, which the
`CallIntrinsic` helpers avoid. Per-op work inside the collection (the `RefCell`
borrow, `same_value`, the entry `Vec`) is the next thing to price, not the brand.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, 5861 tests, four
sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0 (`mean-jitGap` 8.28).

## LANDED (2026-10-30): the regexp match protocol stops encoding its own property name

`regexp_exec_protocol` runs on every `test`, `exec`, `match`, `replace` and
`split`, and it read `lastIndex` with `get_property(agent, re, &JsString::from_utf8("lastIndex"), ...)`
plus `obj.set(&JsString::from_utf8("lastIndex"), ...)` on the failure paths: a
per-call UTF-8 encode and box for a name that never changes, and a full chain
walk for a read whose own property is almost always plain data. Two changes:

- `crux::string::last_index_atom`, so the name is an interned atom (the same
  pattern as `length_atom`).
- The read takes the object's OWN `lastIndex` when it is a data property (a data
  own property shadows the chain for [[Get]], so this is the exact read); an
  absent or accessor own property still takes the general [[Get]]. The write stays
  `set_key`, the spec's [[Set]] with the in-place own-writable-data fast path,
  which also bumps the generation the read-side value cell needs (writing through
  the compiled store's `write_data_property` entry instead is a latent stale read:
  that entry leaves cell refresh to its caller, and 11 fixtures caught exactly
  that, `lastIndex` reading 1 after the reset had landed in the vector).

| probe (100k calls, one row per process, minima of 3) | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `/[a-z]+/.test(s)` | 35.05 | **33.59 (-4.2%)** |
| `/a/.test(s)` (matches, no search) | 15.89 | **13.66 (-14.0%)** |
| `/^[a-z]+$/.test(s)` | 42.35 | **39.68 (-6.3%)** |

The decomposition that led here, worth keeping: a `test` costs **~150 ns fixed**
plus the pattern (`/a/` and `/z/`, which differ only in whether the search scans,
measure the same 155 ns, and `[a-z]+` adds ~200), while a builtin call itself is
18 ns (`mg.get(k)` through an own data property) and a certified leaf call is
5.8. So ~130 ns in a `test` is not the call and not the scan: it is the protocol
around the engine (the encode, the chain walk, `Matcher::new`, the engine's
per-call `tasks`/`choices` vectors) and then the engine's own per-call state.
`Matcher::new`'s two `Vec::new()`s and its `HashMap::new()` are the next thing to
price, and they want a reusable scratch matcher on the regexp record rather than
a per-call one.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, 5861 tests, four
sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0.

## LANDED (2026-10-30): the regexp matcher's task stack is inline

The engine built its task and backtrack-point stacks as empty `Vec`s on every
match, so even `/a/` against an EMPTY input allocated once: the counting
allocator in `crates/regexp/tests/perf.rs` reports 1.00 allocs per
`search_end_at` call, and the engine's fixed cost was 54 of the 60 ns a
`/a/.test(...)` cost. `SmallStack<T, N>` (new module) keeps the first `N`
entries in the matcher and spills to a `Vec` only past that, with the drop
accounting a non-`Copy` element needs (`Task` holds an `Rc<[usize]>`).

| engine-only, 1M calls (perf harness) | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `/a/` on 8 units | 60 ns, 1.0 allocs | **49 ns, 0.0** |
| `/[a-z]+/` on 8 units | 261 ns, 6.0 | **225 ns, 4.0** |
| `/a/` on empty (setup only) | 57 ns, 1.0 | **47 ns, 0.0** |

Corpus `opcost/regexp_test` 32.9 -> **29.6 ms** (-10%), and the jitless column
43.2 -> 38.8, because the interpreter runs the same engine.

What is left in `/[a-z]+/`'s 225 ns is 4 allocations: each backtrack point
snapshots the continuation as `Rc::from(tasks.as_slice())`, and 8 characters of
`[a-z]+` create four of them. Replacing that snapshot with an index into a
shared task log (the choice records the task length, and the log is copied only
when a choice is popped below its base) is the next engine slice, worth ~4
allocations per match on every backtracking pattern.

Gates: fmt, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, 5863 tests (two new
`SmallStack` tests), four sweeps 51,998 at 100%, corpus parity 0.

## MEASURED (2026-10-30): a prototype method read is 10 ns dearer than an own one, and it is the chain, not a trim

The prototype method read was the other candidate off the builtin-call
decomposition (`m.get(k)` 29.2 ns against `mg.get(k)` with the method installed
as an own data property, 18.0). Reading the member alone, 100k iterations:

| shape | ns/iter |
| --- | ---: |
| `var f = m.get;` (method on `Map.prototype`) | 23.7 |
| `var f = mg.get;` (own data property) | 13.4 |
| nothing (the loop floor) | 1.0 |

So the own read is ~12 ns and the chain read ~22: the difference is the compiled
chain path, which after the own-value cell misses runs a map-id-keyed cell probe
(`(map_id ^ name) & (MEMBER_CELLS - 1)`), two cell loads, the link count, then
per-link `(id, generation)` loads and compares from the receiver's direct
prototype, and only then the value. That is a dozen dependent loads and five
branches against the own cell's single probe.

No cheap trim is available. Serving the chain result out of the own-value cell
would be stale: a script replacing `Map.prototype.get` bumps the PROTOTYPE's
generation, and the cell is keyed on the receiver's. The fix is a cell shape that
carries the found link's generation next to the value (a proto-method cell keyed
on `(map_id, name)` with the link generation gate), which is a redesign of the
cell, not a slice, and it would pay on every method call in the corpus.

Not started; recorded so the next session does not re-derive the 10 ns split.

## LANDED (2026-10-31): an env-reading leaf swaps its environment in machine code

A certified leaf that reads a captured binding was the one call shape the
compiled call site could not run in-frame. The probe recorded `uses_env` and
refused, so the site fell to the certified lane on its first visit and to
`leaf_call_env` on every later one: a full Rust round trip per call that
re-validated the record, rebuilt the frame, re-ran `leaf_lookup` (a `RefCell`
borrow of `ecma_functions` plus the map lookup), built the body context and
swapped two `Vm` fields. Measured cost, 1M calls:

| probe | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| leaf, no env (control) | 5.9 ms | 5.9 ms |
| leaf writing a captured binding | 23.7 ms | 13.4 ms |
| leaf reading a captured binding | 19.8 ms | 8.6 ms |

`leaf_fill_info` now records the closure environment and an `env_inline`
verdict: the body captures nothing itself (`context_layout` empty) and reads no
per-iteration head, so `new_body_context` would return the closure environment
unchanged and the whole activation is two field stores. The env lane splits on
that verdict: `env_inline` calls the entry directly exactly like the plain
in-frame lane, wrapping the call in a save/store/call/restore of
`Vm::body_context`; everything else (a body that builds a capture context, or
one that reads per-iteration bindings) keeps `leaf_call_env`.

Two details the slice depends on. The probe path must take the same tail: the
first call at a site is `LeafCallProbe`'s return, not a cached record hit, and
emitting a plain call there ran the leaf against the caller's environment
(found as an `unreachable!("a context slot without a capture-context env")` on
`calls/closure_capture`; the probe now branches on the verdict it just
recorded). And the saved handle rides a Cranelift spill slot across the call,
which the collector's conservative native-stack scan covers, exactly like the
helper's Rust local; `--gc-stress` over four env-call shapes returns the same
values as the plain run.

Corpus: `calls/closure_capture` 34.5 -> 19.4 ms. `opcost/js_call` and every
env-free call row are unchanged, as is the builtin callback lane
(`opcost/array_for_each` 23.7), which is Rust-initiated and does not use this
path.

Verified: clippy `-D warnings` clean; `cargo test --workspace` 5864 pass / 0
fail; four sweeps at 100% (language 23726, built-ins 23821, annexB 1086,
intl402 3365); corpus parity 0, `mean-jitGap` 8.14.

## MEASURED (2026-10-31): the two call floors, and two certified-lane slices that do not pay

With the env leaf lane landed, the call lanes measure clean (1M calls, one row
per process, min of reps):

| probe | ms | reading |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `g(x) { return x + 1 }` (leaf) | 6.9 | ~7 ns/call, the floor |
| `g(x) { return h(x) }`, `h` a leaf | 59.6 | ~53 ns/call, the certified lane |
| `f(1)` with `f` writing a captured binding | 13.4 | env leaf, in machine code now |
| `f(i)` with `f` reading a captured binding | 8.6 | idem |

So a non-leaf JS call costs ~8x a leaf call, and that is the mass in the
amplified test262 rows: `language/.../for-in/head-let-fresh-binding-per-iteration`
makes nine certified calls per body (six `assert.sameValue`, three `fns.x()`),
and at ~53 ns each they are the row's whole 347 ms. Two slices aimed at it were
implemented, measured and REVERTED:

**Running the callee on the caller's ctx instead of building a fresh one.**
This mirrors `self_call_inline` (which patches `buf_end` and the nested frame
only) by patching the callee-owned ctx fields and restoring them after. It is
SLOWER: 59.6 -> 65.0 ms on the probe, 347 -> 367 on the head-let row. The
reason is `JitCallContext::intrinsic_bits`, a 15-word inline array: saving,
writing and restoring it copies 360 bytes per call, where the old construction
wrote 120 once. The array is the one ctx field whose copy dominates.

**Caching the callee-static facts in the call-site record** (the closure
environment, the realm global, the body address, the handler flag, and a
"needs a realm check" flag for an `arguments` body), so a warm call skips the
`ecma_functions` borrow, its map lookup, the body `Rc` clone and the realm
dereference. Neutral: 59.6 -> 60.4 ms, head-let 357 -> 358. The registry lookup
is NOT what the 53 ns is made of.

The conclusion is the one the C3 note reached from the other side: the cost is
spread over the frame carve (`vm.stack` resize plus the per-slot fill), the
scratch save/restore (18 fields each way), the ctx construction and the FFI
boundary, and no single field or lookup is worth a slice. Closing it needs the
compiled nested-call path (the C3 frame work): the machine code carves the
frame, and the callee-owned ctx becomes a pointer to a per-realm template
instead of an inline array, so a nested ctx costs a handful of stores.

Two creation numbers worth keeping, from the same session (300k creates, one
row per process): a plain function expression with no capture costs 264 ns
(`g3`), the same create inside a `for (let x in o)` head costs 443 ns, and the
loop without the create only 57 ns. `SLAG_CLOSURE_PROFILE=1` splits the 264 as
`function-object` 37, `registry-insert` 82 (which includes the
`store_construct_patterns` cell write), `props-batch` 19, `compiled-body` 10,
and ~110 outside `register_function` (the prelude's site lookups and the
step-entry marshalling). Note the profiler's slot 11 ("pre-epilogue") double
counts `register_function` (it marks after the call with the mark left over from
before it), so read `register-total` for that phase, not `pre-epilogue`.
